is a medieval fantasy adventure game. After your sister got kidnapped by pirates, you set out on the trace of their hideout in order to rescue her while travelling the land and seas and helping people across the kingdom.
: This game is exactly like its predecessor: a light straightforward adventure where you walk from location to location, gathering the items, money and resources you need to unlock quests and win fame points to continue on your path. As you do so, the map gradually unveils itself. One change, though, are the skills: there are more of them and they unlock all variety of an item type (many that are gathered on the maps "hidden objects" style) so the quantity of items feels much more massive than my memory of the first game. The setting also is and feels very different than the previous game, and you eventually travel to multiple islands in your quest to fight the pirates and discover the mystery behind their intention.
: The game is just as linear as the first one. There is little strategy save the order in which you accomplish quests, which merely require you to have the proper inventory to succeed. The crafting system is way too over complicated, 90% of the things you can combine and exchange for other things and items you'll barely ever need. Enemies and loot never regenerate, save the occasional animal hunting. There is no replay value to this game: if you played it once, you've seen everything the game has to offer.
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you
This game is so much like its predecessor, in both mechanics, graphics and length, and gets a minor recommendation from me. However, if you didn't like the first
game or were hoping the developers had up the ante, you'll be thoroughly disappointed.

SPAZ is an amazing game! It is a real-time strategy game where you control a small squadron of spaceships from a 2D top-down perspective. Battles are fought by the player taking direct control of one ship while the other 1-3 ships are AI controlled. Resource management is pretty straight forward- all ships are purchased with "rez" and crewed by "goons" that you either recruit or press into service. Ships are highly customizable. I have only two gripes: The written story dialog is terrible, both poorly written and sometimes confusing, and there is some grinding involved to level-up your ships; though overall, the fun game play, simple to use tactical commands, and customization of the ships makes this game a must have.

SPAZ... oh SPAZ, how i love you... Space Pirates and Zombies is a game that deserve... Nein! It NEEDS more attention. Its a great game made by 2 great dudes. They are working (slowly) on SPAZ 2.
I really have nothing, nothing bad to say about this game. The trailer they got is a great way to show off how to game works, what you see is what you get. So if you like what you see then buy it, its a great game.
Here's what i think of the game. The game is a fun little game where you fly around with a small fleet of spaceship. You have a mothership that you can't control and it rebuilds and refit all your spaceships to your need. You start of with only one ship, and gain the ability to use other ships by destroying that type of ship, once destroyed the ship drops a blueprint, collect them to unlock the ship for yourself. The larger the ship, the more blueprints you need. So a small fighter might only need two pieces of that blueprint, destroy 2, collect the blueprint and the fighter is yours. While cruisers and battleships might need up to 8 blueprints, and they usally have alot more health and are harder to kill.
You also get the ability to refit your ships with weapons you want to use. Each ship has its own number of hardpoints, you can mix and match and put whatever you want on your ship. Want to fire kinetic rounds? sure. Lasers? Why not. Plasma balls? It's your ship, your rules.
Now this might be a minor spoiler but they got it in the title of the game so... Story goes that you are a space pirate, each solar system is cut off from each other so what you do in one system won't carry over to the next. To get to another system (a higher leveled one with more advanced ships) you'll have to fight through a UTA Blockade, they block access to the warpgates you need access to procedd in the game, either destroy them all or bribe them to give you access. Each system has 2 factions. The UTA (Military, always blocks the warpgates with blockades). And the Civvies, they control mining and science operations in deep space and usally let you use their facility freely (So you can mine resource, et.c.). You will randomly get a faction rating in each starsystem, sometimes they love you from the start, sometimes they hate you. You'll never know. Pick your side, start blasting ships from the oppossite side and soon you'll make some great friends in that starsystem.
Later on in the game Zombie ships start to appear, and near the end of the game they will be your main enemy. The UTA and Civvies notice the major zombie problem and team up together with you to reclaim the galaxy from the zombies. Zombie ships are unique ships that you can not unlock. They consist of two type of ships, fighting type ships that look like infected normal ships. They will engage anyone mindlessly. And then we got the breed type ships that look like human bodyparts of some sort. They infect ships without shields, if your ship gets infected you have little time to react, either self destruct your ship so the zombies can't gain control of it and use it against you... or make the hard choice and vent the ship of all crew except the captain, so the infection can't spread. It's a hard job late game, but someone has to purge the galaxy from the zombies.
There is also a fourth faction that was released freely with the game. And they are the Bounty Hunters. There ships are unique with specific traits and are also very, very over powered. If you go around in a starsystem they "control" and wreck havoc, you will start to lose respect with them. Lose to much of it and they will warp in when you least want it (in a difficult fight with another faction) and try to blow you out of the space, for the most part they succedd with this. One of the hardest achivements ingame want's you to destroy their space station in the hardest type of starsystem.
So will you use standard weapons like lasers, kinetic rounds or plasma to destroy your enemies? or will you go for missiles and torpedos instead? Why not use EMP weapons and energy drainers to drain all energy from your enemy ships so they can't fire their weapons or escape? Nukes? Sure, SPAZ has them. Drones for carriers, that too. There is alot to do with this game, and it gave me alot of hours of fun.
The only three really bad parts about this game are:
Interface dosen't look very professional.
The story isen't that good, it had one somewhat good plot twist in it tho.
The last "part" of the game, the "purge" all galaxy of zombie threat's is a repeative and somewhat boring job to do. Everything before that is fun tho.

Well, if you like brutal games with dismemberment and clumsy, poorly made and humorous melee combat this is the game for you.
Why do I not recommend?
At a glance I enjoyed this game. It was fun, truely, but then I started seeing the flaws in it. Big holes that couldnt be patched out.
One: Aim Botters. They have them for this game, believe me. "But Draconis, arent you being biased and just QQing about being killed?" No. Go look in my library and youll see I have over 300+ FPS games, most of which have hundreds if not thousands of hours in them. I know what aim bots look like, and how to test them to see if Im right or not. This isnt the kind of game you pre-fire on either, so there arent any legit excuses for "blind shotting" people across a map in the head consistantly.
Two: Block/Parry/Dodge. You have a stamina meter for really no reason other than to say that you get two attacks and maybe three blocks before you cant do anything more. This is up there with Battlefield sprint. A few seconds and its good night for you. Its not a fast combat game any longer. Thisisnt so much the problem as the game's tutorial tells you that you can get a counterblow after a block. That is an outright LIE. You block, then they can block directly afterward.
Three: Speed Hacks. Yes they have them, along with, as far as I can tell, Stamina Hacks so that people can consistantly and progressively attack without stopping. If you ahve played more than five minutes, you will understand there is a visible differance between a constant, instant attack seven times with a pike stab vs you playing with a pike and getting three stabs before your stamina is gone between attacks and blocks.
Four: No VAC or any risk of cheaters even being repremanded. I think they siad they had a cheat protection, but people were very quick to see others behind walls and stop at doorways before they came around to get a free hit.
Five: A whiny ♥♥♥♥♥ass community that made reading chat a huge head ache for me. There is a way to turn off chat I think but I really didnt want to bother. I just stopped playing after hearing some debate about racist words that no one gave a♥♥♥♥♥♥about.
Six: Everyone is experienced but you. This means access to better, faster weapons and more effective equipment. This can be comparable to COD where you are rank 1 and they are rank 40. Sure you have weapons that can kill, just not as well as theirs. And I do mean EVERYONE has this sort of rank. Out of ten servers, I was the only person who apprently bought this game in the last two years, as I was 30 ranks lower than the lowest rank in every server.
Seven: The DLC isnt even being played by anyone. What a huge waste of money. Good thing I got this from Green Man Gameing for like 5$.
Eight: I got kiled by my own team more than I did the opposing team. And I mean about 10:1 ratio. Im not even kidding. Team damage in a game like this shouldnt even be a thing.

Remember Sanitarium? Yes, that old school point'n'click masterpiece made me play STASIS.
I'll keep this totally spoiler free. You're John Maracheck and you've just woke up from stasis on an unknown space vessel. You remember that you were put to hibernation alongside your daughter and wife - both of them seem to be missing. Now you need to push onward and find your loved ones.
As for the gameplay, this is the basic point'n'click game. You gather stuff, combine items and use it on different locations.  As with the other titles of this type, it is a game of trial and error. Beside these, you will also encounter some additional puzzles. Difficulty of these varies. Most puzzles and their solutions are logical, but some are so mind numbing, so better prepare to suffer a crushing defeat and google the walkthrough or bust your head real bad. Great addition in STASIS are death states. You may and will die in the most horrible ways, but you'll also be able to commit suicide and earn Steam achievements. Still, this is no action game and dying is basically triggered by doing something wrong at the right time.
Story is a high point of the game. It deals with different ideas - family, morals and science. PDA's and documents are scattered all around and while they don't have any gameplay significance, not reading these is a HUGE LOSS. Great hints and additional backstory details are revealed this way and they will certainly make you understand main story better.
Visually, STASIS looks and feels like the 90's game. It's the double edged sword. Animations are not really top quality stuff, but everything is highly detailed and if you've been a gamer back then, you're gonna enjoy visual presentation, if not, tough luck - you will probably think game looks ugly (and for what it tries to (re)create, no it doesn't).
STASIS is rich in ideas and retro-futuristic SF design, which combined with the music by Mark Morgan (Fallout, Wasteland) and others encaptures players in morbid, disturbing world. Voice acting, however, could be way better, but it is bearable.
After seven and half hours, the story of STASIS is completed. This is atmospheric, story rich, movie like experience. It is part sci-fi, part body horror that works beautifully and will appeal mostly to old school adventurers who just love great fairy tale and don't mind occasional head splitting puzzles.
GET IT.

I've never been much of a fan of these so called "strategy map games" but I have to admit, that Crusader Kings II (CK2) has given me a lot of enjoyable gameplay and fine moments. Paradox has a certain way to persuade players to their games. I think it's the complexity of the game that lures more prey more human players to play this game. I for one fell in love with the plot and kill system of the medieval politics and way of life in this game.
I'd definitely recommend this game both for single- and multiplayer purposes. SP is good for practise, but the real deal and fun comes from eiher challenging other players from around the world and face the unknown with or without your own companions.
For multiplayer it also works quite fine if one works with his friends to achieve a common goal. No matter whether the goal is just to plot and kill the reigning king or reform the Norse faith under one single banner. Working together, planning, plotting and of course fighting the war is fun and sometimes challenging enough for it to be something worth of fighting for.
As for the gameplay this game seriously has a high learning curve. You really have to spend time reading, learning and just listening to the more skilled players. Most of all, you have to do mistakes because otherwise you cannot learn from them.
(This of course unless you are an übermensch SS Nazi) In addition to the learning curve, the AI is also quite ingenious tactically speaking. The AI knows when to run away and when to charge and destroy smaller armies and units. I hate it when I have to run around Europe to catch a small army of 100 men with my 25,000 men invasion force.

+ Complexity and diversity of the gameplay and actions
+ The amount of fine DLC's in the game (and the fact that only the MP game host needs to have the DLC's so others can play them aswell)

I really enjoyed this game, a dark supernatural murder mystery. I'm not sure exactly what the critics got upset about though looking at the Metascore, but it's not as bad as they have made it out to be.
As others have mentioned it is very LA Noire-ish but it's more forgiving if you make a mistake during your investigation. The story is interesting, voice acting is good, and the atmosphere/music is very similar to an early Silent Hill.
The game has you spend most of your time investigating your death and tracking down your killer. Along the way you can also collect items that tell you ghost stories, interact with living and dead, and help others that have also passed move on. This isn't a hard boiled action game like Max Payne, however you will run across demons during your travels that can be exercised. My thoughts on Fable - The lost Chapters:
I've played this game a lot when I was younger and didn't have Steam yet, that's why it says I've not played it at all and I'm still writing this recommendation. I got this game during a sale just because of the nostalgic feeling and so that I could tell you what an awesome game this is.
Fable was released on PC back in 2005 and got a lot of attention back then because of the freedom it gives the player and the impacts those decisions can and will have on both your character and the environment, which was a pretty much unknown feature.
You start the game as a young boy who's given several tasks, during which you're already forced to decide wther you want to finish them on the good or the bad way. Then, after some events, another tutorial and lots of talking, you're a grown up man who's (amongst other things) trying to figure out why those events happened and who's responsible for your parents death.
You'll be given several quests, you may explore the world and fight numerous enemies, gain exp and gain access to bigger and better spells (which can be upgraded too), weapons (which can also be upgraded, giving them some awesome visual effects) and armor. Houses can be bought, women married (and f*cked, though the screen becomes black), chicked can be kicked around, and whole cities can be murdered.
Cool thing about this game is, it always gives the player a choice. You can play it as a good guy, where you always help the innocent, never steal anything and never kill anyone who didn't deserve it. The more good things you do, the more saint-like your hero becomes, until you have your own halo and literally fart butterflies.
If you do things the evil way, your character grows horns, becomes pale and scares the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everyone he encounters which makes getting a woman to marry you the most difficult task in the game (still a better love story than Twilight!). You can save a lot of money though by simply stealing the things that you need, and murdering an entire city is ♥♥♥♥ing funny!
The hero also adapts to the weapons you use - if you fight with spells most of the time, your arms start glowing, but if you use swords, you'll become a big beefy warrior. Eat much, and you'll become fat, but eat nothing and you'll be thin as a branch.
For a game that old the graphics and dialogues are still pretty good, the soundtrack is great and you'll be entertained for several hours. There may be lots of quests that are nothing special at all, but the freedom you enjoy in between is what makes this game one of the best I've played so far.
There aren't many bad things I can remember because it's been a while since I've last played it, but be sure not to be playing a perfect game. It has its flaws like any other game, but I can't remember anything that makes me want to say "♥♥♥♥ this game".
There seems to be a HD remake of this game on the way (no idea when though), but as someone commented below, only for the Xbox. Don't sue me if that's wrong.
Buy it and enjoy!

Is this a perfect game? No, not by a long shot, but then again, are there any perfect games which aspire to the complexity of narrative and gameplay as Murdered: Soul Suspect? As a narrative exercise, Murdered is very enjoyable. The stories of the various ghosts you encounter are always interesting and sometimes quite haunting. Ronan, the dead detective whom you play, may seem one dimensional at the beginning, but he is 'fleshed out', so to speak as you play, to at least TWO dimensions. But to mitigate this issue are some really interesting characters and stories, i.e. the aforementioned ghosts you meet. Some are quite affecting.
The game is, for the most part, solidly built and I experienced no bugs or glitches while playing the game. Glimpses of Airtight Game's puzzle pedigry show through in several sections, though there is never an explicit focus on that kind of gameplay. Yet nor is there a focus on action. This a much more quiet and reflective gameplay experience, which I wonder is not an explanation of the game's poor reviews thus far. Certainly, it is not a blockbuster, but it feels more like an independent, more closely focused affair which I think many will enjoy if they are open to it.
In many ways, I kept thinking about similar games I played in the 90s. Perhaps it was the interface itself or the mood or the package as a whole. The game is a throwback, so yes it does have obvious shortcomings. The living world which it hints at is very quickly revealed to be smoke and mirrors, but as already explained, I was fine with that. I liked the characters and the ideas and the game played smoothly. I do not regret slapping down the cash for this one.

I was pretty excited to play this game, but after completing the main story-line in under 9 hours I am severely disapointed.
Difficulty:
This game is incredibly easy. It's basically point-and-click. You can't make any mistakes, really. You walk between locations and look for clues, which are very obviously highlighted for you.  I thought I'd have to be solving puzzles, piecing together clues, but everything is spoon-fed to you. The main character must be the worst detective in history, because I was figuring things out way before he was. There's no real threat or doom in this game. I mean, you're already dead, so you can't exactly die. The only obstacle (if you can call it that) are the soul-sucking demons (Which look like Dementors from Harry Potter) which pop up and must be vanquished (Which is also very easy to do. Just sneak up behind them, click three buttons and POOF! Gone).
Story:
The story could be interesting if it wasn't painfully dummed down. There are no complex intertwining stories, no in-depth characters. Everyone is exceptionally bland and cliche. *Spoilers ahead* So you play a detective called Ronan in Salem who has just been murdered by the "Bell Killer". Ronan is exceptionally slow. It takes most of the game for him to figure out that this "Bell Killer" preys on "witches". (It's Salem. That was obvious.) He discovers who the murderer is with the help of a "Medium" who can see/communicate with the dead.
Graphics:
Even the graphics themselves aren't that good. The characters mouths move at random, not really forming any real words. They move their arms and heads around as if they're puppets being pulled by strings. Even the cinematics are poor; clothes have jagged edges, and character's faces have no emotion.
Glitches:
There are glitches in this game which don't allow you to complete current objectives. Also, it's a checkpoint save game, so if you encounter a glitch you must reload from the last save-point (wherever thay may be). I also had a problem of cinematic scenes repeating themselves if I walked into a location where the objectives had already been completed.
World:
There is a very small area of game play. No map needed. You are in a tiny town and you are able to enter the museum, the church, the graveyard, the police station and the hospital (but only when the game calls for it). No free-roaming or exploring. Just walk to the next location (the arrows show you the way) and complete the objective. Then it's on to the next location.
Overall:
This is a VERY boring, VERY easy game. Utterly dissapointing.
Rating:
2/10

I'm a big fan of Fallout 1 & 2. I've been following Underrail since it was first announced. I really wanted to like this game.
Now, I'm willing to admit that I may not have given the game enough time to grow on me, but that's the unfortunate reality behind the ~2 hour return policy - it kind of forces some early decision making. But during that time, the game failed to impress me on any of its major systems: the UI & controls, stealth, dialog, combat.
Starting with the UI and controls, I'm disappointed any time a new release has a camera pan feature that doesn't use WASD. Clicking everything was a minor annoyance, so I won't spend any more time on it. But the UI is horribly small, and the "large" options are still pretty small. The icons are so small that I found myself not even using them. Trade menus are unusable without the filtering options, and those are slow and laborious to use.
Stealth was immediately frustrating, brought about by the combination of needing to click to move my character and the camera and not being able to pause the game. If you could pause the game - no problem. If you couldn't pause the game but you could move your character AND your camera at the same time - no problem. But making stealth where you can't look around corners, can't pause, and have to move the character and the camera with the same mouse? No thanks.
The dialog was... bad. If that's too harsh, then it was a missed opportunity. The beginning of the game is slow, and that can be okay if the activities you're engaging in are... engaging. But the dialog is bland. I felt like the game wanted me to listen to a bunch of talking without giving me any reason to be invested in anything that's being said. Just to be clear, this early game talking wasn't exposition or stage-setting - it was essentially all flavor text. That's a HUGE liberty to take at the very beginning of the game when the game needs to be hooking me with compelling reasons to give it my time and attention.
For me, this is no different than the pilot of a TV show that uses its precious first episode to not setup the plot, setting, and main characters, but to bore viewers with throwaway dialog that doesn't relate to anything meaningful or interesting. It's a wasted opportunity and a waste of my time.
Finally, the combat was nothing but functional. It is no longer acceptable for me for games to do "as well as" the old titles they're modeled from. I want advancements and improvements that engage me presently, and I didn't find that in my short time with Underrail.
Again, it's possible I didn't give Underrail enough time to woo me, but its failure to do so in its critical introductions is itself one of the game's shortcomings. I don't think it's unreasonable to expect modern games to make an attempt at attracting me, particularly early on.
Lastly, I want to mention the pacing of the game. Namely, there isn't any. As soon as you leave your room, you are free to "explore" every level (all 9 of them... I think it's 9) of your starting station. I love exploring, but I need to care about the world, its denizens, and my place in it BEFORE it's of any interest. This is the identical issue I have with the dialog. Why do I want to talk to random stranger #6 when I haven't been given any frame of reference in the world? Why do I want to go exploring in a game that I don't even know if I like yet? I need Underrail to date me for a while before opening its doors and inviting me to come move in with it. But Underrail makes no attempt to set a scene and place the player in it, at least not at the beginning when it really counts.
On this last point, I feel it's also worth mentioning that I've seen people talk about an opening cutscene that talks about the state of current affairs, but I got not such cutscene when I started my new game.

After almost ~170 hours in game, most of which were driven only by my perseverance, I have to change my review to negative. Old review that was written after ~10 hours in game is placed below.
So, the only pros of this game are roleplaying system, basically slightly revised old Fallouts' system, and crafting system. They are interesting and engaging, no gripes.
But the game is ruined by its gamedesign and narrative. It has huge territory and very few quests, and almost all of them located inside a few hubs. No kidding, 90% of game world is an endless labyrinths of look-alike caves/labs/stations with no quest-related content; pure dungeon-crawling and grinding. But in some cases you could actually break quests if you would explore certain locations too early, so you have to grind with caution and check the playthrough before entering another abandoned facility.
So, time distribution of my ~170 hours in game feels like this:
- 40% - lengthy logistics runs through empty locations between loot stashes and merchants (it's a chore even inside the hubs)
- 40% - grinding in the caves/abandoned facilities/subway lines for the reward of couple of level-ups and two broken quests.
- 20% - completing actual quests (which are also sometimes have troubles with design and backtracking for the sake of backtracking).
And the narrative is just plain bad in every aspect. I can't remember the names of majority of the characters that I'd met week ago, all of them are completely one-dimensional, and the lack of unique portraits/models for them doesn't help as well. Main storyline is "go there, check WTF is happening" without any real motivations behind it. And the world lore could be fully expressed in one sentence: "Postapocalyptic (what was the apocalypse, BTW?) underworld community was dominated by one megacorporation that fell apart (reasons for that is also unknown)".
I give up, this game is bloated with low-quality filler content beyond any reasonable limits. I've tried.
6/10, for die-hard fans of dungeon-crawlers with RPG elements.
===================================================
Old review:
Well, it's not from the same league with Fallout 1-2 and recent Shadowrun games, but still a decent RPG.
- Loot variety and crafting system are quiet deep. Non-combat stuff feels more diverse.
- Skills and perk...ahem, I mean, skills and feats with cross-related synergies are nice, too.
- Sometimes it actually delivers that 'post-apocalypse in cyberpunk-ish underworld' feeling which is meant to be here.
- All of the above-mentioned traits are enough to trap you for a long time here.
But:
- Exploration and scavenging are way more interesting than grinding in fights, though it's still inevitable. So there's a bright side and a downside in that. It falls in the same trap where most of single-hero RPGs eventually ends up - you will stuck with your character build, and, therefore, general combat abilities and tactics for a dozens of hours, and variety of tools helps with it only partially. But they had tried.
- There are two systems for gaining xp: combat-based and exploration-based. BUT you can't use both, had to choose one of them at the start of the game. Weird decision, because half of the character traits automatically became less useful. Merging it into one mechanics with little rebalancing would add even more depth.
- Story, world-building, quests, dialogues and characters are 'meh' at best.

This game is a trap. Stay away while you still can.
If there's anything one should gather from my rather long playtime for this game, it's that this game is rather addicting. Don't get me wrong. There ARE some enjoyable bits in this game. I wouldn't have come back to this game after six months and rediscovered all the bad bits if there wasn't. But, yes, there are quite a few problems I have with this game that keep me from recommending it to anyone (or at least, anyone that
I know).
If you've seen any of the trailers or read any other reviews for this game, you probably already know what the gameplay is like. You're at the leftmost side of a level, you go right, hitting anything that looks at you funny until they fall over, until you reach the end and get teleported to another, seemingly identical level. Well, maybe I shouldn't be so harsh. Some of the levels DO seem like they're set up rather well and the combat is rather engrossing. Armed with combos, special attacks, and super attacks (I know there aren't any moves called that, but whatever), the player can very easilly feel like he's a badass fighter in an action anime, running/flying around the screen hitting/slicing badies until finally blowing them up with a large explosion.
Until, of course, they realize the enemies are collectively about as threatening as a one-legged spider with brain damage. The enemies in this game are either legally blind or incredibly stupid because they only seem to acknowledge your presence when you're either right next to them or hitting them across their stupid heads. And when they do notice you, they perform their telegraphed attack once before either forgeting about you or walking slowly towards you. The exception to this behavior is the boss enemies, who have a better grasp on the idea of focussing on players but feel they need to more obviously telegraph their attacks to be fair.
Again, the levels do seem like they're well-made, so these problems with the enemies wouldn't seem so bad if one needed to visit each level only once. Is that the case? No. Levels will have to be visited three, and later even four, times before being allowed to the next one. And that's even assuming you're the right level, because otherwise the game just tells you to level up more, and since levelling up is so tedious, especially at higher levels, it won't be long before you're so familiar with levels that you could draw them on paper while blindfolded (this is assuming you're following the story, of course, and not just playing levels, but since levelling up takes so much grinding, especially later in the game, you might as well).
What also doesn't help with this tedium is the music. I've read some reviews where people have praised the soundtrack, calling it beautiful and epic and the like. And I have to say, yes, the music is rather wonderful...... for the first fifteen seconds anyways, because after that it just loops over again. Even the most beautiful tune in the world is going to sound annoying and overplayed after looping it every half a minute. Add this to the already grating grind settup and what would just be a minor annoyance to my ears suddenly turns into the music I hear in my nightmares.
Of course, a good way to break this tedium would be to play the levels in a party. Yes, this is an MMO after all, and thus you're given the option to play levels with up to three other players. In fact, the game actually encourages it (In a way that I'm not too fond of, but it honestly doesn't get me angry enough to talk about it.). Unfortunately, the only form of communication that the game provides is a text chat, which does not go well with the fast-paced action prevalent in the gameplay. As a result, playing in a party can usually be equated to a giant cluster♥♥♥♥ of screams, explosions, and screen shaking.
Overall, I'd give the whole PvE aspect of the game a miss.
Now, in my opinion, this is where the game truly shines. One of the problems I had with PvE was the non-threatening enemies, and replacing them with one enemy who can actually outsmart you certainly fixes that. And the fast-paced gameplay is right at home in this mode, creating moments where the difference between victory and defeat lies within a nanosecond. I've had matches where both I and, I suspect at least, my opponent were sweating bullets throughout. Matches where I felt like I had to actually contact them and thank them for providing me with such an amazing fight.
What's unfortunate is that I can count the amount of matches like this that I've actually had in Elsword on one hand. It seems like for every opponent pitted against me at the same level as me, there were about fifty who were forty levels below me and fifty who were forty levels above me. This can be blamed on Elsword's rather bad matchmaking system.
So, to summarize on actual gameplay, look somewhere else.
I remember a review talking about how the people in this game are really friendly and playing in the community is fun and how it's so easy to make friends in this game. I can only assume that they were an extrovert and thus able to make friends anywhere else, because, for an introvert such as myself, the majority of the people that I seemed to get acquainted with were people that I wanted to reach through the computer screen and punch in the nose. But maybe I'm wrong on this. Maybe all those annoying players were just a small fraction of the player populace, and the majority of the players on this game are nice, decent individuals who don't get upset when you tell them that no, you don't want to friend them just because you said something remotely funny while in a level. But if that's the case, then it certainly isn't obvious to me.
While I don't seem to agree with them on some things, the creators behind this game do seem to take care of it. Bugs and issues are practically nonexistent, and updates are rather frequent. They also hold events for their players. No matter what day, there's always some kind of event going on in Elsword (which, to me, totally undermines the whole POINT of an event, but whatever.), where any player online during it can get a special item only available then and there.
It just feels as though they're focussed on all the wrong things. It seems like, for every update made to balance the game or fix issues, there's about twenty updates made to add a new costume to the in-game store.
Oh, yes, they have an in-game store, where things in it cost real money. Some items even have additional stat increases when worn. Now, debate can be made over whether or not these increases have any real impact on gameplay, but frankly, it's the fact that there are stat increases in the first place that pisses me off. There's more to be said about this feature, but I feel plenty of people have already harped on it enough that anything I say here would just be a rehash.
This isn't a game meant to bring in new players. This is a game meant to keep old members mindly interested and not think about any other way they could be spending their time, turning the grindfest that is its gameplay into a reasonable sacrifice for getting this totally new accessory only available on a certain day and then doing the same exact thing the very next day. It becomes very easy for one to become addicted to the promise that is a free accessory. The only reason that I got out when I did was because I realized what was happening.
But others are not so lucky. Even today, there are those stuck in this endless loop with little hope for escape. Do not join them. Stay away while you can.

Again this is a game where "recommend" or "not recommend" doesn't mean anything. It mostly depend on who you are, what kind of gamer you are.
If you are craving for an old school Fallout-like game, go for it, you probably won't be disapointed.
But it's 2015 now, and even if I think that some old games ( especially RPGs ) were a lot better in the past, it's not a reason to keep their flaws as current game mechanics, or even putting annoying stuff in a game on purpose. Some examples as a warning for potential buyers :
- the tutorial only covers three things : using a gun, lockpicking, and stealth, because that's obviously the skills required for anyone living in this world. And then the game continues on that way, giving you the choice between a gun, a crossbow and a knife. Ok... but what if I did a Psionic character ? What if I didn't invest any point in ranged or melee ? Though luck, you start without any Psi ability. First you need to unlock your Psi potential by talking to a doctor, whom then leads you to NPCs who could maybe teach you some skills. The first one required me to have 35 and 45 points in Psi to learn stuff, but at level 1 you're capped at 15 points, so you need several levels before learning that. Another NPC only agreed on teaching me a single free skill ( need to pay for others ), AFTER I complete some quest requiring to kill rathounds with... a crossbow. Wait... what ? In order to have a single Psi ability I need to do a quest using a crossbow, but I have no points in ranged combat or crossbow and that's exactly why I need Psi stuff ?
That would be like starting as a mage in Baldur's Gate with 4HP, no spells, no companions and only a sword, forcing you to go melee until you can finally buy some expensive spell after 4 levels...
OK, the game begins to punish you for picking anything else than the cookie-cutter gun/crossbow ranger or melee brute. Fine. Let's start over with a new character.
- another thing is the total lack of map, making it a nightmare to navigate in the maze of metro tunnels. Characters just give you vague information about your destination like if you already knew the levels by heart, and the journal is of no help at all : "complete all the tasks for NPC X and come back to NPC Y". Yeah thanks... I love to wander aimlessly into labyrinths, killing mobs, wasting my ammo and heal.
- merchants will only buy a certain ammount of a certain item, and nothing else. Like, this guy ONLY buys 2 leather armors and one pair of boots. You can stick all your other loot up your♥♥♥♥♥♥.. also, all merchants are cutthroats, I think the exchange rate is like 300% of the base price. HOWEVER some items like weapons have a really high price, and you will probably find enough of them to get a nice ammount of money early enough. I found/looted on ennemies at least 3 or 4 guns and 2 crossbows already, enough to cover my needs in lockpicks and some gear.
- stealth is really stupid as your character's vision is really limited, so you won't be able to see anything past a corner for example. Mobs move really quickly compared to you, so good luck knowing if they are looking in your direction or not. Maybe they should have added some sound, or onomoatopeia to tell you  an ennemy is near ( like in the game XIII adapted from the comic, you can "see" the sound of ennemies step to locate them ). Because there is no way our character doesn't hear a big sentry bot coming his way from afar...
- overall the game is really slow and boring, the character can't run of course.
- the world seems really serious and there is not a single hint of humor like in Fallout or BG. instead the characters will KO you if they don't like your tone.
- inventory is terrible, and some fonts are downright unreadable.
Gonna update this after I play some more. I can't "not recommend" the game despite its flaws, because I guess it's still a nice game, but some aspect will probably turn people off.
EDIT : now some things I like about the game
- there is a lot of loot and your inventory is not too small so you can take a lot of stuff. As you can't sell everything to any merchant you can stock your loot and crafting material in your appartment.
- there is generally several ways to progress : stealth, lockpicking/hacking, brute force, dialogue, etc. For example you can use your lockpicking skill and an omnitool to unlock a ventilation shaft, or a crowbar and your stength. However doing a non-combattant character seems impossible, or at least really hard, as there will probably be ennemies you can't talk with blocking your path. Maybe if you max your stealth, lockpicking, hacking, persuasion and intimidation, and find/buy the right tools ( which requires either luck or knowing the game already to have what you need at the right moment ), AND if you're ready to reload a save a bunch of time to learn ennemies patterns to sneak successfully, yeah it should be doable.
- graphics are nice enough
- you can detect secret passages with a high perception. Not something you find in a lot of games.
- the lighting affects stealth. When you step in shadows, your character portrait will go dark to tell you you're more difficult to spot. Trying to sneak in plain light won't end good. Fortunately most of those tunnels are dark.

As someone with over 2000 hours clocked into this game, I can say without a shadow of a doubt that this is a pay to win game. You can travel through most of the game without cash, but if you wish to succeed at all in it, you will need cash. $10 for a repair scroll. $13 for a marriage (Note, the site only manages increments of 5, 10, 20 and 100 so anything odd numbered requires a larger than your desire purchase), as well as other 'interesting' payment methods. Such as if you wish to expedite your Hyper Skill work and just buy it, it's 550 KC, however, they don't dabble in "pay what you need", so you need to pay 10 just for that 550.
The PVP is by far one of the worst pvp systems I have ever had the sheer disgust of dealing with. It's almost 100% completely gear based. Someone with a highly reinforced weapon and armor 'will' plow through you with little effort. If it's not their gear ending your chances, it's their character. The balancing in this game only grows worse and worse each big update. Chung, the gun user, when built right, now has almost infinite Super Armor capabilities. Making him impossible to combo against. AND THEN IF THOSE 2 aren't stopping you, it's lag. Opponents randomly walking out of your combos, dropping away from them, with 0 care in the world.
MP Breaking is a method to escape combos, but there have been many times where I simply saw them walk away from my attack, no Super Armor, not even any damage, just walked away. It's so infuriating seeing hours of progress in your pvp rank get taken down in 1 to 2 matches NOT because you were outclassed, NOT because you were outskilled, but because the person had stronger gear than you, or lagged, or simply was better than the class you used.
The only redeeming thing this game has is it's community. You can literally trust a stranger with 2 Billion ED (Ingame currnecy) and actually receive your item you payed for. The reason why that's an issue is you can only trade in increments of 700 million, so you will end up accepting a trade twice to 3 times over giving them all your money before you receive your item. They could so easily run away, but they don't, they're trustworthy. Everyone there is kind, enjoyable, very, very weeaboo not gonna lie. But at least they were cool.
The gameplay itself is still enjoyable in dungeon runs, it's fast, fluid action slashing and destroying enemies. And that's enjoyable, or at least it is to me, for 3 level cap characters. But once you get that far, you have to start grinding and start paying to keep up, needing to buy Ores and garbage to make your weapon stronger so you can actually excel at your class. And that just wont happen if you run free the entire time.
With that said, I can't recommend this game to users that want an mmo they can really dive into. This game is worth a look at best, but barely worth truly getting into for the long run. The Pay to Win model becomes all the more apparent as you level up and the sense of feeling cheated out of victory as well as simply too weak (even when you have end-game gear) is a feeling games like this should not generate within their players. It's a sense of worthlessness that you can't ignore, and when you've reached such a feeling, you start questioning if the game is really worth your time, rather than if it's worth your time to achieve the stronger gear that you were just clobbered with.
Now I'm no grand judge of game design, but I don't remember burning through 122 hours in this game.

STASIS is what it says on the tin, a science fiction horror adventure game.  It sets out its goal and it achieves it.
The puzzles are almost all good and clear, with a nice mixture of challenge.  I really appreciated the environmental clues for the statis tube puzzle in particular.  I only found two puzzles I felt were kind of unfair -- the puzzle to get the key to the battery compartments in Project SEED, which is pretty much "use everything on everything until it's solved" and the puzzle for getting the tree sap in hydroponics, which is a timing puzzle based on doing something that is obviously a terrible idea and not obviously a timing puzzle, so when you do the obviously stupid thing out of frustration and an inability to figure out what to do next, you'll probably die instead of getting the next piece of the puzzle anyway; needlessly making the puzzle seem impossible.  Another little hint in the form of emails or diary entries would have take care of either of those puzzles.  The ending is beautiful and perfect, a terrific payoff for the entire game.  It's not a surprise by any means -- I wasn't surprised by any of the elements of the ending, which features a couple twists and turns -- but it's really not about being surprised.  It ends the way it should end, the way it must end.  It ends RIGHT.
STASIS is very much a horror game.  It is NOT a "scary" game.  There are technically jump scares, but I missed about half of them because I often wasn't staring directly at the protagonist the whole time; I was looking around the screen for items to interact with, and I occasionally only knew there was a jump scare because of the music swell.  It's not a very scary game at all from the context of startling you or making you worried that something might kill you at any moment (as an adventure game, that's true, but only if by "something" you mean "the player's choice in what to click on").  But it is absolutely a horror game.  A deliberately paced mounting sense of horror and realization confronts both the player and the protagonist.  There are a couple twists that leave you wondering what, in this space-borne house of horrors, the real "monster" is for a satisfying amount of time.  The actual reveal of the monsters is almost a bit of a let down; considering the abqttoir you've been through at that point to get to them.  But if that seems disappointing, you can always remember where they came from, and the horror of that will keep your stomach turning.  It's kind of a classic, near cliched, story for the genre, but it's beautifully realized and masterfully told.
If you want a horror adventure game, where you're left almost psychologically ill by the end, and you're not going to just turn a corner and jump out of your skin, STASIS is an awesome choice.  I backed the game on Kickstarter and there are no regrets.  A great game.

This game represents all of the unbridled greed that game developers seem to find themselves filled with these days.  In terms of raw micro-transaction COST, this game is the most expensive game on the market.
In addition, this game has been out for quite some time on
prior to being released on Steam.  As a game developer I find Kongregate to be a great community and I've enjoyed seeing other titles such as AdVenture Capitalist, Time Clickers, and Clicker Heroes make amazing transitions over to the Steam community.
The same can NOT be said for this game.
Why?
All the aforementioned titles all had one thing in common.  If you spent money on in-game micro-transactions on Kongregate ALL of those bonuses carried over to the Steam platform.  Players were given the ability to "Export" their save game code and then "Import" it once on Steam.
Even for idle/clicker games that are only on Kongregate this is common practice.  At this point it has become an expected "best practices" within the industry.
Crusaders of the Lost Idols does NOT do this.
Kongregate users have been calling for ages for the ability to import/export save codes.  Even more-so once it was announced that this title would be being released on Steam.  Users repeatedly reached out to the developers attempting to make contact with them.  The devs were silent for over 4 months.
Finally, one day, the devs decided to finally appease the masses and actually engage themselves with their community.  That's when we all discovered the awful truth.  The devs were simply trying to rob their players.
The developers announced they were making the CONCIOUS choice to refuse data transfers to players in their community who spent real money on in-game bonuses.  Spent $50 on chests when the game was first released on Kongregate-only, well you don't get to keep those bonuses.  Better spend another $50 if you want all your perks again!  Eh?
While I have not EVER spent money on this game, and have thus not lost out due to this, I find this to be one of the most unethical decisions I have seen a non-EA/Blizzard game developer make.  It undermines the entire indie community.
Despite the fun gameplay, due to the underhandedness of the developers, I would advise everyone to avoid this game and not support it.  Heck, since it's free to play install it then downvote it with a review.  Players, and consumers in general, need to take a stand against greedy developers like Code Name.

Being a sucker for anything Sci-Fi or Horror (especially a combination of the two) I figured I'd give this game a shot.  I was somewhat hesitant given that I had heard no reviews but after taking a look at the trailer I was intrigued so I picked it up.  No regrets!  From the very beginning I was hooked and felt compelled to finish it.  The story is great and well fleshed out if you take the time to read the abundance of PDAs left behind by the former residents of the ship.  This game is kinda like Dead Space meets Event Horizon with old school Diablo-esque isometric graphics.  The art, music and voice acting acting are all fantastic and several times I stopped just to appreciate the work that went into crafting these environments.  Overall it's one of the best point-and-click adventure games I've ever played and absolutely worth the asking price.  It's not, however, a game for anyone with a weak stomach or an adversion to violence and gore.  I find myself eagerly awaiting the next game from The Brotherhood, this being their first foray into game development.
Pros:  Superb art, music and voice acting.  Fast paced throughout with an excellent story and well crafted characters.  Very strong opening and middle acts.
Cons:  A bit short (took me about 8 and a half hours at a leisurely pace).  Some of the puzzles required brute force to solve and can be a bit frustrating although I pride myself at never having to look up any guides for assistance.  The final act doesn't pack the punch of the opening and middle but it was still satisfying.
TL;DR:  Buy it.  It's worth it.

I'm a big fan of space horror games and this one does it absolutely right.
Very creepy atmosphere and environments. The details really drive home the fact that something strange happened on the ship and I love how it's done.
The gameplay is what you would expect. It is a point and click puzzle solving horror game. The puzzles aren't just random either, they feel necessary and really fit in with the way the story progresses. The game throws you right in too, there are no tutorials for how puzzles are solved or any examples of such. But the answers all exist and follow a locgical path. Moving around the environment was easy. I enjoyed the detailed writtings when you hover over pretty much anything in-game.
Sound design was very good too. Although at some points it seemed like the sound would get too loud and stay that way and not really feel necessary. For instance just walking down a corridor and the music track seems like I should be in a car chase. Other than that though the atmospheric screeching of whatever and the subtle distance sounds really brought the ship alive. I recommend playing this with headphones.
One things I'll add about the sound design is the voice acting. Not really the high point of the game. Although some characters including the player character seems alright, the rest of the voice acting wasn't on par.
The story is all there through PDAs that are left by staff and whatnot. I like that the staff notes feel alive too. They don't just tell you what you need to know but instead have day to day notes that aren't necessary to the story itself, but build this world up and give you insight into a particular persons world. I'm not going to spoil anything so I'll just say play the game yourself and you can decide whether or not you enjoyed the story.
Last thing I'll touch on is the length because most people want to know usually anyway. My steam counter says 7 hours but that was after restarting the game due to playing on a different computer after and not having the save files for some reason. In any case the game is closer to a little over 5 hours I'd say (Depending on your play style). However, the game was a good length overall and it didn't feel like it even should have been any longer. It told the story it had to and did it in a very good way.
For what its worth, I recommend this game. It is a really cool type of puzzle horror game that we tend to not see that much of. By the end I was left wanting more in anticipation for what the developers will do next.

Chivalry for those who dont know is a some what realistic medieval war game.... when it comes to games with solid swordplay there is a lack thereof, good swordplay games would be Devil May Cry, Metal Gear Rising, and The Witcher. Now a swordplay game thats multiplayer? thats almost non existent... though Chivalry is a fantastic game. So the point of the game is usually a red v blue deathmatch, the game focuses on realistic and practical medieval fighting tactics and skills. It takes some practice to get used to the controls but they are pretty solid, the mouse is all the weapon controls and the keyboard is mostly movement. Chivalry has an overwhelming 4 classes to choose from (sarcasm).
Man at Arm: Your traditional sword and shield character, a quick fella with skills like dodging and a constant block (as apposed to a timed block with the sword). Fast speed and little armor, though what he brings in speed he lacks in health, a good 2-3 swings from a beefier character will result in death. Not a user friendly class so use it with experience
Archer: This is your ranged character with the choices of a longbow, crossbow, or slings. Average speed but little armor, though armor is not needed when your killing people from a distance. Personally not my go to character but is still very fun and has some challenge to it.
Vangaurd: This is the pole armed class (personal favorite). Average speed and average armor while using elongated weapons such as spears, pikes, halberds, and more. This is my favorite because you dont die immediatly like a Man at Arms, but you still have range on people when it comes to melee combat.
Knight: Without a doubt the most popular class, slow speed and great armor. This character traditionally uses a broadsword or greatsword, he can definitly take a hit and deliver one... personally I find him to lack challenge due to his beefy characteristics. Recommended class for starters
As for tech aspects the game has decent graphics, solid controls, nice atmosphere and sound, and fair optimization (bigger servers tend to struggle). If youre into the whole Medieval times than this would be right up your alley. I can't wait to see Ubisoft For Honor, it seems very similar to Chiv.

In my honest opinion I think that Deadfall Adventures had everything it needed to be a success but it turned into a disaster. You can describe it as a First Person Shooter Indiana Jones or Uncharted. The game doesn't look that bad and the gameplay is somewhat decent but the more I played it the more I despised it. No matter what gun you use they all feel the same, there's barely any recoil on the guys and they're fairly standard, usual World War 2 weaponry, you can either fire from the hip or aim down sights and that's probably one of the things I less enjoy on a First Person Shooter. Not only to mention it has regenerating health which is something I really hate in games nowadays because you can just go hide behind cover and wait for you to recover full health. The game is extremely linear but it does reward exploration by finding treasure which you can then spend upgrading your health, health regeneration, decreasing weapon spread and recoil etc. The game has some interesting design choices to it such as the use of the compass to find hidden treasure and the ocasional treasure maps you come across on each level, ocasionally you'll come across some puzzle sections in temples that do provide a varied and different experience from the rest of the game and the only help you have to beat them is your notebook, this was probably for me the only strong point of the game. Story wise it's kinda okay, the voice acting is pretty much terrible but it ocasionaly has some humour on the writing. There's also no save feature, only checkpoints which might upset some people, such as me. Overall, considering it's price I don't think Deadfall Adventures is a game you should be looking foward to, it's also worth mentioning it costs 40€ for europeans while it also costs $40 for people from North America which it's a considerable price difference. I'd recommend avoiding it, if you're eager to try it out you might want to wait for a heavy discount.

-Limited side missions
-Small game world by modern standards
-Ronan, and the investigation system, can be really..really stupid
-The facial expressions for pretty much every character in the game sucks**
-Limited number of character models, despite how few ghosts you can interact with
-Probably would have been received better if it was at a cheaper price
**My long review was actually way too long, but the rather awkward facial expressions throughout the game are the most important part of the review that I had to cut out
The (Really) Long review:
STORY 6.5/10 - Chances are, you already realize the Murdered: Soul Suspect is an adventure game based very heavily around a story, and that story quite often falls flat on its face in terms of portraying the sense of whodunit type mystery you would get from anything Sherlock Holmes, or from similar games such as LA Noire. The main story starts off kind of rocky, but as it pans out, and you learn to ignore the hand-holding that occurs during the investigations and some of the sillier plot points (where the game screams THIS IS IMPORTANT), it actually becomes quite intriguing. I found myself actually ruling people out as the Bell Killer, with my mind firmly set on one person from very early on in the game. To my pleasant surprise, I only partially anticipated the ending, and it wasn't something from way out in left field as you would find in an M Night Shyamalan movie. It worked (eventually).
What didn't work in this game, are many of the aforementioned investigations that hold your hand throughout, often making it obscenely clear exactly what happened without ever even looking at any of the evidence at the scene. In most cases, you needed to guide Ronan to each piece of evidence (generally around 10 items), at which point he would make a remark that is often idiotic (and very often the complete opposite of what the item clearly gave me the impression of) about how it may pertain to the case, and after you have collected sufficient evidence, you would choose the items Ronan deemed important in closing the case. Since chances are you already know what happened, you would then need to find the two or three items that Ronan needed before you could move on to the more enjoyable parts of the game. This burden is frequently increased by Ronan's tendency to ignore VERY important evidence, that could immediately close the case, to focus on items that don't really help his investigation..at all. In general, what could have perhaps been the main draw for many people in this game, ended up feeling trivial and even, at times, tacked on as an after-thought. This became especially apparent when comparing the investigative stories to what was probably my favorite part of the game.
Perhaps the most redeeming quality of the game in terms of story, is sadly the part of the game that most people are likely to overlook. Each area of the game has a set of collectibles that you can gather to get a better understanding the lore surrounding that part of Salem, as portrayed through a spooky ghost story. Between these and the investigations, it definitely appears that the ghost stories took a backseat in terms of time spent working on them in the production process, as they consist of a single voice actor describing a very short ghost story, while you look at a spooky picture related to the story. It sounds lame, sure, a cinematic would have made more sense, but at the same time I think it allows you to focus more on the story itself. The ability to successfully portray a spooky story with what seems to be as little effort as possible makes me wonder why this wasn't more of a horror-based adventure game, than a detective-y investigation-y game.
Perhaps the most depressing part of the story is the fact that it is so short, clocking in at only 7hrs from start to finish, getting 100% of the achievements at the same time. I would have liked to see more side missions (I'd say investigations, but there wasn't really any of  that going on), and a generally longer story than the game had to offer.
CHARACTERS 7.5/10 - Ronan is basically a walking cliché for a bad guy gone good guy cop who does more than just toe the line between cop and criminal when he works cases. You can pretty much ignore his character entirely for a good portion of the game as his comments tend to only point out the other flaws in the game. Joy, the teenage medium, even comes off as a rather cliché young pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but her character does evolve rather well. When it comes to characters, the game really shines with the secondary characters, such as Baxter, and some of the Bell Killer's victims that you meet along your journey, who have all interacted with the killer in one way or another, and you get to see how that experience has changed them - for better or worse.
The same split between really good and really boring characters can be seen in the all-to-few number of side investigations that you can find scattered across Salem, where someone may have a problem that you offer to investigate, and inevitably fix. In the cases where the characters are lame, it is often because of the same thing the investigation part of the game suffers from, the answer being too blatantly obvious to not think that character is an idiot for not seeing it. In other cases, it is clear that the character is in a literal limbo, and they need your help getting out of it.
GAMEPLAY 8/10 - First off, the game as a whole  works beautifully, both as a game being played on launch week, and a game in general, as I found no bugs of any kind while playing through the game.
Chances are, part of the reason the game runs so great is because it is just so simplistic. The combat in the game is about as basic as you can get, and would most likely have become very redundant had there been more combat sequences in the game. I had only just started to get sick of dealing with demons by the time I reach the last half hour or so of gameplay. It is very clear that the focus is on story and investigating the crimes of the Bell Killer (see the story section for why that is a letdown).
The world around Ronan becomes increasingly impressive, and creepy, as the frequency of ghosts increases, but in general I got a very Twilight-zone-empty-town feel from Salem, and the ghosts flat out reminded me of the Haunted Mansion ride at Disney World. Ultimately, the living people that populated Salem ended up feeling even more empty than their ghostly counterparts, which I think actually gave me an even creepier vibe from the game, although I don't think that was totally intentional.
While making the world feel a bit more lively is kind of optional, since a gloomier look does make sense to me as you are playing a ghost, I think Salem definitely should have been larger than it was. By the time you reach the credits, you will have only explored just over a half dozen different parts of Salem, and the streets of (a rather small) Salem itself. Sure, the areas are diverse, consisting of everything from a Church, to a Police Station, and a Mental Hospital, but none of the areas are very large, further adding to the small-world feel of the game. On the other hand, with how tedious the combat had become by the end of the game, and how pointless the investigations were (they weren't quite tedious, but certainly would have been soon enough), I think focusing more on other aspects of the game first would have been more important than expanding the world around Ronan.

Strangely addictive...It is hard to quantify what makes this game so much better than that score would indicate.
Gameplay 9/10
A nice balance between running your shop and delving into the local dungeons when you want to restock. You can:
- Simply play the market by subtly marking up your goods received from the local guild and shops and learn the art of profiling your customers and haggling for a slow but steady profit,
- Spend most of your days delving into the dungeons for those high-quality goods that you can sell for nearly pure profit (minus the cost of hiring your adventurer).
- Try to attract new adventurers to your store by changing up the atmosphere
- Unlock new dungeons for faster and greater loot
BUT! Beware, as those debt deadlines can get pretty brutal in the later weeks! Carefully plan out how you spend your days and remember any special orders! The game has enough variety that it rarely gets boring or redundant, but that may differ dpending on your playstyle.
Graphics 6/10
A mixture of Visual Novel style characters and backdrops for story sections and 3D top-down views for gameplay segments provides most of the visual experience. The game feels obviously dated (which it is) and somewhat lacks in variety, but that is to be expected in a game that is mostly procedurally generated.
2D artwork is crisp and nice but fairly low resolution by modern standards. 3D rendering is obviously low-poly and the textures could be a bit better, but animations are generally smooth and do not detract from the gameplay.
Audio 7/10
The soundtrack has a nice overall feel to, but it lacks any fantastic standout tracks.  Most of the music serves as a nice subtle backdrop without getting annoying but after spending enough time in your shop you might just have to go run a dungeon just to get away from the music for a bit!  You probably will not start to have that problem until you have sunk a few dozen hours into the game, though.
Controls Avg. 9/10
Keyboard/Mouse 8/10
Defaults to ↑←↓→ controls instead of WASD and generally has that old-school DOS game key layout, but the controls can be changed (by using a separate configuration application) and are generally very responsive. Perfect once tweaked to your preference.
Gamepad 10/10
Works exceptionally well out the gate with an XInput controller (I use a Logitech F710 in XInput Mode). The configuration application can also be used to alter these controls if something does not feel quite right to you, but the defaults felt pretty natural to me.
Miscellaneous 8/10
Aside from the dated feel, this game comes with a unique premise that makes it feel special.  It offers the kind of variety very few games do in gameplay mechanics without ever overwhelming you.  Most things you want to be able to alter can be altered through the configuration application but here are a handful of "the little things" that might have made the game better:
- In-game configuration menus instead of an external program (you have to do an extra step every time you launch the game because of this)
- Some more hints in-game on how to attract new adventurers and unlock new dungeons (not always obvious)
- More options for resolution, including widescreen options!

This game is portrayed as a thriller and it hasn't failed on that part. However it also implies some horror elements that aren't really present, even with the "spooky" spectres.
As my activity time shows, I've not spent long on this game. I'd say that the campaign is only around 3-4 hours long and all other time is spent simply getting the collectibles or completing the tiny amount of sidecrimes/cases that you can solve.
All in all, this is getting a thumbs down. While the story is good, I can't help but feel that this game was rushed out to help with the new gen consoles rather than be a good game. I also don't think that with the small amount of time spent on thisgame it is worth the £24.99 price tag.

If you played Hero of the Kingdom, then my review will be very short: Hero of the Kingdom II is just "more of the same", and this says enough. If you did not played previous part... well, you can play Hero of the Kingdom II and not worry about storyline. These two games are not connected with each other and their storylines do not cross. In fact, second part contains a couple of tiny references to the first part, but... it does not matter.
So. You move between locations, collect different objects, interact with characters and solve quests. Game is very calm and leisurable, there is absolutely no hurry - just enjoy beautiful surroundings, filled with a lot of small lovely details. In my opinion, art-style in Hero of the Kingdom II is excellent.
The plot is very simple, naive and absolutely predictable. Unfortunately, game is completely linear and there is no replayability. To be honest, there is a couple of quests where you can try alternative way of solving, but it is only a timid and hesitant step on the way to diversity.
Sometimes Hero of the Kingdom II can be quite tedious. Gameplay is mainly focused on searching for hidden objects. Some quests require a large amount of resources, and it is not hard to collect them, just tedious. On the other hand, in my opinion, hidden objects in this game are much easier to find than in the previous part. I still remember how I searched for mushrooms in Hero of the Kingdom - it was a nightmare and I almost hate mushrooms now! In Hero of the Kingdom II I managed to find all items much faster.
I still do not understand what is the meaning of artifacts. To find these items, you need to complete a relatively long quests (I mean - "long" for this simple and short game), then you will get achievement and... that is all. I did not find any use for artifacts. Why this items are in game, can they be used somehow? I have no answer.
Well. Can I recommend this game? Probably, yes. I must warn you: Hero of the Kingdom II will not hold you for a long time, it is a short easy adventure for a couple of hours, nothing more. Still, it is a decent casual game, that is for sure.

EDIT: Game recieved huge update on 8 January 2016 and is now even better. Some of the improvements are:
New gun models (Machine gun is now gorgeous)

Anyways original review below:
By just looking at the screenshots, first thing that probably comes to your mind is:
Holy Mother of Jesus what is this♥♥♥♥♥♥! Why did you even bother?
Well let's look at this and see what it has to offer :)
Game looks decent and runs pretty well. Sure it's no Battlefield 4 (when you think about it, it's not even Half Life 2) and some of the models look a bit cheesy and weird but I think it's completely playable.
There is a whole lot of guns in this, 24 to be presise. You got everything from melee weapons, assault/ sniper rifles to shotguns and RPG. Some weapons like AK Sniper and Crossbow can also be upgraded 3 times.
Maps are huge and quite varied. Locations include some medeval castle, Iraq (?), swamps, city etc.
Game is under constant change and improvement. Developer listens to community and constantly updates the game. Since I bought it, there have been over 15 updates that changed main menu, balanced guns, overhauled campaign mode added multiplayer etc.
Some of the dinosaurs look really cool.
Price. Costs almost nothing. Good price, I like! Yes.
Now, if it looks like I was scraping at the bottom of the barrel to find positives, you're kind of right, because this game is basically Early Access at best.
I said game looked goodish. Well, it kinda goes both ways:
You see, some of the things like shadows, lightning and water are ok, while others are downright terrible like some buildings, trees and ground. Sometimes when you deal very much damage to a dino, it explodes in these half colored bits and it looks just... plain bad.
Dinosaurs behavior is downright crappy. They simply walk aimlessly intil they get shot, at which point they beeline stright towards you in hope of tearing you with your 1 000 000 hp to pieces, at which point they usually die by you hand. Some dinos like raptors can be seen hunting rabbits on some maps, but man that is not something you see often.
Campaign mode is can be completed in about 10 - 15 min. There's nothing more to be said about it, other than it would get pretty damn repetitive if it lasted longer. While maps are huge and some are even great, objective is always the same.
Weapon models are hit and miss. Granted I haven't unlocked everything yet, but some like M99, AWP like sniper, Crossbow and LMG looks pretty damn bad. Same reload animations and models that you can see through. Some guns are also very underpowered while others are waaay to overpowered (M99 and LMG comes to mind).
When you play survival, your FPS will tank in about 5 min, no matter how powerful you PC is. This also happens in campaign and Hunt mode (have not tested online yet), so optimization is needed here.
There are some bugs and glitches here and there.
So at this point I basically teared this game a new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and you think I really hate it.
And while it is kinda bad, even terrible at times, I still enjoy it from time to time and/or after update.
Also, if you think that this game looks bad now, you really have no idea how it looked and played at launch.
I actually respect the developer of this game, for not abandoning this like a quick cash grab, but instead, standing up and constantly working on the game with patches and improvements based on community feedback. Seems like they have ambition to make this into something special in the future and I truly hope they succeed. By looking back on it, I think they are well underway.
P.S.
Game is incredibly cheap. I got it on sale for almost nothing, so basically there were no regrets to be had either way.
