I was really excited to play this game, but unfortunately I believe it doesn't live up to expectations, or at least the pricetag.
+ PROS:
The game is gorgeous. Not only are the graphics really well put together, the art direction is incredibly inspired too.
The voice acting has its ups and downs, but the rest of the sounds in this game are spot-on.
As this is a horror game, it's important that its horrorific elements hold up to disturb the audience, and that they do admirably. This game has plenty of unnervingly nauseating scenes, especially ones centered around body horror.
- CONS:
One of the two biggest problems, this game's plot loses appeal really fast, and I believe the biggest factor in this is simply how it was told.
During the game you'll have the assistance of a certain character, with whom you will occasionally expend a few words. And by that I mean, every five minutes you'll be rehearsing the upteenth variant of "I know this is horrible but you must go on".
I'm no master of storytelling, but it seems to me that the best way to go about this kind of horror plot would be to leave the player alone to metabolize what's happening and take in the environment. I get that the writer probably wanted you to have some human interaction to contrast the horror of the situation, but I don't think the content and frequence of the conversations you have in this game benefit the atmosphere at all.
A second form of storytelling is log entries in the countless PDAs scattered around the place. A decent narrative strategy, if not for the fact that:
1) They're too verbose, mostly irrelevant to your present situation and the way they're written feels samey after a while.
2) They decidedly outnumber the items you can pick up for puzzles while being more visible, which makes their presence a thorn in your side while you're trying to solve a puzzle.
As for the plot itself, if you know your sci-fi tropes you'll have it figured out in a matter of minutes. The problem is that 99% of the time the game consists in "find a way to get to X", so you tend to forget about what you did a minute ago since you've moved past to a different room.
Despite having found a couple of interesting puzzles, the vast majority is just busywork. There's plenty of closed doors/hatches/lids that need something to open them, and not much else. This creates a further problem: since most of the time your objective is the same (open the path forward) you eventually lose your focus on anything that lies between you and the next door, and you end up not knowing what you're supposed to do exactly.
On top of this the game has a certain annoying tendency, especially early on, to pad the playable area with empty, useless rooms and corridors.
Letting a couple of glitches silide, the interface has a few problems too:
- The cursor is too ambiguous. Most of the time the "eye" indicates something you can examine but not interact with (as in, not even use items upon), but occasionally you do. On the other hand, the "hand" pointer mostly indicates things you can either pick up or "use", but every now and then a spot will only be interactible by using an item on it.
- No subtitles for anything that isn't a conversation between characters.
- You can't skip text or cutscenes. Since in this game you can die you'll probably have to once or twice, which will make having to sit through the same empty dialogue again really frustrating.
As far as the horror elements go, Stasis is exceptional. The problem is that most of everything else falls short: the dialogues and personal logs all blur together, the sci-fi elements are left extremely underdeveloped, and the puzzles only occasionally keep up your interest.
At a lower price it would probably be worth it  just to experience the incredible visuals and the atmosphere.

Overall 39/50
Strangely addictive...It is hard to quantify what makes this game so much better than that score would indicate.
Gameplay 9/10
A nice balance between running your shop and delving into the local dungeons when you want to restock. You can:
- Simply play the market by subtly marking up your goods received from the local guild and shops and learn the art of profiling your customers and haggling for a slow but steady profit,
- Spend most of your days delving into the dungeons for those high-quality goods that you can sell for nearly pure profit (minus the cost of hiring your adventurer).
- Try to attract new adventurers to your store by changing up the atmosphere
- Unlock new dungeons for faster and greater loot
BUT! Beware, as those debt deadlines can get pretty brutal in the later weeks! Carefully plan out how you spend your days and remember any special orders! The game has enough variety that it rarely gets boring or redundant, but that may differ dpending on your playstyle.
Graphics 6/10
A mixture of Visual Novel style characters and backdrops for story sections and 3D top-down views for gameplay segments provides most of the visual experience. The game feels obviously dated (which it is) and somewhat lacks in variety, but that is to be expected in a game that is mostly procedurally generated.
2D artwork is crisp and nice but fairly low resolution by modern standards. 3D rendering is obviously low-poly and the textures could be a bit better, but animations are generally smooth and do not detract from the gameplay.
Audio 7/10
The soundtrack has a nice overall feel to, but it lacks any fantastic standout tracks.  Most of the music serves as a nice subtle backdrop without getting annoying but after spending enough time in your shop you might just have to go run a dungeon just to get away from the music for a bit!  You probably will not start to have that problem until you have sunk a few dozen hours into the game, though.
Controls Avg. 9/10
Keyboard/Mouse 8/10
Defaults to ↑←↓→ controls instead of WASD and generally has that old-school DOS game key layout, but the controls can be changed (by using a separate configuration application) and are generally very responsive. Perfect once tweaked to your preference.
Gamepad 10/10
Works exceptionally well out the gate with an XInput controller (I use a Logitech F710 in XInput Mode). The configuration application can also be used to alter these controls if something does not feel quite right to you, but the defaults felt pretty natural to me.
Miscellaneous 8/10
Aside from the dated feel, this game comes with a unique premise that makes it feel special.  It offers the kind of variety very few games do in gameplay mechanics without ever overwhelming you.  Most things you want to be able to alter can be altered through the configuration application but here are a handful of "the little things" that might have made the game better:
- In-game configuration menus instead of an external program (you have to do an extra step every time you launch the game because of this)
- Some more hints in-game on how to attract new adventurers and unlock new dungeons (not always obvious)
- More options for resolution, including widescreen options!

L.A. Noire is an amazing crime thriller. You get to do varying detective tasks. You conduct interviews with whitnesses and suspects. You search the games beautiful world and look for clues as well as secrets and easter eggs. The game is about 19 hours in length for the story mode and a few side missions sprinkled in. It makes it well worth the 16.99 CDN it is currently on the Steam Store for. It also goes on sale almost every Steam sale. The story is very gripping as you solve corruption in the upper leadership of the police force and the municipal goverenment. There is a few plot twists and shocking moments in there as well, which makes for a really great overall experience. I can not say too much on the plot from here since it has to be played to be truly enjoyed. One more of the things L.A Noire did extremely well was the characters. You always feel like you can relate to the characters in certain parts of the story and they feel truly human, with human qualities. This makes L.A Noire an extremely rewarding game to play, and I reccomend you pick it up, despite its age and older graphics. After all the game is more about the story, rather then the gunfights and flare of the graphics.

I thought i'd pitch in my two cents, since I imagine many of you may be in the same situation as I was; wanting to buy the game but discouraged by negative reviews.
Well, never fear. I can tell you now that if it seems like you want this game, then you should just get it. It requires a lot of forgiving, but when it works, it's pretty amazing, and very unique - one of the highest fieldety games of this genre by a passionate developer.
The Good - The combat is fun, and never ruins the pacing. There's always time to explore. The graphics are phenomenal. Some UE3 limitations pop in from time to time but the overall effect of the art design, lighting and most textures really is brilliant. And hell, the setting. Do you want to go shooting Nazi's, Commies, and Mummies? Good.
The Bad - in a way, the game does deserve its negative reviews. The voice acting and animations are juuust that little bit off, but endearing in their own stupid way. The puzzles aren't really puzzles, just guessing games or connect the dots environmental obstacles. The shooting, while fun, isn't weighty enough; and the aiming is a bit sticky. And let's just say that from time to time the game breaks consistency in some very, very frustrating ways.
However, i've not run into a bug, or a glitch. From a purely objective standpoint, it's technicaly proficient. And yes, I suppose it's mediocre. But I don't care, I love the ancient civilization adventure genre. And if you do too, you'll forgive this game and soak in the incredible atmosphere. Another bland shooter this is not - check out NecroVision for another shooter set in a visually intense world by the same developer.
Besides, when was the last time you shot a Nazi in the face?

I've never found a strategy game better than Crusader Kings II. I've owned it for nearly two years (ignore my playing hours, I actually have two copies of CK II; one from gamersgate, and one on Steam I picked up off the humble bundle), and I LOVE it. It's stunning in depth and complex like few other games, yet I found it easy to pick up and learn. Anyone who likes royalty, strategy, or family politics will love this game.
Graphics are great; beautiful even. Very few strategy games I've played have such beautiful graphics in every area - character portraits, interface art, maps - normally something out of those lets you down. To mention it comes with its own, original music - beautiful, fitting classical pieces.
I've found it to have infinite replay-ability. Not only because there are so many different characters you can try out (nearly anyone in mainland europe, and with DLCs all of India and the middle east), but because it has a great AI that always makes the world different each time. In the footsteps of real medieval europe, inheritance can change the map fundamentally. Play historically and rebuild the empires of a dynasty, or just conquer a whim - both are fun.
This game is also constantly updated. Paradox has a great DLC policy where you get nearly every bit of content without the DLC just in the updates - all the DLCs do are to make characters playable, introduce new starts and new interface themes. So if you don't want to pay, you don't have to; you still get most of the experience, and you won't be left behind if you want to play multiplayer with others. There is no DLC wall. Not to mention DLCs can be easily turned on and off via the launcher.
So much content has been added since I began playing, and the game is always getting better - just recently they doubled the map size, an enormous amount of work for Paradox, nearly 2 year after the game came out.

I've waited patiently for STASIS for a long time, since I backed it way back in 2013, and now that it was finally here, I really looked forward to playing it.
8 hours and a bit later, I can't say that I am anything but disappointed in the final product.
I am willing to overlook the multiple bugs I experienced along the way, and also the clunky and cumbersome UI, but the quality of the game itself is really lacking.
I've played and loved all the old LucasArts point and click games, and more or less all the Sierra ones as well, so I am not adverse to the genre at all, but STASIS really suffers with a lot of puzzles being click-everywhere-until-you-hit-a-hotspot or try and combine items from your inventory until you get some that works together no matter how unlikely that combination may seem.
There are many puzzle in this game that are highly illogical to me, that I only solved by brute force, but luckily at any given time there are only a few rooms available to interact with, so trying everything is never too tiresome.
Graphically the game works fine, consisting of pre-rendered screens and animations, and mostly they are very atmospheric and works as they should.
The voice acting is pretty good too, it gets a little over the top from time to time, but generally its pretty good.
This leaves the most important part of the an adventure game, the story, and the writing, and this is where STASIS falls completely flat, in my opinion.
The story is all over the place, characters are inconsistent across the story, and there are way to much back story that are inconsequential and just seems like simple filler. Oftentimes the writing gets extremely poetic, for lack of a better word, and it feels like the writer(s) has had heavy use of a thesaurus just to use big words, and that just annoys me. (This is absolutely personal taste, I'm just not a fan of using big words just for the sake of using big words)
All in all, the most important part of the game is where it fails the most, and because of this I simply can't recommend it.

STASIS is excellent. Describing it as a "point and click adventure" doesn't do it justice; it's a finely crafted piece of entertainment, conveyed through extremely detailed isometric graphics and animation, and atmospheric sound and music. It's a very unsettling game, and it pulls no punches when it comes to being bleak, particularly in its uncompromising third act. The storyline initially appears simple, relying on established and well-worn sci-fi horror tropes, but it goes in a far more interesting direction that it first appears, and the closing moments of the game will have you reassessing what you thought you knew about the story.
There are some flaws; the voice acting for the main character is of a high standard (he really goes for broke in the third act), but the supporting characters are weaker, although for a low budget indie game it's surprisingly good. The "Alien / Aliens" references are a bit much; I love a good homage, but they're everywhere, the game doesn't need to fall back on such references. A couple of the puzzles are a bit of a stretch, not necessarily in knowing what to do, but figuring out how to do it. The puzzles are mostly of a high standard though, and the game moves from one section to another with a limited number of rooms and objects so that figuring out solutions isn't too daunting. After Mass Effect 1, I was really looking forward to the sequel - and It didn't disappoint!
Whilst it's graphics and gameplay are improved (quite a lot I think), it's also a slightly different style of game. Where in ME1 the story is somewhat standalone (not unlike a film), ME2 is more like a TV series where the grand finale at the end sees the results of all your hard work (or not).
The main plot is secondary to the recruitment of your very own "Dirty Dozen", and the game feels much more open than its predecessor.
Combat is far more fluid and fun, and the classes feel more balanced than before. Eqiuipment, ammo, weapons and everything else is far more streamlined, and after a few missions, I found that I didn't miss the old (more complicated) system at all.
The only poor part of the game is the scanning of planets for minerals (a tedious task if there ever was one), needed in order to upgrade your ship and equipment.
I would also strongly recommend the narrative DLC.

I hate to give bad reviews but I had a really hard time finding the good in this game. From poor character development, the occasional illogical or stupidly easy puzzle, primitive first person shooter experience, and cheap rpg aspect, I had a lot of trouble getting as far in the game as I did. I will say that there is a layer of nostalgia as the storyline and environment liken to Indiana Jones movies a bit, but if you want to watch an adventure film do just that and bypass this game.
My points in more depth:
- Poor character development: Jumping right into the story the characteres prod with one another endlessly with mundane and all to frequent jest. The dialog and voice quality is lacking any intelligent use of pause, and becomes annoyingly predictable.
- Puzzles are not very enjoyable after the initial nuance, in that the basic principle to shoot the block, or match the faces with the cheat sheet (in game little "Perk") is overused. Other puzzles were somewhat unique but either lacked a logical or discernably logical hint, like the rotate floating particles to make a shape puzzles. One such puzzle was eventually solved through trial and error, and didn't end up making a recognizable image. That was frusterating.
- The first person shooter aspect is usually what draws me into a game. The satisfying plink of the well placed stealth head shot kill. Sadly this game's fps setup is a strict point and shoot. It reminds me in a way of hyperstudio from years ago where you defind a region, and if you "crouched" the region go slightly larger. Click anywhere in the region and you hit the target in (to make things easy) a random location selected from a finite and small preset. Oh yes, and the shotgun is just stupid - small amounts of ammo, no effective spread, and incredibly weak power. Besides headshots what's not more fun than rounding the corner and point blank blasting the baddie with a shotgun? Well, in the game your out of luck because even at point blank range it'll take three or four shells. Sure, we're talking older weapons, and sure, the enemy might have body armor. But at close range in the kevlar you're going to be at least knocked back.
- Lastly, the rpg aspect of this game was pretty bland. A simple grid of powerups that are all vanilla. Shoot or reload faster - upgrade health pool, longer more powerful flashlight. Sure these are great and all if those are the starting base talents for a more complex tree. Sadly this is it for the game, for the trouble of running around and looking int every possible hidden corner in the game you get to aim a little better, and upgrade the once "interesting" combat mechanic (flashlight to weaken and kill zombies). In my opinion a good/fun rpg is one with talents that change how you play the game, and do so with very unique means. Take the classic fantasy class differences between melee, stealth, and magic combat structures.
In short, I think the designers of this game tried to do a little too much in incorporating too many game archetypes into one. Sure, it's possible to create a great game in this way, but sadly this one stretched itself too far in too many directions, and its playability or "fun factor" if you will, suffered for it.

The game was pretty much panned by all critics. In Deadfall Adventures, I never really felt any sort of adrenaline rush from any enemy encounter. The enemies are way too bullet spongey, so it's best to set the combat to easy and save yourself some time; the combat is simply unsatisfying and dull. The AI is laughably terrible and using your flashlight to defeat mummies is no new concept. Metro Last Light used this same mechanic, but it added to the intensity of the battle, which is not the case here. The story, setting, and characters are all extremely trite. The dialogue is painfully bad, and I couldn't care less about the plot, which is sad because I was initially very excited to play a FPS that was inspired by Indiana Jones. Your female companion is often ridiculous to rely on in battle, and much of what she does seems not only poorly programmed but often glitchy.
The visuals are the only impressive aspect of the experience, but the animation is very poor. I've been doing 3D modeling and animation for only 2 years and even I could have done a better job with this game's animation. It's just one more blatant problem that works against any sort of immersive experience this game intended on providing. It's a shame, because they must have had some really good artists working on the game. The only saving grace is that cutscenes are skippable. I suggest that anyone playing this game should exercise that option.
As far as exploration goes, the puzzles are both frustrating and insulting to one's intelligence, though they aren't as frequent as one would expect. Some puzzles are very obvious while others are difficult for all the wrong reasons, such as knowing a solution but being unable to execute it due to bad programming or confusing hints. There are treasures to be found, but not many, and it doesn't feel like you accomplished anything in finding them. Platforming is nonexistent, as the character can't jump high enough to actually get on top of objects in the game. Even if you could, the incessant invisible walls would keep you from exploring off the extremely linear path the game forces you to follow throughout its entirety.
I played this game for a few hours on another account. I really wish people wouldn't judge reviews based on the hours clocked by steam, though I understand that many users are too quick to form a negative or positive opinion of a game. This is something I have run into multiple times, especially when reviewing games that I played extensively before Steam added a system to keep track of the time spent in-game by each user. I promise I would not review a game before giving it enough of a chance to sway my opinion.
I mean no offense to those who worked very hard on this game. I know it took a lot of effort and many, many people poured a lot of hopes and dreams into this project. The premise was what sold me on the game. I took a risk and preodered Deadfall Adventures. As much as I was let down, I still have faith that the developer can create a game of a higher caliber. I hope that the developers will learn from the mistakes made on this project. I wish I could say that I enjoyed Deadfall Adventures, and I could see the potential buried deep within the final product. Sadly, the potential never really surfaced. It was more like something I projected onto the game. Still, I hope they try again after learning from their mistakes.

I don't even know where to start to review a game like this. It's a strategy on a massive scale. I should probably state that the initial learning curve is steep -- very steep.
**Note: Do Not Try To Learn This Game By Doing In-Game Tutorials (They Are Bad), Watch Some Great YouTube Video Resources**
Unfortunately the enjoyment comes after the learning curve, but when you hit that breaking point, the fun factor is overwhelming. It took me months of having this game to get past 5 or 6 hours of playing, but when I hit that, I can't stop playing it.
Starting in 1066, things are fairly slow for the early years of your first ruler, but it's best to learn in this time, and at this pace.
Some Highlights: Council. Your council will be made up of 5 different councillors, all with their own unique abilities to influence different aspects of the game -- from spying on neighbours, to training troops (personal levies), to fabricating claims on other states (you need a reason to allow you to go to war, so this is a must).
So, if you've not played this, or if you have put in under 5 hours, you ought to push a little bit more, and hit that point where this game turns enjoyable.

Full disclosure: I was aware of this game long before it ever became a reality, and backed it on Kickstarter, so that may have influenced my reaction.
That said, it's not exactly unknown for Kickstarters to disappoint their backers, so I am very happy to report that while I have a few minor issues, STASIS is in most respects exactly what I was looking for when I laid down my money. It's a fairly meaty, beautifully pre-rendered isometric horror adventure game set on a deep space research ship called the Groom Lake, one that has taken advantage of the remote and isolated nature of deep space in order to evade ethical and legal restrictions on the types of biological research they're doing. It's not a completely original scenario, of course. There are plenty of horror games set on some sort of ship or space station that has gone horribly wrong and killed off its inhabitants. But if it's a well-worn trope, it's a well-worn trope for a reason: it resonates strongly, and STASIS is no exception to that. It does add a couple of layers to the horror that I haven't seen elsewhere, though: protagonist John Marachek and his family weren't inhabitants of the ship, nor did they intend to go there as part of some investigation or rescue mission. No, they were in the titular stasis on a family trip, and the Groom Lake abducted them for use as experimental subjects. John didn't bear the brunt of this, although being summarily ejected from stasis hasn't done him any medical favors, but he's got no guarantee the same can be said for his loved ones.
So you have an immediate and compelling goal: find your family, and get the hell off this ship before it's too late. And since John is a completely unequipped civilian contending with a ship that's been the death of everyone aboard, that is going to take some doing. Fortunately, John is resourceful and dogged in his determination, and before long he has communications, at least, with a lone other survivor to help guide his quest. Unfortunately, the Groom Lake is a really, really terrible place, falling apart where it's not actively trying to murder John, and the methods required to progress are frequently pretty stomach churning. There's a healthy amount of body horror and other visceral unpleasantness, and it should say something about the tone that one class of achievement is for discovering the game's easter eggs: which inventory items you can use to have John end his existence prematurely. But not easily. Yeah. It's pretty freaking bleak.
But how is it as a game? Well, I do wish that the resolution were higher. The game's backgrounds are all prerendered (and, as I say, gorgeous - the quality of the screenshots were my initial hook into the game), so it's understandable that that limits resolution options, but it's a little weird that 720p was the one resolution chosen. I'm pretty sure most people can do better by now. Oh well. I also wish that you could skip through dialogue. Not because I'm one of the heathens who skip that stuff first time out, because the story was absolutely one of the things I came to STASIS for. But because this is a game where you can die, and while most of the time it's something you yourself initiate (often by doing something obviously stupid) and pops you back maybe a screen or so, there are a handful of instances where it comes right after a lengthy dialogue exchange without a chance to save. Beyond that, it's a very solid adventure game. Puzzles are generally quite fair and mostly logical as long as you've noticed everything you can interact with and found all your inventory options (although I had to resort to hints multiple times since there were several instances where I didn't). As I said above, some of the solutions are quite grotesque, but they evolve naturally out of the situation and the very limited resources without any weird leaps of logic like in many classic adventure games. You can die, but it's because you missed some important step in whatever you're trying to do most of the time, with only a couple sequences having any relation to your timing or reflexes. There are plenty of logs and things to look at to set atmosphere, and some really fantastic sound design. And all told, it took me around 9-ish hours to complete and then snag the last few achievements I missed. Quite fair for the price, I'd say.
So do I recommend STASIS? Absolutely, as long as you like your horror bleak and unrelenting.

Stasis is an amazing isometric point and click horror adventure game(damn thats a long description).  As a horror game its hits on all the right notes, rather then focusing on jump scares which loose their value at an exponential rate and wouldn't really work for an isometric game, stasis rather focuses on the ever constant mood. The set pieces are what they are, bloody, goory, and just out of your vidision to get a complete picture of exactly you are looking at. As you might imagine, this lack of view is actually a boon to the game as it allows the player to fill in far more horrific items they may dream up to fill the holes. While you may have no problem sleeping, playing the game you will force yourself to consider ethics and morality not within the confines of the game (there is no choice) but your own as you explore this "S.S Horror Ship".
As an adventure game it manages to miss nearly every pitfall many recent point and click adventure games run into, game logic. Stasis, when it comes to puzzles are firmely placed in real world logic, meaning the puzzles are based off of knowledge you already posses, rather then say a game like Deponia(which I still enjoy), where the puzzles are over the top and becomes a exercise and understanding the game logic then finding the puzzles. Being from a Isometric standpoint there is a few very scarce issues of not being able to see what you need to see or interact with due to the darkness of the object or how it looks relation to everything else, but as i said, these are scarce.
Stasis has but one flaw and that is its menu system can be clunky or annoying to work through. The game menu is "chunky" for lack of a better term and hates to remember your volume settings. In addition some puzzles that have a menu system lack a certain responsiveness making it confusing occasionally what you are suppose to be doing.
Stasis manages to pull off what I consider the best kind of horror that a horror game can provide, forcing the player to look inward as they progress through the situations presented to them through the game that they have no hope of fixing, only moving past.

This Review Is In Regards To The New Expansion, And Not The Base Game
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Plains of Eidolon was meant to open up the cramped spaces of Warframe to an open world, freedom and fluid gameplay experience. It didn't, at all.
We now have a large beautiful looking landscape, with absolutely terrible mechanics at every turn.
The Missions:
Plains isn't just some tileset you go out onto inorder to find challenges, it's a mission map like all the other tilesets. You take missions in the form of bounties, which are multiple stage missions (similar to in base game you have multiple waves/stages), however in Plains it's incredibly easy to have a Bounty stage fail due to bugs, bad design,♥♥♥♥♥♥luck. Congrats, you just wasted 20+ minutes of your life.
The missions you get for the bounties are basically all the same: Capture a Commander, Escort a Drone, Blow Up Some Supplies, etc. There is very little variety and it gets repetitive very fast, which is a huge problem because you needs TONS of faction rep to get anything rewarding out of Plains
ArchWing/Travel:
The ArchWing should never have been a consumable. We have had these frames sitting in our ships for ages, now we need to go fishing and grind crafting mats to make a consumable "Okay, you can use your archwing now." item?
Furthermore, the amount of time you spend bullet jumping across the landscape to reach the City gates to "extract" after missions, failed or not, is way too damn high. Want to make it even more miserable? Do the Plains with public matches and get people who don't go to the door to extract, have fun, may as well go put Netflix on.
Class Balance:
In a game that is already suffering terrible with certain Warframes being hand over fist better than others, Plains completely shakes that up and makes it a hundred times worse. MANY MANY frames have abilities and skills very much based around maps that are indoors and close range. Well, now we are outside and a majority of my favorite frames abilities are absolute trash without corridors that funnel enemies into useful range settings.
So Much Grind, So Little Payoff:
Plains is nothing but a grind, the "boss" of Plains, the Eidolon, is literally a 40 minute fight and the rewards much like the Bounty system, are lackluster....like, really bad. Faction grinding for items feels terrible, everything about this whole Investment VS Reward structure in Plains feels completely jacked.
I was really , really , really looking forward to PoE. I probably should have expected much less from DE.

The game is actually pretty good. Short, but good. The story is absolutely fantastic - well written, well presented. There are a couple of problems I encountered - keyboard controls felt awkward, so I had to switch to xbox controller, the whole "investigation" thing is pretty linear. But what saved this game for me was the sheer amount of LORE and background for everything happening and what happened. Hell, even the town and some of it's past events are real. But also not only you can "read" newspaper articles or you dead wife's diaries - you can also poke around the city to find some ghostly remains of city's past, reveal some well-narrated backstories and so on.
It is pretty linear in it's investigations, but outside them you have your town which is kind of open-worldish, but not really. Nice little touch is the ability to read people's minds - and even though they sometimes repeat - the amount of "thoughts" is pretty big and also reveals some lore.
The "ghost" mechanic is great and executed well - the only bad thing I can name is that in tight spaces (there are not a lot of them, but still) you can easily lose your sense of space because of your "ghost noclip" ability. Oh, and demons are kind of annoying, but not too much, and they are pretty rare.
The real bad thing is that this game is pretty short. If you ignore all nice details you can possibly complete it in 6 or 5 hours. With all the poking around it will take around 9-10, but not more. Though the story is good, really good. The whole story made me not regret buying it.

NOCLIP - The Game is a game about the ghost of a man who attemps to solve the mystery of his own death.
Story - 9/10 Fitting uncountable cliches but is very well written. Being a mystery story, I suggest that you avoid spoilers.
Atmosphere - 10/10 Very tight and immersive atmosphere.
Graphics 9/10 - Looks like it should look in 2014, but a little edgy at some details.
Sound 10/10 - I have nothing to complain about. Excellent voice acting.
Playability 9/10 - No plotstoppers for me. NOCLIP - The Game has some minor issues, but does not desperately need a patch.
Gameplay 2/10 - That is the reason for all the scathing reviews.
In NOCLIP - The Game you play as a ghost. You can walk through walls and people - hence the name. You can also possess people to read their thougts, solve some puzzles and get your clues. You can even possess the cats and control them to access some areas. Later you get the ability to teleport.
Clues - they are basically just collectibles with an occasional tiny puzzle attached to them. You cannot fail the puzzles, it is always just trial and error. Each investigation just consists of getting all these clues.
The game is full of other collectibles. They unlock some background info and additional ghost stories.
In attempt to make NOCLIP - The Game a bit challenging, there are fights against demons. You can beat them with a QTE or sneak your way around them. These fights are very repetitive and annoying.
And that is basically it. No other gameplay elements. This is not an adventure game, this is just an interactive movie with a boatload of collectibles.
At least the level design is very open and nonlinear, partially due to NOCLIP. You can also return to old levels for the collectibles you missed. Sadly, you cannot do this if you complete the game. there is only one save slot and the last savepoint is just after a point of no return, luckily the only one in the game.
Conclusion: Do not buy NOCLIP - The Game for the gameplay, buy for the story and the atmosphere. But you can get that as well if you watch a decent walkthrough, which saves you some money. Actually playing it only benefits you with achievements and trading cards.
Frankly, To The Moon has the same issue as NOCLIP - The Game: excellent story, but awful and repetitive gameplay, kind of like collectible hunting as well. Yet To The Moon is praised by the press. I understand the bad reviews for NOCLIP - The Game, but I can hardly understand the difference.

Man, this game is beautiful. Deadfall Adventures has the setting and story of Indiana Jones, the style of Uncharted and the gameplay of... a generic first person shooter. You play this game from a first person perspective which is actually a very nice twist on the genre. You'll be traveling to different parts of the world to find hidden treasures, solve puzzles and chase bad guys.
Like I said, the game has the vibe of Indiana Jones. It all looks very colorful and very adventurous. It has awesome, detailed graphics and horrible, horrible voice acting. A damn shame, because the rest of the game is actually worthwhile, but the voice acting is one of the things that drags the game down. The other thing that drags the game down are the firefights. It's inaccurate and doesn't feel realistic. It's important, because near the end you'll be fighting off more and more enemies.
The story is fun in that it doesn't take itself all that seriously. It will be fun as long as you keep that in mind.
There are also loads of treasures to be found; some can be found in the open, some are hidden and can be found by simply exploring and some can be collected by solving puzzles. These puzzles are usually simple to solve and can be completed in just a few minutes. If some of these puzzles were only a bit harder it would've given you a better feeling of accomplishment.
Doesn't take away the fact that it's fun to try and find these treasures. Treasures can also be used to upgrade your character, but I didn't notice much of a difference when I first started the game and when I eventually finished the game. He still felt like the exact same guy to me.
Checkpoints are sometimes awkwardly placed so if you die while trying to solve a second or third puzzle you might have to start all over from the beginning. This can be frustrating but usually it's just a couple of minutes. Still... annoying.
Deadfall Adventures wants to be a first person Uncharted and in a way The Farm 51 has succeeded in doing this. Next time, keep the graphics, improve the voice acting and shooting aspects, make the puzzles (a bit) harder and you'll probably have a great, fun sequel in your hands.

This game states that it has permadeath, I believe because the game thinks it is hard. As of yet, I haven't found anything hard about it, but I have found a TON that is annoying. A chunk of that comes from the characters themselves. I'll get to that.
The world looks nice, but becomes repetitive VERY quickly. Each zone, and they're large, has one tileset that they use, and your eyes glaze over it in no time. There's the occasional decoration around, yes, but they typically cause graphical glitches in the form of black lines appearing next to the object, and sometimes enemy. That's really nice, when an enemy walks around looking like someone tried to paste it to the game directly out of paint. As such, each rooms basically looks the same. Assuming the room doesn't crash your game. Which happened to me THREE TIMES in the 70 minutes I played.
There are items you can find in treasure chests, in the form of potions, bombs, and power ups. Potions don't persist if you leave the room, (Not sure about other items, I didn't want to risk it.) So if you find a room with three potions that you accidentally opened, and you only have room for one, sucks to be you! Potions gone! For that matter, you can also somehow use items while in the menu checking your stats. Lost a bomb that way! Guess I don't get to open that wall till I can find another, yay.
The enemies are actually kind of cute, although their art style stands out from the characters in a big way, making the characters look even chunkier and flat. While they look good, the placement of the enemies is extremely boring and uninspired. They're just in your way, waiting for you to show up, sometimes just the same enemy for rooms and rooms (six rooms straight of just floating swords. How fun.) On occasion something will drop from the ceiling, or a flyer will fly though the floor and walls because why not. None are in the slightest bit dangerous, and most can't even drop down or climb up ledges, making them completely helpless.
There is dialogue, but I never get to read it because I run around while mashing the shoot button, which skips dialogue. Great.
The music is okay. I didn't get to hear much, honestly, and what I did hear was a fairly short loop, which, while nice, got annoying fast, in particular because I could HEAR WHERE IT LOOPED. Speaking of sound getting annoying, some sounds are just louder than others. There are pikachus in the game, and when they do a shock attack, a LOUD buzzing noise plays that is very jarring. The same noise plays for bombs.
Now, on to the characters. There are eight
characters. I attempted to get each one to level ten to get a good feel for them, but the game had other plans for me.
Gojar is the first. S/he (I'm not sure) is a swordsman, and suffers from being a melee character in a game where you can shoot. As such, he sucks. His gimmick is he has a higher speed stat than the others. This caused me to collide with enemies constantly as the dude shot around the room. Actually kind of funny. Possibly my fault as I was in a hurry.
Thirakor is next. He is also a swordsman, with a mighty beard. His gimmick is that he does high damage, and has good defense and HP. That's about it. Actually kind of satisfying, as his high damage and slow speed allows you to basically move forward mashing attack without worry. Can't shoot, so he's still not very useful.
Farog is third. He is ANOTHER swordsman. Is old, and has a sweet fu manchu. Appears to be a mix between Gojar and Thirakor. Does more damage than Gojar, less than Thirakor. Is faster than Thirakor, slower than Gojar. Woo.
Agroha is fourth. He has a large spiked shield, and has no attack. He simply moves close to enemies, and they take damage. If he moves too far, they clip past the shield and damage him. Incredibly boring, and you're forced to use him to open doors, because someone made automatic doors that only open if some shmuck sticks a spiked shield into a specific wall for some obscure reason.
Larilak is fifth. He can double jump. Because this would bring him dangerously close to being a good and fun character, his stats suck, and his weapon is terrible. It's a spear that does low damage, and only damages directly in front of him. In a game where it sucks to be melee, he has even worse melee.
Arajam is sixth. He's a mage. He fires blasts of magic. This means he can shoot, which makes him useful right? NOPE. For some mystifying reason, his shots go over the heads of small enemies like rats or crouching slimes. If he crouches, his shots fire from the exact same place. He cannot attack small enemies, of which the game has mostly consisted of so far. Combine this with corridors with small roofs, and he gets wrecked trying to get around enemies. Someone actually reported this issue on the 12th of may. It got a dev response, but nothing was changed. At all. Is completely useless because of the inability to shoot low. Another power of the mage is the ability to shoot magic statues to open doors or make magic blocks appear to avoid danger. If you open a door this way, it will be closed when you come back. TRAPPING YOU IN THE ROOM. Forcing you to bring the only other mage to come get them out, or to use a summon statue to bring the mage back to safety. If you just have your magi left, you can break your game this way. Good job dev!
Gela is seventh. She has a bow, and is literally the only good character. She has decent speed without rocketing around, and has decent enough attack to do satisfying damage. She can also shoot, AND she can shoot low enemies too, making her the only character you'll ever want to use.
Ciya is last. She is also a mage, and somehow gets stuck on walls a lot. Suffers all the same problems as Arajam. I could not get either mage to level 10 as a managed to get them both trapped in different magic statue rooms. I admit, the second one was my own stupidity.
I made it to the second zone, which for me was the crystal caves. They were pretty for three rooms, then became bland and repetitive. After that, I had no motivation to play anymore.

In L.A. Noire, you play as a detective in an episodic crime thriller. Each episode consists of a single crime, and has you collecting clues, interviewing witnesses, catching the bad guys, etc. The most interesting mechanic is conversing with people - trying to figure out when they're lying or when to bring out evidence, but the whole idea falls flat. Everyone's "tell" is to twitch and squirm like they have bugs crawling in their nose, so there's no doubt when you've got a liar on your hands. The map is completely open-world, which sounds like a plus but it doesn't add anything in an episodic, story-driven game. It's too easy to solve each case, so they all play out more like a movie than a game. The lack of gameplay could be written off if the crimes were worth writing home about, but they're nothing more than basic, cookie-cutter police reports. Don't play L.A. Noire, it’s not the 40’s detective game you’re looking for.

Deadfall Adventures review:
Deadfall Adventures tells a fairly tame story with larger than life characters and many moments where the action heats up with some cool scripted scenes. The puzzle element is welcome, but in some instances really hinders the pacing of the game. Sadly, the game's characters are simply not likable enough to step beyond being generic, and as a result the story aspect of the game is largely inconsequential. So, what you're left with is a fairly competent shooter, that cleverly mixes in puzzles, throws in some multiplayer and co-op and wraps it up in a neat package that plays pretty well. However, there's simply something lacking from the game in every department, that borders on being dull and uninspiring. As a result, Deadfall Adventures doesn't reinvent the wheel, or tries to, and merely offers a mediocre but pleasant action adventure, that's worth a play but is not necessarily an essential purchase, and certainly not up to par with its peers in terms of quality. If you like a bit of puzzle solving, shooting Nazis and are bored of military shooters, then Deadfall Adventures is perhaps worth checking out, although perhaps it would be prudent to wait for an inevitable price drop.

I've never found a strategy game better than Crusader Kings II. I've owned it for nearly two years (ignore my playing hours, I actually have two copies of CK II; one from gamersgate, and one on Steam I picked up off the humble bundle), and I LOVE it. It's stunning in depth and complex like few other games, yet I found it easy to pick up and learn. Anyone who likes royalty, strategy, or family politics will love this game.
Graphics are great; beautiful even. Very few strategy games I've played have such beautiful graphics in every area - character portraits, interface art, maps - normally something out of those lets you down. To mention it comes with its own, original music - beautiful, fitting classical pieces.
I've found it to have infinite replay-ability. Not only because there are so many different characters you can try out (nearly anyone in mainland europe, and with DLCs all of India and the middle east), but because it has a great AI that always makes the world different each time. In the footsteps of real medieval europe, inheritance can change the map fundamentally. Play historically and rebuild the empires of a dynasty, or just conquer a whim - both are fun.
This game is also constantly updated. Paradox has a great DLC policy where you get nearly every bit of content without the DLC just in the updates - all the DLCs do are to make characters playable, introduce new starts and new interface themes. So if you don't want to pay, you don't have to; you still get most of the experience, and you won't be left behind if you want to play multiplayer with others. There is no DLC wall. Not to mention DLCs can be easily turned on and off via the launcher.
So much content has been added since I began playing, and the game is always getting better - just recently they doubled the map size, an enormous amount of work for Paradox, nearly 2 year after the game came out.
My ratings?
Music - 9/10
Graphics - 8/10. Only thing that could be improved is player portraits might be higher-res.
Gameplay - 10/10
Replayability - 10/10
Updates - 10/10
Support - 9/10
Overall - 9/10.

This game surely can be a lot of fun. Spoiler alert.
When you start a game. you wake up in the middle of nowhere with no tool in your hand (even though you can unlock different tools that you can build each time you level up.) You see creatures you dreamed of playing with as a kid as long as you liked dinosaurs. Must be fun playing this with VR.
You find out that you can build so many things using the resources all around you. You can tame creatures and even let them breed. How cool is that? You can go anywhere on the map and really you can play out your imagination however you want within the game's capabilities.
Some of the downsides of this game I noticed are:
1.The A.I. system:
It's frustrating to see your Trike following you only to get stuck between two trees all the time in the forest. Sometimes your creatures can get blocked by other creatures which cause your creatures to run in one place perpetually.
Also, your enemies are pretty sharp at detecting you. For example, let's say you are on the top of a ridge with your friendly longneck rifle with a attachable scope, peering down at the surroundings below you while picking out your target dinosaurs or creatures. And for the sake of an argument the distance between you and your immediate target is an equivalent of 100 yards. (You can shoot a creature from quite a distance in this game.) One shot lands on the creature and it knows where you are and starts coming after you. I mean this sort of AI is what you see in COD with their perpetually bad A.I. I wonder if Studio Wildcard will do about this or it might be just inherent in this game and nothing will be done about it.
2.Resource requirement for making and reparing tools:
It doesn't make much sense to require 50 or more metal ingot to build a rifle. I meant, have you ever seen a metal ingot? Ofcourse sizes may vary but usually it's a large hunk of a metal and requiring 50 to build a rifle just doesn't make any sense. And I'm only taking about one example, you will find other several examples that are just as ridiculous and it can easily slave you to resource farming.
3.Multiplayer Experience
It took some amount effort to figure out how to play with friends via LAN because the game doesn't offer a simple solution to this. Running a server on your own computer and playing ARK on it can cause some serious RAM usage.
Be prepared to have at least 16GB or RAM if you want to run your own server and play on it. On my rig, it was consuming around 12~14GB or RAM. When it was nearning 14GB I could feel some lag issue even though I have no problem running this game at 1920X1080 pretty much all things maxed out.
The overall experience is still good and this game can be a lot of fun whether you play alone or with friends.
I wouldn't recommend playing it online with strangers even though it can be fun, it is also offset by numerous toxic players.
Have fun!

The sequel to Hero of the Kingdom that was released in 2013, Hero of the Kingdom 2 takes much of the same formulae as the original had, and improves upon them. For those not familiar with the first, Hero of the Kingdom takes the Hidden Object formula, and mixes it with RPG and Adventure to make a nice casual experience that allows the player to experience the game with little to no pressure. Allowing you to either sit down and clear through the game in one sitting, or to boot up and play the game when you have a little free time. Anyway, on with the breakdown analysis!
(TL:DR version and Conclusion at the bottom)
The game starts with the protagonist and their sister wandering the countryside, looking for a place to call home. Their family, and their old home, were destroyed by a earthquake, with them being the only survivors of the event. They are found by a kindly old man, who takes them in and brings them to the fishing village he lives at. After running a couple errands, he comes back to the village only to find that pirates are raiding the village, and holding his sister captive. But before he can get close enough to his sister, he is knocked out.
He wakes up, only to find the pirates gone, and a couple of the townspeople badly injured. A trip to the nearby herbalist provides him with a couple potions necessary to tend to the wounded. Once he knows the townspeople are well, he sets out to find a boat in order to chase after the notorious pirates who have captured his sister.
Just like the first game, the storyline is that of a rescue mission. But, It has enough differences to it that it's not a sort of cut-and-dry copy of the original. The original is only referenced through a bit of obscure dialogue, so one could play this game without even needing to play the first.
Same as the first game, as they yet again took a minimalistic approach. But I do suppose it works for the formula they went for, so I suppose they opted to not fix what wasn't broken, and instead put their resources to the art and gameplay. But fortunately, this means those familiar with the first game, will find absolutely no issue in navigating the UI.
Very similar to the last game, but there's definitely some improvement here. There's actual multiple ways to make profits should you run out of things that would be obvious to sell, as opposed to the single and extremely slow method in the first game. There is also other islands to explore, as opposed to a single landmass. There's also a new skill you can unlock, which is the ability to pick locks. Which is quite nice.
But, aside from that, things are relatively similar to the last game. In that you'll unlock new things to find as you learn new skills, of which these new things will spawn or activate throughout the world once you learn the skill, requiring a bit of backtracking to find everything. And interaction is done solely with a mouse, to click on objects to collect, exclaimation points to trigger quests, and on creatures to fight, so long as you've the items to fulfill the requirements.
The graphics are well executed, everything containing a sort of consistant style so as to not make things look completely out of place, but also not blending completely in to the background. This can make things look as though they fit in their environment, but not insanely hard to find as well. Which is a problem I've seen quite a few Hidden Object games have.
All the art resources are also made by the staff working on the game, which is another such thing that I've seen games of the HOG genre cut corners on. So definite kudos to the artists of Lonely Troops.
The music is quite nice, fitting the settings well. Obviously it's not the kind of music that one'll get hooked on, but it's definitely good to listen to for the duration that one is playing for. Sounds will also play depending on what is in the current view of the area, so you will definitely hear the difference between a bustling city full of people, and a forest stocked with wildlife and boar to hunt.
- Storyline is simple, akin to the first. A mission to rescue your sister!
- Easy to play casual gameplay.
- Graphics are well done, and don't look out of place.
- Music and sounds that fit the location.
- More ways to make money than the last game.
- Good amount of Achievements.
- Minimalistic UI as in the first game.
- Game is very casual, making it a boon for those who like it that way, and a strike against it for ones looking for more from their experience.
- Game is short, just like the first game.
- Even more backtracking than the last.
- Little to no replay value.
It doesn't try to be groundbreaking or something overly different, it settles in to it's own element peacefully, while making improvements over the formula set by the first. It doesn't try to bring too much to the table like I've seen happen in other sequels, and what it does offer runs smoothly with absolutely no glitches or bugs. All in all, it's a enjoyable little game, and good to play for both people new to this series of games, and those playing this one after the first.
I hear a third game is in the works already, and I'm sure that it will improve more over the formula as this one has. And I'll have to be sure to pick it up myself to play once it's released. But for now.... Thank you very much for taking your time to read my review~!

(After finsihing the game I have to change my recommendation. The story ended up going in a direction that just left me feeling angry. Everything I wrote below is still true though)
Apparently this game was KickStarted, I didn't actually know that from the trailers, since they look very slick, but once I got into the game I started to see the signs of a budget that was a bit too small.
If you have played games like Sanatarium then you will recognise the kind of horror this game is going for. Even this cutscenes look like they were lifted from a 90's game.  The good news is that the one thing it doesn't lift from the 90's is the puzzle design...on purpose at least.
One of the biggest problems with this game is that there seems to be critical lines of dialogue either missing or not triggering. A prime example is when you go into a morgue, in the corner there is a large door that the game tells you is a furnace. I will say that one of the things I love is that you only have to mouseover an item to get the description of it instead of having to click on everything. The doors inside the morgue are all iced over and what the game expects you to do is use a♥♥♥♥♥♥soaked rag you got much earlier in the game. You wrap the rag around the gears that open the furnace and then open it. The gears will jam and start heating the room up. If you stay inside the room at that point you will burn to death but if you run out and then return you will be able to get access to the corpses inside the drawers.
The problems with the puzzle is that if you interact with the door to the furnace before putting the rag on the gears nothing will happen. Your character will do a fiddling animation and that is. The door doesn't swing open then close again, your character doesn't make a comment. You are given no clue as to what is supposed to happen. I figured out what I was expected to do partly by guessing and partly by blind luck. It was made easier by the fact that the door and gears where the only things I could interact with.
On top of that I had no idea why I was doing any of this. The game does such a bad job of communicating what is going on a lot of the time. That you end up having to just muck about with the three or four interactable objects in any given set of rooms till a solution presents itself.
Another problem I have is that sometimes the perspective will screw up. The character model will be huge compared to the objects around them. Sometimes the character will pass in front of parts of the environment that they are clearly supposed to pass under. A group of pipes hanging from  the roof is a good example.
On top of that there seem to sometimes be sections where the descriptions or line of dialogue where either written or recorded before a area was finalised. This can lead to weird moments like a part early on where you come across the body of a member of the crew. You talk on the radio to another member of the crew about how there friend is dead. The only problem is the corpse is still twitching around on the floor. This also happens with objects in the world, there is a hologram dancer that is said to be dancing to a silent tune. Which would be fine if it weren't for the fact that loud dance music is playing at the time.
I don't know how much of this is glitching and how much is just the result of a tight budget. Even with all these problems I still enjoy the game. It doesn't exactly do anything super new and you will spend a lot of time reading people's PDA's But the writing is really strong, a trio of PDA's you find in a security station really stand out to me.  The voice acting is a bit of a mixed bag as well but there is nothing unforgivably bad and it kinda plays into the Pulp Horror vibe for me.
So yeah, even though I have some problems with the game I really enjoy it. The puzzles, when I know what they are, are logical and don't employ any moon logic. The game  moves along at a fair clip and the writing is mostly pretty strong. There are some cool ideas hidden in here, particularly when it comes to how some of the people on the ship dealt with the situation.
If you like point and click adventure games of the old breed then I would give this a look. Even if you don't like those kinds of games I wold still give this game a whirl.

Managing expectations is important. Perhaps it was a mistake on my part to expect a story that works not only on a basic three act structure level, but also leaves room for arguing about a metaphor, detailed analysis and interpretation. Not that there is anything wrong with a more straightforward storytelling, especially if it's finely crafted, but the number of science fiction clichés that present in STASIS is just too large: Unethical Scientific Experiment gone wrong, Evil Megacorporation, Insane Over-Obsessed Scientist that just have to Play God because... clichés.
I guess you can argue that this failed experiment can be interpreted as a metaphor for a stem cell controversy; evil scientist who violates medical ethics is a warning reminder of unethical human experimentation and that such sets of principles as the
and the
could not be violated; and Megacorporation is supposedly an anti-globalization statement. But for that assumption to be true, those topics should be actually developed and expanded upon. Instead they exist only to justify the horror setting and as a mechanism that propels protagonist from point A to B.
It's important to manage expectations, but it also important to look at things in a fair way. And it's hard to argue that for a small South African indie studio STASIS is a huge accomplishment. Crafted mainly by just two people this game boasts some pretty decent visuals, while also managing to lend several genuinely effective jump scares (in a point and click adventure game!) and have one pretty disturbing (

Wow, where do I begin? This game is an excellent next step in the idle game genre, but I really don't think you need to be a fan of idle games to enjoy it. Unlike most idle games I've tried, it really is a fun game first: the fact that you progress even while the game is closed just feels like a bonus feature.
The biggest differentiator from most idle games is the formation system, where in addition to pouring upgrades into heroes you also have to place them on the battlefield. Crusaders have skills that affect the heroes around them, making it a really fun puzzle game to try and maximize your damage in different ways. Unlocking new Crusaders, formations, and equipment open up a lot of really cool options for formations that keep the game fresh and interesting even after you've played it for a long time ( I'm glad Kongregate doesn't track time, and I'm a little worried now that the game is on Steam!).
Another crucial thing is the reset system in this game: in most idle games you can reset your progress for some bonuses, but then it just feels like you're playing the game over again but faster. In Crusaders when you reset you get bonuses as well, but you also have the option of taking on really crazy challenges for a run instead of just playing the normal game. Challenges that change the formation really bring out that puzzle game feeling, and you learn techniques and tricks from them that you can use in your normal games when you try to go for deep dives ( going as far as possible before resetting ).
I know this review is pretty glowing, but every problem I've had with the game over the months I've been playing has been addressed by the devs, and there's no sign that the updates are slowing down. I've been really impressed with their open communication with the players, it's not something you get from every developer these days.

This game is really fun. The story hooked me in right from the start and never let go until the 'yell at your tv' ending. I find the gameplay mechanics refreshing and fun. You are a ghost so you can't directly interact with most things, but you can look and piece together clues leading you through the games story amazingly well. I don't think i ever got frustratingly stuck or bored of the gameplay. The story and gameplay flow together nicely. And the characters! I found them all to be believable, with no cliche cardboard cutouts among the main characters.
The collection of all the items in the game adds more reason to search through the levels and adds a nice layer onto the story with collectables about the main character, the enemy, and even the town itself. The world feels very historic. Some might argue that it is too linear, but I personally liked that places were blocked off or I would have spent hours rifling through large buildings, getting lost XD
Maybe my only complaint about the game is that there is no map, and since you can go through walls, it can get disorienting. I get that a ghost cant really carry around a map haha, its just a little nitpick, overall I loved the game and would recommend it to anyone looking for a great story and a fun time :)

I've never found a strategy game better than Crusader Kings II. I've owned it for nearly two years (ignore my playing hours, I actually have two copies of CK II; one from gamersgate, and one on Steam I picked up off the humble bundle), and I LOVE it. It's stunning in depth and complex like few other games, yet I found it easy to pick up and learn. Anyone who likes royalty, strategy, or family politics will love this game.
Graphics are great; beautiful even. Very few strategy games I've played have such beautiful graphics in every area - character portraits, interface art, maps - normally something out of those lets you down. To mention it comes with its own, original music - beautiful, fitting classical pieces.
I've found it to have infinite replay-ability. Not only because there are so many different characters you can try out (nearly anyone in mainland europe, and with DLCs all of India and the middle east), but because it has a great AI that always makes the world different each time. In the footsteps of real medieval europe, inheritance can change the map fundamentally. Play historically and rebuild the empires of a dynasty, or just conquer a whim - both are fun.
This game is also constantly updated. Paradox has a great DLC policy where you get nearly every bit of content without the DLC just in the updates - all the DLCs do are to make characters playable, introduce new starts and new interface themes. So if you don't want to pay, you don't have to; you still get most of the experience, and you won't be left behind if you want to play multiplayer with others. There is no DLC wall. Not to mention DLCs can be easily turned on and off via the launcher.
So much content has been added since I began playing, and the game is always getting better - just recently they doubled the map size, an enormous amount of work for Paradox, nearly 2 year after the game came out.
My ratings?
Music - 9/10
Graphics - 8/10. Only thing that could be improved is player portraits might be higher-res.
Gameplay - 10/10
Replayability - 10/10
Updates - 10/10
Support - 9/10
Overall - 9/10.

After seeing this on a winter sale, I decided to spend the four dollars and go for it. The game is a point and click adventure turned RPG set to a pirate-themed world. I would put "Hero of the Kingdom" in the same light-RPG flavor that made the original Pokemon games so popular: You're making progress regardless of the order in which you do things.
The game is open enough and short enough to keep one's attention for a few hours at a time, which is a positive because there appears to be very little replayability. The collection quests work very well with the resource management, and there is never a sense of impending urgency to do plot points. I consider myself reasonably capable of puzzle solving; a 100% completion run took a little over 6 hours with no guide.
Pick it up if you don't mind some gentle chiding from a game rather than direct scolding for failure. A word to the wise, this game does require a strong eye for details. If your eyesight or monitor resolution aren't the best, take caution. Other than that, it's a superb bargain-bin time filler on a rainy afternoon.

So WHAT THE HELL IS IT?
It's basically a casual adventure/puzzle/hidden object game.
You follow the fantasy story with a hero, although you don't see him on the screen. You don't "walk" with him, just move between static 2D screens (with basicaly animated backgrounds and moving-arrows on the border of screen). You also collect resources, find hidden objects, but most of the time you're just trying to figure out what to do next.
Few important thing:
* it is VERY easy. You cannot die or get stuck irreversibly and you have always a hint available
* it's ok for kids, no cursing or brutality
* the gameplay is almost casual. I can imagine it could be well played on mobile phones
* ..but having said that, it is FAR MORE complex and longer, than average casual game
+ / -
+ it has some very simple rpg elements (you don't have to get "lockpicking", for example, but if you help npc XY, you can learn it and make money that way. The same with Herbalism, Hunting etc..)
+ 100% achievement easily reachable (and somehow fun to get)
+ about 5 hours gameplay
+ not many similar games around. The closest thing would be old point'n'click adventure games  (or hidden object games as "Abyss: the wraiths of eden")
- story is a bit cheap
- absolutely zero replaybility
Can be finished with 100% achievements in about 4+ hrs, during one continuous play.
I bought it for 4$ and yes, that's about worth it - can be surprisingly fun to play, if you don't expect much.
p.s. if you played first one, this is just more of the same.

STASIS is about as jolly as you might expect from a developer who cites Alien, Event Horizon and Sunshine as some of his inspirations. The Groomlake is a massive derelict in a decaying low Neptunian orbit, and it really looks and sounds the part. It should've been called the RV McGrimy though, IMHO.
According to the
, it took 12 hours to implement each scene in STASIS, and every room and object is pre-rendered from detailed 3D models. You won't see much asset reuse - no two rooms or corridors look alike, and there's lots of them. As the ship is all shot up as well as on security lockdown, you don't exactly navigate it the way the architects intended, which adds a lot of variety. There's also elaborate clockwork mechanics for airlocks, tram cars etc, the lighting is beautiful and moody, and the art is undoubtedly a labour of love.
OK enough gushing - I'm a professional. Entering smiley/frowny face mode:
In conclusion, this is a great game for the patient - those who like to soak up the atmosphere, explore for clues, find hidden objects and read all the backstory.

Disclosure: I backed this game on Kickstarter, and I don't regret doing so -- the project delivered exactly what was promised, which already puts it ahead of many Kickstarters.  I can't recommend the game for the reasons below, but that doesn't mean that I think the creators failed, or that the game shouldn't have been made. It's a successful project that unfortunately produced a mediocre game.
The good: Many of the horror scenes, particularly those involving the physical/personal horror of terrible things happening to the main character's body, are effective.  Most of the puzzles are organic to the story (no cat-hair mustaches).  The graphics are fine overall (with one major issue; see below) and the pre-rendered cinematics are excellent. The sound design (excluding the voice acting) ranges from good to great -- the environmental effects in particular are disgustingly evocative. I don't think the game is too short (and it doesn't end in a cliffhanger, so thank you for that).
The bad: The graphics are too damn dark.  I am not bothered by the single fixed resolution available -- the level of detail and overall quality looked fine to me, even on a large monitor.  The problem is the gamma. There are too many scenes where you can't see important things, even with the brightness cranked all the way up.  I get that the designers were trying to make the game dark and atmospheric, but watching a dark unrecognizable shape navigate its way through dark unrecognizable corridors to pick up dark unrecognizable objects gets old.
Also, there is far too much pixel hunting for a game released in 2015.  That was maybe okay in earlier eras of adventure games, but there's absolutely no reason not to have a "hold down this key to see all the hotspots" option in a modern game. A few times this even extends to room exits being difficult to find, which is flat-out unacceptable.  I don't mind a hard game, I don't mind a game that kills the main character in a wide variety of arbitrary yet amusing ways, and I don't mind a game that refuses to hold your hand, but I do mind a game where I have to sweep the mouse over every inch of every screen in order to be able to proceed.
On the plus side, only a handful of the puzzles fall into the "guess what I'm thinking" category, and a few of them are quite clever.
The ugly: The story is mediocre at best,  and I don't mean "it grossed me out too much" or "it was campy but fun".  This game takes itself seriously ... which is unfortunate because nearly everything is badly written. While the game's attempts at physical horror mostly succeed, its attempts at psychological horror mostly fail.  The spoken dialogue ranges from awkward to awful (and the voice actors seem to have been encouraged to chew on the furniture, especially the "mad scientist" villain). The in-game PDAs (which are entirely optional) reveal the crew of the Groomlake to have been a bunch of stereotypical misfits who collectively manage to tick all the boxes on the master list of dysfunctional interpersonal relationships. Even the inevitable betrayal (I'd say "spoiler alert," but really, by now we all know that there has to be an inevitable betrayal in this style of game, right?) is justified by its perpetrator in a way that makes absolutely no sense.
I really wanted to like this game -- and, as strange as it may sound, I don't regret backing it on Kickstarter, nor do I regret playing it. There are some geniunely horrifying moments in there mixed in amidst the overwrought dialogue and the cliches. In fact, there are just enough good things about Stasis to make me think that its creators might have a really good adventure game in them.  If there was a recommendation setting for "don't play this game, but I think you should buy it anyway, so its creators make enough money to try again" I'd pick that.  As it stands, I can't in good conscience endorse the game, because it has too many flaws to be a worthwhile investment of the 6-8 hours you'll spend finishing it.  But I don't hate it, and I genuinely hope that its creators will try again.  In fact, if they go back to Kickstarter for a new game, I'll back it. I sure hope they hire an editor for the script next time, though.
Final thoughts: There probably is a price point at which I could see my way clear to recommend Stasis, but not at $25 (which is the price as of this writing). If it drops to $10, which I'm sure it eventually will, any fan of adventure games will no doubt find something to like here. A small team made a game from scratch and that's an accomplishment worthy of respect.
