One of the drawbacks of grand strategy games is that they have the tendency to feel mechanical and isolated.  CK2 is one of the few games in this genre that does not suffer from this problem.  Its RPG elements put a human quality to the game.  You have a character you choose a wife, you have kids and you raise them up.  Instead of staring at numbers or faceless hordes of identical troops you are dealing with family members and rivals who have a face and a name.  That being said the game still includes a heavy elements of classic grand strategy.  You can conquer the world, and become the biggest empire.  The diference in this game instead of being loyal to a country you are loyal to a dynasty and a family.  Your motivation is not nationalistic conquest but to secure your dynasty in the world.  This mixture of elements makes for an addicting experience and one that is unique on every playthrough.

At first glance, this game is extremely intimidating. The UI and overall gameplay are complex and hard to understand without tutorials; even with the tutorials, the game is just confusing. It doesn't help that you are never really given any goals or anything to do. Now, you may be wondering, why am I saying these negative things if this is a positive review?
Because those are the things that make this game great.
Crusader Kings II gives the best interpretation of Medieval government, diplomacy, warfare, and royalty in any game. Ever. While it lacks the fancy battles of Medieval II: Total War, it brings in mechanics like functioning diplomacy and levies for a much more realistic and fun grand strategy game. On the topic of complexity, a newcomer may find the maps and tabs to be excessive and stupid. Once you realize their function, however, you will find them indispensable. I mentioned earlier that this game has no clear cut goal. This is probably the best part, as you really define your own experience. Work your way up from Count to Emperor. Or don't. Maybe your personal goal as a Spanish Catholic is to finish the Reconquista. Maybe you want to convert to Islam and teach Christendom a lesson. It's completely up to you, making for a unique and personal playthrough every time.
Your main incentive to get off your♥♥♥♥♥♥and achieve stuff is your dynasty. In the beginning, this may just be you and your personal family (if you are starting small), but by the end you will have a branching royal dynasty who may even be on the other thrones of Europe. Crusader Kings II has you play as a ruling member of your dynasty, and mixes in your character's personal life into the mix with your strategy gaming. Many events will pop up about your character making choices in regards to their spouse, children, friends, and enemies. This gives you a personal attachment (good or bad) to your character as well as others, making each playthrough even more unique.
To conclude, I'll bring up another plus: The modding community. Mods have added minor tweaks as well as moved the game into the fictional universes of A Song of Ice and Fire and even The Elder Scrolls. They add even more replay value to a game that will keep sucking you back in no matter what. Thanks for reading.

The game has a visual style that's unique, deeply creepy, and very well done.  It's dripping with atmosphere reminiscent of the "Alien" series.  It's surprisingly long.  The soundtrack doesn't seem like much at first, but gradually builds into something amazing all on its own, mainly by respinning a single melody in increasingly different ways until you're hooked.
The game might feel positively ENORMOUS if you stubbornly refuse to ask for hints.  You can get stuck in quite a few places.  Puzzles are logical once you realize what they actually ARE, but the game is frequently unclear (and occasionally outright misleading) about what your immediate objectives happen to be.  The game is extremely linear though, and shepherds you from one small, self-contained area to the next.  So, all together, this ends up feeling like an adventure game from the golden age of adventure games: incredibly difficult, but not unfair.
It's worth noting that some of this difficulty comes from the need for pixel-hunting, and not infrequently either.  And, depending on your monitor, you might have to manually wrest control of the brightness level options that the game offers (that really don't get very bright at all) and ramp up the gamma instead.  This does help you see, but damages the game visuals.  The art team did an amazing job with style, but in doing so created a visual scheme that often leaves you feeling like you're lost, blind, and in the dark.
All in all, it's a great game, dripping with style, and only held back by pacing problems resulting from frequently getting stuck.  Depending on your preferences, all of that might be welcome news.  If not, walkthroughs have sprung up recently to help past the thorny patches.  Defnitely worth playing!

I don't think anyone will ever accuse STASIS of being a
game. It all looks a little dated, some of the animations are a bit awkward & unnatural and it all looks a little rough around the edges.
something doesn't have to be pretty to be beautiful. And not to mention this game is just dripping with atmosphere.
From the meticulous created environments to the haunting screams that echo throughout The Groomlake's vast hulking shell the world Chris Bischoff throws you into is both terrifying and captivating. I would quite happily spend hours exploring these corridors over and over again, admiring all the tiny details hidden amongst the blood drenched bulkheads. But that may just be because I am terrified to discover what horrific creature awaits me around the next corner.
And like any good point 'n' click the puzzles in STASIS tread the fine line between logical and fiendish. Creativity and patience are rewarded (don't forget to read all those personal logs) whereas carelessness will inevitably end in failure and the occassional amusing death.
It may not be pretty but there is a definite haunting beauty to this game and I highly recommend any point & click aficionado or horror game fan give Stasis try.

So I grabbed this on sale about a year ago, and sent 3 copies as gifts to a bunch of my best pals, and guess what? We went crazy all night over this game.
Starting out, control felt weird, but this quickly changed over the first 10 minutes as I got used to the flawless, fluid control scheme. The game is responsive, and character animation was fast.
As for Graphic, this game for built for portability, so don't expect some Battlefield Standard graphics here. It can run on Integrated Graphics on my other laptops, but I played this game on a Dedicated GPU, making framerates over the top, which added to the overall experience.
Gameplay wise, I have to warn you, this game, will make you have sorethroats, spasm attacks, uncontrollable laughter, and make you throw tantrums at your friends. In this 1v3 game, the objective is to outlast your opponents/'Friends' by using evil item pickups. Some overpowered ones are dodgable, and the weaker ones are hard to pull off, making this game very easy to play, at the same time competitive. Having 5 characters to choose from, i have no complains as it only helps to differentiate whom you want to scream at!
Community wise, the community is quite a friendly one, but has the occasional hiccup of a laggy player, due to international hosting. No complains in this sections.
Overall, this game has brought me loads of fun, and sorethroats. Pros outweigh the cons, making the game a valued one. Recommended to anybody whom wants to lose a friend:p

Preface: This game is so good that halfway through this review I became a poet.
For an early access game, it plays as a finished one with a few small bugs. They don't really hurt you other than being a mild annoyance because you don't lose anything for losing. On the other side, you don't gain anything for winning either. BUT you do gain the glorious feeling of winning and being a god because you gave it your all and managed to beat your three opponents.
Bugs like the camera getting stuck off the map I am pretty okay with but the only thing that is game-breaking for me is when you dodge a grappling hook (the "dodged" text appears on screen) only to find yourself hooked 1-2 seconds later. My internet connection isn't bad, I get 1mb/s on a bad day but I feel like it's a connection issue of some sort.
Rare bugs aside, I absolutely love this game! The community is amazing, it's easy to find nice people to chat with. When your room drops to just a 1v1 a lot of people let you catch up if you fall behind a bit and you for them, creating a beautiful environment of harmony as you run and swing across maps in the most friendly manner conceivable. Though you may never see that person again, the experience renews your faith in humanity, puts a smile on your face, and makes you yearn for more.
The gameplay...glorious. I had played as much of the story available online on the website(as a flash version I believe) and I knew i had to get it. Little did I know at the time what true glory still awaited me. Then the light of multiplayer racing shone down upon me and I got trashed by a pro in the most fabulous fashion imaginable. Oh how he swung so beautifully, his releases and jumps so perfectly timed, and his item usage so exact I would think he were a watch maker. True art I experienced that day, I was so stricken that for a moment I became a poet solely to express the moment. I gradually learned the ropes (haha great grappling pun) and now I too can create art with flowing movements, though still not yet as gloriously skilled as the god-child I had witnessed, but enough to give me the strength to open cans of whoop♥♥♥♥♥on occasion.
The beautiful feeling of pure awesomeness when pulling off an amazing move, whether it be dodging something in a manner that even you did not know was possible or just barely managing to pull ahead far enough to win, is more than enough to consider this game well worth the money spent.
11/10 would buy again. Thank you for producing such glory and allowing the commonsfolk to bask in the light of heaven itself.
note: I saw some people saying they would play more if they had a controller. I do actually have a controller, but I have not actually tried using it for this game yet. It is possible that it would offer a better experience but thus far, I have experienced nothing but pure joy whilst playing solely on a keyboard. If another player is advantaged by using a controller, I have not yet noticed.

Taking a spin on the flip-side of the JRPG equation, you play the proprietess of one of those ubiquitous item shops that you would have been constantly visiting (had you been the adventurer of this tale) to sell off items and purchase better equipment in order to aid your ascent up the ladders of fame.
Recettear focuses on stocking your store with worthwhile goods, haggling prices, establishing a rapport with the local adventurers, and meeting payment deadlines in order to remain in business. Work supply and demand to your advantage, capitalizing on itemshortages and the overstock of other stores. Finally, hire adventurers to visit local dungeons and hunt for treasures with which to stock your store.
One of the truly funny games out there, Recettear plays as both honestly enjoyable game (though the dungeons can be a little long if you're anything of a completionist) and parody of existing genre-tropes.

I missed a lot of good games, when they were actual at their times. This list is just enormous and I will need a thousands of hours in my life to complete my backlog. It was kinda hard to remember about every game I wanted to play/finish, when I was a pirate and didn't have all my games at one place, like Steam. Now it's much more easier, I can organize everything with steam, making own groups and categories.
So the same thing was with L.A. Noire. I started to play this game literally 3 times and never finished it for different reasons. Now, when it was released, I was faced to a dilemma - either I spend extra money once again just to play it on big screen on PS4, or on switch to play it somewhere in public or during some kinda trip, or I can just save my money and don't pay twice for the product I already own on Steam. Well, I chose the last option, but to be honest, that's only because I didn't own neither 4k TV nor PS Pro, otherwise I would definitely go this way.
Being a big fan of police crime drama TV shows, I was kinda excited about this game and was looking forward L.A. Noire, especailly knowing the fact, that game made an innovation step in motion capture progress in video games. The whole game is based mainly on interrogations where you should define either your suspects lie or say truth to you. At this point I should say, that this technology with all their face expressions looks a bit creepy and outdated sometimes, doesn't feel the same as it was in 2011. Then I felt like, maybe I made a bad decision and I shoulda grab the remastered 4k game on PS Pro, but after checking some videos on Youtube I realized that the difference is not that significant.
Speaking of the game itself and the whole plot game can be a bit disappointing. If you expect some mind-blowing plot with an unexpected twists and multiple choices/endings or whatever - you better cool down. The whole game is pretty much linear and divided into 5 parts. By parts I mean different departments you gonna work in, investigating crimes. Almost every case in game, except of DLC cases, is connected to others and here we come to the disappointing part. Mostly, after each case, in every department, you will realize, that you arrested and convicted the wrong guy. And it happens almost every time, so the closer you will be to the end of the game, the harder it'll be to surprise you with anything in that game.
One of the most important parts in this game is that era where events occur - America 1947, Cold War. The whole atmosphere and feel is just amazing and it lets you fully dive and enjoy that period. I was also impressed by that enormous work which developers have done on the characters and dialogues, every single detail, every topic during conversations lets you know that you are in the 40th now. Outstanding work! Still looks great in 2017.
Ok, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:
+ Love detective genre
+ Enjoy sdolving puzzles and investigating everything by yourself
+ Adore the atmosphere of the America 1940th
+ Wanna play a good game with a good story, but don't expect anything mind-blowing, like I did.
Avoid this game if you:
- Don't like to pay attention to every small detail and think a lot
- Want to play something short in one-two sessions. I was even a bit annoyed by the length of the game, it's so freaking long, such a rare thing in a nowadays games, where you can finish the whole game just in few hours
- Are already a mature man, pushing 30. I guess the whole plot of this game is full of cheesy predictable moves, which won't be able to impress you or keep you interested at your age.
I must also clarify that I enjoyed this game and I can recommend it overall, just not for everyone, so I would go Neutral, if that would be possible on Steam.
Enjoy!

I noticed in the updated versions for consoles they've changed the truth,doubt,lie to 'good cop' 'bad cop' 'accuse' which actually makes even less sense but I've finally figured out just why the interrogations (which some people flaw the game on) are a bit vague.
The logical approach would have been to have some multiple choices for Cole to say but what we get is the option to 'truth/doubt/lie' the suspect and then Cole shouts out something mental and we curse an 'x' in our notebook.
Then I realised it's because we're watching a film! We're not Cole, we're watching Cole.
The interrogation scenes intentionally become part of the drama because we become nervous about what crazy thing Cole's going to say to screw everything up.
If we had a choice of what his question is going to be we'd get it right every time because - through cutscenes - we've been privy to more information than he has and because we're old hand multiple choice point and click savvy gamers. So the interrogations ramp up our drama because we're watching Cole fumble in the dark, see?
I'm sure it would be a duller game if we could pick and choose what Cole says as we'd be smarter than him and just sail through every interrogation as we'd just eliminate the crazy and fit it more to what we know and wouldn't shout at a pregnant lady with her dead husband on the floor behind us. I guarantee if you've played this you've experienced the dread of pressing a button in case Cole goes off his head and blurts out the crazy and that's the whole point! You didn't make a mistake, Cole did! It's just like you shouting at the TV and saying 'No! You idiot! Why would he commit suicide if he just bought groceries!'
The game owes a lot to the film adaptation of L.A. Confidential which is great to watch as a companion piece. It features some of the same historical characters from the film as well as similar subplots and themes and even some of the same first and second names thrown around, hell even one of the minor actors of the film appears in the game!

A truly amazing combat/exploration fallout-inspired game with great character build variety, decent balance and plenty of content 9.5/10
Comparison to fallout:
Even though it's similar to fallout 1,2, it's way more combat-based than fallout. Roleplaying part is pretty redundant and irrelevant in this game. Don't get me wrong, there's plenty of great quests but the game is centered around combat, exploration and crafting.
Character building:
Amount of perks is enormous and you may specialize in very different and distinct builds from psi-augmented unarmed fighter to chemical gunslinger with electronic augmentations or stealth-based crossbow-wielding trapper with a freaking discharger sledgehammer. All those builds are actually viable and the game is balanced well enough. I've tried so many builds and developing new ones is the most fun part for me: you can tell that by my playtime.
Crafting:
Crafting part is very well-made: there's relatively few recipes(about 40 or so) but every recipe may use different tiers and types of ingredients that result in different items. For example with a single recipe "chemical bolt" you may make all kinds of bolts from tranquilizer to acid-infused.
Comparison to beta-versions:
The game was great even while it was in beta stage but after release it just became better in every aspect and a lot of content was added as well.
Misc:
Some parts of the game like single-use items may seem weak at first but trust me, after your 4th or 5th character you'll find out that there's actually no useless items at all, but some of them shine only if you find out how to use them properly.
Things you may not like:
- Game world is enormous in size and there's no in-game map, so you're expected to keep it all in your head which may prove quite challenging(similar to dark souls and such).
- Vendors not only have limited cash to buy your junk, but they also accept very limited amount of items(like weapon dealers only buy 1-3 firearms) so you'll have a to stash, disassemble or just leave a lot of pretty expensive stuff because no one will want to buy it.
- Graphics are not terribly astonishing neither technically nor artistically. Overall graphics feel a little "indie". No, they're not bad, but this game is definitely not about graphics or fancy shaders.
- Game has some scaling issues on very high-resolution screens, namely fonts become too small. It won't be a problem on any currently standard resolution around 1920x1024 or less.
Verdict:
If you like fallout 2-style combat and exploration, don't even think, just buy this game because it's amazing.

I don't write many reviews but, I think I've sunk enough time into this game to give my thoughts. And my thoughts are- Pretty darn good. Sure, when I first got the game I had the same problems most have, I looked at itm the tutorial and repeated a hundred times. "What the %$# do I do?" But when things start to fall into place and you know what's going on and how to control things. It's wonderful.
I love history, and this game is reliving, and rewriting history all in one go. Ever curious to what would have happened in 800ad if Ireland united and took over all of Britannia and became a medieval superpower? Try it out! It won't be easy, starting as a lone Irish count working your way up to unite ireland while staving off the vikings, scots, welsh and english (sometimes others!) But it's rewarding to look at your family tree, see your starting count "Count Bob of Connacht" and look down to his current living great gandson "Emperor Bob III of Britannia." And relive all the intrigue, war and crazy things in your head that happened from A to B for your dynasty.
It doesn't end there. The "Irish Empire" is born- You really think the Frensh, or the Holy Roman Empire is going to let you have all the power untested? You think  aJealous half brother count is not going to start a revolution. Should you make them fear you, love you, respect you? Combinations of all? Go completely crazy? The choices are endless, victories and defeats.
Ireland aint yer thing? Well with all the DLC you can really be anyone, Original game gives you access to most of the European nations of Catholic and Orthodox beliefs. Old gods lets you start form a earlier time period and play any Pagan religion. Sword of Islam allows any Islamic nation and so on!
Mods are also great, giving more and more gameplay. Ever wanted to play "Game of Thrones" on CK2? There's a mod for that. Want to start in "The old gods" time period and make every nation no larger than one territory and see what empires arise where? There's a mod for that.
Endless game, endless fun.

I sadly cannot recommend this game.
Does it have impressive graphics? Yes! Does it have solid gunplay? Yes. But that is bascially it. I really liked the first game but this is just more of the same and some additional bad stuff.
Note: I only played this game on the hardest difficulty level on Ranger mode. That means less supply, no HUD, so basically more immersive. BUT: While the game teaches you the basic controls (which should not be new to you, if you ever played an FPS) it doesn't explain controls that are specific for this game. If I hadn't played the first game I would had no idea that you can keep the flashlight button pressed to get out the dynamo to charge your batteries. And I skipped a lot of weapons until I found out that I had to keep the use button pressed to pick up a weapon. And later in a car I had to press every button to find the one that starts the engine. One may argue that it improves the immersion of the ranger mode but if have to open the control options several times to find all the buttons, this is stupid. And there are also hand symbols on your screen when you can open a door so that breaks the immersion as well, if you argue like that.
Also: For a game (world) where resources are apparently rare, you find way too much of them. So many times I couldn't pick up ammunition (even for my main guns), gas filters or medicine and this just feels stupid if you see yourself as a scavenger in a postapocalyptic world. And later in the game resources are suddenly very rare and it's then even more stupid that you can carry a lot of ammunition that you will never use (because you have a seperate ammunition slot and limit for each type of ammunition but you can only carry 2 guns at the same time) but not a single additional gas filter later on. Some sort of inventory management would have been better here I feel. I also got stuck later in the game without gas filters (sorry for looking around too much...) and no medicine (because it all of a sudden became very rare) and I really lost the will to keep playing the game. It's not that the game was too hard. I could have avoided that situation. But together with the bad boss design (more below) and the not that interesting story, I felt no urge to restart the chapter and try to make it better.
For a game that is called Metro, you also play too much outside later in the game. While interesting at first, it just get tedious with the need to frequently change your gas filters every 3 minutes or so (what kind of filters are that?). The outdoor sections are just annoying and you often don't know where to go because it's not apparent where you can go or jump over or where you'll find invisible walls. You have a clipboard with sort of a compass that shows you the right direction and you'll need that very, very often. But you can't really see the compass if you use your night vision goggles that you also often want to use in the dark sections of the game... The good parts of the game are the close quarter or underground sections but these also feel exactly like playing Metro 2033.
There is also a Karma system that determines the ending of the game (like in the first game) but for me, the system makes no sense. Why does listening to a boring story increases your Karma (or whatever)? And there was a situation where I had to decide to let someone die or rescue him, but I had no idea how to rescue him (again no button prompts or so in Ranger mode), so he died although I wanted to help him... So be prepared to watch the "good" ending on YouTube after finishing the game.
Another large problem I have with this game is the boss design. These are just large creatures that take a lot of bullets to kill. But this game is not made for this. It has good, realistic gun play but no real dodge or cover mechanic so you just run around the enemy in circles and shoot at him until it's dead... Wow... I mean that is some way to deplete your resources and find a reason to pick up new ones.
The fight against human enemies or the normal creatures on the other hand is fun. In Ranger mode, enemies die from a headshot but you die very fast as well. I found that very rewarding. But this comes with another problem: The sneaking. You can avoid a lot of the fights by just staying in the dark, killing enemies silently or sneak around them. But the reaction of the enemies to your sneaking is very, very basic. They either don't see you at all, see you for a short time, but think it was probably nothing after shortly searching for you or instantly see you if you are not in the dark. They also seem to ignore their friends that die next to them from a throwing knife (that for some reason instantly kills an unaware enemy but not an aware enemy). You are basically invisible or visible for everyone. These are not solid stealth mechanics for me. I prefer the shooting anyway but on the hardest difficulty you normally have to sneak or at least kill some enemies before you get detected.
Conclusion:
This game has a lot of potential but doesn't use it correctly. Play Metro 2033, especially the Redux version, and you'll get a much better game that focuses much more on the underground section with occasional surface sections that feel much more terrifying. Last Light, in my oppinion, adds nothing that improves its predecessor.
I also had problems with crashes every 5 minutes in the middle of the game and I did not found a solution for that. I was somehow able to finish this section (maybe a graphics card driver update solved the problem) and continue but together with the fact, that the intro logos of the game take like 2 minutes and ARE FOR SOME STUPID REASON NOT SKIPPABLE, it got very, very annoying.

The mechanics in this game are very intelligently thought out. You can tell it was made meticulously and with love. It's very well balanced, and the framework is good enough that I hope it's used to create future games with. The story is pretty good too, but what really shines and keeps me playing for hours is the user experience. It's just a joy for the kind of RPG fan I am. Isometric. First person. Mature and unmanipulative themes. Honestly, this game deserves to be up there with the greats in the genre. Full support and a big thank you to the developers.

STASIS feels like a AAA 90's computer game. The animation and visuals of the human models have a distinct 90's quality to them. It's not a bad thing at all, but for some reason the nostalgia center of my brain is going nuts while playing this game, even though it's brand new to me.
It also plays like early PnC adventure games. There is no hand-holding. There isn't a pop-up telling you what you need to do if you get lost. There are some modern twists like not having to switch your 'verb' as that is done automatically whilst also changing the icon to reflect the action, such as an eye-ball to see and having the text automatically appear. There is also PnC 'logic' which is kind-of whitewashed via the computer logs that you read, but still, some of the puzzles when thinking about it from a larger perspective don't make much sense. Why would a spaceship be fraught with so many bugs?
There are also some Myst-style sections/puzzles intertwined as well. Close-ups of panels that need to be operated. Nothing that is as hard as Myst-type puzzles, but some of the order-of-operations style puzzles that Myst seemed to have burned into my brain are present.
The atmosphere is executed very well. The isometric (Sidenote - I love isometric games) viewpoint is not only easy-on-the-eyes from a visual standpoint but facilitates the horror themes of the game. A fixed perspective with enough of an angle to foreshadow events is a great way to heighten suspense.
STASIS feels like a hidden gem from the past.
Recommended.

This is a wonderful little game that harkens back to the days of Planescape and Sanitarium. A game where you must think, and not react simply pulling a trigger to anything that moves.
There's a lot to be said about a game released in 2015 that shares most of it's qualities from a game made in 1998. A lot of good things.
Stasis nails the environment, the atmosphere and the element of tension. The thought that at any moment something could end you. Waking up and feeling like there is nowhere safe, and having no idea what is happening, that feeling, captured perfectly.
I can say with 100% conviction, that I have always wanted to go to space. Growing up on the space coast tends to make one have fancy thoughts of space operas and flying cars. I can also say with 100% conviction, that if space is anything like this you can take me off that damn list of canditates
There is screaming all around you, but no clue what it is. There's a helpful person on the radio and a less helpful person who has issues with helpful person, and by association, you.
The animations are smooth, the audio is wonderful.
So far in my time with the game, I've woken up (I'm always cranky at this point in my day). I've realized I've lost my kid and wife somewhere on this trip of ours. I've made a new friend as well as enemy and chopped someone's arm off. I have also blown myself up a couple of times as well as having been consumed by sludge zombie things and to really top it all off, I've taken a face-full of acid. And that's just my first few hours with the game.
This is another game that I can see becoming a classic, not because it re-defines a type of game, but because it takes something that worked years ago and makes it pure. Playing this I had flashes back to when I was younger and playing any of the old isometric point and click games, and that is awesome. There aren't enough games in the world that are solid enough to remind me of what gaming used to be like before everything became DLC and season passes. It's nice sitting down and knowing that I can play this game all the way through if I have the nerve to do so.
So, for the question of the hour. Does Elenath recommend this game?
Without a doubt. For the price you can't beat the story and immersion.
You get to kill yourself over and over again just to see if that pool stick was really needed for this puzzle. Pointing this out again, It's a game that makes you think your way out instead of shoot. So if you're here for John Woo Vs Space potatoes get out now. But if you're inclined to use that beautiful bowling ball on your shoulders and figure out what you have to do, then this is a game for you. Best way to say it is it's a slow, beautiful top down space game that shares some elements with Dead Space and the mystery of Event Horizon.
There's also (I think) a nod to Boondock Saints. So win win.
Price at launch will be 24.99 with a 20% discount for the first week making the standard version 19.99 or the Deluxe with all the goods 32. (soundtrack, wallpapers, art book and game) in my humble opinion go with the latter, the music is worth the price difference alone.
My final comment is that there is a great story buried in here, that requires you to wander around and explore to get it. The people that you find, or find what's left of them, you care about them before everything went to hell. They are written as if they are real people, something that sometimes is lost in games.
Despite this games visuals, there is nothing 2D about it.

John Maracheck sets off on an inter-planetary holiday with his family, but when he wakes up from cryogenic sleep he finds himself on an abandoned spaceship (The Groomlake). Disoriented and alone he begins to unravel the dark and perverse history of the ship while driven by the hope of seeing his wife and daughter again.
Gameplay progresses by solving puzzles and interacting with the environment, but the creators made sure there is more to it than just mouse-clicking! By hiding subtle hints necessary for progression in the multiple journal entries of the (now missing) Groomlake crew members you are immersed in the lives of many people; each with their own aspiration, inner conflicts, insecurities and imperfections - it is through their narrative that the storyline truly unfolds and John's experience connects all the dots. The story is set in the future, yet it touches common themes of humanity throughout history.
The visuals are often grotesque and yet amazing. The lighting and sound track sets the perfect mood for each scene to the point where John's emotions become your.  As one of the Kickstarter backers back in 2013 I can honestly say the wait was worth it and I can't wait to play it again, because I am sure I missed some exciting and yet shocking piece of the Groomlake history on my first run.

Like I said in my original review. The game draws obvious heavy inspiration from classic sci-fi, from Alien, to System Shock. The developers did their homework when it came to building a creepy and mysterious atmosphere. One thing I have noticed though is that Stasis isn't really all that scary. Creepy? Sure. Atmospheric? Definitely. Just not scary. The setting and story are the only real selling points here, but that isn't a bad thing because Stasis does both pretty well. The gameplay itself is rather standard of the point and click genre,  combining items, finding where and how to use items, puzzles etc. No surprises to speak of really but I will say there is no hand holding either, you've got to pay attention and be clever. I got stuck more then once and sometimes puzzles were vague and obscure at times, however these moments are rare though. What kept me playing Stasis was how the game feels almost like a movie mixed with a game. There are cut scenes and story moments that really do an awesome job of building the universe. I wanted to know more and it gave me just enough to chase the carrot. The voice acting is solid and helps build the tension. John's reactions to things make you feel like you're there. The graphics are spectacular for a P&C game, as are the music, and sound effects. They need to be for what they aim to do with this game. In all the journey of Stasis is incredibly well done and fun. The story itself has some standard tropes that I hope have a twist. I can't comment on this until I complete the game. Which should be fun and soon!

Warshift is a mix of two games that many of you probably don't know about - Battlezone 2 and the PC version of Wargames.
It is basically a lane style RTS game in which you produce structures which send automated units to attempt to destroy your opponent. However instead of you sitting in orbit doing nothing or whatever the backstory typically is for an RTS, you control a drone on the battlefield directly - giving you a direct FPS element.
You use your drone to stand near energy sources to activate them, then switch to the RTS overhead camera to build things. You can technically play in RTS mode only but the AI is limited at best, especially since your command drone can transform itself and fly in the air depending on which type of command drone you picked.
Unfortunatly this is where the game starts to fall apart. Unlike the aforementioned Battlezone 2, you can not dedicate yourself into one or the other role. You can not place buildings or order your troops, give buildings production orders, nothing while within the FPS mode. Anything to do with the commanding aspect you have to do from the RTS view, which in the heat of battle can and will get very, very annoying.
If you stick in RTS mode, then your command drone (known as an Avatar) can not access many of its abilities and fights very poorly. So its a constant balance between the two modes, when really the RTS view should be almost totally optional like it was in, again, battlezone 2.
Unit choices are rather poor - I don't even see the point in building infantry for example, they just feed the enemy avatar experiance points. I know its supposed to be this FPS-RTS hybrid, but there's really not enough here to justify the RTS component in many respects.
While I do recommend this game, that is only because there's been fairly constant patches which have added new content. However that recommendation will change if the base issues with the game don't eventually get solved. It has a lot of potential to be a fairly great game, but I'm afraid it is just not there yet.
PS. It does have multiplayer vs the AI, however only one person plays as the commander. The others can only control their own drone\avatar so its almost purely a FPS experiance for them.

STASIS is at the border between old and new. The transposition of the usual sidescrolling camera to a fixed isometric camera has the same general purpose just with another perspective that serves the narrative in a different way. The point and click mechanic, the pixel hunting and the puzzles are just a number of elements that remind me of adventure games of a different time, when this genre was focused on brainteasers and not a story driven cinematic experience (and by cinematic I don’t mean locked at 30fps!!!). But the game doesn’t go out of its way to address nostalgia. The fully voice acted dialogues and the full motion video cut scenes bring the game to a more up to date standard.
As a horror game it takes inspiration from movies like Alien or Sunshine and applies the theme of being trapped on a space ship with something dangerous on board extremely well. It builds suspense and mystery through storytelling and the use of gore, sound and the fight for survival without having to fight anything.
Looking backwards and analyzing the elements of this game, it seems STASIS is at a transitional point between the two predominant styles of adventure games (with a little more focus on the retro style) and this might be the key to satisfy both the old school and the newer fans of the genre.
The game has its flaws, but looking at the bigger picture they don’t mean much. STASIS is a five years labor of love from two brothers that poured their hearts and souls into this project (which is a little disturbing considering the game’s theme!) and their debut game is an adventure horror blast.
Pros:
+ A gruesome atmosphere for a 2D isometric game

Personal Log – "I don't have much time left. The screaming stopped a few minutes ago... I'm likely next. I believed in what I was doing, in what WE were doing – I want to make that abundantly clear to whoever finds this. You don't just cure Alzheimer's, diabetes, CANCER, without getting your hands a little dirty. Ethical standards didn't – haven't cure JACK♥♥♥♥♥♥– but I did; my team did. We make these sacrifices, live with the mistakes, suffer the nightmares... so you can snuggle in your beds at night with your loved ones, blissfully ignorant. You may scoff but the way I see it we're both equally complicit.
"They're breaking through now but I'm not afraid. I'll greet Death with a familiar smile.
"We're old partners, as it were."
STASIS is an isometric, point n' click, sci-fi horror adventure game. Is it scary? No, not particularly. I was unsettled at points, uncomfortable, grossed out... akin to an experience at Applebee's, but never was I scared. Is it wholly original? Again, not really. It took a lot of fine points from the likes of Dead Space: is there an everyman, missing loved one(s), mad science gone wrong, creepy lullabies, and helpful (but mostly absent) support?
Check, check, check, check... check! That's a LOT of checks.
Is it good though? Is it fun? That's what's important after all – critical even!
If you're a fan of this genre I think you'll have a good time with STASIS. Besides a clichéd, predictable story, a few point n' click gameplay pitfalls, and some sporadic, minor graphical glitches it's a pretty fun ride.
You're one John Maracheckplease, disoriented space schoolteacher everyman aboard the Groomlake, a science research vessel orbiting Neptune doing totally legitimate, above board ethical science stuff. John hasn't the foggiest as to why he's on board, though he likely signed up for the totally legitimate, above board ethical science stuff and just forgot... it happens! John's wife and young daughter are missing and it's up to him to find them. Not an exactly an enviable task, especially when you're on a derelict spook ship.
As John Maraschino travels from deck to deck he'll talk to a select few survivors (disarmingly pretty science lady, wacky scientist turned God) who guide and impede progress, filling in narrative along the way. John Marrakesh also stumble upon PDAs (future PDAs, suddenly relevant after the mass smart phone extinction of 2049) from the Groomlake's crew, though they unfortunately usually follow the same general story structure: “I love my job,” “This job is kind of shady,” and “Please God forgive me, I have so many regrets about this job.” Despite this I still read each and every email, personal log, and report I could find. They're very believably written and frequently serve to provide different perspectives from other survivor experiences you'll read during John's travels.
The sound and graphics marry to create an immersive, atmospheric experience. Like I said earlier, STASIS really doesn't have any scares but the environments, denizens, logs, and IMPLICATIONS of what's happening on the Groomlake give it an excellent creepy tone. This gritty sci-fi reality definitely has a storied history, and every component (the science, the tech, the ethical shortcomings) feels real and plausible. You get the sense that things weren't every really great on the Groomlake to begin with, truly the Delta Tau Chi fraternity of space research vessels. Each deck and each individual room is unique, meticulously crafted, and coated from ceiling to floor with different flavors of horror, backed up by spooky horror ambiance.
Gameplay is standard point n' click fare: you'll collect various knick knacks and trinkets during each level to solve some thoughtful, clever puzzles to progress. Sometimes the solution is obvious, sometimes you have to hunt for clues (drawings taped to PDAs for example), and sometimes you'll pound cylindrical pegs through square holes,cursing the damnable fools who brought you into this ♥♥♥♥ed up world. For the MOST part STASIS avoids traditional, obtuse point n' click adventure puzzle tropes but boy do they creep in during the mid game (looking at you empty handgun). Still, as someone who doesn't play many of these kinds of games (I prefer Silent Hill pachinko) I managed to beat it in just over nine hours. There are also some fun death fail states that can occur if you screw up a puzzle or put John in a dangerous situation – though these become frustrating real fast when the solution isn't clear.
Overall I enjoyed my time with STASIS, like visiting an old friend. It looks good, it plays well, and it doesn't overstay its welcome. You'll probably get frustrated once or twice but that's the price we pay when we play point n' clicks. It's also unlikely you'll play it again unless you're hunting for achievements so do keep that in mind thrifty readers.
Fans of the genre would be remiss to skip this one... fans of sci-fi too.
How else will you educate yourself on the Eugenics War?

i've been looking for an rts/fps game for years now, i've approached dozens of titles before laying my hands on this one, and let me tell you this: this is THE ONE.
there had always been several issues with said games, and Warshift overcomes all of them:
- often the fps part was weak. in warshift the fps part is the BEST ONE
- some games had everything but no co op vs ai, Warshift has co op vs ai, and it's great
- even when a couple of games could do all of the aboves, the connectivity was so bad that i dropped them. Warshift has its own masterserver and you can also play lan

last point: even though this game is officialy out of early access, the developer (yes, one guy alone) keeps updating it and working on it, wich is amazing

This game is  really, really bad Bioshock game. It is a passable shooter overall, but a terrible Bioshock game.
I don't really know how to call these exploration rich multi path shooters like Prey 2017, System shock 2, bioshock, so I will just further call them Bioshock games, or refer to Bioshock one as a reference point. I love bioshock one a lot, and it will be obvious throughout this review.
I played the game on hardest from start, with no Vita chambers or guides, and chose to save little sisters every time.
I can't subject myself to the horrors of this game for a second playthrough though, to know the alternative path.
So, what are the problems that I see here?
First of all, crashes to desktop. Constant ♥♥♥♥ing crashes to desktop. I considered myself lucky when I didn't have a single ctd within 30 minutes of play. The more things going on - the more probable is crash to desktop, which lead to staggering 12 ctd's during the last chapter of the game. Just so annoying.
But the things that really grinded my gears were design choices.
It was like this game was 100% developed by a marketing department. They know all marketable, easily recognizable elements, but they don't understand why they made Bioshock 1 a great game.
Big daddies were a cool thing? Everybody loved them?
Okay, then let us make you play as one. Without changing the core mechanics of the game of course - those are important.
So you are still a very fragile, sneaky type that requires ingenuity, precise aiming and wit to overcome the opponents. Nothing wrong with that, but it makes you suit an accesory. What would be the point of big daddies in the first place if they were as fragile as you? You die from a couple of explosions, or 5-6 shots. Just a rusty bucket wearing normal fps protagonist, not a powerhouse that big daddy is supposed to be.
Oh, how could I forget the drill. The drill is a disgrace to a family, and a clearly inferior choice to a firearms.
In bioshock one, I used the wrench throughout the entire game. Here, I just couldn't. Stealth is really poorly fleshed out, causing real damage with the drill requires fuel, which is kinda limited, and most tonics and upgrades that make drill awesome appear in the last third of the game.
Back to everybody loves the big daddies - anpother great idea - just make them a common enemy now. During two last chapters of the game, they replace around 50% of splicers. They are still boring and weak despite that, so yeah.
Ok, what else? Remeber Frank Fountain? That fight wa the best part of the game!
No, it ♥♥♥♥ing wasn't. Fountain boss fight is boring and terrible, like every boss fight in the game. Just enjoy your highly mobile bullet sponges(Big sisters), that kick you back with melee attacks all the time on every single level of the game. These fights are boring, uninspired, unchallenging, and just a waste of ammo. Thank god the ammo is cheap and easy to get. Worst of all, finall boss is just 2 big sisters...yay...
Also bullet sponge splicers as minibosses. That is also a thing.
Bullet sponges are a nice segway to another point. Gun design.
It is atrocious. Gun's don't really have a nice audio or on screen feedback, nor they do any serious damage without full upgrades and some damage up tonics. It results in gunplay not feeling really well, which is a shame for any shooter game.
Although headshots with headhunter from the Rivet gun are quite satisfying. Too bad that there are no iron sights, and even in the soom mode crosshair is just enormous.
About the terrible sound design - soundtrack is terrrible and glitchy as hell. When in the middle of the game it bugged out, and subjected me to 30 minutes of walking around with constant ♥♥♥♥ing nervous violin build up(feels awesome to be shopping with those sounds), I just broke down and diabled the music completely, which I recommend you to do too. Wait, I don't recommend you play it at all.
What are other cool things from Bioshock one which are missing?
Level design. Bland and uninspired. All locations are already mixed up in my head, and I finished the game within two days. I still can remember almost every single location in Bioshock one. Those are beautifull, and somehow connected to the madness of Rapture, each in its own unique way.
Encounter desing is ATROCIOUS. Pure♥♥♥♥♥♥ Most of fights you are going to have is you standing in one place with enemies pouring at you. It is just like the terrible part in Bioshock one, when you had to defend your little sister from splicers, but whole game. Enremies constanly appear out of thin air when your back is turned. It is especially aggravating because you can actually track that with weapons that levae traps. Not once and not twice after trapping the whole length of corridor before little sister standoff, I have noticed that enemies just spwan at a certain point of this corridor - with all the traps behind that point magically intact, and all traps after that point triggered. ♥♥♥♥ing shamefull design that it.
Bioshock one had a nice system, where first splicer shot at you always missed. Well, that system was for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Real men just get shot in the as by splicer that appears out of thin air behind your back. Yep. Nice.
When it is not arena kind of fight, it has a couple of interesting moments, but exploration mixed with combat is one of my favorite things in this kind of games, and here it feels more like an arena shooter than anything. I missed the moments where I could get a drop on a couple of splicers that were, you know, actually doing something, not running at me from their spawn point.
Oh, pacing. How I lament your death in this game. Number of situations in which false urgency is needleslly created where non should be, or you are locked in some room with exposition pouring in your ears over radio...I can't describe how much I hate this moments. Also, the boring drag of a level after percieved climactic finale appears here, just like in Bioshock one.
AI is incompetent. Friendly bots AI just completely breaks from time to time, making bots related plasmids and tonics worthless. Enemy get stuck a lot. Generally enemies are just running at you, shooting or swinging. Boring.
No plot twists. What the heck. Expecting the plot twist was my sole reason to keep going despite everything I didn't like, and when none appeared, I was sorely disappointed.
I understand that Sophia Lamb was a countepart to individualistic, self centered Andrew Ryan. But unlike Ryans (or should I saw, Ayan Rands?) ideas, her ideas are completely bonkers, not sympathetic or interesting in any way. She is a moot villain with moot ideas and moot motivations, and she wants everyone to become a part of conciousless amorphous greater good blob. At least it is fitting.
No memorable characters. There is no interesting mid game enemies, nothing like Sanders Cohen. I loved the guy, and was really expecting for someone to show him up in this game, but nobody came even close. Damn shame.
Hacking even worse than it was before. I know many people didn't like it in Bioshock one, but this new system is a lateral movement, not in advancement.
This is a tiny section for things I liked.
Plasmid and weapon dual wielding feels great.
Drill specialist tonic is a great idea - shame you can't get it and drill vampire earlier in the game. And multi leveled design of location isn't great for drill figths in the first place.
Your daughter is bona fide badass. Fighting together with is most fun I had in this game.
Naming and reparing turrets and bots with handy man is neat. Too bad bots AI constantly broke.
Despite location design being bad, they are vast and kind of pleasant to explore. Multi layered format is a blessing and a gift - it can be quite an interesting battleground, when you are not getting shot in the back by some guy on the balcony.
In conclusion, and tl;dr, your time will be better spent replaying Bioshock one, or playing Prey 2017, if you want more of the same.

Preface: This game is so good that halfway through this review I became a poet.
For an early access game, it plays as a finished one with a few small bugs. They don't really hurt you other than being a mild annoyance because you don't lose anything for losing. On the other side, you don't gain anything for winning either. BUT you do gain the glorious feeling of winning and being a god because you gave it your all and managed to beat your three opponents.
Bugs like the camera getting stuck off the map I am pretty okay with but the only thing that is game-breaking for me is when you dodge a grappling hook (the "dodged" text appears on screen) only to find yourself hooked 1-2 seconds later. My internet connection isn't bad, I get 1mb/s on a bad day but I feel like it's a connection issue of some sort.
Rare bugs aside, I absolutely love this game! The community is amazing, it's easy to find nice people to chat with. When your room drops to just a 1v1 a lot of people let you catch up if you fall behind a bit and you for them, creating a beautiful environment of harmony as you run and swing across maps in the most friendly manner conceivable. Though you may never see that person again, the experience renews your faith in humanity, puts a smile on your face, and makes you yearn for more.
The gameplay...glorious. I had played as much of the story available online on the website(as a flash version I believe) and I knew i had to get it. Little did I know at the time what true glory still awaited me. Then the light of multiplayer racing shone down upon me and I got trashed by a pro in the most fabulous fashion imaginable. Oh how he swung so beautifully, his releases and jumps so perfectly timed, and his item usage so exact I would think he were a watch maker. True art I experienced that day, I was so stricken that for a moment I became a poet solely to express the moment. I gradually learned the ropes (haha great grappling pun) and now I too can create art with flowing movements, though still not yet as gloriously skilled as the god-child I had witnessed, but enough to give me the strength to open cans of whoop♥♥♥♥♥on occasion.
The beautiful feeling of pure awesomeness when pulling off an amazing move, whether it be dodging something in a manner that even you did not know was possible or just barely managing to pull ahead far enough to win, is more than enough to consider this game well worth the money spent.
11/10 would buy again. Thank you for producing such glory and allowing the commonsfolk to bask in the light of heaven itself.
note: I saw some people saying they would play more if they had a controller. I do actually have a controller, but I have not actually tried using it for this game yet. It is possible that it would offer a better experience but thus far, I have experienced nothing but pure joy whilst playing solely on a keyboard. If another player is advantaged by using a controller, I have not yet noticed.

I've logged about 12 hours on this game so far and I've so far only purchased the endless mode DLC, so about twelve games. Maybe more. Dwarfs is a free to play strategy arcade game in which the player takes the place of an omnipotent god/guide/being/etc. The player guides the dwarves that start underground in a cave in an attempt to get a high score by doing things like defeating enemies, digging minerals, and so on.
If you want the short version of this review: If you like strategy, and you want something you can play in the off time, get this game. It's free, it's fun, and perfect for a "Lunch time game". If you want to get more out of the game once you buy it, I highly recommend you get the Endless mode DLC. If you want a little bit more in depth, here goes.
VISUAL AESTHETICS:
The game looks very good, and a lot of love and personal style went into creating everything. The dwarves in particular are very adorable to me, and everything oozes with character. Something worth mentioning as well is how well the visuals coincide with the gameplay, in that extra efforts were taken to ensure that the player was not lost or confused at any point, though there are still sometimes where it gets very easy to get lost in the deep caverns. All in all, the game isn't next-gen and people who are even looking at this shouldn't be expecting groundbreaking graphics. It's cute, adorable, varied, and knit together well with the gameplay with a fantastic style.
SOUND AND MUSIC:
There are a few songs on the soundtrack from this game and they're all very relaxing and gives the game a very zen feeling, most of the time (When lava/water/boss fights break out, it's kinda like running out of air in Sonic...) But the music is fantastic otherwise. It's very well paced with the gameplay, and it never feels like it tries to portray something its not, like some games have. The sound effects aren't very special, some fighting, some clattering. I think one aspect that shines though is the voice of the Dwarves themselves, they're very cute and add to the charm of the game. I think if one played this game repeatedly for hours, the music might get tiresome, but it shouldn't if you play it with moderation.
GAMEPLAY:
So, the big one. How does it play? Pretty damn well. The player has a pool of gold to start with, and the Dwarves dig automatically in random and unpredictable directions. Every wall they dig generates a small amount of gold, and can dig up minerals to get more gold. The player can click and drag a line to a destination on a dwarf (or strategically lay it out on his path) and he will follow that line until it ends, digging whatever lies in his wake, but this costs a small amount of gold. This priority makes controlling the dwarves fantastically fun, and easy. Where does the challenge come from? This game is by no stretch of the imagination easy, even on easy mode. The challenges come in three basic forms. Lava, Water, and "What lurks in the Darkness when you dig too deep." Basically, every game you initiate will always have caverns inside, their contents being unrevealed until you choose to dig into them. The three things I just mentioned above will literally pour out, and if they flood your starting location, that's game over. But the player is given the tools to dispose of these problems, which cost money from your gold pool, but for this review I won't go in depth on. As your cave gets bigger and bigger, managing these problems gets tougher and tougher. The player needs to make tactical decisions made primarily on luck ("Does that cave have baddies? Or lava? Nonono, ♥♥♥♥ that, seal that♥♥♥♥♥♥") or split second reactions because their dwarves tunneled into a cavern full of lava and ends up leaking it through a bunch of tunnels.
Every order in the game is given, but no result is immediate, it's similar to Dungeon Keeper or Evil Genius in that regard, combine this with the aspect of you can't liberally pause time like you can in a game like Dwarf Fortress or Crusader Kings II, this becomes extremely difficult, and that's where most of the challenge comes from (You can however speed up time which just helps the game along and increases its user friendly nature!). From there, it gets more difficult when you start unearthing the boss fights, Goblin Shamans, Spider Queens, and the dreaded Lich Lords. With even harder difficulties, and a bunch of scenarios to boot and DLC if you so desire, the gameplay is fun and inviting. In the base game, you can set your timer for as little as five (5) minutes all the way up to sixty (60) minutes. Despite the strategy involved, this makes the game absolutely perfect in terms of time management. You can pop on for a quick 15 minute game and be done before the kettle boils or its time to go to work. All in all the gameplay makes Dwarfs excellent.
AFFORDABILITY:
This game is free. Not much else I should say there. The only thing you should really buy for this if you want a great time is the endless mode DLC, which is 2 bucks. If you want to fully support the devs, every DLC costs 18 dollars in total. It's great, afforable, and fun. If you like strategy games, you have no reason not to install this game, and buy the endless mode DLC.
REPLAYABILITY:
This is arguably Dwarfs strongest suit. I've yet to get tired of this game, I love it and every game is enjoyable and different. For those of you that want high scores for leaderboards and such, that is available to you. I personally don't enjoy them, but the score in this case is still used fantastically to measure your performance, edging you to just give it one more shot, in a fashion similar to tetris. The caves are randomly generated, the scores are limitless, and the Dwarves do not stop. Keep digging on and on, and see how good you can get.
CONS AND CRITIQUE:
This is a great game, but every great game has a flaw or two. My main complaint is with the end game, where you need to be able to bounce between places in a flash, you can navigate to problems pretty easily the first time, but after that you need to remember where they are. I once lost an extremely good run because a Lich Phantom I forgot about destroyed my base. This could've been very easily been remedied with the incorporation of a mini-map. There's also a few minor complaints I had where there's no way to repair the base or the outposts, which I can kinda understand why and these are meant (usually) to be disposable games, but in Endless Mode at least, I felt like that should've been a feature. Those are really my only complaints about this game.
OVERALL:
If you like Dwarves, get this game. If you like Dwarf Fortress, get this game. If you like strategy games, get this game. If you want a game you can play whilst eating a bowl of cereal in the morning get this game. This is definitely one of my favourite arcade style games to have come out in a while, and I encourage anyone who meets the criteria I listed to get this game. And if you don't meet the criteria, I ask that you at least give it a shot. It's a small download, and a 15 minute game certainly wouldn't hurt. The tutorial is user friendly, or you can just dive right in. In five words Dwarfs is:
Arcadey and Amusing Digging Adventures.

You will love this game if...
- You like games that don't hold your hand
- You like games that allow you freedom to customise your characters and experiences
- You like games that TRULY reward exploration and investigation
*Legit, if you don't sit there scrolling over the map looking for hidden chests, ladders, ledges, etc, you're doing it wrong*
- You like high strategy, turn based combat that rewards forward thinking and planning
- You like finding, using, selling or collecting loot
- You have 1 or more friends that will play with you. This game shines in multiplayer
The handful of little annoying bugs and glitches are completely and utterly outweighed by how captivating and enthralling this game is... And it's still in Early Access... I see a lot of complaints that the story isn't long enough, or really focusing on the bugs, lets get real.
Bugs:
- Sometimes your helmet will blink and flicker a bit
- Sometimes your characters won't be within range, or have line of sight on a target they clearly should
- Accuracy percentage seems to be a bit off, 80% chance to hit is more like 30%; anything under 90% is trouble
That's... About it...
Story is too short? Well then play the rest of the game kid. You can speed run the "story" in like 20 minutes if you wanted, the real fun comes from exploring the world and finding everything else there is to do. I honestly can't believe how good this game is for an EA release and I can't wait for the full release come September. Could not recommend highly enough.
Things I would like to see in future:
- More races.
- More in depth customisation options for spells and abilities. Think Champions Online or the Oblivion Spell-Creation. (asking for a lot, I know)
- A little control over what armour looks like on your character.
- More spells, more synergy between spells. This is already great, but why stop at great!
The more points I list, the more I realise I'm just asking for more of the game. Give me more of the game mate.

It's quite fitting that the first serious recommendation I do for a game would be Fable: The Lost Chapters.
You know how some people tend to play Deus Ex whenever it's mentioned because of how much they love it? In this case, Fable is my Deus Ex. Ever since I played it on the Xbox in 2004. I was hooked.
The game truly gives you a feeling of connection with your character, as you play as him from a small child to an elderly, war-torn man. Although some characters are rather dull, most are well-done and well-written for the context of the game. Even when I was an evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who slayed every villager in his sight, I still couldn't bring myself to killing certain characters.
The story itself is excellent, dropping you in the mystical land of Albion where beasts of all sorts roam. The main villain is revealed rather late in the game, giving you a chance to explore and understand the environment you were put into without being forced to fight a singular individual. I, personally, enjoy the setting of the game, pitting you in a medieval-esque surrounding.
The game gives you a nice sense of freedom when choosing your playstyle. You can be a stealthy archer, a brutish barbarian, a wise spellcaster, or a combination of them. I did a run using only fire spells, and another as a spell-archer. The possibilities aren't endless, but you have quite a bit of freedom in choosing how you want to play.
And to top all that off, the music is absolutely brilliant. Have a listen:
On some bad notes, though, the morality system seems rather extreme. The game sets every quest for you to become either some sort of saint, or a completely evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. To put it into an analogy, you're either giving candy to an orphan, or you're kicking said orphan in the teeth.
Almost all cutscenes use canned animations, which can be a bit of an eyesore later in the game, and of course there are graphical errors and glitches that might scare some people away; It's understandable, seeing as you can SEE UNDER THE CHARACTERS' EYELIDS.
The game is also a bit too easy. As long as you have a steady supply of potions that you can buy with gold that's easy to obtain, you can't die. If you really wanted to have a feeling of difficulty, you would need to throw out all of your resurrection vials and try to limit your potions. That's pretty much the only way to make this game harder than it is.
All bad points aside, I truly enjoy this game; even enough to call it my favourite game ever. I sincerely recommend this game to anyone reading this. It may not be the most immersive RPG in existence, nor could it stand up to the likes of Kingdoms of Amalur in gameplay, I still say you should give it a try by any means possible.
That being said, though, stay away from the sequels to this game.

I like the style of the Hero of the Kingdom series. When I played the first one, it took a bit getting used to, but being able to move all over the map with a few clicks makes going back and forth to get things to solve a quest so much easier than any 3D adventure game where you have to walk or run to get around.
Just like its predecessor, your progression through the game is relatively linear, and though it is not strictly speaking necessary to win the game, it does give one a certain extra satisfaction gaining all the achievements, which is possible to complete after reaching the winning conditions of your main quest and storyline. Judging from the global statistics, rather a high number of players actually choose to complete all achievements, which is an achievement for the game's creators.
Speaking of story, it is your typical slightly clicheed fantasy adventure story, where even the twists are hardly surprising, though a nice touch to what would otherwise be a bit too predictable. Still, its familiarity makes the game a bit more casual, which suits it nicely.
Like in the first instalment of the series, a bit of bartering might be necessary to reach the funds needed to achieve all goals. I assume that hardly anyone plays this without having played the first one before, and so I'll not say any more particulars about the game mechanics.
I felt that what you had to do in this game, though of course similar to the first one, was sufficiently different to make it feel fresh and fun again for the 4 hours or so that is needed to complete the game. My playtime ended up being a bit longer as the game was left on when I was AFK, and also I had to find those last hard-to-spot eggs and lost crates to complete my Steam achievements as I was so close at the end of the game I thought I might as well.
Coming from a 1920x1080 15 inch display laptop, I felt that the things you had to find were slightly easier to spot in this one than in the first game. Perhaps a tad bigger or clearer, whereas the individual blue mushrooms of game one left me looking a bit longer.
All in all, this game was more similar than different from its older brother, and think that's a good thing. It dares to be different, and manages to go against the trend of over-production that has crippled the gameplay of some adventure games over the last few decades, though it is by no means retro in its use of graphics as there are hardly any visible pixels in sight.
The simplicity of its user interface might seem to belong to a different era, but I think it makes for highly playable and enjoyable minimalism, making a game that I feel is well worth the ticket price.

There isn't much not to praise in UnderRail. It's a work of love from a developer who clearly deeply enjoyed the old Fallouts, XCOMs, Wasteland and Jagged Alliance, but due to todays technologies and an attention to detail, it's become so much stronger.
Explore the caverns, passages, ruins and beating heart of the UnderRail; the underground remains of our future civilization, sprawled across the Metro system which has been beaten by time, scarred by combat and given refuge to competing groups, deadly enemies, politics, and scavengers, stragglers and survivors making their way.
With a fantastic combat system and range of very well designed traits and abilities, you'll constantly be learning and trying new things as you descend further into the world of the UnderRail, eventually finding the even wider and more intricate lower levels..
There's a level of detail that brings everything up a level. Most characters and groups are unique enough to be interesting, oddities, mobs and items are all fun to read about, and the history of the world is scattered around waiting to be discovered
Combat and abilities have been balanced strongly and never feel spammy, boring, or badly designed. Finding advantages and alternative approaches to a situation is encouraged, and keeps you thinking and involved throughout every encounter.
* A fantastic lack of restriction and forced objectives/interactions means you can do whatever you want, pretty much from the get-go, even if it's stupid or suicidal, which helps add to the exploration and immersion
* Fantastic combat and a deep yet balanced skills and abilities system mean that making new unique characters is easy, and fun, and lends to more replayability
* Like Metro 2033, the setting is just right for the atmospheric sound effects and music. They match really well and help create stronger immersion
* A useful crafting system and economy, which aren't overstated, help add depth for those who want to spend time on it
* The long playtime with good pace and content throughout, and the heaps of re-playability deserve special mention
* There's a strong lack of explanation and tutorial elements. The wiki helps, but new players can often go wrong with combat and other abilities
* Small UI problems like text sizes, and the odd bug or two
UnderRail is exceptionally well priced at just £6.49/7.99€/$9.99 at the time of review, though this has been rumoured to increase after release. With 60 hours+ playtime it's currently a must-buy for anyone who enjoys this genre.

* The regular experience system should probably be chosen by new players as the Oddities system requires more involvement

Elsword is an amazing game to play with friends and family, game is pretty fast paced and has a more in depth combo system than it may seem with two basic attack keys and 4 or so active skill keys. But I do not reccomend this version... while it may say I've been playing the game for 53 hours, I should note I first started playing Elsword as far back as Closed Beta for NA.
The problem with this version of Elsword is being it has slowly creeped from something you didn't need to cash to play, into something where it seems your credit card is becoming more and more of a vital tool to keep up, speccialy if you wish to remotely even buy anything in the market that's been inflated to a point any in-game ED(Gold) you get will only really be spent on NPC services.
The host as well hasn't proved shy of converting free features into cash features. Skill Notes for example have been converted into a mostly cash feature, they improve skills you can learn in some way or another. But unelss you wish to get a skill note for a lousy active skill nobody chooses for very good reasons. Due to how the skill trees work in this game, you often won't even pick up the worse skill in a choice since picking Skill X will lock Skill Y entirely, making many if not all quest earned skill notes left unused. (If you plan to play the Korea version, this point is null as skill notes are a mob drop over there.)
And then going back onto the economy... an in-game gamble box will give cash players many of what they'll need.. and more. So don't expect to be able to sell your rarer drops to them except for Secret Dungeon drops. This is because the gamble box gives them much more of the same items you can find in-game form mob drops... without the grind. This has resulted in an in-game economy where only cashers can trade with cashers and very few if any F2Ps can actually buy anything of note worth, the aforementioend skill notes bought with KC can be traded after being bought... but the ED to KC rate will make it far too much ingame gold for one out of 6 skill note slots..
While I do enjoy the game itself as well... a game mechanics wise and as a fun arcadey co-op beat em' up, I have to advise players to stay away from Elsword NA. Look into other servers instead, I'ms ure if you google a bit you can discover many other servers of which may be a far superior alternative.

An unrealistic and overly technical political simulator, buggy even at this late stage, with extremely weak military aspects.
When you aren't inexplicably 'forced' into peace due to a 'war score' percentage, money magically vanishing from your accounts as a reward for the victor even if he has no army or possibility of victory (or means of taking the money) then expect to be trapped in an endless grind for the tiniest scraps of money, staring listelessly for hours at the successions of a dynasty before you're permitted to interact in any meaningful fashion.
I'm amazed I'm saying this, but even the Total War games, silly as they are, offer a more realistic, involved and entertaining experience than this game - if only because of the lack of arbitrary, illogical rules relating to declarations of war.
There's no underdog here, no flexibility or opportunity. Do not expect to take a nation from humble beginnings to greatness. Only the colossal nations in the preset historical bookmarks can effectively grow.
The Paradox view of history is that it functioned as a machine according to strict rules, and that even 'plots' and 'intrigue' could only be carried out according to a manual of etiquette with no logical coherence.
If you don't relish the idea of a family management game, in which you'll spend 80% of your time waiting, 15% arranging marriages and 5% staring, bemused, at the latest bug or crash report, play something else.

Crusader Kings II is a Grand Strategy game based around familiy dynasties, political power mongering and in short - trying to make sure you have the biggest wealthest family in the world. The game spans ~400 years of historical time between 1066 to 1453 and offers historical events and references that you can either choose to follow or create a new alternantive timeline from. Do you start a 'War of the Roses' battle? Does YOUR family takeover the Papal?
Building relationships, marriages, alliances and faking claims is the key. If this sounds all very Game of Thrones then you're right - it is. Crusader Kings II is the best GoT game on the market at the moment, and that's all thanks to engine being used.
Crusader Kings II is the end result of many years of creating and improving on Paradox's Clausewitz Engine (the engine responsible for Cruaders Kings, Europa Universalis, Hearts of Iron franchises). If you're familiar with those games, you might feel familiar with CK2, but the truth is this game goes beyond what the engine has produced before hand.
The Clausewitz Engine is in sense the major selling point behind CK2, so while the graphics aren't anything special (and are little more than 3D Marker Pieces) the true beauty unfolds as you play.
I can't think of many greater feelings than the moment you're 50 year plotting to get your Grandson into place of power from his lowly Duke title to Lord pays off. Sending your Master of Whispers into a neighbouring region to spread lies and cause dissent amongst the vassals, while you forge a plot to fabricate claims to the title and ursurp the Lordship. So good.
Paradox have managed to support the game well since release in the form of DLC Expansions, which have opened the game world up and expanded the 'fringe' empires to be just as complex as the 'key' European ones. However they've also supported the game with post-release patching and balancing, so they're not ones to sitback and take your money.
