A few minor bugs, and not nearly enough multiplayer maps, but still an awesome, thrilling experience.  The RTS side of things is polished and well done, requiring your attention across the map as you battle for resources and the destruction of the enemy's avatars.  Said avatars can get a bit overpowered late game, but this is usually because you threw too many units at them at once, which I often did early game.  The Shooting side of things is easily the best part of the game.  Finding a coop game with a good commander, with you running around the map trying to help where you can is truly an awesome experience, especially when the super-units come into play.
That being said, the game has a few glaring issues.  Namely, the lack of maps.  The game has only four maps.  They're incredibly detailed, especially for an RTS, but still, far too few for a release game.  Also, there are far, FAR too few units to choose from.  There are two infantry units, three tanks, two fighters, and the dreadnaught.
This lack of troops, and minor bugs and physics quirks, are the main problems the game, but they easily made up for by the sheer scale and awesome theme of the game.  Play it like an RTS, zoom out, tilt the camera back, and scroll through the center of the map, and you tell me that isn't ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.

Graphics. A major upgrade over the first game. Smooth, dynamic, colorful

A.I Teammates now relialbe
The Bad
Inconsistent dialogue options.
Some special abilities seem over-powered.

I was first introduced to the world of Chivalry through a Half-Life 2 mod of pretty much the same name. The game featured a variety of classes, weapons and styles of playing making for an interesting medieval-themed combat game.
This more official release of Chivalry, under the name "Medieval Warfare" whom a friend of mine recommended me to, seemed fun. I thought it may be a superior version of the mod and would provide for an even more in-depth feeling of what it's like to battle it out oldschool in the medieval ways aaaand.. it did. Kinda.
The game presents itself beautifully with an epic intro and gorgeous music with a great setting and mood that rolls in almost immediately the moment you engage to dwell into the world of Chivalry. The graphics feature a richly-detailed environment with a great attention to being authentic, so no magic spells or dragons or futuristic space marines and guns. Just good ol' sword & shield, or bow if you're not one to throw yourself into the very front of the battlefield, or perhaps you feel like brutally bludgeoning someone with a warhammer if you so desire. GREAT. The only thing I can really nitpick on is very minor bugs and glitches, such as the ragdolls stretching or twisting themselves into hilarious but kinda gross fleshy messes, or just getting stuck in random objects just to either slowly drift away from said platform to fall to your doom or meet some other gruesome demise.
As for the music, it's a beautifully orchestrated ensemble performing traditional middle-age type of compositions, most of which are cued in a fitting manner and never feels out of place but feels natural with the game's flow and approach.
The game features several game mods that'll keep you busy and offers several types of gameplay. The free-for-all, team deathmatch, King of the Hill and Objective-based team games. I might have missed one or two, but you get the drift i'm going for. All of which are pretty fun for the most part and are what you'd expect if you're familiar with any multiplayer games who usually possess these type of scenarios for players.
The problem for me personally started showing gradually throughout the gameplay. While it maintains the original fun from the mod, with the weapons and character classes all having their own specialties, strengths and weaknesses, something is kinda wrong though. Now, don't get me wrong, I think it can be pretty exciting to be in a pretty epic man-to-man swordfight and the overall fast pace of the game makes for pretty heated battles, BUT, I feel like the physics in the game aren't quite as polished. You see, I think it's a bit odd when you're in a battle and your foe can somehow do a 720-degree spin, while wildly swinging his sword in the air and somehow still land pretty devastating blows to your torso and / or head. - Or how a weapon such as the Cudgel is pretty much a given win once you get a couple of hits in, giving the player no chance to either attack, kick or parry any incoming threat and instead just kinda have to stand there and hope that they might have a chance to hit first or sneak up on you once they respawn. Or how someone can incredibly enough parry a sword from the front and back simultaneously. Obviously it all boils down to how a player chooses to play and any kind of "exploits" or "superior" strategies are of course gonna be the ideal way of keeping a top score for MANY players, however, I feel like these type of things can kind of ruin the gameplay experience for some as even I haven't always felt like my death in a battle was rightfully "justified".
All in all, this game has alot of potential and positive things going for it, but there are those little things I believe are holding it back just a little bit. However, judging by the price tag and frequent updates and what seems to be a dependable team and ever-growing community, I still recommend this game if you've got a little more money than you can handle at the moment.

Fable is one of those classically good games with very nice production value. It's primarily an action RPG where you play as an epic hero as you quest through the lands.
The game is full of humor and riddled with sidequests. But bare no bones about it, Fable is not a smart game by any stretch of the imagination. It's an action game first and an RPG second, and if you're determined enough you can beat the game without buying any equipment or levelling up your character in any way, I know this first hand.
So don't go into this expecting a game with the intelligence of Baldur's Gate, or any of Molyneux's other games, because it's not. Thankfully, the PC port is pretty solid and it features a completely extended part of the game after the original's ending.
Overall it's worth the 10$ on Steam and keeps your attention, but it's not anything to break an appointment over.

No question is a di-rect decendant of Fallout 1 and 2 as so many here have stated. What more can you say to that?
The good:
-Crafting of guns, armor, electronic devices, grenades, chemicals, even ammo

-A fun and creative range of combat options (kneecap shots, crippling melee blows, setting enemies on fire (hells yeah), knife throwing, even psychic attacks.
-Can even set up 'ambush' scenarios with caltrops, traps, and molotovs.
The Bad:
um not much...
-steep difficulty curve, unforgiving at times (you need to learn what armors protect best in many situations)
-not a lot of personality to the dialogue at times (though it has improved a lot)
-a lesser sense of a 'real' community in the towns (not much going on in the background)
If you're a fan of old school turn based RPG's....you owe it to yourself to check this out. This is an experience you should not cheat yourself out of. It's worth every penny and more.

Elsword is sort of like a 3D Maple Story in it's own way. So if you enjoyed that, you might like this.
From the begining it can get qutie repititve really fast. It's not like most MMOs where you have an abundance of quests to do, rather, you only get a few quests per level. This can get pretty frustrating past level 40, as it forces you to either dungeon grind or field grind (Fields are areas with monsters that you can do repeat quests over and over. It's very stamina efficenet on weekdays, and gives a fair amount of xp.) Ereda Island is also a nice alternative if you're looking for PVE mixed with PVP. It's stamina efficent and it gives good exp.
This game does have a stamina system. When you run out of stamina, you can no longer dungeon or gain exp from monsters in field. While most would be turned off by this, I personally don't find myself ever running out of stamina. This might be because I enjoy playing plenty of characters though, so I switch often. On weekends, stamina is unlimited.
I can't really think of many things that are bad about Elsword, persay. Some would call it pay2win, due to the only way you can aquire costumes and such is through the cash shop. Plenty of players are able to play with no trouble and never spend a dime on the game. I have personally cashed, but I do remember what it was like not to cash as well. Not being able to cash limits some things, but I wouldn't say by much. You could also buy KC (The cash shop currency) from other players, but our economy is quite terrible right now so that may not be an option. Whether you cash or not does not limit your ability though, and those who think like that are silly.
I think PVP is the one reason why I think this game is great. The combo system and how everything works together is very interesting. Unfortunately, many people are quite rude in PVP and those who are considered the top players have a large ego. Prepare for the salt if you decide to PVP. (I do not recommend PVPing before at LEAST 45 if you decide to, due to level differences. If you choose to PVP before then is at your own risk.)

I’m pleasantly surprised by how entertaining and charming Hero of the Kingdom 2 was. It’s a short, casual game that’s a unique blend between the genres of
and
. I’ve never played anything like it, and I think the developers have a great casual game formula going. Basically, your hero explores the countryside, a city, and neighboring islands while helping residents and gathering items and money in order to complete the main goal of saving the hero’s sister. It’s a delightful, family-friendly game and while I would recommend it to anyone who likes casual adventure games, I think Hero of the Kingdom 2 is especially good for young children.
Keep in mind that the RPG elements in the game are very LITE – so, if you’re after a more traditional cRPG experience, this isn’t quite the game for you. While your hero learns skills, there are no stat allocations, nor can your hero make any choices that can alter their adventure. Also, combat is very simple – if you have the required items needed to initiate combat, you WILL win.
Another warning is that Hero of the Kingdom 2 will only take a few hours to complete (it took me 4 hours). While the actual gameplay mechanics are delightful, and while the game appears very polished (the musical score is particularly high-quality), it’s far from being a cost-efficient game on Steam. The price/time element is definitely something to consider here, considering that there are many <$10 games that you can buy which can provide at least 50 hours of gameplay.
If/when the developers work on Hero of the Kingdom 3, I would like to see minor interface improvements (for example, I believe that the hero’s health and gold amounts should be visible at all times). Most importantly, the developers need to work on storytelling and refining sentence structure. Here’s a snippet of game text:
“The workers did a good job. But they should work with tools more carefully. They have broken my saw.”
I wish the developers the best of luck with Hero of the Kingdom 3, as they’re innovating casual gaming, but I also hope that the future game text is presented with more polish and professionalism.

Let me start with the TL;DR:
WOW.
(And I mean that in the non-MMO kind of way.)
This game is amazing.
The Witcher 3 is being released today (been waiting for it for a year and I already bought it) and now I'm seriously doubting whether I should install it or just continue playing UnderRail. It's just that good.
Don't play this if you want an easy hand-holding fairy-tale with flashy graphics.
Do play this if you're looking for games like Fallout 1/2, or maybe a little Jagged Alliance or even somewhat like single-squad X-Com... Only, this one just might be better.
It's been ages since I've seen a game with such a deep and diversified character development. Without dividing your options into classes or anything such, there's so many different ways to build your character depending on what kind of playstyle you're looking for and all of them are viable and fun to play.
Despite the old-school graphics, the game manages to create an atmosphere that really sucks you into its world.
It's also the first game ever where crafting objects is actually something I find interesting. The crafting system is so deep and complex and yet so simple to use and very rewarding.
Character progression is fun and well-paced and there's no annoying level-scaling. Nothing feels as good as returning to those gangers that forced you into a bribe earlier and returning later to give them some payback with your new equipment and skills. The game gives you a lot of points to put into skills but also a lot of skills to spend them on, allowing for a lot of diversity.
The storytelling is good and the many (side-)quests are very diverse instead of all the FedEx quests often seen in other RPGs. There are often different ways of accomplishing your goal, allowing you to use stealth, persuasion, look for other solutions or just go in guns blazing. Everything works and there's no wrong of doing things.
The world itself is large, complex and rarely forces you to follow a single path. Without a real map, quest markers or other form of hand-holding, it also makes exploration really feel like you're exploring an unfamiliar dark and dangerous underworld where danger could (and often does) lurk behind every corner.
And then there's crafting, and the psi-powers, and the C&C, and so much else to tell...
Anyhow, I could go on for hours, but I'd rather spend that time playing the game.

I'm a big fan of RTS's...and I always like RTS's that include some First person elements.  However the only one I found was executive assault, which at last play had some nasty crashing habits and wasn;t the best looking game.
So, I entered into warshift with a pinch of salt.  I was pleasently surprised to not only find a good looking game, but one with useful tutorials too that teach you the ropes.
Edit:  Having plated a few missions now, I'm finding the game is quite enjoyable.  That said, as a casual gamer, I do enjoy the ease of them...not too hard and not too easy.
The FPS and RTS modes are easily accessable with a simple push of the tab key.  Your ability to level up your combat avatar, the unit you use for FPS modes are also pretty good as it encourages a moderately aggresive strategy and discourages turtling, as you need to fight to level up your army and get to the really good stuff like the dreadnought.
So far I have only seen three avatars, a amphibious APC, a amphibious tank and my personal favourite, the raptor mech, which seems to have flight and siubmarine abilities as well as some nasty weaponry to unlock for each.
There are of course, the usual RTS problems such as unit AI pathfinding but a simple brief redirect manually makes that easy to solve.
The fact that energy modules (used to power your buildings and mining platforms) are also limited to three buildings only, which encourages that your forces spread out to claim the neutral energy modules before making your own.
Next is your 'ark', the equivilent of the construction yard or HQ in most RTS's.  This nice baby is also a large scale training and building platform.  Any unit or building that you have reached the level for can be built and deployed from this.  It also has the ability to fly between the maps 'landing zones' which are the only points on the map where the arks can land.
These are very important due to one last limitation I like.  The superweapons, known as orbital strikes, are also deployed from the ark, with the catch that they have a limited range.  This makes them less offensive and more defensive, stopping what I call 'superweapon spam' (which is the method of turtling up against your enemy until you are able to fire superweapon after superweapon at them) by your opponent in MP.
All in all, this game is proof that cyril should be given a high end job in the game dev big leagues.  The fact he put this game together solo is a testament to his skill and while it has a few bugs (the pathfinding problems I mentioned) the fact that is the ONLY bug, again proves that this person deserves support.
Final score
Graphics: 9.5/10
The graphics on this game are beautiful and even though game debate warned me to run it at medium, it runs like a charm on high.
Gameplay: 8.5/10
This is a little easy and while I like RTS's to not be punishing, this may not be everyones cup of tea. It would also be nicer to have a longer delay between mission complete and the victory screen appearing so players can savour their victory.
Unit and abilities:  9.5/10
The units are nice and beefy, and the superweapon abilities feel like they pack a punch too, something some RTS's have missed since supreme commander.  The 'combat avatars' however seal the deal for me as does the third person shooter mode in them.  Its always nice to join in on your armies fun and its nice to see this done right for once.
Final score:  9.1/10
This RTS is brilliant and any casual RTS fan should give it a chance.  Its a nice looking, fun RTS and a fantastic work of art, given its development team consists of one person.  Its worth being given a chance to shine.

Mass Effect 2 is an amazing action-rpg with great third person shooting mechanics.  The combat is very fun but not what makes Mass Effect so unforgettable.  The highlight is the characters, the way you interact with them, and the choices you make.  The characters are fully fleshed out and many of the game's missions are dedicated to gaining your allies' loyalty and learning more about them.  The ways you interact with them and decisions you make in the game, or have made in Mass Effect 1, have consequences both grand and subtle.  They combine to make the game one of the most personalized gaming experiences out there.
Many triple A games aim to deliver an epic experience, and I won't claim that they fail.  But Mass Effect 2 is probably the most epic game I am familiar with.  Its epicness cannot be overstated and in fact its epicness is quantitatively thrice as large as the epicness of other triple A games whose epicness is the main selling point.  Yet despite the incredible epicness of Mass Effect 2 (and I am in no way discrediting the power of epicness), it doesn't neglect to add incredible depth to its characters and choices.

How do I describe ARK: Survival Evolved? Bugs, glitches, and crashes, all of which leads to frustrating gameplay.
They're still releasing major content patches for it (each of which ends up breaking something), but haven't fixed long outstanding bugs. They have a name for that in the gaming industry, it's called ALPHA. Beta is when major gameplay elements are finished, and is when polish begins. This game has almost 0 polish, so it's still in alpha, not even beta. The game works, but barely.
Collision is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Hitting/gathering rocks/bushes on the ground is a crap-shoot. It's not clear at all where the collision is for those things. You eventually learn some techniques for gathering them, but it's tedious. Collision with dinosaurs is annoying as well, as they'll constantly push you up against a wall while following you, making you unable to move.
Pathing is nonexistant for tamed dinosaurs. The biggest draw of this game is taming dinosaurs, using them as raiding/hunting buddies, and riding them. It's awesome, but for tamed dinosaurs, there's 0 pathing. If they're following you, they want to move STRAIGHT towards you with 0 variation. They'll constantly get stuck on trees, fallen trees, rocks, cliffs, other dinosaurs, and anything in their path. They have no snapping mechanic to re-gain lost dinosaurs, so travelling is slow and tedious as you have to look behind you every 20 seconds to make sure the idiot dinosaurs didn't get stuck on something and will be lost forever in the damn forest.
Why not just venture alone? Well, this game has huge difficulty spikes. There's a myriad of dinosaurs that can knock you unconscious and just pummel your body on the ground with nothing you can do about it. So, having tamed friendly dinosaurs near you is important, and extremely annoying.

Yes, I do wish the game conveyed even more clearly how to execute the more difficult moves (and didn't just expect me to patiently learn through trial and error and watching other players), but ultimately I do feel it's less my fault than the games' for me not being able to carry on. - Am I looking puzzled as an action? I am saying they look puzzled?
4: *you wonder why the dialog is all in 3rd person, since you can barely tell what's a thought or action or what's actually said out loud (and to whom)*

5: *you facepalm at the ridiculousness of it all; you don't know who 'you' is referring to*
Other than that, it's a wonderful game. Of course, the dialog is 1/3 of the entire game, so that's a MAJOR issue.
Also, the dialog was written by a non-native english speaker. It's obvious, and slightly irritating since, beyond the above issue, there are some dialog options which make no sense whatsoever, yet can mean the difference between your character living and dying in the game.
Example:
NARRATOR: *you see a runed vase with an inscription warning you to not pull the lever unless you have fund scrolls to tell*
(and yes, all descriptions come in the form of dialog with a pretend person named "NARRATOR", instead of just describing the scene in a normal way. Very hokey, and a constant immersion killer.)
1: *you pull the lever, confident you are ready*
2: *you break the vase*
3: *you open the vase and absorb the entity inside*
Wait.. What?! WTF does "have fund scrolls to tell" mean? Which optin shold I be choosing? How do I back out? PS: You can't back out of dialog, so you MUST make a choice. Your guess is as good as mine what the non-english part is supposed to mean, but the rest of the game is decided in that moment and there are no take-backs.
So, yeah, awesome, awesome game, with the most ridiculous dialog/narration I've ever seen.

Basically, if you enjoyed Hero of the Kingdom I, this is more of the same, and when I mean more of the same, I
mean more of the same.  The gameplay structure is mostly untouched, as is the UI/map/sound/etc. and that isn't really a bad thing here.  This series is a causal resource-management set of games and the familiarity between titles makes it very easy to jump right into this.  You'll be collecting x amount of items y and z so the miller's wife can sell you bread without skipping a beat.
The story is super generic fantasy and comes with a stiff English translation.  The visuals are very nice and the style really works well.  There are no annoying technical issues or gimmick gameplay bits to get in the way of you fetch-questing for the rest of the kingdom.
There are a couple of downsides, though.  HotKII is a bit longer than the first game, but this is mainly because item amount requirements can get kind of sizable and repetitive at times.  Building the boat is probably the biggest example of this.  The other problem I had is that there is some pixel-hunting required at times for items that don't visually "pop" from the rest of the art and don't have an "action" command signposting them.  There's only a couple of instances of you having to do this to progress but it can be quite annoying when you can't find the blacksmith's toolbox or whatever since it's super tiny and just blends into the background without doing anything in particular to draw your eye to it.
In short, if you liked the first game, you should probably pick this up.  If you've never played the first one and find this in a bundle a year from now, it's a nice, little resource management game where you can't find yourself in a fail state and is oddly relaxing and addicting to play.  It'll take about five hours or so to see everything there is to see but it's an enjoyable, light game that is ideal for zoning out and chilling.
One last thing, you can continue playing after beating the game, so unlike the first one, there's no worry about a point of no return.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This quite simply is the bang for your buck paradox game you know well. Crusader Kings II is set in the  dark ages of Europe. And several factors are already in play from the start of the default game.You start out as any lord of Europe. From the count of Norfolk to the Emperor of Byzantium. The following situation faces you. (Edit) They also added to the depths of Mongolia. If Yurits and eating fish is your niche.
The remains of Rome are declining in the east. And the Muslim hordes are still on the offensive in Spain and in northern Persia against the remains of the Zoastrians. Keepers of the old Persian Imperial Traditions. The Lords of Russia are shattered and  infighting. Leaving great chance to a crafty and respectable warrior.
Western Europe is in a stable. But inevitably declining status quo. The French King is faced with an issue. His greatest General and overall vassal William is leaving France to become King of England. Making a French dominated England as a rival quite the possibility. The Holy Roman Empire eyes French holdings in the modern day Netherlands  with envy and seeks to take it for themselves. Spain is divided between 3 Christian lords and one powerful Muslim lord. The Christians face the greatest chance they have had in quite a while however with the Muslim lord being of lesser stature. Whom is losing his grip on his African holdings. With an intelligent and brave warrior king. Iberia may yet be under the cross again.
In Scandinavia. The last of the vikings are chafing under the new found power of Christianity. The Lord of Norway still holds a lot of power. But is distracted with affairs in England. Where he claims England for the Norwegian crown against the local King Harold. And Duke William. Sweden has just formed.It still has several Norse Worshippers within the realm. And may be brought to be the last viking Kingdom in Europe.. Denmark has long converted to the cross. Fearing a Christian invasion from the South. The King of the Danish with several tactical marriages holds the oppertunity to unite the scandinavian realms under his grip. But must tread carefully due to his size and lack of an army.
The middle east is in a similar situation to Western Europe. Egypt is under the power of the Shia Fatimid lords. Whom control both Jerusalem and Mecca. However they are facing major sectarian issues. In the regard of Religion. Islam is split between two powerful lords. The Sunni Sejuk Turks in Persia. And the Fatimids in Egypt, Were it not for Byzantium. The Sejuks would be invading Europe proper. No concern should be held by the lords in the west if you do not take the reigns of the Sejuk. If you do however lead either lords. They have the power and ability to rapidly become the true Islamic nation.
India is DLC based. But I will briefly mention it
5 Kings. All ruling vast domains of varying cultures and religions. They contain advanced cities. Massive armies. And wealth beyond measure. Their one problem? They are very inward focused due to internal conflict and the nature of the religions of India. With a caste system and religious warfare rife. Many see no chance for the Indian Kingdoms to unite into one Empire. But if it is done. The Sejuks in Persia stand to fight off the Indian hordes which will have to invade through the mountains of Afghanistan. India is a great oppertunity. But more than skill is needed in this untamed land of mystery and old legends.

Fantastic gameplay, even in an alpha state. That's the short of it, the long of it is a little more complicated.
This game's got a lot to offer even in an extremely unfinished state as it is, and I'll probably change my review when the next story segment comes out and likely again when the game's released as a finished product. As it stands, without voices, with missing dialogue, with missing assets, and occasional bugs, this is still a beautiful game that, while short, offers some pretty in-depth character customization, even up to level 8 or 9.
The elemental effect/terrain altering magic from the first game is back, and better than ever, with a few new combinations, as well as the Bless/Curse quasi-elements that can transform an already dangerous fire patch into a lethal Cursed Flame that sets enemies or allies aflame with immolation that can't be put out with water, or transform an annoying but avoidable oil patch into Blessed Oil that fortifies allies instead of slowing them, making it a detour you WANT to walk through for a buff rather than a hindrance to walk around. I constantly found myself wondering how best to use my action points to turn terrain to my advantage rather than simply cluttering up the field with dangerous patches of fire, ooze, or electrified water.
Creating characters is even more in-depth than the last game, and many of the old skills from the first game have either been changed or removed for more interesting ones. Summoning is now its own skill tree, and is best paired with spells that create environmental effects, or simply on a Lizard who can breathe a patch of flame wherever they want, as the summons, a totem and an "Incarnate" gain the element they're conjured on, either water, fire, poison, oil, or blood. Even with all the spells at my disposal, I still found myself favoring the weapons I'd chosen before, as even with a hundred spells at my disposal, sometimes it's nice to just smack someone with a big sword.
This game can be very, VERY hard, but often in a Dark Souls way. Usually you'll know why you died, and can reload to try to fix it next time. Enemy casting a lot of fire spells? Make sure to purchase a rain scroll or use more water magic to counteract them, or simply stunlock the enemy to death and try to pick apart the enemy's strategy. It's pretty rare that you'll encounter a fight that you simply cannot win when you first encounter it, unless you go into the battle extremely underleveled (If you're more than 1 level below your opponent, you're probably going to lose). Generally fights last a while, so make sure to prepare for both long and short combats as it's rare that you'll go into a fight completely outclassing your opponent, and be prepared to burn potions and the like, as they WILL give you an edge in combat and it's generally not worth trying to tough it out without them. There's apparently an entire mechanic for food, but I've never gotten good results from it and the buffs generally arent worth the action points it takes to eat it, so you can't simply down six cheese wheels to heal to full.
The storyline's not quite as good as the gameplay, sadly, but I'm pretty confident that with voice acting and some tweaks it will get far stronger. The quest journal's still hardly worth looking at unless you've totally forgotten what you've done and feel like looking through a complicated and user-unfriendly transcript of everyone you've ever spoken to. The journal could definitely use a change as it was often hard to maintain who's quests were what and with four characters with FOUR SEPARATE JOURNALS THAT OFTEN HAVE SEPARATE QUESTS it's quite difficult to keep everything straight. Thankfully it's easy to just start walking in a direction and you'll probably run into some enemies that are either your level or much, much higher, leading to a quick-reload and a different path taken. The storyline itself introduces a number of people, Dalis the Hammer, Bishop Alexandar, a blind elven seer, and far, far, FAR more, each with a complex backstory that almost everyone's happy to narrate to you at the drop of a hat, which can get a little overwhelming sometimes, but it's an inherently wordy RPG, so that's just par for the course.
The story's tone is classic Larian, with a serious and epic plot that tries to be grim and po-faced when the rest of the world is made up of goofy talking skulls, riddling rats, mad witches, puns, and adorable dog quest-givers. Although the main storyline ends up looking a little out-of-place, it's nice that it's there and that the game's not simply a permanent comedy routine. I will say that some will find the tone kind of schizophrenic, and although I'd agree with that I'd also say that it's not a game to be taken seriously, and is instead more a sandbox for one or more players can wreak havoc or play within the rules.
Character customization is a little lacking at the moment, but that's almost secondary compared to the great animations each race/gender has, as well as each armor set looking different on each race, with an emphasis on eastern cloth for Lizards, or a hardier iron look for Dwarves. Spells have intricate and impressive effects, even for basic spells such as "Throw a rock" or "hit someone extra hard." While the hairdos and facial options presented to each race and gender is pretty small, it's generally enough that you probably won't get your characters confused.
On an entirely different note, the game's graphics and representation is amazing. I love the vibrant colors, and beautiful tropical locale for the start of the game. The one big downside is that the first part of the game takes place in a giant prison, but the atmosphere is that of a tropical resort, with sunny skies, beautiful coral beaches, and a shanty-town that looks more like a run-down tourist town than a brutal gulag for wizards. Although it wouldn't be nearly as pretty to look at, it would have been nice to have a more oppressive environment to start in, and escape to the tropical paradise later on, for contrast. That being said, the shadow effects playing off trees and logs, and the drop dead gorgeous beaches make for an impressive opening, and when the future chapters of the game are released, I'll be most excited to see the environments they take place in.
To sum it all up, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic. Worth a look if you enjoy slower-paced RPGs, even though the storyline's only about 1/3rd complete. With almost all of its flaws coming from being an unfinished alpha and very few coming from the actual design or gameplay. Pretty much fun in every aspect, with an insane level of combat and character customization depth, this game is absolutely worth your time.

Now that I've beaten the game once ''I played as Fane btw and got his signature ending'' I can safely say that this game is the best rpg I have ever played in my life. It might be the best one ever made too. Here are some reasons why: The story itself is incredibly engaging unlike anything I've seen with the only game comparable to this might be the witcher 3.
The combat is really fun and interesting,which is a huge step up from the first game where combat was kinda damn boring tbh.
The world of this game is incredibly charming and feels real,sure the voidwoken are attacking and magic is anywhere but you know what I mean.
The game is not predictable,there are a lot of twists in the story that you honestly would never see coming, especially if you play as Fane.
On top of those reasons the game is really damn long,I RUSHED the game to the ending on easiest difficulty and it still took me 58 hours. Only reason for rushing it was that I only had about 5 days to play the game before I had to get back to work. I know for a fact that I skipped at least 50% of the content,so even on explorer mode the game would be at least 100hours long if you want to see all of it. When I get another break from work I will start playing on bit harder difficulty as the Red Prince and I'll try to complete the game rather than rushing to see the ending. Now that's already more than worth 44.99 but what if I told you that you can play the entire story on multiplayer mode? What if I also told you that this game has a Game Master mode that literally turns this game into visualized dungeons and dragons? No I'm not ♥♥♥♥ing with you. I tested the gm mode and you can do A LOT with it. I already bought the game for one of my friends and if this ever goes on sale I'm buying it for my entire ♥♥♥♥ing D&D group just so we can use this game to play D&D. It's not exactly the same thing as D&D because it still uses divinitys game mechanics but who the ♥♥♥♥ cares since this game's mechanics are ♥♥♥♥ing perfect anyway. So this means that this game literally offers infinite amounts of gameplay if you've got at least couple of friends to play it with. As long as you can make up the stories and adventures you can keep playing,much like the actual pen and paper dungeons and dragons. And that's something no other game can say,I've never seen another game with a system thats done as well as the GM mode here. Some games have tried it but failed miserably,here it just works.
TLDR: So here's what you get for 44.99: Incredibly well made single player rpg with deeply engaging story and lore,a multiplayer option so you can experience said story with your friend and a GM mode that is easy to use so the game offers literally endless hours of gameplay and has infinite possibilites for you and your friends. Btw entire game is voice acted and the voice acting is really well done.
If you like RPGs even as a concept you will love this game. Just ♥♥♥♥ing buy it.

Camera zoom/navigation is very strange and difficult. You have to manually pan the camera, and/or use the mouse to move, but the camera doesn't follow behind your character like in typical RPGs, but above and at weird angles, so sometimes you can't see where your character is facing, and you have to manually pan the camera to see what's ahead. Graphics themselves don't seem that bad, but the entire game feels like something you would expect maybe five plus years ago. There also isn't any audio/narration to speak of apart from generic background music, so there's a lot of reading in dialogs, like an old Gameboy era RPG. I like the exploratory options available, but....it was impossible for me to really get into the game, and fighting/combat felt weird, even in Explorer mode. I had tutorial mode turned on, but it still took a lot of googling and trial and error to figure out how it's meant to work.
---
Edit: Came back to the game after Early Access, and I still hold to my previous points about the weird camera and controls. Still, after struggling with it for a while, I kind of got used to it, though it still isn't as immersive as I'm used to. The game itself is kind of addicting in a mindless kind of way (e.g. investigating stuff, choosing the best armor/equipment and skills, etc for tactical purposes).... but somehow it's not really as immersive story-wise as I would like... Still, it's not as bad as it was before; takes some getting used to, but you get used to it after awhile. Some aspects of the controls (e.g. the tactical view/aspect of it) reminds me of Dragon Age Origins, but it's just not as immersive so it's hard to connect with the story/characters. Even when I set auto-zoom on dialog start, the zoom angle is all strange and cuts off part of the character's head. In general, the camera and movement controls are just strange... but the game does grow on you after a while. The ending is very disappointing though, and there are parts that just don't make sense. It was mildly entertaining while it lasted, but I left feeling unsatisfied. I probably won't be replaying it again anytime soon.

A well presented game that rewards mastery of the controls.
Dustforce is a speedrunning game, in essence. Major focus on completing the levels as fast as possible, and the mechanics are inclined to reflect that. Movement is fluid and quick; after a little while of learning the controls you'll find yourself breezing through the beautiful enviroments and dispatching areas of dust. And that is where this game is unique, in that you have to not only go fast but to clean the room of dust/leaves/slime as best you can. Going fast by itself will not get you the best grading (although usually the dust is used to indicate to you the best possible path you can take, think of it like coins but more specific.)
This game features smoothly animated hand-drawn graphics and shows an incredible amount of attention to detail, without obtrustructing the gameplay. Leaves fall gracefully when you dust them away, old attics have a neglected ambience to them, it all fits together wonderfully.
The soundtrack is worth mentioning on its own merit. Many peaceful, relaxing or energetic tunes for this surprisingly high-octane game make playing it a pleasure. I can't properly put it into words but I think this game is worth buying for the music alone.
The game also features multiplayer and a plethora of custom levels with a wide community. I haven't really tried it out myself though.
In conclusion, a lovely game that I honestly should spend more time playing.

It's a pretty good game in general for people who like things like Fallout 2 and such, however there are a few problems that just makes me not being able to recomend this game.
The first one is the developers not really listening to player imput. They have their idea of the game and they will not change things that are clearly bad design just because they are trying to be different... They at least do fix bugs and try to get everything in working order as soon as possible, but the development will not be influenced in any way, shape or form by the players even if certain mechanics are bad or things are not balanced properly.
And that pretty much is the rest of the problems of the game.
Balance between different combatstyles highly vary with some being absolute overkill and others not being good at all. Granted the game hasn't launched yet so there may be some more balancing down the line to make this better, however I wouldn't hope things will be balance at launch, in fact I don't expect them to be balanced in any other way than mods.
The game like so many others in the genre has a carry weight limit and very early on it will seem like this is ok, until you start finding things like sledgehammers and metal armor which weight far too much and make even a very high strenght character barely be able to carry anything... I can understand realism but a game is supposed to be a game at the end of the day and carry weight only do one thing which is breaking game immersion by forcing you to constantly stop what you are doing to go unload. This is made worse with the game having respawns in some areas.
Worst than that is the vendor system. Now many games in the genre have vendors with limited supply of money and this much is part of Underrail, but if the problem was that alone it would be fine, however Underail also features vendors who only buy certain amount of items and in limited quantities too. What this means is that you can never sell all your loot, you'll be forced to leave a lot of loot behind or wait for vendor reset which I belive happens every 45 minutes.
So what does this means? Well you've cleared a place, you've spent a very long time going back and forth placing all your items in some container with easy reach, now you only have to sit next to the vendors for 3 hours to maybe be able to sell everything... So yeah the game pretty much forces you to leave stuff behind. Now even if you leave stuff behind you'll still have more money than you'll ever need, that is not the problem. The problem is that if you are not rewarded to go out of your way and explore, you might as well just do the main missions and rush for the end. There is no incentive to go out of your way and do side questing nor exploring.
Remember the above problem? Well you still have too much money, that is yet another problem of the game. You can buy anything you need at any time which means the economy is not good at all. You'll only ever be without money very early on but quickly you'll go from no money to I can buy the entire store.
Then we come to the crafting. It has been made slightly worse in some aspects, it was made better in anothers. There are some feats now to improve crafting but overall, crafting still isn't worth that much. Crafting doesn't keeps you ahead of the curve. For the most part of the game you will buy/find better weapons than what you can craft and when you finally start being able to craft better stuff, you are really close to the end of the game. No point in investing in something that will only pay off in the end, not to mention that you won't even need the bonus.
And these are the major problems with the game. It really is a shame because when i first played it the only problem was the crafting. All other problems didn't exist (well there might still have been some balance issues but they weren't as bad). the game has a lot of depth to it, from character creation to character development and to how you engage in combat. The story is ok as far as I've seen. Definitly not Obsidian level by any means but still good enough.
The game had all the opportunities to be the next Fallout. Granted with a bit of a Metro spin on it. Hero of the Kingdom II is a very casual and relaxed game. There's no stress, no time limits and no 'action' to speak of. It's entirely based around economic puzzles; gathering resources in many forms and bringing them together to progress. Some you need to spend, others stay with you. It's simple enough, with the real test being the ability to remember where and how to get what you need. For an example, remembering how to get hay when later in the game you end up needing some for a cow's bedding. -- And yes, that's about how the average quest goes. You'll be slaying monsters as well, but you do it in the exact same manner. "Now where can I get a shield, a mercenary and a torch to slay a giant spider?"
Even then, it's fun. It's very genuinely fun. I do need to warn you that the story, writing and dialogue are all awful. It is a very fun game to play with friends. One of my favorite indie games.

+ Cyril Megem, the 1 sole developer who has worked on this game for over 5 years made something absolutely unbelievable. He is the game designer, artist, and programmer.....and he made Warshift.
+ The graphics are AMAZING, there is so much detail on the ground or up in the sky. The explosions, the vehicles, the environments, the atmosphere, everything feels like a AAA game. You could honestly say this is one of the best looking RTS games to have ever been released.
+ The gameplay is innovative! You can play the game like a normal RTS from a top view perspective building a base, an army, and strategizing when to attack and defend. However, you also have a special "commander" unit which you can actually take full control of and play like a 3rd person action shooter.
+ Some of the "Commander" units can transform and instantly go from ground to air to sea, and it feels and looks GREAT!
+ There is a ton of upgrades that you can purchase for your commander units as you level him up by using him to destroy enemy units, and these iniclude a large diverse selection of weapons.
+ The levels themselves are VERY LARGE with plenty of space to navigate around, and are all have diverse environments. One is even in space!
+ The controls feel great as you seemlessly switch from Strategy to Action Mode, and then from Ground to Air to Sea vehicles. They are all user friendly, and easy to learn, almost natural in fact.
+ Epic soundtrack
- The campaign is very short and consists of 10 levels + 4 tutorial levels which will take about 2 hours to complete.
- There isn't much of a story or characters development which is a bit unfortunate as the missions don't feel very rewarding.
- I felt like the enemy AI cheats at times, instantly rebuilding turrets, or have commander units that can obliterate my units in 1 hit and then go invisible and run away before I could even react.
- The AI of your own units can be very stupid, and they will often decide to randomly drive across the map to their own doom when you are not looking. Disabling the AI control will make it so they can not attack when an enemy gets close without your command.

Overall opinion: Great game once you get into it, however the learning curve is steep and tutorials minimal. Would definitely recommend it for anyone interested in these types of games.
More detailed info that may or may not help in determining whether *you* would like this game:
1. This game is difficult to get into. There are in game tutorials that explain things briefly - but that's exactly what it is, they only explain things. There's no Age of Empires style "Draw a box around your units, and move them from flag to flag" style of introduction - it's text boxes and some flashing buttons showing where what buttons are, but never going into too much detail. Watch a beginner's guide or tutorial on Youtube instead, or just get into a game and see what goes where by trial and error.
2. The game is very open-ended - there is no set goal other than to make sure your dynasty member is always in control of at least one county. If that fails, it's game over. (Incidentally, this makes every playthrough different.) You can set your own goals or see where the game takes you (my last game ended up with Ireland converted to Russian culture, and Holy Roman Empire fully converted to an Orthodox heresy) - there is just something so satisfying in seeing all the pieces of the puzzle fall into place, and the master plan coming to completion.
3. Graphics are functional. Not the highest quality, but they show what is required effectively. This game doesn't seem to be too taxing on the computer.
4. There is no direct control over a character. The "you" character will be a portrait and stats screen, and random (to an extent?) events displayed as pop-up windows will provide you with choices that you can take for your character, which may provide your character with better (or worse) stats or traits. These random events often involve RNG too, so it's always a careful gamble on which option to pick - there rarely is a "better than all others" option - it's all carefully balanced trade-offs.
5. There is very little micromanagement to economy.
6. There is very little micromanagement to armies and war.
7. There is a lot of micromanagement when it comes to politics, scheming, plotting, and political marriages. This is the bread and butter of the game.
8. Game soundtrack is good, and varied enough to not get boring - you'll be listening to it a lot, as the only other sounds are various notification sounds. There's a folder with the game soundtrack files, so you *may* be able to use your own music instead. Don't take my word on this though.
9. Writing behind random (and not so random) events is great! There's a sense of humor, and vague references to real historical events or tales, reading them never gets boring. You may get the same event portrayed from different characters' perspectives too (if you happen to get the same event with different characters in different positions), and see that there's more to the event than either situation alone would tell you.
Last but not least: there's a demo of this game available on Steam - at least was on the time of writing this review. If you're at all uncertain regarding whether you'd like this game, give the demo a try. This game is definitely not to everyone's tastes. I'm really enjoying the 100+ hours I've played so far, and I feel like I'm only starting to get into it - based on that, I'd definitely recommend trying the game if you're into grand strategy games, but not necessarily into micromanaging battles or economy.

An unrealistic and overly technical political simulator, buggy even at this late stage, with extremely weak military aspects.
When you aren't inexplicably 'forced' into peace due to a 'war score' percentage, money magically vanishing from your accounts as a reward for the victor even if he has no army or possibility of victory (or means of taking the money) then expect to be trapped in an endless grind for the tiniest scraps of money, staring listelessly for hours at the successions of a dynasty before you're permitted to interact in any meaningful fashion.
I'm amazed I'm saying this, but even the Total War games, silly as they are, offer a more realistic, involved and entertaining experience than this game - if only because of the lack of arbitrary, illogical rules relating to declarations of war.
There's no underdog here, no flexibility or opportunity. Do not expect to take a nation from humble beginnings to greatness. Only the colossal nations in the preset historical bookmarks can effectively grow.
The Paradox view of history is that it functioned as a machine according to strict rules, and that even 'plots' and 'intrigue' could only be carried out according to a manual of etiquette with no logical coherence.
If you don't relish the idea of a family management game, in which you'll spend 80% of your time waiting, 15% arranging marriages and 5% staring, bemused, at the latest bug or crash report, play something else.

So far I'd say I have spent more time in the hangar costumizing my fleet and trying to figure out the best trade offs to be made than actually blowing up enemy ships. This game has a very decent variety of weapons, sub systems, mounts, armors, shields, engines and all that good stuff you can apply to your ships in order to costumize them. Ships of all classes and sizes are available (fighters, support ships, battleships, mining ships, mass bomb carriers), you just have to unlock them by a very simple unlock system (blow up the ship you want and collect its black box from the remains). After I played the first one some time ago I thought it a good idea to test the waters in the second game. Catching it while it's on sale for release is a good idea. I finished the game with 5 hours on my steam clock, but that was also idling for about 25 minutes off PC. Is it worth the time/cash ratio? I think so.
The game is identical in how it feels to the first game. Great artwork, tons of collectables, a relaxed soundtrack with a nice atmosphere for it. All in all the game really does feel fairly polished. There was a really annoying quest which seemed to ask for unreasonable things as it felt still early in the game however you can scrounge around testing your detective skills by finding necessities along your quest. I also feel like this one is actually possible to lose if you mismanage your materials before you get to a point where you could properly take advantage of all locations that offer a chance to make some money.
There might be a bit more balancing yet to come however the game is definitely possible to complete somewhat easily. For the style of game I'd say the only thing it's missing is a way to track quests. I had to cycle the map a few times to remember what my quests needed when I was processing a few at a time. The only thing that really peeved me at all would have to be when buying/selling lots of materials the button to do so really has an annoying delay. Mind you extremely minor and in no way really affects the game.
As with the first game there's next to no replayability outside of enjoying the story again. Adding to that the story is not exactly ground breaking or outstanding but it is detailed enough to at least give you a nice sense of what the character is feeling. With significantly more battles to take part in though could spend a good hour just killing things.
So if you can pick this up while still on sale, it's worth the small pricetag I believe. If you don't have a sharp eye you might spend a fair bit of time just looking for everything which adds a bit of it's own 'I spy' feeling to it. Rating on the style of the game I'd give it an 8.5/10. Could have been longer and would have liked to see maybe temporary areas with loot for one time chances, or map extensions and more quests.

I went into the game with a mindset of not wanting to think much and just wanted something relaxing and casual. Hero of the Kingdom definitely provides that. The story is simplistic with some predictable twists and turns but nevertheless the overall resource management present in the game and some hidden object finding makes the game interesting enough for me to complete it. The background music is nice and certainly fits the theme of the game really well. It varies accordingly to the situation and the different sound effects does enhance the story telling by a bit.
I would love to see the game ported to mobile devices.
All that said, I must play more hidden object games to see give any comparisons of any sorts.

Rapture. It's been a while. Welcome back to the city of dreams, built by the illustrious Andrew Ryan in an attempt to build the perfect place where the wealthy and prestegious may live their lives as they deem fit. Unfortunately for you, they deemed that taking  a whole crap-ton of the gene altering drug ADAM was fit. Oh, and also stuffing you inside a suit of armor and forcing your only goal in life to be protecting a drugged up, sick, twisted child. So there's that.
That's right, in this sequel you play as your worst enemy from the first game, a Big Daddy. Turns out, its been about eight or so years since you played as Jack in the first game. A lot has changed since then. Now, not only do you have to deal with Big Daddys, but also Brute Splicers, which are giant bulky versions of the normal Splicer type, as well as Big Sisters, which are Little Sisters who grew up and were weaponized.
In terms of story, there was no way that this game was ever going to live up to the original Bioshock. However, it still does a fairly decent job of providing a gripping narrative, while not quite as shocking. The second half of the game is where this plot really shines, though I won't go into too much detail.
There were several improvements to the gameplay that I found worth mentioning. First off, that hacking minigame is gone thank the Lord! Instead, we are given a realtime hacking game where you simply have to press the button when the arrow is in the green zone. Much less irritating and less time consuming. Also, we are given a hacking weapon that allows us to hack from a distance! And also place tiny turrets, which I think I used once. That was how useful it was.
The thing that bugged me the most while playing was the Little Sister protection Mini-Games. I feel like it was simply to buffer game play time (the game is considerably shorter than the original) and they were not fun! When you kill a Big Daddy, you are given the option to adopt a little sister to gain more ADAM. She does this by leading you to bodies, and then harvesting the ADAM from the corpse, which would be fine and dandy if it didn't take a million years and you weren't brutally attacked by half the enemies in the entire freaking game. And you had to do this twice per Little Sister. I eventually just stopped, because I had enough ADAM that it wasn't even worth it.
My main complaint about this Remastered version was that originally, the game refused to start. When I got to the end of the loading screen and tried to start the game, it immediately crashed. I was forced to go into one of the game files and change a number from a 2 to a 1, which you can find a fix for by searching "Press Space to Crash" in Google or whatever search engine you use. Unfortunately, while this fixed the crash for starting the game, there were still several crashes that I experienced ingame. The only advice I have for that, is save. Save constantly, after every big fight or anything.
All in all, I enjoyed Bioshock 2. While the Remastered version has its problems, I would not let that be the only deciding factor for purchasing this game. If you enjoyed the first game, do yourself a favor and just play this one. Good luck! And watch out for those Big Sisters, okay?

Great platformer. The level design is the best I've seen from an indie game - each level has themes that are developed without ever being too repetitive, and yet it all fits into the game's core gameplay without any need for one-off mechanical gimmicks. Restarting is fast and stages never have any sections that are too easy or make you wait too much.
The levels are somewhat long and yet more lenient compared to other games in the "hard platforming" subgenre, which results in lots of proper, well-paced tension while playing, whether in trying to recover form a failure or from finishing the last section of a level. Far too many of said platformers get stuck in lolhard-land, where fun comes down to retrying pixel-perfect jumps in a 10-second level hundreds of times.
My only serious criticism is perhaps about visuals getting in the way of gameplay. For one, the fluid animations can get in the way of understanding the actual coordinates of your character, which is especially frustrating when dealing with dust blocks. Also, there is no way to immediately see if you have jump charge or not. That is something I'd say would be a much better use of the glowy aura than the special attack, which can be seen at the bottom of the screen or outright memorised for certain sections of a level.
A minor complaint is with how poorly the game explains some of its controls. That's somehat aggravating given how you're required to know unintuitive techniques you're never told about to access certain levels. For instance, the fact that you can slide off a U-shaped ceiling and back into a wall without jumping if you have enough speed.

Without writing a full novel here, the bottom line is, this game will reward you with an old-school experience of a proper RPG. If you're yearning for something akin to the old Fallouts, buy this and you won't regret it.

The good:
It's a fun surivial game that lets you tame dinosaurs and keep them as pets, allowing you ride them around on land, in the air, or underwater.  The dinos also level up over time as you use them, giving you a choice of stat points to make them stronger, faster, carry more weight, etc.  There are multiple maps to explore with different dinos available on each one, and even the option to transfer your character, items, and dinos to other maps, only leaving the structures you built behind.  I'm still learning all the things you can do in this game even though i'm nearing 100 hours into it already, but its been very enjoyable to explore and figure things out as i go.
The bad:
Very grindy unless you are on a server with increased rates, especially the taming process.  Even on a server with increased rates it could still take hours to tame some dinos, even longer for high level ones.  Not only that, but you have to babysit them to keep them tranquilized and fed while they are being tamed, if you run out of materials before they are tamed then you better hope you find some more nearby.  The flyers are also very dumb sometimes, if you have them help you in battle they will occationally chase the enemy down and abandon you completely, either getting themselves killed or lost in the process which is extremely frustrating.
Overall it is a fun game to play solo or on a dedicated server with friends so you can setup the exp/drop/tame rates and other stuff to make things more enjoyable for everyone.

SPAZ is yet another game that the screenshots and trailers do no justice. The game was made by only two people.
The universe you are set in is randomly generated and has a small amount of customization in size. The smaller the universe, the harder the difficulty between each galaxy. The bigger the universe, the longer the overall game and the more stretched out resources are. The game tells you not to do your first playthrough on the hardest difficulty. I immediately went and ignored this because I love a good challenge.
And boy does SPAZ deliver. You have up to three of your own ships in play at once. You can manually control one of the three ships at any time and the AI will take over the other two. The combat can go beyond mindlessly killing at times in the harder difficulties and thought is needed to plan out what you are going to do. Getting a game over is rare but progression is also challenging.
Good for casual and hardcore players. I'd write more but I've run out of room.

Do I recommend this game?
Sorta.
I'm not sure where to start, so let me tell you all the good parts.
Positive Critiques:
First off, the game is free, which is awesome!
When you first load in, the amount of options is amazing!
Everything you do is up to you: Your play-style, where you go, and who you face!
The story is very good and they are constantly adding to it.
The most recent update (at the time) added "The Plains of Eidolon," which adds an entirely new landscape that is huge.
You can do tons of bounties to explore and conquer throughout the plains, each with varying difficulties.
There are tons of planets, factions, weapons, and other players to join you in your adventures.
Speaking of players, there are so many people that are willing to join you!
One under-appreciated factor is the optimization. You can run this game on almost anything.
I have a low-tier gaming PC and I run this game at maximum settings (Which is gorgeous) with at least 200 fps everywhere!
You can check my profile for my PC stats :)
Negative Critiques:
First off, this game takes alot of time, unless you are willing to buy in-game currency then it isn't as bad.
At first, there is alot to do and progress is happening the whole time, until you decide to do more interesting things.
Let's say you decide you want this new weapon. Well, you can't just buy it, trading for the exact parts takes alot of time and patience, and farming for the loot takes FOREVER.
While there is alot to do, it can start to feel stale after only a few hours or so. Each mission ends up feeling like the same thing, just in a different location. I personally take breaks a week or two at a time.
Conclusion:
The game is good, it just takes alot of time and patience to fully enjoy it. It is more fun with friends and a clan than by yourself by a long shot. Optimization is very good, plus IT'S FREE!

In my opinion Dustforce is the best game ever made, at least in the platform genre. As mentioned before, Dustforce deserved all the attention and fame Super Meat Boy has gotten. Sadly. Dustforce somehow just didn't make it to be the mainstream, popular and acclaimed platformer it deserved to be.

Once you get comfortable with the movements, dashing, and  attacking enemies, there shouldn't be any problems in reproducing the same moves over and over again.
The soundtrack is great, the graphics are fine, and there aren't really any negatives I could mention. There isn't any reason why you shouldn't pick this up for such a low price.

This is one of my favorite games. The controls and movement feel so good. In the beginning when you haven't learned the mechanics it feels sort of clunky, but as you improve the game develops a really nice flow. This makes mastering levels really satifying. In most platformers I just want to make it through each level and move on. This was the first game where I found myself revisiting levels just because I wanted to do a better job.
Another great part of this game is the way they handle the learning curve. There are plenty of levels that a beginner can approach, and each of these helps teach you the tricks and strategies you'll need to tackle the more difficult parts. They never spoon-feed you any technique, but instead let you develop it yourself as you work your way through. It almost feels like your character is leveling up and learning new abilities throughout the game, but it's actually just you getting better.

After playing ARK for nearly 500 hours since buying it in Early Access, and recently buying the new Abberation expansion, I feel I can finally write a proper review of ARK. For me, my feelings of ARK are very mixed. I have a very love-hate relationship with this game. While I want to love the game and recommend it to my dino-loving friends, I simply can't, because the core game mechanics are so unforgiving, and the game quickly becomes frustrating and unrewarding. Some people enjoy this, but as someone with a job (like everyone else) and plays games for fun in the evenings, If it wasn't for cheats and mods, I would have given up on ARK a very long time ago. And while I give credit to Wildcard for doing sponsored mods that add a lot more fun to the game, I can't suggest the vanilla game by itself because of this reason, as much as I would really like to.
I love the game because;
- It has amazing graphics, with gorgeous environments and dinosaurs which spawn in an array of beautiful colour combinations. I love the designs of the new creatures and environments of the new Abberation expansion, as well.
- Some of the best dinosaur models and animations I've seen in a game, and I'm looking forward to the dinosaur TLC pass soon on it's way!
- I loved the base building part of the game. It allows you as a player to be as creative as you want, whether you enjoy creating enclosures for your dino's or making unraidable fortresses.
- Enjoyed exploring the map to find the dossiers, and uncover the story of ARK, which adds a bit more purpose if you're just play PvE, like I did.
- Inclusion of bosses in the game to add more purpose to the PvE experience.
But, I also hate this game, because:
- It is incredibly unforgiving, and quickly becomes unrewarding.
- An entire evening can be spent gathering resouces and building what you need, only for them to be taken away in an instant due to how easy it is to be killed in the game. This is where you rack up hundreds of hours in the game, and it becomes repetitive and frustrasting.
- Taming dinosaurs take far too long, unless you are on single player or a server where the taming time has been drastically reduced. This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't so easy to lose your hard-earned dinos in the game, having to start again.
- The building mechanics are very frustrating. The snap points are unreliable, and buggy. You can't pick something up again once you have placed it, having to destory it in which you only get back half the resources you used to build it with, so you then have to gather the rest of the resources again to build it again. This is also where all the hours start to rack up, given that the buggy snap points make it so easy to misplace something.
- Dinos constantly get stuck on trees and rocks. It's very easy for you and your dinos to get stuck somewhere, and if you have dinos following you, it quickly becomes a slow, arduous task to try and travel across the map.
There are probably points I have missed, but I just wanted to focus on the main mechanics of the game for my review. If there was a 'neutral' or 'mixed' option I would have gone for that, but since there is only a yes or no option, I have gone for yes, because despite the game being the most frustrating and irritating game I have played, I have enjoyed it, as well. But I really wouldn't pay £50 for it.
I've spent a lot of hours in ARK using mods to make fun dinosaur enclosures, as well as exploring the beautiful environments. But I honestly can't say once games like Jurassic Park: Evolution and Monster Hunter World comes out, if I will come back to play ARK much.
Finally, if you do plan to buy this game, just be prepared to die A LOT, rebuild a lot, and wait around a lot. And then repeat that, again and again.

This is the FIRST early access game which I purchased and didn't feel like I was robbed in broad daylight - and I've tried a few. This hidden gem, which took me a while to find, turned out to be one of the most addictive, immersive, challenging games I'd played in quite a while. If you loved the Jagged Alliance series, the original Deus Ex, Fallout and Shadowrun -- this game takes a lot of what made those games great and puts it all in one neat little package. I've found this game to be relatively challenging, but not in an annoying way - there are always multiple solutions for pretty much any situation one might find themself in. The graphics aren't the most amazing thing on the market, but I got used to them fairly quickly - they do have some character of their own, and do well to immerse one in the game. Almost 20 hours in, and it still feels like I am learning, like everything is still brand new. Very impressed with this game, particularly the writing, the design and the mechanics. This game is pretty much a must-have for those interested in turn-based RPG adventures and for under $10, buying it is a no-brainer.

I basically have everything set to epic, grass to middle (for both) but shadows to medium (for terrain) and low (general shadows). This game has literally blown my mind. I started from zero with my son on the Ragnarok map and this game is easily the best purchase I have made in years. There is so much to do, so much to see and explore. There are dungeons, ruins, caves, weird advanced tech and even notes from explorers long gone. In a way this is the game that looks how No Man's Sky should have looked like. Huge dino's that actually have varied animations, and decent AI. They do sometimes get stuck, but to be honest seeing a T-Rex devour countless creatures and just watching AI battles from a safe distance never gets old!
I could go on and on about this game.
Anyone unsure about purchasing this game should only worry if they have a low end video card. The game itself has incredible attention to detail. Even your hair grows with time and you need to cut it. Personally this game feels like a mix between most survival games, with a pinch of SIMS, Pokemon and games like Skyrim/Oblivion (but without questing or human npcs).
It is amazing - just trust me on this. I am a super whiney person and I have enjoyed bonding with my son over this game.

This is the first review for a game I have done, but this game has earned that honor.
I've played one solid session of about 10 hrs and the ride was crazy to say the least. I went from moments of shear joy and excitement as I tamed my first trike and pack of 3 raptors, to moments of pure rage and anger as I got murdered time after time by that stupid rex sized bird/Godzilla hybrid from hell (Therizinosaur).
I started on the south east corner of the island, on of the “easy” areas. Took my time figuring out controls and how everything worked. Before too long I had a small house and was advancing to lvl 20. I tamed my first trike, followed by a few raptors. I didn't mess with any of the dinos that were bigger than me because they looked like they could ruin my life. But then it happened, the Therizinosaur that had left me alone for 8 hours decided "hey lets go ruin this noobs life".....and that is what he did. It was dark when he first attacked, I was hanging out by my small house, doing what I don't remember, my dinos were set to roam around so they were not around. I lit a torch, was turning around when then music changed and there it was, the Therizinosaur, like the Spector of Death.....it was over in less than 3 seconds, I was dead, thrown who knows how far by his razor claws. Normally I wouldn't care, I had died many times already, however this was different, before I made it to the respawn screen, I saw written in red, that the same Therizinosaur that killed me, proceeded to murder my dinos, the ones I and grown to love and care for. He murdered all 4 of them, all while I was lying dead on the ground.
Words cannot describe the hatred I felt at that point, I normally don't get this invested into a game, but this was different, this was personal. HE WAS GOING TO DIE! I would kill him in his sleep!
So, that became my purpose in life for the next hour. I got everything I needed to build a stone towers, plenty of tranq arrows to knock his @ss out, and a pike to impale him on, and then I would hack him up to pieces. After a while I was ready for revenge.
I lured the pos to the tower and proceeded to turn him into a pincushion with tranq arrows. Needless to say I knocked him out. I wish this is where the story ended, with revenge completed and rebuilding begun. But that would be to easy. As I delivered the first few pike thrusts I heard something getting closer. Frantically I looked around, and there they were, two more Therizinosaurs within spitting distance, and they were coming straight for me. They tables had turned on me once again, the two Therizinosaurs tore me apart. Now my home is surrounded by 3 Therizinosaurs who don’t want to leave, have killed me who knows how many times, murdered my pets and countered my attack in a manner that let me just staring at the screen in disbelief. It was at this point I googled the Therizinosaur, and just to add insult to injury, found out it was a MF Herbivore!!!!
Needless to say, this game is hard, but that won’t stop me from exacting my revenge, I will now murder all three of those Therizinosaurs for what they have done to me and my family……
10/10 would watch myself and pets get murdered, followed mission of revenge and hate any day of the week!
