Youtubers Life is a Strategy / Simulation game where you have to design your own YouTube-Channel. So far there are 2 different channel types between which you can choose: Gaming and music.
Gaming: Haven't played it for quite some time, so my experience is limited to the earlier stages of the game, but it was always pretty funny and entertaining. It never feels to easy or to hard to play, you always have to work for your money at the start and things get easier from time to time, as soon as masses will follow you.
The card mechanic in editing your videos is pretty cool, even though I think there might be a bit more potential in this since it doesn't feel like you've got a choice on the order in which the active cards will be given to you to choose 1 out of 3.
Lately I've been playing the music channel and besides some bugs, which are not that bad in general, get fixed pretty quickly (more about that later) and are to be expected since it's an Early Acces Game, it feels really good.
The music channel is a pretty cool new way to become famous on the virtual YouTube-platform and for me it feels a bit harder than it was for the gaming channel, but that's not to be meant as a negative point.
You've got to buy instruments and music rights on your songs (or write your own ones) instead of buying consoles and games.
The core game stays the same and that's good, since the new channel option isn't meant to be a new game, it's just another way to play the same game, always keep that in mind.
New features are the option to play concerts live on stage and with the live concert-feature, there has also been a new feature to determin whether the result will be good or not (on live-concerts only):
It's a bit like a guitar-hero minigame and it fits really good, exept for the small bugs, but as already mentioned, it's a BETA, so if you play this game now, expect bugs.
And now for the last point of my written review:
The developers and how they react to feedback, etc.:
I've reported a few bugs by now that I've come across in this game and I'm really amazed by the speed and quality of the developers here in the steam-forum. It usually takes less than 1h for a dev to answer your bug report / feedback / whatever and for my reported bugs it took about 1-2 weeks to have them fixed. That's not just fast, in support-developer cooperation terms that's supersonic speed! I know I'm not the only one to report most of those bugs, but still, I've got to say, that's really amazing!
Now for my conclusion:
Stability: 10/10 (no crashes or similar)
Graphics: 7/10 (I don't think it's necessary to have GTA V-like graphics here, to that's alright that way. Like this it's also less ressource-draining, which is also a good point.)
Sound: 3/10 (While creating videos you'll get the same sound effects (shoutouts from your character) time and time again, which is pretty annoying, and while recording music / playing live concert there is no sound, so that could be improved in the future).
Gameplay: 7/10 (Short-time: Lots of fun, really interesting; Long time: Pretty entertaining, but repeating content a bit, but not that bad)
Bug-fix: 10/10 (Never seen such a good support on any other game. Awesome!)
Final: 7/10

Also, the dinosaurs are SO clippy, they're constantly locking you in place by glitching into you, knocking you off something, or getting themselves stuck somewhere.
Basically, this game makes you grind and grind to get to experience high quality, albeit dramatically unoptomized graphics. To be clear, I have a really powerful PC. 1440p@144hz monitor and a 4k@60hz monitor paired with a GTX 1080 TI, 16GBs of 3200MHZ DDR4 ram, i7 6700K, m.2 SSD. This game still performs very poorly at non-max settings (like often dipping into the low to mid 20FPS).
If you want pay for this game and play on a private server to test it out, mod the hell out of it and go in with very low expectations other than being able to experience the visual gimmicks, because the "quality" content stops there. The game is an extreme disappointment if you go in excited and wanting to invest serious time into it.

Youtubers Life is a fun little cartoony game, that being said the price is a little too high and I would reccomend somwhere near 8 USD. The downside to the game is that at first, it has a very nice steady paste with unique events but eventually becomes repetitive hard work the further you get. This style caused alot of youtubers to play it which skyrocketed its popularity but after a single run, they all quit and never came back, and I think that's most of the audience right now.
Now that's not to say it's bad. At first, the game was a big hit and everyone was playing it, but as time went on, the game slowly dropped until it became pretty unpopular but the people who tried it for themselves (besides the actual youtubers) stuck around and instead of the developers ceasing most developement due to lost popularity, they still went and updated it quite a bit to the point where a whole new channel type was added in.
In terms of graphics, the game feels a little recycled because 1. Most of the clothing is retextures 2. Most of the models aren't that different and alot of them are re-used even though that looks bad 3. Overall, the graphics were recycled and cheap excuses but the lighting & particles are good
I like how the game has a bit of a life simulation aspect added in which broadens the activity board if you ever get bored of just doing youtubing. Speaking of broadening, the game is supposed to have gaming, music, fashion, lifestyle and cooking as cannle types. This is a little reasonable although most youtubers do 1. games 2. pranks 3. fashion so it's gonna be unique in that aspect. Now that would be fine with me except that since they don't exactly have a big developement team, broadening the scale causes each individual channel type to feel like (for the most part,) the same so it actually loses a bit of its quality.
The sound is nice and some of the tunes (for example, the halloween song) but the voice acting is terrible because they didn't make it even remotely similar so every voice is very different (which shouldn't occur if they all speak the same fictional giberish language).
One big thing that angers most people though, is how you're expected to make more and more videos based on how many subscribers you currently have. This might not sound too bad but near the end-game, you're forced to make videos left and right to fufill the needs of your fanbase, and while they do have collaberators to try and make things easier, you can't take a break even if you wanted to which is really annoying and starts to ruin the game.
Overall on a scale of 10, I would currently give it an 8 because while it is a fun little youtubers game with just the right amount of extra life simulation to make it fun at certain times, it still get repetitive and hard as it progresses which starts to make it less and less fun.

While buying the base game in itself is not that expensive Paradox tends to keep making new content about twice a year, while it's very nice and adds replayabiltiy it brings about three major problems and one minor one.
1. Every year you will spend $30 bucks.
2. Not buying it means the version you are playing will introduce features that make the game feel off as new mechanics are built around content that is blocked off to you.
3.As the mechanics change so do a lot of the rules, so suddenly you find yourself in a situation where you go to bed with a stable empire in a game you've been playing 50 plus hours from 860 - 1330 only to find yourself in a massive civil war because the numbers where arbitrarily changed.
The game has a few unbalancing issues, it's really hard at the beginning until you start snowballing. Unfortunately the mechanics to try alleviating the snowball effect (liberation armies, adventurers) will either crush you because you were too small or they will be an annoyance at best (sometimes a too frequent one at that) There is little to no reward for facing these challenges. It does however let you occasionally loose, sometimes you get beaten, sometimes your plans fail and it's not game over (Unless it is however one of those adventurers then your hosed.)
The games positive aspects are pretty amusing and I could spend hours talking about the time my son assassinated me to take the throne or you skillfully killed, manipulated and set up that sweet moment. The AI does occasionally goof but the moments where things come together far outshine it... Unless you're playing small... Never, EVER play small, start small maybe but never stay small. Unfortunately there are often times when you're just sitting there waiting and twiddling your thumbs... it seems to become less of an issue, (With DLC of course) yet if you're playing as a Catholic or Muslim surrounded by others of your same faith you could be spending ages with nothing to really do... The Arch Duke of God let me do something fun before this person dies.
Combat is pretty much a numbers game, although there are times when tactics and troop composition DO matter so it's something to pay attention to.
Finally Multiplayer... is very janky...very very janky.

There is a bit of a learning curve up front, but this game is a gem once you get going. Along the lines of Starscape (which I've previously recommended), you are gradually exploring the galaxy using small ships deployed from a larger mothership. As you go, you will develop relationships with local civilian or military factions, fighting missions for them to gain experience and advance your research. Upgrade all aspects of your mothership and deployable crafts, and iteratively gain the ability to explore more of the galaxy.
Oh yes, and there's zombies, too. Good times.

I Can't Escape: Darkness is the spiritual successor to "I Can't Escape" (feels like a direct successor :P). The gameplay has been polished up, a bit more depth added, and visually improved. The audio is also superior.
Pros:
- Replayability is high due to Procedural Generation of mazes/dungeon.
- It's not a "Jump Scare" game, but rather a tension building game as your resources dwindle in increasingly difficult areas.
- Music and Atmosphere is very strong* (* - see caveat in cons)
- Distinct Style and polished feel make it superior to the previous iteration of the game
Cons:
- Some of the sound effects are a bit weak (the music at atmosphere noises are great though)
- Hard to notice when an enemy is attacking/approaching you, and the direction isn't clearly stated (a necessity in this type of game movement)
Notes:
- Won't give you an immediate adrenaline rush for any moment that I found, instead focuses on the slow burn approach (suspense)
- Is definitely an indie title, with a limited budget - the graphics are 'good', but won't blow you away.
- Fairly low system requirements make it easily accessible
- Game Session Length is pretty short, save function is optional though in case you don't have the time to commit. (I very rarely had sessions over 30 minutes).
If you'd like to see the game in action, I did make a video, but only loosely cover the pros/cons in it (felt an itemized list was better saved for the text review)

Crusader Kings 2 isn't fun for a guy that enjoys a conquering-type of wargame.  CK2 feels like a medievil relationship game (like Sims almost) instead of a conquest game. The 'Metro' games are excellent. They are based off the popular post apocalyptic fiction book by Dmitri Glukhovsky. Metro Last Light does not follow the story line in the book, instead it is a direct sequel to Metro 2033 (the game and book). Metro LL (last light) is a game I believe everyone should try.
If you have heard of this game, which you probably have, it is not unknown that this game is visually outstanding. On my GTX 970 I had the game maxed out with a high framerate, well the majority of the time. Entering the mission often made my frames drop but thats too be expected with this game. The attention to detail is phenomenal, every part of the Metro has been carefully engineered with precision to create the look of a worn and dying civilization. This attention to detail creates an immersive and atmospheric game.
Just like the original game Metro 2033, Metro: Last Light is played from the perspective of Artyom, your player character. The story takes place in post-apocalyptic Moscow, mostly inside the metro system, but occasionally missions bring you above ground.
As a first person shooter, the gunplay has to be perfect if the developers wish for success, they have got it right. There is a small selection of weapons, which was suprising, but the customisation compensates for that. Who needs a sniper when you can find a revolver and add an IR sight and a stock; even a suppressor for you stealth fanatics.
The games plot is excellent. The Metro is very atmospheric and immersive thanks too the excellent graphics, the slow paced solo guitar music and the excellent plot. I won't go into detail as I don't want to ruin the stroy for anyone who hasn't had the pleasure of experiencing the Metro games. Essentially you, Artyom, wipe out the Dark Ones with a plethora of nuclear bombs- or so you thought. Intense radiation plagues the streets; which has caused mutation in many species turning them violent, untamable and monstrous.On the way you meet people , meet the civilizations (Hanza, Reich, The Order) and have a great time. There is a sexual nature to some of the scenes so do take that into account. The game does seem to throw enemies at you sometimes which to me could be the downfall of the gameplay.
The music is good in this game, as of now I don't have a good headset so the audio isn't of a good quality; but the music and sounds in this game were great. One of my weaknesses in games is that I somehow block out music and it tends not to register in my mind, or my brain disregards it- but I have listened to the starting music multiple times and it creates an aura of atmopshere, a post apocalyptic atmopshere. As you listen you can imagine the sadness in the citizens of the Metro, its played by one person- with a guitar ,I'm not sure which type. He is playing slow notes in a memorable tune which masterfully creates atmopshere.
The gunshots in this game sound on par with modern military games which is great, the sounds of the beast are definately threatening and after you encounter one, you are always weary of hearing a battlecry of the beasts.
As this game is set in Russia, they had to find talented voice actors that could speak English with a Russian accent, they did a good job overall, although some of the charcters were clearly faking the accent which at some point sucked me out of the immersive grip that the Graphics and Gameplay had on me.

Overall this game is a must play from me, works great on PC with keyboard and mouse, and I'm guessing a contoller would work well too. The game has great gunplay and a stellar story line, which can be let down by the feeling that the game throws hordes of enemies at you for nothing else than to make you have more gametime. The music and SFX are good but the voice acting feels lacking for some but most characters are excellently voice acted.

Elsword... truly conflicting on whether to reccomend this game or not. It's truly a fun game when you're starting off. Going from one class to the next, or learning new combos for characters is a great experience. However, when it's all said and done, it's very repetitive. After you've gotten a character past level 40 (Around after your last class change for a character.) It begins to feel like any PvE is copy and pasted, with almost constant use of the same skills, or combos. And for those who like PvP there is a noticable amount of unbalanced characters.(Many people may fight this matter, but some characters /classes have a ridiculous upper hand) whether you decide to play as these characters and have PvP be a complete drag, or fight against them and enjoy fighting a very unfair fight. Also, players can pay to have the ability to use twice as many skills, giving them a large upperhand against those who won't pay in PvP. Overall though, I'd reccomend trying it out. See for yourself, some people really enjoy some of the mechanics of the game, and while it can become a drag. There are some things to coax you to continue playing. So try it out. Other than time, what have you got to lose?

You don't have to switch between weapons and plasmids - you can now set someone on fire and shoot them at the same time. Like to set bees on people? By my guess, oh and don't forget to pin their skulls to the wall. Wanna summon bots and set bees on them too? Oh yeah!
The only BIG issue is that this game will crash - a lot. You'd think the dev would have fix the performance issues but apparently they want to take a leaf out of Cohen's book, tidy it up with graphical upgrade but do nothing about the gameplay issues. AND IT IS SO FRUSTRATING!
The DLC - Protector Trials is a miss for me. While it is interesting to have restriction placed upon you while splicers spit fire and burp lighting all over the place, it got tedious REAL QUICKLY. Like doing it once is fine, but THREE times to get those stars? Really? REALLY?
But Minerva's Den, ah, Minerva's Den. That DLC is worthy of its name and its reputation as one of the the best story-driven DLCs in gaming history. Right next to Dishonored's Knife of Dunwall and Brigmore Witches DLC.
My suggestion is that if you want to buy the remastered version, do some homework about how to minimize the performance issues this game has. DO NOT come in expecting a smooth, non-crashing gameplay, that is a futile wish and not worth your prayers.
Do your homework, search the internet on how to fix the graphical stuttering, audio dropping in and out, texture streaming and the like. Cause apparently developers are demanding players to do their own troubleshooting for stuff they should have ironed out before putting this up in the market.

Styg works really hard on his game, I just wish he spent more of his time working on adding content than changing features that functioned fine as they were. I purchased this game long before it was on Steam (January 2013), and played through it and had a good time getting to the end of what content was there. I then proceeded to play through again another time with a more traditional build than my crossbow/psi build that I had started out with. I'm really glad that I did, too, because I just haven't been able to enjoy the newer versions of the game that have been released since then.
Whereas most games that were short on content likely would have added a lot more content long before now, and not bothered fooling with things that were working as intended, Styg has gone around adding item durability, messing with the XP system, making merchants refuse to buy your loot and other things that frankly haven't benefitted the game in my opinion. If he had spent the time that he has spent messing with the economy adding content I imagine you would be able to get all the way to Core City by now. Instead far too many of the updates over the last year fixing things that weren't necessarily broken.
Styg is devoted to his game, and the product is clearly moving in the direction he wants it to, Underrail is well worth the price of admission and a must play for any fan of the original Fallout games, or turn based tactical role playing in general. The game receives regular updates and has an interesting world to explore, I just wish I hadn't spent so much time in the game before the strange economic changes and dreaded item durability were incorporated, so that I wouldn't have known just how much more fun I would have with it had those changes not been made.

Before playing BioShock 2, I'd heard a lot of mixed reports on it; some saying it was terrible, some saying it was better than the first game, and a lot saying something in between. I managed to generally glean from all this that the gameplay of BioShock 2 is significantly better than BioShock, but the story's worse. Having now played BioShock 2, I can now verify that this is true.
The main premise is that it's eight years after the first game, and some Rapture hotshot—who somehow never got mentioned in the first game, despite apparently having massive power and influence—has made the Objectivist utopia all Orwellian, through some evidently Hitler-level oration ability. (This gave me some System Shock 2 flashbacks, especially when the horribly mutated enemies kept running at me yelling "Join the Unity!" or something similar, although this game was a lot worse at making it clear why Communism is bad.) It's functional enough, but it has the Portal 2 problem where the first game was perfectly good and self-contained by itself, and tacking on an extra plot just feels unnecessary and undermines the definitive conclusion of the last game.
The gameplay is, conceptually, almost identical to the first: shooting, plasmids, gene tonics, food, audio logs, hacking, all that jazz. However, a lot of specific aspects of these mechanics, large and small, have been improved. First, mouse movement feels a lot smoother, which goes a long way towards making gameplay feel better and faster. Second, you now can use plasmids and guns at the same time, which is a great idea. Third, the hacking's been changed from the pipe minigame to just a put-the-needle-in-the-right-zone minigame, which I'm sure will make a lot of people happier (and is probably an objectively better mechanic) but kinda bums me out. Also, you can get extra bonuses if you're good enough at hacking, and there's a special gun exclusively dedicated to hacking if you're tired of the hassle of stunning machines, then running up to them. Fourth, gene tonics aren't divided into categories any more, but are all in one big pool that you can unlock more slots of; this makes customization a lot easier and more fun. Additionally, reloading's way faster; there are more weapon upgrades; there's more of an effort to differentiate the different levels of plasmids with new effects; and the camera now films instead of taking single photos, doesn't require film, and gives bonuses besides just damage upgrades and tips you could've figured out yourself. The end result of all these changes is that the game feels a lot more fluid, energetic, and fun. You can be creative and dance around enemies, like in the best Old-School FPS.
However, not everything's improved. The Little Sisters are the biggest example. In the previous game, you killed a Big Daddy, then either saved or killed his Little Sister. In this one, you kill a Big Daddy, then adopt the Little Sister (you're also a Big Daddy, by the way) and take her to two specific corpses, at each one protecting her for a minute or two as she takes her sweet goddamn time harvesting it for ADAM. At any point during this process, you can kill her or deliver her to a vent, which rescues her. Going through all this rigamarole is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ around Siren Alley, I started just putting Little Sisters in vents as soon as I got them, because I didn't need extra ADAM
badly. Even so, the ability to get more ADAM per Little Sister means that they give you gifts less often. Also, dealing with all the Little Sisters in a level spawns a Big Sister, which is basically a tougher, more agile Big Daddy who hates you for some reason. They tried to improve the Big Daddy/Little Sister element of the first game by putting in more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, not getting rid of the pointless moral choice.
Also, Vita-Chambers are still a thing, which is annoying. Their only purpose is to make it so you don't have to try to progress. I eventually started not using First Aid Kits or any weapons besides my melee, because if I died, I could just respawn and be back at the scene with none of my progress lost in seconds. I debated not using them at first, but decided against it because I wanted to get through the game fairly quickly and effortlessly.
Also, the UI looks worse, the First Aid Kit and EVE Hypo caps have been lowered significantly, and you can now eat health items even if your health is full, effectively wasting them.
On the more neutral side of things, all the weapons have been traded for new versions that look cooler and more powerful, but are functionally identical (the Thompson is now a minigun, the pistol is now a rivet gun, the crossbow is now a spear gun, etc.). The one exception is the  drill, which replaces the wrench but is waaaaaay better at everything, and a hell of a lot of fun. The new weapons are entertaining, but the fact that these much more powerful devices do the exact same damage makes it seem like all the enemies have gotten more powerful, too.
The game looks a lot nicer than BioShock.
The money cap is now $100 higher, which means that it took me slightly longer to hit it and then never use any of my money again.
You can't go back to previous areas any more, although I'm pretty sure nobody used that feature in the first game, so I don't really mind.
You finally see how plasmids get into you.
The game's a lot more setpiece-based; fortunately, a good amount of those setpieces are quite good, and the rest are inoffensive.
I had to go into the game files and change a 2 to a 1 to make it work; even then, it was kinda crashy.
Overall, BioShock 2 is more fun to play than BioShock 1, but it's not nearly a match in the story department. Whether that makes it better or worse is up to you, but for me, the overall experience was...just fine. It passed the time. It certainly wasn't an atmospheric tour-de-force like BioShock mostly was, but it was okay on its own merits. Buy it if it's on sale and you just want to pass a few hours, I guess. That's my boring opinion, and I hope it's useful to you.

Warshift is a RTS/3rd person shooter hybrid. Those who remember and liked Battlezone will feel similarities at once. Scroll down for a tl;dr.
You command a futuristic force that is built around an assault carrier (think helicopter carrier of modernity) fighting an enemy. The lore has human cyborg based army fighting against an alien invasion of a colony on a remote planet. Your assault carrier serves as a command center of any classic RTS, serving as a core for a base. Barracks, factories, turrets, resource extractors, infantry, tanks, aircraft... your typical RTS bread and butter. I mean that in a good way. In addition to it, you are also able to jump into the battle controlling an avatar, which is a particularly powerful vehicle (there are several different versions, from a good old tank to a flying submersible dinosaur looking walker to a katana armed jet pack commando) that enables you to tip the scales into your favour when ordinary units clash. This means you are effectively a  one man fire brigade, moving from area to area lending hand where attack is most dangerous if on defense or moving together with that big bunch of tanks and infantry you just sent toward the enemy base on offense. If you get yourself killed, you respawn after some time in the carrier. In addition to these RTS and action elements, there's the dash of RPG in ability to level up and equip your avatar with different weaponry as well as equipment providing passive increases to various stats while inside the carrier.
First off, a warning: It is at the moment very bare bones, with only a few skirmish maps and a campaign that is lacking any real story (that can be found on the website and is very short and basic anyway) and explicit story-wise connection between missions. Campaign missions are themselves for the most part just a streak of skirmishes or if not that very lightly scripted but still using same maps as skirmish. People looking for a quality single player storyline experience should keep clear for now because that's something they won't find here at all. What remains is skirmish and multiplayer.
Now that that's out of the way, the game is otherwise great. The core mechanics are all working properly from my experience. Gameplay is there and it feels pleasant enough, with only details to complain about and those are being communicated to the dev who is very active and deserves a big round of applause. For example, Battlezone veterans might notice the lack of any ability to command while in action mode, which is a bit of a pain as it requires lots of swapping between action and rts modes. But the dev announced he'll implement ways of ordering building from action mode, so it's being worked on.
Apart from some minor buggy issues (the now apparently famous invulnerable alien fighter in one tutorial mission that sprang up after a recent update that made people decide the game is totally broken but that actually doesn't prevent you from finishing the mission in any meaningful way), things work very well.
What needs to be kept in mind is that both RTS and action parts are fairly simple. This isn't a full blown RTS with massive amount of micromanagment potential, since player's attention is divided between the two aspects. The combination is well done and at least for me taxing enough to be engaging and fun while not being exhausting. The only issue I have in this department is the sometimes confusing moment that ensues after I swap from strategic to action mode in the heat of battle as it takes a couple of seconds to figure whats where.
What I like:
- A well thought of modern take on the underrated Battlezone rts/action hybrid genre.
- Cool looking graphics with impressive moments (large battleship hovering above your head pounding on targets beneath it while being pounded by equally large enemy counterpart some way in the distance as an example).
- Pleasant gameplay with lots of explosions and satisfying action - in a word: fun!
- Massive potential for the future.
What I don't like:
- Still very bare bones as explained in the first paragraph.
- Absence of any commanding ability in action mode forcing lots of rts to action to rts swapping which takes some time to get used to.
- Occasional bugs and quirks that were never game breaking for me, but they are there. Unit behaviour comes to mind here, they tend to... do things. That you never asked them to do. That gets them killed. But you can easily reign them in if you notice it and react in time. Also somewhat irritating way you can get stuck on a fairly small rock while driving a tank and then have to slowly back off and drive around it. Terrain negotiation could use a slight modification for these cases. But this too is a minor issue and once you figure what youre not supposed to drive over it's no longer a serious problem.
Apart from this, the game controls aren't exactly fully explained. For example the ctrl + 1 group designation isn't mentioned anywhere but it's there. Also units and their stats, resources and what they are used for, as well as tooltips are left for you to figure out and read during playing the game, without the ability to pause the game to read or understand them. This means that it's up to the player to figure many details for himself. While it's not neccessarily a downside (I kind of like the "what does this button do" approach), it's certainly there and will be a problem for many. I suspect the reason is in the fact that game is still being worked on intensely so things were added after the tutorial missions were designed.
So tl:dr:
It's still a rough game that will repulse those seeking for a complete, static and done product. But it's very fun, the core mechanics are there and are all good, majority of the roughness comes from the fact that campaign is very basic and game at the moment includes just a handful of maps that are used for every mode of play. Which is in my opinion a great thing because it means all that's needed is expanding on the already set basis, no fundamental reworks needed. If you are ok with playing a game that's being worked on but that is fully functional in it's core, then supporting this dev and buying it is worth it.

Though I haven't spent as much time playing ARK as other reviewers here did, but from the time I did, I must say that I enjoy the game a lot. However, take that with a grain of salt because I can see how the game would not be for everyone and I can also understand why some people give it bad reviews. It's a mixed bag, depending on what you enjoy in a game. Keep in mind that this is a subjective review and I know not everyone will agree with it, but maybe it can help out new people who are considering getting the game.
The Good:
As I'm still new, I haven't seen much of the game world and the available islands. I love exploring, seeing new places (biomes) and new dinos. This usually results in me getting completely obliterated by a wild dino, but I take it as part of the adventure. There is a lot to see and many things to find and tame.
If you're a new player, expect to get the Pokemon "gotta catch them all" syndrome int he first few days, where you will just want to tame absolutely everything you see. The taming itself is fun too. Every creature has different food requirements or mechanics to tame it which is enough to keep it interesting for quite a while. The levels on the creatures also make it exciting to try and find a higher level creature to tame for yourself.
The survival mechanics (food, heat) aren't too severe and add a little extra thing to kepp an eye on. As long as you us common sense and don't, for example, go into the snow biome with your naked butt sticing out, you should be fine.
Overall, it's a fun game that always has something that you can do when you turn it on - from farming some materials to upgrade or build, through taming dinos to get those materials, to just running around exploring new places.
The Bad:
The game doesn't feel finished when it comes to the technical aspects of it. There are many glitches and problems with it, which can be very immersion-breaking for many people. Dinos and players get stuck the structures you build can get glitchy and clip. Personally, this isn't a huge issue for me, I tend to just laughat these sorts of bugs, but I know that many people hate them. Though the devs are slowly fixing them, it feels like new problems pop up just as fast as they fix the old ones.
The game itself sometimes crashes on me or just glitches out in crazy ways. This may just be a problem on my end, or not be the case on official servers, but I'm not sure. The latest example I have, which happened yesterday, is falling through the world, getting ported up to the surface, falling again, repeat until the server admin ported me to a safe place.
You also need a pretty good pc to be able to play the game on higher graphical settings. My game is on high and I don't lag, but I'm pretty sure that weaker computers wouldn't be able to get a full experience from the game when it comes to graphics.
The Mixed:
I feel like certain specific mods are required to make the gameplay experience better. For example, mods that allow you to pick up the items you place on the ground which would normally stay glued to the ground until you destroy them. If you place something wrong or just decide to redecorate, gg, destroy it and try again. This wouldn't be a problem for things like walls (you don't pick up walls in real life, after all), but for small objects, there's no reason why you shouldn't be able to pick them up.
Official servers, especially pvp, can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥with big clans bullying everyone. But there is always an option to just not play on those.
Overall, it's a fun game that has a lot to be enjoyed. I would reccomend it to people who can overlook the bugs or are not bothered by them too much.

Despite the barrage of negative reviews I currently see in the 'most recent reviews' list , L.A Noire is a good game. It captures a great aspect of the Noir aesthetic , presenting interesting cases and characters.
===WARNING - this is an old game (getting a remaster November 14th I think lol) , so the graphics are nothing special. Framerate caps at 30 , this is due to the whole facial-movement thing going on , so I advise not to change it. ===
The gameplay is moderately fresh , you can read expressions , which gets more difficult to do as the game progresses. You then decide whether to believe , doubt or expose their statement as a lie. Of course , if you think the person is lying , you need evidence to prove it.
L.A Noire can also be described as a story-rich 3D point-and-click type game , since most of the time you will spend is either searching for clues at a crime scene or shooting , or driving your car. Mostly investigating crime scenes.
The game is split up into five major arcs: Patrol , Traffic , Homicide , Vice and Arson. My favourite out of all these is Arson , whilst my least favourite is Vice. About the story , this is a detective story. There aren't any massive twists , and mostly the culprit will be someone you have to investigate , and have no emotional ties to. That's where the game falls flat.
It seems very bland. It
fun to investigate a crime scene and power through a case like an intellegent beast , but at the same time , there are no twists. It would've been exciting if perhaps in homicide , Rusty was the killer of the last case , but it was an extremely generic outcome.
I love the Arson desk because it's very story-oriented (it's the last desk you play through) , it also has a few twists you may or may not expect , and the cases are intruiging and seem more structured and important.
All in all , I don't think L.A Noire is the best detective game ever , but it has left a great impression on me , so much so that If I were to rate it on a scale , it'd be an 8/10.

This is the best game I have ever played. Not a statement to be made lightly.
What sets Crusader Kings II apart from other strategy games is the simple fact that your country doesn't matter. This is a design choice, but it is also a huge plus. Once you realize this, the game opens up and becomes immense fun.
So if your choosen country doesn't matter, what does matter? Your family. This is a game about expanding the influence of your dynasty, your blood-line. Your country is irrelevant in the grand scheme and that is what makes this game so great. You could attempt to take over the entire known world with military might(have fun putting down uprisings repeatedly), but it is much more rewarding to use smart marriages and devious scheming to put members of your clan in all of the positions of power in the known world. And don't forget keeping those bitter, pesky nobles happy.
The options become endless. I have, as a small time Irish King, had an uncle elected Pope. Without ever leaving the isles, in that same save, I put a Nephew on the throne of both England and France(the deaths of everyone in line for those thrones who were not of my dynasty were purely a coincidence). Later I used those alliances to take Scotland and push into Spain. I fought in a Crusade, and was awarded the Kingdom of Jerusalem(which was promptly given to a son, and gave my Dynasty yet another throne). I acquired more land and fame by marriage. I married the Queen of a small Kingdom, and upon our deaths, all of that land passed to my heir.
The amount of detail in this game is unsurpassed. The things you can accomplish if you set your mind to it, endless. I can't give this game a higher recommendation.

A wonderfully in-depth mix of RPG, strategy and history. Start with a chosen character, from the lowliest count to the most powerful emperor and choose a time in history from the Dark Ages to Medieval, and build a dynasty whilst you re-write 5 or so centuries of history depending which expansions you own. The game is based on the relationships between thousands of characters, and through marriage, scheming, intrigue and war, you can make your mark. When your first character dies - and there are a vast array of ways to meet your maker - you will continue as your heir. The game plays out as a pausable, real-time system, with events popping up that give you little multiple-choice vignettes to add colour to proceedings. RTS fans will likely find the combat simplistic, but the real beauty of this game is not how good any one of its systems is - it's the way they combine together to make an epic story unfold before you. Your dynasty will have a rollercoaster ride of rising and falling fortunes, but as long as you have at least one province, you're never out of it - in fact, there's nothing more satisfying than clawing your way back from catastrophe and the game does a fantastic job of making failure fun.
There's a wry humour throughout, and CKII is far from a joyless history lesson. Not only that, the level of replayability is astonishing. The choice of rank, culture, size of nation and historical start date gives a vast variety and the expansions, often discounted, widen this even further, as well as adding new rules and scenarios. Mods are also available and even a (rather expensive) save converter that lets you carry a completed CKII game into Europa Universalis IV. The forum community is nice and helpful and the Paradox website also contains a lot of AAR's of people's games - worth a read to get a feel for the gameplay.
I can't recommend this gem enough to anyone who enjoys strategy, RPG or even RTS type games, and wants something different, or to anyone who likes Paradox's other efforts.

Tahira: Echoes of the Astral Empire is a good, little game. While I enjoyed it, I've seen some reviews here absolutely gushing with praise and I can't quite understand them. It's a good game. Is it incredible? No, not really. The story is good though nothing particularly amazing and it desperately needs a sequel to tie up some loose ends and to resolve the cliffhanger ending.
Most of the reviews compare Tahira to The Banner Saga and for good reason, since the combat is nearly identical with only a handful of small differences. Graphically, it is almost disintguishable from the Banner Saga during combat and if you told me they were part of the same series, just covering different locations or something along those lines I'd believe you. Where the Banner Saga let you choose between targeting the opponent's health or guard, Tahira forces you to work through the guard stat before you can whittle down the health and dispatch the enemy. You only have three different classes to work with (four if you count Tahira, herself, being unique to the other characters you use) with a serious lack of ranged options. In terms of story and choices, Tahira comes up a bit short. There are only a couple of choices you can make (as of the writing of this review I can only clearly remember one though I'm 95% certain that there was another one) and they don't really make any difference. Where the Banner Saga prompted you with choices that had real ramifications for the story and the combat, Tahira is more like reading a novella with combat segments after each chapter.
While this may all sound a bit negative, Tahira really is a good, enjoyable game. However, I would only suggest that you temper your expectations a bit. It is rather short and the ending comes up rather abruptly with a fairly large cliffhanger. The combat is good though nothing groundbreaking and some of the later battles can get a bit dull as Tahira's response to up the difficulty is to just throw more and more enemies at you as oppose to having different objectives to accomplish. The music and artwork are both very good and the Middle Eastern inspired setting is a fun and refreshing viewpoint that we don't see in enough games and could certainly do with some more of.
If you enjoyed the Banner Saga, you'll enjoy Tahira. They are, like I said, shockingly similar. It is not, however, perfect and it's similarity to the Banner Saga works against it. I feel bad constantly lining the two games up and pointing out this or that but they really are that similar. However, in the end, I have to give Tahira: Echoes of the Astral Empire the thumbs up.  Pick it up, especially if it's on sale, you'll probably enjoy it.

A modern day isometric turn-based RPG that is almost an instant classic. If you lived in the era of isometric role playing games such as Fallout, you will quickly fall in love with UnderRail. It is charming because even though it maintains a retro style with artwork and gameplay elements, it also feels intuitive and innovative in it's own right.
- The "oddity" xp system in this game suits it perfectly. Players must find items called "Oddities" to gain experience and level up instead of grinding through enemies and objectives to gain xp, players are forced to explore in the manner which suits them most in order to gain xp. Whether you engage combat head on with every opponent or avoid them with stealth or manipulate your way into places with persuasion, you will be equally rewarded with xp. This means players are rarerly forced into combat and a diplomatic or pure stealth playstyle is not only plausible, but enjoyable.
- The crafting mechanics are finely tuned and well-balanced as of the recent patch. The crafting system makes sense and the skills are very rewarding to invest in but are not a necessity by any means. The player can go through the game crafting his own gear, stealing it, looting it or buying it. Crafting will eventually lead to higher quality gear though which makes it feel like a worthwile skill investment.
- The skills in general are all well balanced. There are a few nuances, such as unarmed combat and the evasion skills being underpowered compared to using melee weapons and wearing heavy armor, but still are definately viable if you don't mind the extra difficulty.
-The psionic abilities and skills in this game are great. It provides variety in combat along with the various traps, throwables, consumables and ammunition types to make combat feel layered and strategic.
- The depth in dialogue is lacking and the plot does not feel fleshed out yet or immersive. Mind you this game is still an alpha and the content is currently being worked on for the next big patch. It will provide much more dialogue and lore and add many new areas to the game to explore and immerse in. The game right now can be finished in 15 hours if you are playing at a fast pace. However there are many side quests and distractions to keep the playtime around 30 hours.

WARSHIFT is unique. Maelstrom was the first game I played that had the same mechanics and elements as this game. However, Maelstrom was broken and outdated. I was lucky to find this. I was on the main store page and saw the three newest releases and this was one. Clicked it because why not? Read the description and immediately bought it, then looked at the videos and pictures. This game is great, and I completely support this SINGLE developer and his work.
TL;DR version is at the bottom.
WARSHIFT is a great game in its current state. Yes, there are a lot of bugs and issues presently, but the developer is working on them daily and keeps pushing out new patches here and there. He listens to the community by reading all issue threads, posts replies, and tries to fix them immediately. For a single developer he sure puts his community first. That alone deserves a recommendation!
Anyways, WARSHIFT is a mix of mostly Real-Time Strategy and Third Person Shooter. The game consists of up to 3v3 matches either co-op or PVP. The RTS portion is left to the commander of each team who is allowed to build his base and train the units. The other two players are support avatars and are locked into the third person experience.
The RTS experience is limited currently. There are a few structures currently on each team but only some have a significant use right now, like the drilling platform, factory and barracks. There are a bunch of units available to train as well. You can also set your factories and barracks' to auto produce a custom queue of units which will automatically move towards the enemy and attack anything along the way. Of course, commanders get control of their avatar too.
The third person experience is very fun. There are a bunch of avatars to choose from (presently more for the humans than aliens), each is different with its own weapons and upgrades and special ability. There are a bunch of weapons of different types and a bunch of different upgrades of different types as well. As you deal damage with your avatar - in direct control or not - you gain experience and levels. As you level up you unlock more items and gain stat points to improve your avatar's abilities.
The bugs? There's a bunch. I work closely with the developer as a sort of community moderator. I have posted a thread
where all of the known issues and bugs I've encountered --- or the community --- are posted. I'm constantly updating it and this is a good reference if you are unsure about this game in its unpolished state.

EDIT, 14.10.2015:
TL;DR
"Unfinished, depthless, mindless dino shooter."
"MOM I DONE MAED A GAEM get the camera"
"Steam quality control, hello?"
This game has had a major overhaul and the developer notified me of this through a friendly comment on my last review so I decided to give it another go.
This revamped review may be biased because of that. Be critical when reading.
Please also note that I've not had the patience to play through the entire game as of writing this review.
There are a few things I do like about this game now. I'll start with those.
* This game has lot of content for its asking price
- 11 maps
- 17 or 19 weapons. It's a bit unclear.
- a few dinosaur types, zombies
- Four gamemodes in addition to four bonus gamemodes (8 in total)
- Multiplayer (currently in beta, whatever that means)
* Maps
- Fend off a castle against a dinosaur invasion, or take to the snowy mountains to go dino hunting.
- Good location variety is what I'm trying to get at.
* Player progression
- It has a currency system. You gain currency from killing dinosaurs and getting headshots.
- You use the currency to purchase new weapons or upgrade your existing ones.
* EXPLOSIONS
- Michael Bay directed the survival mode.
* Uh, performance?
- You can most likely run it on either a lemon or potato.
- Bugfixes and optimisation are in the works it seems.
Now for the things I don't like about this game:
* Core gameplay
You pick your weapons, pick your map and mode, and click on dinosaurs.
* AI
The AI in this game is broken. All enemies have awful pathfinding, so you'll mostly see them get stuck on terrain. A lot of times the AI doesn't even react to getting shot - especially from far away.
Enemies also have weird spawn locations, so the hardest part of this game is actually finding the dinosaurs. In addition they sometimes spawn inside you or right next to you, which is the only time you're likely to die in this game.
Give the AI better pathfinding!
* Maps
The maps all feel very rushed and badly designed. Why is there a tower on "Africa" if you can't climb up there? Why does "castle" feature a cool castle if I have to go outside the walls to even find the dinosaurs? On all the maps, there are numerous spots where you can place yourself to bug out the AI, if you have the patience to find the AI.
Give the maps purpose and backstory! Why are there dinosaurs getting stuck on terrain in this wintery landscape?? Do I need to track down and defeat the ancient yetisaur?
* Weapons/gunplay
The guns I've tried feel boring. The devs have put some work into making the guns feel a bit meaty by making your crosshair bounce around a bit when you fire. I've noticed no bullet drop, no bullet penetration, no tracers and bullets dont leave marks if you fire at any prop in the world. The guns aren't all awful, they just need some work.
* Inventory
(I think) You can carry all the weapons in the game at the same time and all bullet weapons have a shared stash of one ammunition type. Weapons have magazines which need to be reloaded after depleting them.
The devs could've done so much more with the inventory system.
* Graphics
Game looks about ten years old. There's varying texture and model quality all over the place. Some things look better than others. Lot of things look either awful or unfinished.
* Physics
- nope
* Sound
Either someone has diarrhea or that's a dinosaur yelling.
Dinosaurs don't make sounds when stomping around, or while doing anything else. There's just a diarrhea roar when you spawn.
GET IT? -STOMPING AROUND-
Just to summarize - nothing is fleshed out at all. Everything feels either broken or unfinished.
Everything that makes a game cool or good is missing. With the exception of exploding dinosaurs. That part is okay.
In my opinion this shouldn't have made it onto Steam to begin with.
* Other things
- Standard unity launcher in addition to an options menu where you can turn off shadows, bloom and music.
Conclusion:
I want to recommend this game - I really do. I like the concept, I love dinosaurs, the asking price is nice. I want to be nice. I want to say, "hey this game has its moments!"  But the game is a turd. It's a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ And not even a polished one.
Waste of time.
I would absolutely recommend it as a gift for someone you hate though.

Seeing the reviews already posted, I have to agree with both sides. This game is fantastic. It is an amazing concept that has been transfixing people since Jurrasic Park and again with Jurrasic World. DINOSAURS!! The taming is good, and a fairly basic premise. The bases you are capable of building are superb (if you have the time; especially in vanilla). BUT, the bugs are absurd for anyone playing something other than at leas 50x rates and modded. For some fairly un-powerful dinos, this is a ridiculous ability to have. And then there are the Giganotosauaruses. These have been the topic for debate since their release. I think they are way too powerful in the wild and not worth the hype tamed. First off, it takes SOOOO many tranqs (of any kind) to knock them out that you would need to have a large group of people all with Ascendant level longnecks each with 200 darts to knock out the thing. And then once it's tamed, you find that all the stats go way down. OH!! And if you fall while on it, it will kill you :) So yeah. the bugs are bad. But all in all, as long as you are careful and aware at all times, there is no reason you shouldn't enjoy this game. And as someone with almost 1800 hours in ths game, I say that honestly. Modded or official, it is worth it.

The amount of detail in this game is unsurpassed. The things you can accomplish if you set your mind to it, endless. I can't give this game a higher recommendation.

A wonderfully in-depth mix of RPG, strategy and history. Start with a chosen character, from the lowliest count to the most powerful emperor and choose a time in history from the Dark Ages to Medieval, and build a dynasty whilst you re-write 5 or so centuries of history depending which expansions you own. The game is based on the relationships between thousands of characters, and through marriage, scheming, intrigue and war, you can make your mark. When your first character dies - and there are a vast array of ways to meet your maker - you will continue as your heir. The game plays out as a pausable, real-time system, with events popping up that give you little multiple-choice vignettes to add colour to proceedings. RTS fans will likely find the combat simplistic, but the real beauty of this game is not how good any one of its systems is - it's the way they combine together to make an epic story unfold before you. Your dynasty will have a rollercoaster ride of rising and falling fortunes, but as long as you have at least one province, you're never out of it - in fact, there's nothing more satisfying than clawing your way back from catastrophe and the game does a fantastic job of making failure fun.
There's a wry humour throughout, and CKII is far from a joyless history lesson. Not only that, the level of replayability is astonishing. The choice of rank, culture, size of nation and historical start date gives a vast variety and the expansions, often discounted, widen this even further, as well as adding new rules and scenarios. Mods are also available and even a (rather expensive) save converter that lets you carry a completed CKII game into Europa Universalis IV. The forum community is nice and helpful and the Paradox website also contains a lot of AAR's of people's games - worth a read to get a feel for the gameplay.
I can't recommend this gem enough to anyone who enjoys strategy, RPG or even RTS type games, and wants something different, or to anyone who likes Paradox's other efforts.

Dustforce is a calming game. The game isn't labelled difficult for nothing, but the game is probably a very different tone than most you'd find under the category. Between the calming visuals and the serene soundtrack, I never really got that frustrated like I would in other difficult platformers: instead I got determined.
That's part of the magic of Dustforce. It's one of those games that really lets you take the game at your own pace, do levels how you see fit. There's no plot or story which allows you to explore whichever unlocked door you want to first.
It's a very easy game to get into, with challenge ramping and testing you throughout. The entire game is essentially a tutorial. Unlike similar describable games though, there is an endgame there.
Enter the community. You can watch the top run that anyone has done in the game via the replay system. You can see how any of your friends tackled the level. You can see the guy who shaved a few frames off your time and see what he did differently. Anyone you meet who plays this game extensively is also incredibly friendly and just welcoming new faces to the game. It's got to have one of the best video game communities I've ever been bare to witness.
So pick it up, try it out, see if it's your cup of tea. You might be surprised how fun cleaning can be, and how far you can take it.

A very impressive little game that ticks pretty much all the boxes for me. Great tactical battles, compelling story, intelligent dialog, nice art, and a UI that doesn't get in the way. I heartily recommend it to anyone who enjoys turn based tactics.
If you know Banner Saga's combat system, you'll be right at home. This is a good thing, very good even - it's an excellent system which deserves to be reinterpreted and iterated upon. There are interesting differences, but most importantly the battles you have to fight are open-ended, large scale, and challenging.
The is no strategical layer to speak of. I prefer that to Banner Saga's trainwreck of one, to be honest.
There are very few choices and branches in the story, which would have been welcome, but it's not a terrible omission either. The setting for the story is original, believable and interesting; the characters, while not developed that much, are likable. The story line itself is enjoyable and engaging.
I typically don't place too much value on dialog, but I've been positively surprised here. It's interesting and smartly written, while staying short enough to not get in the way of the story or the gameplay.
The art is also quite similar in style to Banner Saga's, and that's also a very good thing. Clearly the budget there is not quite the same, but that other game (being one of the most strikingly beautiful games in recent memory) is not a fair comparison. The first impression might be a bit less than overwhelming, but it grew on me quite well.
The UI is maybe the thing I have the least good things to say about, although it's not really bad in any obvious ways. It looks a bit meh, and sometimes demands a few more awkward clicks than seems necessary, but nothing major.
On the whole, the largest negative I found about this game is how short it is, as it left me wanting for more. Hardly much of a negative though, is it ?

A challenging platformer that's comparable to a more tactical Meat Boy: rather than the goal just being to get to the end as fast as possible without dying, you're also tasked with cleaning up as much dust/leaves/trash/etc on the ground as possible (by running over it as you traverse the level), and in as large of a combo as possible by sweeping it all up in quick succession, while also dealing with the occasional small group of enemies.
While the controls feel a bit different than what you'd normally expect out of this sort of game, they're actually very well made once you've had some time to get used to them. The gameplay is rock-solid, the soundtrack and art are comfy, and the higher-difficulty levels provide a great challenge.
My main gripe with the game, and consider this an important disclaimer if you're anything less than really, -really- good at platformers, is the system for unlocking new levels.
Levels have 5 difficulties, which for purposes of space we'll call A, B, C, D, and E. By default, you have all of the A levels unlocked. Completing an A level and getting an S rank for both dust cleared and max combo (called SS rank) earns you a key to unlock a single B level. Likewise, earning SS rank on a B level unlocks you a C level, SS-C unlocks a D, and earning SS on all of the D levels opens up a bonus hub world containing the E levels.
It's important to note that to earn S-rank for each category, you must score absolutely perfectly. That is, clear -all- the dust from the level, and have a combo that stretches all the way from the first patch of dust to the last.
If you earn less than an SS rank, be it SA, AS, BB, CD, or whatever, you only earn a portion of a key. So in example, earning BC rank on two A levels would get you a single B key and some progress towards the next one, as opposed to the two you'd have earned if you had scored SS ranks.
This brings up the pretty immediate problem that, if you don't have the skill and/or patience to keep retrying to earn SS on every level, you'll never unlock the more challenging (and at least for me, the more fun) parts of the game, especially considering that dying, or even just getting hit, automatically disqualifies you from earning S for combo unless you start the entire level over again.
While this isn't a huge issue for A and B levels for anyone of at least moderate skill, C levels already ramp up the challenge significantly, and D levels are pretty much Meat Boy tier in how many times you're going to die trying to beat them (don't even get me started on the E levels), so this system ends up locking out a lot of players from a significant portion of the game merely because they weren't -absolutely perfect- at it.
This aside, I do recommend the game to anyone who likes truly challenging platformers, as there's a light at the end of the tunnel that saved this review from being a Negative one: Should you find yourself in the same situation I did, having a lot of fun with just the challenge of beating the levels, but no fun at all at the prospect of going back and spending hours trying to perfect them, something you may simply not have the skill to do, the game has a community-made mod called Dustmod that, among a whole lot of other functions, lets you switch your save file to NG+ with the click of a button, unlocking all of the levels and letting you play the entire game without having to worry about rank.

The only drawback I find is that your objectives are not always clear, and on the later stages the game throws what seems like endless numbers of enemies at you until you complete the objective. It can get a bit frustrating when the enemies just keep coming and swamping you.
There are certainly some issues, especially the relative shortness of the game story-wise, and the combat can feel like a grind, but hopefully the developers are able to make a sequel to improve things. I for sure will be on board with that!

Tahira is an indie turn-based RPG with large battles, very enjoyable combat mechanics and an entertaining story.
Even at the full price (of only 15 Euro) there's really no reason not to play this (unless you absolutely hate turn based games).
Highly recommended! :)
The battles in Tahira are a lot larger than in most turn-based RPGs (e.g. in some battles you control 20 units) and there are usually some side quests and varying victory conditions.
There are some fun and interesting features like ambush, were you can hide some of your units, which makes them invisible and removes them from the usual turn order. Those hidden units can be revealed any time during the battle, even during the enemies turn, to use the element of surprise and attack with additional bonuses.
Just like in Banner Saga, you won't have many mage units and your units have 2 defensive stats (HP and guard). Unlike Banner Saga, you don't get to choose which stat you want to attack and a lowered HP does not decrease your damage output. Instead, a unit without guard points can get hit critically more easily.
Guard can be restored, but HP cannot be healed. Also, battles are divided into several smaller ones and your stats are not restored after everyone - You need to plan ahead.
At the current battle, my army consists of knights, heavy mercenaries (think barbarians), light mercenaries (ninja-like) and Tahira herself (mage). Also, a hero joins for every class in your army, which is basically a stronger version of its class.
So far, the only one with ranged attacks is Tahira, so a lot of the tactics in this game comes from positioning and combining the special attacks of the different characters.
It's not your usual high fantasy setting or story. The story is well written and mainly presented within dialog boxes. I didn't like the art very much when I looked at some screenshots before I bought it, but now I have to say it fits the game quite well. Especially the combat maps look great!

REWORK:: My initial review may have been just, however unlike most of the♥♥♥♥♥♥posted to steam greenlight the Dev is actually working with the community to better the game. Needless to say this was a huge step in the right direction for Dinosaur Hunt Africa Contract warranting me to re-do my review. It was nice to hear that the developer is placing time into his game that he cares about similar to the dev for UNLOVED. Okay so contrary to the previous review was written on a previous build but the game seems to have done a complete turnaround.
The combat seems to have improved with the dinosaurs now moving alot faster than their previous. With that said it still has some flaws with damage taken/done but nothing to detrimental to overall enjoyment. It was also nice to see some small things changed I.E. animations so the dinos don't just slide around at a really slow pace, the dinosaurs actually seem to carry a weight so props to the dev to knocking that out. On top of that the progression seemed to have a change as well with each level having a set of actual objectives to complete rather than the old version which was nothing more than go in kill one to two dinosaurs and leave. So this was also a pleasant surprise.
Overall the game is certainly progressing in the right direction to become something worth owning especially with it's fixes from it's original version it may be worth the small 99 cent pricetag. The amount of fun you will have with it is pretty much based around what you enjoy. Is this what it would be like to hunt dinos? I really still don't think so and I also don't think this game was made for me but don't let that stop you from giving it a go. In it's current build with what time I've spent with it my 2-3 major gripes are relatively small. For one you do too much damage to the dinos nearly one shotting everything especially with the shotgun. 2 the dinos spawns are random and so are yours so you may spawn next to or even on top of a dino and some of them have the ability to kill you in 1 hit and revert your progress on the level so that would be nice to see fixed. And lastly an addition of a more refined UI and shop would be nice to see but polish certainly should be the last things on a devs mind.
To finish this review I would like to say thanks to the Racing Bros (The Dev)  for contacting me and informing of a new build so I can give a more fair review to the new build. This game is bait.
It looks good and sounds good on paper, with even a nice sounding name to call its own, yet once you actually start it up, you soon realize that this is nothing but a cheap production to grab some money.
The game actually has the nerve to claim it was better with audio enabled (honestly, which game isn't?), yet has the most amateurish voice acting I have heard in quite some time. The lines sound as if they had been recorded with a smartphone or something with the "actors" themselves sounding more like the dev team's friends/family members. And the worst part? They never shut up. Same lines over and over and over and over and over again. Please, just make it stop!
The humor is rather weak, too, mostly revolving around weak stereotypes such as pokemon go players filling the streets and being a hindrance (it's even funnier because Pokemon Go was a phenomenon that died as quickly as it became popular, thus not even being relevant anymore)
The "story" cutscenes try to be funny but ultimately just aren't as the supposed "punchline" is just a dumb realization. The whole design of the cutscenes is rather childish with the protagonist's wife being stuck on the toilet, having run out of toilet paper or the protagonist smoking weed. Huehue, Toilet jokes and weed. Hilarious.
The gameplay itself is rather straightforward. You walk from left to right, dodging pedestrians. Sounds funny enough, but becomes rather frustrating fast. For one, you are supposed to "nearly" run into them and dodge them at the last second to gain a speed boost, yet it isn't clear what exactly counts as a near evasion and how closely you can pass a pedestrian. I sometimes found myself avoiding people I thought I had run into for sure, then the game told me I ran into people I thought I would easily avoid. Ultimately, it doesn't seem to make a huge difference anyway as you can run into them as much as you want and suffer no penalty whatsoever. I have once been repeatedly run over by cars with no sign of ever losing any health. In fact, I don't think there is any form of health system in this game at all. On the top left appears to be a green bar which I once ASSUMED was health, only to realize it never depleted itself in any way at all. No idea what it's supposed to do and at this point, I doubt I will play this game again to ever find out, let alone care. You can also "excuse yourself" two times per level to supposedly be granted immunity for running into people once. I tried it and nothing seemed to happen. Not that it really mattered, since running into people had no effect in the first place.
The level design is also rather odd. There was a level in which bicycle riders kept coming at me in waves repeatedly, often times appearing in such a way that it becomes impossible to dodge them. It soon becomes annoying to even try, so you just take the hit and deal with it. I found myself often times stuck on screens in which there just wasn't a way to advance without running into anyone at all which seems really odd for a game which supposedly is all about avoiding pedestrians.
In the end, it's a game with nice pixel graphics and a cool idea behind it which suffers from a horrible execution. Not worth any money at all, imho. Don't buy. You could have more fun going outside and running into people for real. At least they would actually sound like people and say different things every time you did it, too.

...is a third-person action investigation game. Returning from World War II, now-police officer Cole Phelps is quickly singled as a brilliant detective where his case investigations has him facing the corrupt forces that rule Los Angeles. This review takes into account all DLCs.
While the game is set in an open-world city with drivable (and commandeerable) vehicles, this is not a 1940s-set GTA clone. Each case works as a separate chapter, you start your day being assigned a case you must investigate with your partner, being given a specific location to drive to in your department-supplied car. At each crime scene, you must uncover clues, interrogate witnesses and gather information to figure out where to go next.
Investigation has its own neat set of mechanics: spot clues laid about on the ground, on furniture, or on victims. As you pick them up, you observe them by moving in your hand on a 2-axe 3D fashion, spotting marks, inscriptions or additional information. Witness interrogation consists of asking the questions in the right order, each answer chained to additional information depending on whether you correctly assume the answer to be truthful, doubtful or false (the latter must be backed by proof you select from your already accumulated clues or testimonies).
Additional investigation mechanics include solving puzzles, secretly following or trailing people by car or on foot, or contacting the office whenever you need additional information such as location addresses or followup messages from collaborating personnel. Driving and shooting are pulled out directly from similar open-world games.
The campaign has a good length to it, totaling 22 different cases across 4 different desks: Traffic, Homicide, Vice and Arson. Each case is very distinct, it can be easy to miss clues, mess up interrogations, charging a culprit with a lack of evidence or straight out charging the wrong person. You'll often be able to progress in the story without a 5-star success in some cases, but sometimes you'll have to replay an entire investigation and figure out where you went wrong and try things differently.
Where
really shines is in its characters. Even though graphics haven't aged that well, this game pioneered facial recognition in video games: each face is a 3D rendering of an actor who spoke each line, many you'll recognize from various TV series (yes, Leland Monroe's face and voice really is John Noble, aka Walter Bishop from
), and while their facial articulations may seem overdone at times, they are usually very believable with top-notch voice acting, you'll spend a lot of time looking at faces and twitches in an attempt to see if the person in front of you is being honest during interrogation. The script is also very good, and most people you come across have implied motivations of their own.
Fictional late-40s Los Angeles is beautifully recreated, filled with people and almost a hundred real-life time-appropriate cars including hidden special car models. There are also collectibles to find and landmarks to visit. 40 optional side quest will be made available as police calls you get during your investigations while driving from point A to point B, giving you additional incentive to get to know the city.
There's a missed opportunity with this open world: there are no stores, no activities to do in the city. When you conclude an investigation, you begin a new one the next morning, and that's it. There is no building you can enter unless it is related to a case at some point or another, so unless you really care about collectibles, you won't feel any urge to explore the city. The developers obviously put a lot of heart in creating the city, but it is left unmemorable. As for all the cars, you'll stick to your supplied car for convenience, assuming you don't simply let your partner drive to skip directly to the next location.
The overarching story is lack luster to some degree, supplied as chatter during driving segments, or small cutscenes in between cases. Sure, the flashbacks help flesh out your character, but his personal life is barely explored. Important moments such as
come as a complete surprise as it's barely hinted to, and overall contributes to making you relate very little to the protagonist. To top it all off, the last few chapters feel rather rushed, giving the game an unsatisfying ending.
There's a lot to be found in this game you won't find elsewhere, and it requires observation, thoroughness, and most of all enough patience to redo some cases until you succeed. If that sounds like you, I strongly recommend you give
some of your time!

*SPOILER WARNING. DO NOT READ BEYOND THIS IF YOU HAVE NOT YET PLAYED LA NOIRE*
This game was amazing. Despite the frequent mechanical glitches, and broken driving gameplay, I found myself completely immersed with L.A Noire.
That being said, I found the ending ridiculous.
Cole Phelps, the main protagonist, was an honest, compassionate man filled with integrity, serving in the LAPD to right his wrongs commited during WWII. So why did he have an affair with Elsa? This was incredibly out of character. He spoke highly, if rarely, about his wife and daughters, and when talking to Elsa, showed no romantic or sexual interest. So why would he throw that all away?
Moving on, after he is exposed by his partner Roy, as a scapegoat to cover up an LAPD scandal, he is hated by everyone in the force for being disloyal to his wife. However, this is the 1940's. Men are racist, homophobic, and sure as hell cheat on their own wives. So why all the hate for Phelps?
Thirdly, Phelps dies at the end. Understandably, RockStar love love loves to kill off their characters, but this seemed a bit far, as for most of the game, Phelps was an honest man living in a dishonest time.
I wish I could recommend but at the same time not recommend this game, but as I cant, I will give it an overall positive review, as the gameplay was excellent.
