Tahira was a fun, but brief, adventure that in the end, felt like the first hour of a really good movie.
It ended when the character and story development was JUST starting to get rolling, JUST starting to hook you in--and then abruptly, it's over---clearly paving the way to a sequel or two.
Which, incidentally I'll be buying--because Tahira seems to have nailed a lot of the fundamental aspects of gaming, correctly.
Most of your time, and I mean 90%, will be fighting. And the fights are large-scale, multi-staged, arenas which make for some pretty triumphant moments if you use the battle mechanics correctly to your advantage.
The battles are fairly long, with scripted events, and virtually every battle is a fight against overwhelming odds, which at first glance look impossible--but it's pretty gratifying to 'hulk smash' their superior forces.
I've been a strategy and turn/based strategy fan since the term came into existence, and in Tahira, was content with the level of balance and difficulty that I ran into. What it lacked in dyanmics in terms of NPC skills, it made up for largely in the size and range of options of the battle fields. Essentially, while there weren't a lot of individual skills, there was a lot you could do with what little you had--so in the end, it was still fun and challenging.
The graphics/animation are hand-crafted and look wonderful, similarly, the sound effects and music quality are well chosen.
My largest gripe with the game is that it ended too soon--I don't want a half-scoop of ice cream! :)
In terms of improvement, I think the characters could be better developed, and more dialogue could have been added to the game to make it seem longer. Dialogue between characters did not include descriptive elements (only direct, spoken lines), which I think is a missed opportunity for immersion into a well crafted, mystical environment. Humans relate to emotions--and if players can become privy to the internal dialogues and states of protagonist characters, they can relate to--and connect with them better; this is the difference between a comic-book and a novel. And as Tahira is a story driven game, it would be greatly improved by adding narrative and descriptive elements to add to it's already solid combat systems.
Overall, I'd give it an 8/10, for 3 guys, it's quite a job well done. I hope they use this game as a template to launch future games with expanded character abilities, subtantially more dialogue and descriptive elements, as well as special attention to individual character (personality) development.

This is the type of game that you can instantly tell was a labour of love.
Being entirely hand drawn, the art goes a long way to speak for the determination of the devs behind it. To buck the trend of drag and drop 3D rendered games that now heavily populate the market takes a mad man, or three as it so turns out. Mad as it may be, their efforts cumulate in the visualy refreshing journey that is Tahira. At no point have I felt that I've seen this all before or played through games so similar as to instigate a sense of deja vu. The rich artwork is only futher complimented by a stunning soundtrack and deep storyline that add to the immersion. The interplay of the three act to create a novel like experience, where you feel as though you are turning the pages of a fantastic book.
The combat requires a great deal of thought and planning, especially on the harder difficulties, leaving wrong moves harshly punnished. Aspects of the battle dynamics could be improved as to keep a greater flow, although it is the nature of turn based tactics games to be stop-start.
If you were a fan of the Banner Saga or Fire Emblem way back in the day, this game is for you.

EDIT: I've changed my review to a "do not recommend", because there's a game-breaking bug on a boss fight where the boss is simply unresponsive and no work-around. Doing some research, this has been an issue since the first version of Metro: Last Light, and since it's still in the redux version that means it's just ... well, it shouldn't have a game-breaking bug in it. As such, I can't recommend the game.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Pros:
+ Russian-style post-apoc
+ Great story
+ Choose your Play-style (stealth, run-n-gun, violent, pacifist, hardcore, tourist, etc)
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Neutral (you may or may not like):
* Corridor-style shooter where you are given a direction to go and have to work your way through it (ala Half Life or Wolfensteinas as opposed to open-world games like Fallout or STALKER)
* gratuitious T&A ... post-apoc world, and women are working the oldest profession in the world (being hookers). There's one hooker you can pay to give you a dance. I don't mind that, any of it. What annoys me is that once you're stuck in that chair there's no way to cancel her dance, and she keeps dancing for a full minute. When she stops you immediately see a "give bullets/money" signal, so you think you need to pay her a tip for the dance. No. That just makes her dance more. Right after you pay her to dance again you see a quick blurb up in the left-hand corner of the screen saying "press 'up' to leave'. Why can't I do that to leave any time she's dancing? When you're playing this game and your girlfriend walks by behind you... and notices you're NOT stopping the dance out of respect for her catching you getting a virtual lap dance in a video game, you end up having awkward conversations you'd rather not have with your girlfriend. "No, I'm not a perv, dear. This stupid game simply won't let me stop the ... oh, ok here we go... jesus, apparently that makes her dance some more! NO! I'm NOT A PERVERT! HONEY, LISTEN TO ME! *sigh* I'm sleeping on the couch tonight, aren't I?" Honestly, I feel like the game locks you into a minute-long lap dance with this hooker simply as masturbation material for horny guys. Need more then a minute? Ok, give her 5 more bullets and she'll dance for another minute. This whole situation just seems like gratuitious fap material purposefully coded into the game to serve that only purpose.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Cons:
- player moves really darn slow, which is ok when other humans are moving just as slow, but not when you're stuck in the middle of a bunch of really fast mutants leaping at you and eating your face off
- cut-scenes or certain scenarios force you into situations your play-style wouldn't suggest you'd fall into (eg: you can stealth large parts of the game, but certain parts force you into run-n-gun).
- several "wander through the town" areas that can be interesting, but slow down the pace of the game
- sometimes hard to tell what you're supposed to do or where you're supposed to go; some boss fights are confusing (thick russian accents and all signs in-game being in russian don't help)
- crouching to sneak is really getting old in games... I'm tired of getting a♥♥♥♥♥♥eye-view of the world just to be stealthy. People can be stealthy by walking normally. I wish this old "crouch to activate stealth" FPS trope would die already.
- on more then one occasion I had someone stealthily dead in my cross-hairs, I shot, and it's like the bullet deflected off their face to just alert them to my presence instead of blowing their brains out... that was a bit annoying
- You can stealth sections with human opponents, but mutant enemies seem to home right in on you forcing engagement.
- When mutant enemies do show up, it seems there's an outlandish number thrown at you, and they are tough as nails (tougher then human opponents), so there's just this huge gap in difficulty as things go from moderately do'able to "holy cow, I'm gonna die!" as you progress from human to mutant sections of the game.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
It's hard to talk about Metro without comparing it to STALKER (another Russian-style post-apoc game franchise). Both have that dark, gritty, Russian-style atmosphere, but they're both unique. Both mix sci fi into their post-apoc mix, but in different ways. They both have supernatural + radiation mutations + mad science elements, but in different ways. They both have factions, but in different ways.
The biggest difference is that STALKER games are more open-world, choose your mission, while Metro games are more about laying a path in front of you and making you forge through it.
I recommend both franchises, though. They're both great, especially if you like Russian-style gritty atmosphere.
I grew up as a child of the 80's, and heard all the US indoctrination propoganda of "red scare", "better dead then red", etc bull**** during the Cold War. But, I'm also an anthropologist at heart. I was always fascianated by the USSR and Russia. In the states, everything we saw about them was delivered to us like we were looking at an alien world and alien species. Then Gobechev tore down the wall, the USSR fell, Russia came back as a superpower, and (regardless of what the media propogates) Russia is an ally of the states now, along with Japan, Germany, etc... it's like people you were fearful of are now your old friends.
I love games like this, because they humanize what seemed like an alien thing in my past. I get to walk through places and see the architecture, the technology, etc, etc, even if it's in a game. These games are also great, because there is no "United States vs. USSR" bull****. It's just a post-apoc setting, and that is all about survival and trying to help each other, regardless of who you are. So, it just helps tear down old prejudices and puts things into a different light.
Anyways, enough babbling... if you like Wolfenstein: New Order, or Fallout, or post-apoc, or Russian-style gritty settings, Metro & STALKER franchies will not disappoint.

Playing Guild of Dungeoneering is a charming and fun-filled experience.  You send your characters into dungeons that you create and level them up from 1 during each quest.  Leveling happens fast by just fighting a monster the same or higher level than you.  You can also collect a piece of gear from each fight to make your hero tougher (and sometimes more stupid).  Levels and gear are reset for each quest.
This may sound grindy, but you don't meta-level anything, except your guild, and there is no need to redo any quest once you complete it.  Characters can get Battle Scars (if you leave this feature enabled) that can augment them, usually for the worse from my experience.  You will get more powerful characters as you advance the plot and Tier 1 characters don't hit or defend hard enough for Tier 2 or 3 dungeons, so bear that in mind.
There is an element of randomness in the game.  To control for it, just don't over-stuff your deck with cards.  Sometimes selecting gold is better than your loot options.  Also, many times the best play in the dungeon building phase is to leave things as they are, if you've got a decent set up already.  Your main source of gold is the quest objective.  Discovering the dungeon, killing monsters and selling gear only gets you pocket change.
At times the game got a little tough, especially at the end.  You can, at times, win by drawing the right card and lose by drawing the wrong one.  Card games are like that!  But if you picked the right character and gear for the dungeon, this doesn't happen too often.  Although drinking from the wrong fountain can still get you killed!
I really enjoyed The Bard's mocking songs, but I played this game casually over two weeks.  I would pop on for a few dungeons here and there, when I needed a smile!
Not recommended for people who take gaming or themselves too seriously.

TL;DR
For being a free, this game is completely worth what you get. You have agility beyond belief which allows for more than a 'CoD like shooter', and extensive modding which doesn't "dumb down" the player at all. Quite literally billions of mod combinations! This game has a fluidity which doesn't allow for a review to do it justice. What does that mean? Well, the nearly monthly, FREE updates, can completely change this game. With the Plains of Eidolon just on the horizon, this game will go from mission based to open world. This is the sort of game that gets updates which seem like Warframe 2. Imagine Destiny, but Destiny 2 was a free update. It's a great game, honestly. Not P2W at all, and is SO generous you'll probably spend money just to donate to DE! I highly recommend this game. Why not try it? It's free!
Intro
Warframe, a universe thriving with lush, hidden lore. The place where a species of technologically crude, and industrious Grineer have made home. The place where a plutocratic, advanced, and money greedy Corpus have made home. The place where a technocyte plague known as the Infestation has made home. Ah, and of course.. the place where you, the noble, honorable, Tenno; have made home.
Warframe Pros
Warframe is a free to play done right, everything in this game can be earned for completely free. You know how I know? Well, I've been getting EVERYTHING for free, and have spent a fair amount of hours to get this info!
This game has thousands of mods. Unlike its 'comparable' Destiny, this game has more than a dumbed down skill tree. This game has a modding system. One which lets your power have billions of stat combos.
This game allows for player to player trading. Whether you're looking for 'prime' gear, or platinum (premium currency), trading has you covered. There are people willing to trade you for mods, gear, and platinum.
The UPDATES, now this is a big one. This game Warframe has had so many updates, nearly on a monthly basis that it could EASILY have had a Warframe 2 by now. For a game being completely free, these updates are WELL worth your time. I mean hell, for the first time, we're getting an enormous expansion adding open worlds! (which we all know will be expanded to every planet).
The memorable moments. One, undeniable fact, is that this game gets sweeter as time goes on. With monumental quests such as The Second Dream and The War Within, this game will blow you out of your socks. Though, for some, this can take up to 100-200 hours to get to. It's crazy, but gives you the best feeling and memory afterwards.
Your Space Mom. Every Tenno needs to feel like they have someone.. SOMEONE! For the longest time, in the game, I was closest to my dear space mom. The Lotus!
The soundtrack is absolutely gorgeous, I know this is a random one but it can really hit you in the feels later on. Try looking up "This is What You Are - Keith" <- It'll bring you to a Warframe song that is too good..
Warframe Cons
The grind can be unrelenting for some. For people like me, the grind was never bad because of my constant progression, but for people who aren't patient or want things quickly (in a progression system) this might be a bit too much.
The lore is very hidden. There is a story, but for some major lore, and theories on it, you'll have to look it up on YouTube. If you'd like a good series I recommend StallorD
The enemy scaling. For some people who love a hard challenge, the enemy scaling might be too much. Not exactly the ENEMY itself, but more specifically the ARMOUR on an enemy. It can be insane to even damage an enemy after level 100.
Improvements?
These are simply opinions on minor things...
Dojo improvements. I think Tennogen should be introduced for the Dojo, more decorations should be added, AND massive group builds. I'm talking about decorations that require a load of resources. That way if you have a large and active clan, you'll have special things that show your true power, and riches!
On 'Finisher' animations for the Nikana backslash, a mark/bodysplit hould happen. What I mean is that you do a diagonal slash across the enemies back, yet no deep cut appears, or body splitting? I dunno, just a request!
Final Words
Now please, note that this is all speculation and pure opinions! I love Warframe! If you have any questions, need help in game, a clan to join, or notice anything spelled wrong, or anything I should add.. please feel free to drop a comment in the space below!

I loved this game!
I’m all about good narratives in games.  It’s something that is RARELY done well, if at all, and this game really forces you to engage with its colourful story from start to finish. It doesn’t give anything away at the beginning, and because of this, it pushes you through a wealth of heavy and staggering commentary on the world we live in today, from the war in the Middle East, through to religious and cultural intolerance and intersectional feminism.
It’s really nice to see a female protagonist in a game that isn’t immediately portrayed as naïve due to her sex, and I believe this was done intentionally because of the stark contrast between Tahira’s character, whose main motif is self-actualisation and growth, overcoming familial turbulence and the pressure of becoming a leader (much the same way a man is taught to), and the other main female character “The Hammer” who seems to have already conquered that particular hurdle, and is now confident in her self and her sexuality, but does not let it get in the way of her ability to kick♥♥♥♥♥
I would be very interested to find out if the Hammer was used as a device to remove the burden of sexualisation from the main character, which is often a concern for me in a lot of games where the female characters are overly sexualised and the male characters overly domineering.
Overall, it’s a bit wordy, and that would probably affect a player with the attention span of a gnat whose main goal is to get straight to the battles. However for me, it is important to let yourself experience a new world first and immerse yourself before you get into the combat, which there is PLENTY of once you reach a certain point, believe me. The story comes together with the game's beautiful original score and fine artwork, giving it a pleasant cinematic quality that only fuels your thirst to get to the end.

This game's a really good remake of the NES version of Bionic Commando (which seems to be a sequel to the arcade version, sort of). The developers stayed faithful to the source game, and even the soundtrack is almost all remixed versions of the original tunes. The gameplay is solid, and there's some really cool complicated maneuvers you can pull off with the bionic arm. Every level has something in it that lets you go to a different level, so you always feel like it was worth your time when you clear an area. There are quite a lot of hidden areas and items to find, so be patient, as getting to the items can involve some really tough platforming. There's no ammo limits on any weapons, and all of them are useful for different things.
Overall, a great remake. Its more polished than most remakes of games, and this was published in 2009.
(One thing to note though- there is no V-Sync option, so sometimes there's some screen tearing, but only in very few sections.)

Bioshock 2 is an amazing sequel to the first game which learns from its predecessor and improves upon it in a lot of ways. The story is set a few years from the 1st part and you play as a Big Daddy, Subject Delta, in a quest to reunite with your long lost little sister, Eleanor Lamb who has been taken away by her mother, Sofia Lamb to play an integral part in the development of Rapture after its decline in the 1st game. Its a great and emotional story and deeply shows the father-daughter bondage as explored through the eyes of a Big Daddy.  There are some new characters and some old ones making a comeback through audio logs found just like the 1st game which explain the stories more.
There are some great new tonics and plasmids as well as weapons at your disposal to take down the enemies in the game. You fight the regular splicers with 3 new enemies in the game- Brute Splicers, Alpha Series Big Daddies and the Big Sisters. I have to say the combat is more challenging in this game than the first one. I played on the medium settings and died quite a lot of times whereas in the 1st game i never died once. When you find a Little Sister you have to protect her from splicers while placing strategic traps and turrets for her and your protection while she gathers ADAM, the in game currency through which you purchase various powerups. In a nutshell, the combat is satisfying and fun.
I played the Remastered version and apart from some texture improvements I didn't notice much difference between this and the old game. I did suffer from two crashes in the main game. I was lucky on that as I read on the forums that many people have faced lots of crashes and unable to progress in the game at all. Apart from that the performance was smooth for me and it was fun to play this game maxed out on a current generation video card.
I also played the DLC for this game "Minerva's Den" which I have to say is one of the best DLC's I have played in recent years of any game. Its a touching story and really expands on Rapture's behaviour on how it manages its security systems, air supply, vending machines functioning through an artificial intelligence known as "The Thinker" which was hidden from the rest of the city in a secluded part known as "Minerva's Den". Its fun and challenging to play and expands the story lore a little bit more.
I would recommend the game as well as its DLC outright and if you are a fan of the first game you will love this game fully. Buy it :)

Continuing the trend of Mass Effect is Mass Effect 2, cutting out all the fat and gristle of its predecessor to leave nothing but well-tuned gameplay. Initially, I felt as if the game was short and somehow more shallow than the original, but then I played them both through again; the first game feels suffocating in the amount of busywork there is, the constant inventory twiddling to make sure everyone on the squad had the best guns and armor, hanging out at the gear lockers for a half hour at a time, as well as the removal of the endless segments of planetside driving, looking for some mineral deposit or picking up some random item. Instead, you have the not-entirely-enjoyable but easily-avoidable "scanning for minerals" minigame that you can go to whenever you need to stock up to buy upgrades. The action is higher-paced and the game flows better, all-around. Rarely do you see an improvement on greatness, but here you have one.

After spending time with this game, I can personally say it's phenomenal... iiiiif it runs for you. I've seen the reviews, and some people have had serious issues with it; I personally have experienced none of them, but it's very much worth considering either way.
That in mind, I'm going to outright admit that part of what I'm about to say is probably gonna fall into the realm of 'only the biggest nerds will care as much as I do', but I'm gonna say it anyway. I've seen some people criticize how this game handles story delivery, and I can see why they don't like it; a lot of the game's story- spoken, anyway- comes from other characters monologuing at you, or monologuing into diaries you can find throughout the game. This is honestly a 'your mileage may vary' type of story delivery, but I personally think it works in this context- you're playing as a Big Daddy, and most of the time the main sounds they make are whale impressions. Bad ones, but whale impressions nonetheless.
Buuut some tend to glaze over some of the more subtle ways the game delivers its story- through the environment. There's lots of little things you can pick up on if you look around- from literal writing on the wall to the general condition of your surroundings, and all sorts of other details. Sometimes the game is decidedly unsubtle about it, but an interesting aspect of this method is that, if you don't care about the story, it doesn't forcefully present its full breadth to you; if you want it, you can find it easily; if you don't, you can ignore it easily.
This combines with some absolutely phenomenal gameplay-story integration. Plasmids and Vita-Chambers exist, and the story acknowledges it, and even exploits it at times. You can respawn basically infinitely in most circumstances, and the characters in the world... or at least, the sane ones, are aware of it. It produces a product that honestly feels basically seamless in many regards. Add in excellent environment and sound design and you have a recipe for an extremely immersive- and sometimes even a bit terrifying- experience.
It's not all sunshines and rainbows though- I will say that the gameplay could use a bit of work. The game likes to starve you of items and money if you're not being incredibly (and dare I say excessively) religious about searching bodies, and tracking down loot, and it can get extremely punishing because of it, even on the easiest difficulty. This doesn't sound like too big of a deal, but with the finite resources available in the world and the fact that it usually takes resources (particularly first aid kits, since it's often hard to avoid damage during fights) to get more of them. But other than that, it's generally pretty well-designed, with a wide variety of weaponry to use and a huge amount of options in all sorts of different situations. Things can get a touch repetitive sometimes, particularly with the Little Sisters, but otherwise the gameplay is very solid.
The runtime of the story is a bit short, but the Remastered version does come with both DLCs to offer even more playtime, and with how expansive the levels are, and their many secrets, plus four different endings (if I remember correctly), there's plenty to go back and do even after you've completed the story once. Ultimately, I'd say it's worth the 20-buck price tag.

A hardcore, rewarding speedrunner's platform game. Watch other players' replays in-game to see how the pros route the level (great feature!), master your favorite character (each of them play differently, and the differences are even more notable in high level play), complete the simpler levels to unlock progressively more insane stages (and possibly the most challenging secret stage zone I've ever seen), and feel the power of your own improvement.  Visit
to get involved in the running community and save all your replays - a sure way to track your own rank and improvement.  This game becomes more fun with every minute you put into it.

The problems are mostly within technical nature of these port. The most annoying one is the controls with mouse and keyboard. However this is optimized for a control stick on a game pad, which means one basically have to imitate the control sticks movement with the mouse, bah! The draw distance is short and so when one travels from one place to another there is a lot of micro-stuttering when the game loads new areas and it's textures. This even more annoying because the game runs with only 30 fps (due to hard coded facial expressions) and so frame rate drops are rather common and noticeable. Rockstar has loaded it's social club "crap" into this game presenting you a twitter feed of the Rockstar's twitter account (with lot of gta online info lol), This means there is another DRM on top of steams in this game.
In summary i give the games content 4 from5 stars, the port gets 2 from 5 stars.

This is a multiplayer based game around Medieval Times Europe, with a rank system that judges what weapons you can unlock and then use on other enemy players.

You'll soon find a server you can stick to, because it has a good ping, good players, and good people.
But you sometimes can find the exact opposite, so be careful.
Sometimes you'll find CS:GO'ers who just ruin the games, but they're very few in number.
But they always exist in every game, so its fine.
The devs seem they want to give us a Medieval Times multiplayer VS game, and they have done it well.
The gameplay is based on very accurate and sensitive hit detection, and parrying/blocking based on stamina.
All in all, a very good game to play if you feel like rushing into a warzone with knights and yelling Vanguards.

It is difficult to believe that Tahira: Echoes of the Astral Empire is the product of just a three-person development team. Such is its outstanding quality. However, the team at Whale Hammer Games have put together something quite magical. It is a heavily story-driven tactical turn-based combat game that places you in the world of Tahira the princess of Avestan. You must guide her and her merry band of followers throughout one of the most arduous nights of her kingdom's history.
Inspired by real-world travels throughout the Middle East, Nepal and India the game presents players with a well-crafted and meaningful world that will have you fully immersed within it. My initial expectations for the game weren’t particularly high because this is the team’s debut title. However, it becomes immediately clear that the game was made from the heart and is definitely a passion project.
The highlight of the game is the story. Its complexity and depth unveil itself as it progresses.
The writing has one clear tell-tale sign of superb writing. This is the fact that it repeatedly made me wonder and deeply question which side Tahira is truly on. Firstly, she personally appears to be of a pure heart. However, there is the fact that the land that her father ruled has experienced so much hardship. There are countless tribes and other nomadic people who fear and hate the current rule. Consequently, a crucial plot line – should you so choose to read into it – is whether the current rule is the right rule for the people of the land or whether those who have come to transform the land are doing the right thing.
Therefore, I believe that the game is making a political statement on the United Nations occupation in the Middle East. Because of this, it makes the game a timely release regardless of which side of the debate you find yourself in. Perhaps your worldview will change or become more educated through the playing of this game.
However, there is a potential downside to the game within its wonder. Those who prefer to have equal parts action and the story may be disappointed. There is much more story within the game than there is combat. Of course, players do have the choice to bypass the story segments by clicking through them. However, I am left to wonder what the point of playing the game would be without experiencing the story at least once.
A further downside is that the story is linear. This would impact those who would like to experience multiple playthroughs in the hopes of unlocking new content. However, it is a relatively minor quibble.
I have found myself becoming much more appreciative of outstanding artwork lately. Therefore, laying my eyes upon the artwork featured within the game sent me to artwork heaven. The screenshots may look relatively basic but it is very pleasing to the eyes.
Full credit for the artwork goes to Peter ‘Simmo’ Simpson.
The turn-based combat is a big reason why people would be invested in the game. Thankfully, it delivers a very solid all-around effort. There is a nice amount of content. There are a number of mechanics and classes each with their own strengths and weaknesses that are introduced throughout the game.
Without a doubt, my personal favorite is The Claw. They are ninja styled combatants who have a power titled ‘vicious strikes’ that enables them to use the game’s ambush mechanic to rip through multiple enemies before they have an opportunity to realize what is happening to them. It’s very cool.
One bonus to the combat is that there are multiple ways to win each encounter. This enables players to utilize a strategy that works for them while maintaining flexibility and variety where combat will never feel too repetitive.
However, there are a couple of weaknesses in the combat that deserve criticism. The first is that I would have enjoyed seeing a greater emphasis on formations. The game introduces formations early in the game but then struggles to utilize their strategic realization throughout the game. You’ll likely only ever use them when you are in a position to utilize certain skills. This, sadly, isn’t often enough for my liking.
Ultimately, I believe that the combat offers enough room for strategy but it could have been improved.
Although I am a fan of the presentation I would have appreciated voice acting throughout the scenes. The music is solid throughout, however, it becomes rather stale when there is no other sound throughout much of the narration.
There is so much dialogue that I almost considered adding the ‘Visual Novel’ tag to the game on the Steam store page.
Yes. The game has been Steamified by the addition of 8 trading cards and 18 Steam achievements. These achievements have been designed to ensure that the hunters play multiple playthroughs of the game. Some of them are more difficult than completing a single playthrough. For example, ‘Play it Safe’ requires players to complete a playthrough and ensure that Tahira, the game’s main character, never takes HP damage. Do note that this is not ‘defense’ damage and consequently does not mean that she cannot take any damage.
Tahira: Echoes of the Astral Empire has captured a gigantic piece of my heart. There are not too many games that are released these days where I feel that I owe it to myself to complete it multiple times. I am now interested to read about the places and the people that have inspired the game. This is something that I haven’t really experienced from a piece of media since I read The Kite Runner for the first time.  Therefore, I recommend the game not only for the great story and solid gameplay but for the profound cultural effect that I am enjoying it for.

Warshift is an amazing and also very difficult breed of an RTS with FPS aspects. Graphically speaking, it’s beautiful. The effects look flattering. The models are spectacular. At the time of writing this review, there're not that many buildings to be built at all. Just some basics. Long range unit brewer, short range brewer, defense systems, etc. The combat, however, is very fun. With many abilities to choose from, it is not easy to be disappointed. You can be a living dragon type creature (not flying, though), a fire-breathing one, too! I could see how this game could be described as a 4K dream in the future since I have been able to play some very action-packed battles with stable frames ranging from 45-60. It’s definitely worth picking up during a sale, heck, get a few for you and your friends. It’s a blast to play. I once missed 20 minutes on one battle, it just flew away. Time well spent!
The controls are difficult to remember for the first few times you’ll be playing a match. Otherwise, the game is solid. The mechanics work fluidly together. Playing with or against AI is actually quite of a challenge. You can choose from a decent pool of maps. Battles can go on for quite some time. It’s just a very good and difficult strategy game, to be honest. Just the FPS mechanics that make it truly special. It really, really reminds me of Airmech (an amazing F2P game on Steam, you should check it out). Both games are amazing, so try out Airmech as a “try before you buy” type deal, you’ll most likely stay playing both Warshift and Airmech.

Don't let my time spent on this game fool you. I've been on board since Raven's release and it's been quite a roller coaster in terms of my opinion of this game up until now.
Elsword is a great game, don't get me wrong. The mechanics are solid, I haven't run into many glitches, and the general feeling of the game when playing is unique. Being a 2D fighting game, scrolling is to expected when it comes to dungeons. Elsword does it very well. Each dungeon has its own theme and get more fun as the game progresses. With the addition of fields, players have an alternative to obtaining EXP. PvP itself also rewards players with EXP, but in much smaller doses. Skills are flashy, each playable character feels unique, and overall, the game is pretty easy to pick up.
However, some key things set this game back two steps whenever it advances one. Mechanics are solid but latency issues and ping play a large factor in being able to PvP well. More often than not, I find myself dying to lag than skill, even when the other person is better anyway. I've won my share of lag matches, and I always feel bad when a genuinely good player gets beaten because of the awkward connection. Dungeons rehash a lot of the mobs. Certain effects can bolster and change a mob, but for the most part, it just takes more time to kill it. Speaking of which, every dungeon's boss save for the secret dungeons' are extremely easy to kill. It takes two to four 200-300mp skills to down most of the bosses. Some dungeons are too long, especially toward levels 30-40, and feel as though they are just intended to burn precious stamina. Killing mobs in fields also costs stamina, but that was very minor in my opinion. The PvP matchup system runs by what seems to be just ranks. This can cause a lot of problems as some high level players who have already attained high ranks lose matches on purpose and "derank" in order to climb back up and farm for AP, which is currency only obtained through PvP. Skills themselves are not a problem, but more often than not, I find myself using little to no skills on the trash mobs throughout the dungeon. Leveling up in general to get more skills is a pain, especially that dreaded moment when the next quest is level locked and grinding is the only option. Grinding itself isn't that hard, but the community is not very friendly to grinders. The community itself is mediocre. Rudeness and trolls are abound in PvP, loners and the occassional leech can be found in PvE. Another non-game related problem besides the community is the economy. Massive prices, ED being extremely worthless, buying one's way to win through the cash shop etc. The cash shop itself is Pay2Win, and even though it's possible to overcome that (skill notebook, bank perks), it's extremely inconvinient and requires tons more effort. Some features that give the game a very different feel and the player a much easier time are locked down permanently without cash (skill slot B, pets).
Of course Elsword is a good GAME. That's about all it has going for it. Everything that contributes to the game other than the actual mechanics kind of break it. If you can put up with all that as long as I have, then kudos. Elsword is enjoyable, but only so much so.

Grappling hooks are insanely awesome in gaming culture.  They're a major staple of the Zelda franchise, for example.  The Bionic Commando: Rearmed game showed some promise being one of the few 2D games I'd be excited to play that had a grappling hook mechanic.  Unfortunately, that mechanic was not implemented in an intuitive way.
Yes, yes, I was getting to that.  The game doesn't work out-of-box.  It is missing the PhysX driver it requires.  It comes bundled with PhysX as part of the install, but it doesn't install the correct version.  You require this legacy driver:
(Thanks, support forums!)  That thankfully won't replace your latest PhysX driver, but it's a hoop you have to jump through just to get the game to load its initial agreement screen.  Then, you have to scroll through a lengthy contract with your arrow keys and finally agree to it before you can see the main menu.  At this point, I was already kind of upset with the game, but it had more issues going forward.
Yes, those two things exactly!  The controls were lacking a jump option, and the grappling mechanic was not as fun as it should have been.  I've seen free Flash-powered browser games from 2004 with more charm and elegance in their grappling mechanics than this game had.  I've seen better shooting mechanics in old arcade games from the late 80s and early 90s.  Compared to Contra or Metal Slug, I don't understand how anyone could recommend this game.
If this game has any nice points, it's the UI design.  Mind you, parts of the UI were non-functional, but most of it worked and looked very stylish.  It's a unique UI and worth the experience, I suppose, since the game was free.

The storyline for ME2 focuses much less on developing overarching elements ontop of what was established in ME1, opting instead to develop meaningful relationships with a large number of interesting characters and a touch more comedy.  Big introduction, lots of neat character development, big finale.  This works out great and seems designed to leave more major plot developments for ME3.
Gameplay feel has improved significantly, aside from some awkward default key bindings.  There's much more variety to progression with a few new abilities, guns that can be found laying around, upgrades and unlocks that can be bought with credits or built with raw materials, etc.
Planet surface exploration has been removed entirely, thankfully, aside from missions discovered as anomalies upon visiting certain planets.  Don't feel compelled to probe up more raw materials than needed for upgrades, or it'll take you a while and provide little benefit.
Overall, a solid improvement over ME1.

first of all 2K didnt do much 'remastery' here - i mean yeah the graphics may be improved a little bit - but they basically left all those glitches and bugs from the first game into the remastered version.
and ofc as a lot of ppl have stated in their reviews, the remastered version crashes every few hours, without ANY warning. maybe you were loading next area, maybe you just finished hacking a vending machine, maybe you were looting corpses... that doesnt matter. your game would simply freeze, then all your unsaved progress is gone.
and the last thing - the thing that made my mind up about giving a thumb down on the remastered version - is that certain achievements are bugged. namely any achievement involving an in-game counter to count numbers, for example - "Rapture Historian", an achievement that requires you to collect every single audio diary in the game.
tl;dr
for those who have bought the original version - dont bother. its plainly wasting money.
for those who havent bought the original version - IF you dont mind save often and the fact that you cant 100% complete it then... hell, why not give it a try :P

The gameplay, much like it's predescessor, is a turn based RPG a la classic fallout and in my experience is much faster paced than fallout and Divinity: Original sin. The difference in gameplay from Divinity: Original sin is that the action system is more compact, some attributes were replaced to make things more simpler, defence from physical and magical attacks as secondary "health" bars instead of %reduced, a character past system that gives you new dialogue, and that the dreaded rock paper scissor persuasion system is gone. Many sees the changes as a double edges sword as it removes the more familiar aspects of the game, but to me it was very easy to learn which may have been the intent of the studio and you can take this as a negative or a positive.


Better than previous system in my opinion
The player dialogue changes i very much appreciated, especially the removed rock paper scissor system, the character past dialogue is interesting and suprisingly incredibly useful as you can get minor help from NPCs, an example would be "MINOR SPOILER"
.


It's different though not much better than the previous system in my opinion.
The gameplay and combat is still quite similar to it's predescessor, but much more fast paced and flashy, especially the new source magic though some of it can be underwhelming. Many of the combat changes seems to be based around the new magic and physical armor system, particularly the damage dealt within one round of combat seems to have been bumped up by a lot both NPC and playable characters compared to the older system.
The difficulty around the armor system can sometimes be glaring because magic, to me, is a much greater threat than physical attacks because of the almost ridiculous amounts of dangerous magical effects that enemies utilize like
compared to the physical debilitations,
being the most dangerous physical ones. The good thing about the new system is that as long as you have the type of armor the effect/element affects the debilitation will only be applied when that armor bar is fully depleted, though some can see this as a negative since i actually liked the willpower/bodybuilding system.
Physical combat is still a very good way to do focused damage on one particular enemy, but is more devastating on one with little to no physical armor as  a well placed  barrage of arrows and melee hits can dispatch those enemies very quickly, though the same can't be said for monsters fighting against the playable characters unless the players are underleveled, but a proper and well built team can still kill enemies 3 levels higher than them.

Great indie title that can be approached in a variety of ways. On easier difficulties and on large planetery systems it plays like a Diablo-esque version of Beat Hazard where you grind enemies for research (xp), goons (prisoners) and REZ ($) in order to improve your fleet. On higher difficulties and smaller galaxies you need to approach things more cautiously and you'll need to plan ahead. There are many types of ships that you can unlock by reverse engineering their hulls and each ship can be upgraded with a variety of weapons (rocket launchers, turrets, lazers, drones, etc). The game offers a per-planetery system alliance mechanism, a research system involving  dozens of technologies that directly effect your ships (engine,hull,etc), a trading system, some randomized missions and events. Combat is real time but there's also a pause button/tactical screen. There's more than meets the eye in this one.

Before commencing this review, I would like to note that this is a game that should really be played using a gamepad.  The default controls use the keyboard but the game does not work well when it's played that way.  If you don't own a gamepad you may not necessarily have the best experience with Dustforce.
I'm not normally the type of person who enjoys platformers, especially fast-paced ones like these, but something about Dustforce resonates very strongly with me.  I entered the game wary, as the complicated gameplay and challenging levels that I had seen were intimidating, but in under two days I've put over ten hours into it and I haven't had this much fun in a video game in a long time.
I suppose this is a difficult game to review objectively, but if you're an obsessive perfectionist like myself then this game will likely have you playing for hours at a time without slowing down.  The good music, relaxed atmosphere, and very fluid animations of the game make that much easier to accomplish.  I suggest that even if you aren't a fan of platformers, if you like a game with many testing challenges to overcome, then you should definitely buy this one.  It's worth every penny.

Although the game appears to be in its infancy, it's no doubt that it is
most beautiful Unity powered game, and while I'll admit that the third person vehicular combat doesn't make the RTS aspect any easier, I feel that the combining of a vehicular action game and an RTS renders this game the start of something great.
While the RTS would otherwise be standard fare, the piloting of your combat avatar (your hero unit) plays a crucial part as you would need to queue up a build order, fly to the desired energy node with your avatar and deploy the building to ensure control of energy node. To keep the player seated in their hero unit, infantry and vehicle production buildings are 100% automated. Take note that this really doesn't make the RTS aspect any easier, since you'll also need to turn the tide with your personal vehicle as well as build air units from your spawn point since you can't be everywhere at once. My main gripe is that the AI is nothing short of brutal even on easy (though i dunno if that has to do with my personal skill with RTS, so if anyone else owns this game, I'd like to know that it isn't just me.)
Personally, I cannot help but note that everyone loves to hate Unity because of this aspect, but I'd like to think that i'm not lying when I say that this game looks gorgeous and I'd go as far as to say that it'll take a long time until Unity games look as good as this. My primary dislike in this regard is the lack of advanced visual options.
Looking at both the gameplay
the graphics, you can imagine how surprised I am to realize that this is completely done by one person. While I believe that Shigeru Miyamoto's philosophy about rushing games applies to WARSHIFT, I'm hoping that the money I give to Cyril Megem will go towards eventually finding likeminded developers who will help with the completion of this product.
One thing which i think would help the game a lot is to give co-op players the ability to ping the host over the minimap and/or allow them to enter the RTS view. As it currently stands, there is no hotkey to signal the host whenever co-op players free up power supplies.

Visually the game looks a lot like SSX 3, but you can change the screen size to match current monitors and add antialiasing. You have a selection of about six skiers, and you can customize them with different clothes and gear. I was a little disappointed in the overall lack of customization. It's enough that you can pick an outfit you like, but you probably wont be satisfied with the selection of hats, pants, and jackets. Either way I've seen more customization in other snow games (Amped comes to mind). It's not bad, but it's not great.
Gameplay is challenge based, and remember it's a freestyle game so no races. Challenges come down to gaps, rails, pickups, and score challenges. The skiing is very smooth and responsive. Big jumps feel satisfying, and nailing a huge off-axis spin feels great. Crashes are physics based, so your character rag dolls down the hill and your skis fly off in all directions. The game also has controller support for two players with customizable buttons. I personally use a wired xbox 360 controller and it works fine.
There are about 5 mountain environments to traverse, all various backcountry areas. So far each run is about 2 minutes long from top to bottom, with multiple runs per different area. It is NOT a single mountain. Instead you select a mountain on the main menu and then select which run. The challenges are interesting enough to keep you occupied, which is good because there isn't any story. Also keep in mind that this is a semi-old game, so the music is completely dated.
So why do I recommend this game even with limited customization, old music, and no races? Because the core gameplay is very solid and intuitive. The skiing is fluid and feels great for an arcade style game. I also haven't experienced any pc problems with this game, so it is very stable. For ten bucks, you could do a lot worse. Is it the best ski/board game I've ever played? No. But it's also nowhere near the worst. A very satisfying ski game for the price.

This is a tough one. The game is very clearly not finished, or not polished I should say. The UI is disgusting at best, buttons often times just don't work in the main and pause menus, the game could be optimized a bit better as even on a beefy computer, frame drops were abound while controlling the "avatars" directly.
However, even in it's raw state, there's very clearly a solid idea here, and there's not a doubt in my mind that, eventually, this will be a great game. But it stands that there are some glaring flaws, or at least shortcomings.
The idea of directly controlling your units in an RTS game isn't new per-se, but I can't think of a single game outside of the Men of War franchise that lets you do it, other than Warshift of course. You also have plenty of traditional RTS gameplay, base building and whatnot. Additionally, those only familiar with MOBA type games will be pleasently suprised to know that unit creation buildings will by default send squads of soldiers marching to their dooms in a fashion almost mirrored by DotA or LoL. Traditional RTS players will also be happy to hear that you can choose to control these units yourself all the time if you so please, your "avatar" included. Speaking of the avatar, it's a little dissappointing that it's the only unit you can direct control during the match, unless I missed something (not a whole lot of playtime after all), but maybe thats just the Men of War fan in me wanting to send a lone infantryman to do the work of a batallion.
If you're on the fence, then it really comes down to why. If you simply want assurance that the game is functional, then you've got yourself a purchase here. If you're looking for a finished product, then give it some time. I'm going to give Warshift the benefit of the doubt, and a portion of my paitence, and I'm not going to refund it just yet. However, if the finished product is indeed what I'm seeing here, then it may just be the last time I trust an Early Access game.

I cannot recommend the remastered edition as to not reward the poor behavior.
Bioshock 2: Game Review
The game returns to Rapture, after the events of the original title. This time, the player is a Big Daddy, trying to rescue a little sister from Lamb who seems to be running the once thriving city under the water. Once again, players dawn guns and plasmids as they make their way through swarms of splicers, big daddies and big sisters.
Bioshock 2 doesn't stray far from the original game, which is a problem. The first game had a sense of wonder and exploration of a paradise in shambles with a sinister ambiance.  Sure the levels are different, but I didn't find them nearly as memorable. Almost all the splicers return with few editions, and since almost all the plasmids and weapons are the same as the previous game, there just isn't a lot of variety to expand upon. They also dropped the crafting system without much to replace it. I suppose the protecting of little sisters as they gather Adam counts for "new."
The story is also not as compelling. In the first game, the player is immersed in Andrew Ryan's dream of a libertarian utopia that ripped itself apart. Every element of the game reflects the decadence, amoral science, and self-serving attitudes of Ryan's world. Lamb exists within Ryan's shadow. Her Utilitarian beliefs just don't resonate due to having no manifestations of her ideals on display. And the story takes a long time to get started. I was probably half way through the game before I felt invested into finding out what was going on.
Little changed in the combat. Plasmids on one hand and guns in the other. But there is no radial menu to select weapons from and considering that weapons don't automatically shift to a different ammo once depleted (each weapon has 3 ammo variations), I often found myself cycling through empty weapons in frustration. This is compounded by the camera and hacking tool both being on the weapon wheel, in the middle of it no less. I've never had to rebind so many keys to feel some level of comfortable with an fps. Plasmids have the same issue. I found myself not wanting to unlock more of them because it was already cluttered and using the F key for 8 plasmid slots is not feasible. They also oddly removed the ability to recharge your evo at will, having to wait for it to be spent.
The Protector Trials DLC, which comes with remastered, and pretty lame. If you didn't get enough of protecting little sisters in the main game, enjoy another 24 of those.
Bioshock is one of my favorite games, and much like Lamb, Bioshock 2 just can't get out of the shadow of its predecessor. It doesn't really do much better, and lacks in a lot of areas that made the first one great. I would give still give it a positive review, albeit a luke warm one.
Edit: Minerva's Den
Easily the best part of bioshock 2. Playing it I realized how cramped the main game was. Lots of tiny rooms that we just thrown about with no rhyme or reason. Minerva's Den adds a new weapon, new plasmid and was a better story than the main game and it didn't crash once, plus all the achievements work.

First things first, I want to point out how difficult it was for me not to give this game a big red thumb down. I'll make sure to go into detail about why this choice was such a challenge, but let's start with the game itself.
Bioshock 2 is the (obvious) successor of the widely-acclaimed Bioshock. The game was received with mixed-feelings. Despite having favorable reviews, all within the 4-5 star range, the game suffered critique from fans of the original. I've always had a working theory about this. I believe that most people who didn't experience the first prior to the second found it as an enjoyable game, whereas those that did experience the first had higher expectations and therefor felt disappointed. I fall into the second category, I do not feel that Bioshock 2 compares to the original. That being said, I don't think Bioshock 2 is horrible, I mostly feel it's "okay".
The environment of Rapture has changed in the near decade since our last visit, although not as much as you'd expect (some of those posters are tough, damn). Strangely, it seems that although there were multiple ends in the predecessor, Bioshock 2 seems to takes place specifically after one of those endings. Splicers have managed to maintain their dirty habit, some now having a more extreme appearance than last time. Society as a whole has remarkably held up somehow. With all that said, for me it doesn't feel like Rapture. It looks like Rapture, it has the same art-deco design, same crazy denizens, but something feels off. Honestly I feel it might have to do with level design, in Bioshock the levels are made very fluid and have a sense of claustrophobia to them. I didn't have that same feeling in Bioshock 2. If anything Rapture seemed very expansive, with massive areas and several story buildings.
Gameplay-wise quite a few things have changed. Players are now capable of using plasmids and weapons simultaneously, which some people might mark as an improvement but I find myself at times stumbling around my keyboard and juggling around between a spear gun and a frosty Winter Blast. Keybindings have been rearranged weirdly enough. And walking is no longer an option, you're sprinting from now on buddy. The hacking mini-game has been revised as well, you no longer tell father time to take a seat when you decide to mess with pipes! Is this an improvement? I'm not entirely sure. I never found myself during my two playthroughs really jumping around and gunning gene-junkies down while hacking something, so it didn't really change much. A bit quicker though I suppose. And they've added the gatherer function, you get to play Big Daddy and defend your little sister while she does her eight to nine and drains adam from rotting corpses while hordes of splicers come to investigate. Probably one of the more innovative additions to Bioshock 2, though it does become stale after awhile.
Here's the big subject for me, story. The story in Bioshock 2 is, while I hate going back to an earlier statement, but it's simply "okay". Was I sucked into the plot? Not really. Did the tragic history of Delta and Eleanor tug at my heart strings? Old ticker just kept chugging. Really the only character I felt helped build my image of the world of Rapture was Sinclair, but he stands alone. Words aren't coming to me right now, the games story just didn't leave much of an impression on me. It's an  interesting tale but sadly it doesn't live up to its predecessor (Levine 4 Lyfe).
Now for what you've all been waiting for. Why did I struggle to give this review that nice cyan blue thumb?
This game is a mess.
I mentioned the crashing issue that's a prominent subject in my Bioshock 1 Remastered review, but in Bioshock 2 the issue is near terminal. I may have crashed for each hour of gameplay, each time without warning. Another issue with the game is the achievements. When I have to find a guide on how to do simple game related achievement then there's an issue. Some are just impossible without some digging, and trust me there are guides on the subject. During my second playthrough I had collected one hundred and twenty audiobooks and still hadn't unlocked the achievement for finding one hundred. These problems just make it so difficult to enjoy the game, especially when you crash and have to retrace almost a half hour of gameplay (please don't make Groundhogs Day the Game a thing). At one point I swore I'd give Bioshock 2 Remastered a negative review.
And the real kicker here is that the Remastered version doesn't really offer much more than its original. While the Bioshock Remastered obtained commentary, a museum, and several puzzle games, Bioshock 2 mainly just got a slight polish. With all the bugs it just feels like a worst version of the none-remastered version. It made my playthroughs feel like a job rather than a pastime. I genuinely hate that later I just had to accept that I had to save for almost every block I ran (because you can't walk).
Now onto a more jolly subject before tying this review up onto a teddy bear with a bow, some Adam, and hey I'll throw a gene-tonic in there too! Let's talk Minervas Den! Oh, I'm forgetting the Protector Trials. The Protector Trials are a way to pass time. Anyways, onto Minervas Den. If I had a genie in a lamp I'd ask him to first sound like Robin Williams and then ask for him to somehow swap Minervas Den and Bioshock 2, let Delta be DLC! Minervas Den is such a fantastic little story, while the plot is somewhat generic it at least left me with an impression. Rapture Central Computing, while borrowing some level design from Bioshock 2, is just so much more interesting. A crazy new weapon and plasmid, a new Big Daddy model that looks like it should be guarding the gates of heaven, all these great things and they all had to be confined into a DLC! Oh, and lastly, if I hadn't driven the point home yet: Sigma > Delta.
So I'm not entirely sure if I've made the right choice giving this game a thumbs up, but I still think if you're a fan of Bioshock you should experience its sequel. You may enjoy it, you may not, but you won't know unless you try.

Traditional platforming has never felt so graceful.
If I had to sum up dustforce in one word it would be “Understated.” Everything from the stylized visual aesthetic, to the almost silhouette character sprites, the animations, enemies and even the level design all hold themselves with such dignity. The small flashes of flare that you get, when performing your special ability and the slow motion finishing move at the end of each level all give you a sense of “Yeah, I just did that, whatever.” As you calmly walk off from your amazing display of platforming prowess without even looking back.
Mechanics wise, dustforce is a great example of giving the player a single minded goal, and the tools to get there. I forgot where I read it and i hope they don't mind the unattributed quote but it sums up so perfectly the mentality I draw from the game. “Dustforce is not content to let you be content with yourself.” Again apologies for probably butchering the original quote but it is so true.
Dustforce has a tiered level structure where you unlock keys to higher tiered levels by completing previous ones to a certain proficiency. While simply completing the level from start to finish may be enough at the start to work towards a few keys and level, you will eventually need to break past your preconceived limits. This system of partial completion still progressing the player is great for giving the player control over their own difficulty curve and doesn’t fall into the pit of so many other challenging platformers where you get stuck on a single level and cannot progress.
Another thing it does great is support the players journey of self improvement without being overbearing. After completing any particular level you are given access to the high scores from the community. But where other games may stop there dustforce then records the exact run of that player so that you can view it whenever you want in its entirety. I cannot tell you the amount of times I was stuck on certain levels but then was able to completely change my approach after seeing a “pro” do it in front of my eyes.
But no game is perfect and Dustforce is no exception. The physics and movement in the game is very momentum based. If you are unable to continue your exact series of boosts and ramp launches you will find your experience rather jerky. When it works it makes speed runs a visually awe inspiring art, but when it doesn't you find yourself spamming jumps off walls at odd angle into spike pits or off cliffs.
I would recommend this game to anyone that loves tried and tested platforming mechanics with a stylish coat of paint and some really nice quality of life features. And to anyone that loves the feeling of becoming one with your controller, eye's glazed, as you become one with the game and skirt even the most precarious platform dungeons with grace and ease.

(Please note: My playtime on Steam currently does not represent how much I have actually played L.A. Noire - I also own a copy on the PS3)
L.A. Noire is a great game, albeit flawed. The facial technoloy is astounding and really does a great job of getting down the faces right, unlike OTHER games (Mass Effect: Andromeda
). The gameplay itself is pretty cool, too. On the surface, it looks like another standard Third Person Shooter trying to mimmick the overwhelming success of the GTA series. Once I started playing, however, I was pleasantly greeted to a game full of more mystery and intrigue than gunfights and punching. Yes, there are bits where you do shoot people, but the developers make it clear through cleverly implemented mechanics that shooting isn't the focus of the game.
If you despise stories in games, don't buy L.A. Noire. If you do, really do give this one a shot. Despite how bland it might look at first, it's one of the most original and brilliant games of the early 2010s. That said, it isn't without it's faults, such as:
1) The PC Port itself. Listen, the PC port here isn't astoundingly bad, but it's FAR from perfect. There are some reports that it doesn't run well at all on Windows 10, it works fine for me, but just be aware of your computer's setup before buying. There are some other issues, among them is incredibly low framerates on computers that are more than capable of running this game. I was one of these people, but thankfully, there's a good chance that some simple tweaking in the configuration program before running could help fix the problem for you (if you're having this issue, you can find instructions
; it worked for me). The game itself is capped at 30 FPS due to the facial technology being unstable at any framerate but 30, but it's very much possible to uncap it - just be careful as doing this has proven to have some consequences.
2) The first missions are kind of... ehhhhh. They're not terrible and are decent at introducing the player to the game's mechanics, but they could have been done allot better.
3) The Open World doesn't really need to be in the game. Despite having a giant map to explore, which faithfully re-creates L.A. in the time period this game is set in, there's little reason to explore it and this game is very linear. I mean, VERY linear. Unlike most Open World games, you don't drive to a location to start a mission, or do specific tasks (like walking around or waiting) to get more details in games like Nier: Automata. Nope. The missions start by themselves, have virtually only one way of being completed, and usually are followed by a cutscene of some sort. I have nothing wrong with this, but it seems to me that, again, the Open World isn't at all necessary to gameplay.
And that's about it. If you're looking into buying L.A. Noire but don't want to deal with the so-so PC port or have to deal with aging hardware, the good news is that Rockstar is actually re-releasing it on newer consoles this November. There will also be a Nintendo Switch port, for people who think that every single video game known to mankind needs to be ported to that system... for some reason.

It's golf.
It's playable concurrently with people you like to hang out with. Y'know.. friends.
It's Golf With Your Friends.
In the seven months since I purchased this game, the developers have added two courses, increased the graphics quality, and made the game much more stable. There's even a mechanism added to save your favorite game settings into presets in order to access them quickly.
Many of the holes on the courses were designed with the help and creative input of players, and the developers have added little honorary plaques at the tee areas to show their appreciation. I'm not sure that is a great thing since most of these holes are extremely difficult! That being said; it's definitely the struggle of scoring low in front of your friends that makes this game so charming.
Everyone plays at once and the default setting doesn't allow golf balls to contact one another. There's a default two minute timer on each hole so it really can be a fun social experience where you aren't waiting your turn all the time.
I've been in public games with up to twelve people as well as eight friends at once in a private game. We've tried a bunch of different rule changes out. It can be pretty chaotically fun. Everything from game world physics to the shape of the golf ball can be modified. Imagine twelve people playing with tennis-sized balls shaped like cylinders.. on bouncy ground and in low gravity.. where everyone is richocheting off of one another. Or, you could play with lower strokes-per-hole and a lowered time limit in a hyper-competitive match. Lots of different options means Golf With Your Friends can be absurdly fun to play.
Once, in a public game on Oasis (before the fourth course was added), a developer stopped by and asked us questions about what we liked and any bugs that we noticed as we played a full game together. I'm told that happens relatively often. That's pretty nice to see in an Early-Access title.
The one major quibble I have is that loading the new haunted course hangs the game every single time (since at least 10/16). No matter who's hosting, we have to wait patiently with our Task Manager open while the game recovers itself.
I highly recommend this game because you can play it with anyone and the price is extremely small for the amount of fun you'll receive. Enjoy!

~~My first review~~
Let me first explain my negative review. Ultimately, I wouldn't recommend this game to myself. Rather, I would recommend Dustforce to masochists, personal enemies, and professional platform gamers.
I really wanted to like Dustforce. The promo videos made it seem like one casually 'ninjas' and floats about beautiful 16 bit levels collecting cobwebs like Sonic collects rings. Not quite.
The concept itself is interesting. The goal is to travel through obstical courses as fast as possible. Along the way, you must run through patches of dust and hit "enemies" in order to clear the level. This is a 2D speed-running game.
The physics and mechanics make absolutely no sense to the uninitiated casual game playing plebian like myself. It can be frustrating, repetative and time consuming simply jumping from platform to platform in the overworld. This is where you wander around finding doors to unlock, which represent individual levels.
Compare with titles like Super Meat Boy and Cave Story. These games present challenging and interesting game play, while having control schemes and movement that are predictable and intuitive. Dustforce DX creates simple levels, that are made challenging by a character that is difficult to control. Essentially, they took a relatively simple concept and made it difficult to enjoy on account of sloppy, tendinitis aggravating controls that are frustrating to learn and maddening to master.
Further, the actual levels are fairly uninteresting and easy to get through. The challenge is that in order to properly complete a level, simply getting through it is not enough. You need to get the fastest time possible without missing any dust. This means repeating levels until you have every move perfected. This ends up being more busy work than anything else. You could easily spend a thousand hours trying to perfect each level. Combined with controls that assault your hands, it can be a very unforgiving process of which I quickly grew tired.
I suppose in the Genre of repetitive games which slap you around and demand perfection it succeeds. However, I guess I'm not a fan of games where developers decided the best way to make a game challenging is to make the character barely controllable. I feel like back in the days of original 8 bit graphic platformers, this would simply be called bad controls and it would be relegated to 2 and 3 star reviews. These days there are gamers who specifically enjoy and excel at games with lousy controls, and I suspect if you're one of those people you will find a lot of fun in spending countless hours punishing yourself on Dustforce.
Recall the viral flash game where the object is to control a sprinters limbs to push him over the finish line, or rather see how far you can comically stumble and hobble across a track. This is the same concept taken to it's inevitable extreme...
OK, it's not THAT bad, but you'll be spending a half hour trying to jump onto a ledge just to get to another stage... only to discover that you don't have the key to unlock it. Oh right, keys.
In order to unlock all the levels, you will need to complete the stages with perfect scores to accumulate keys. Ugh.
Summary;
If you are considering using the standard keyboard layout, either get an ice pack for your hands or forget about it. The game is barely playable on a game-pad, which is far superior to the keyboard controls.
If you're a demi-god with spaghetti fingers and the ability to pick up outrageous controls, and have a lot of time and patience, I guess you will LOVE this game.
If you're a casual gamer who likes simple controls, and doesn't want to invest the hours it will take to teach your hands to waltz like noodles through endlessly repetitive levels of dust ninja then get Super Meat Boy instead.

I didn't go into this expecting much and ended up pleasantly surprised.
Please note that as I write this it's still in early access with only one career path at present. That being said at this writing there's still quite a bit of content to explore. It's something of a tycoon/management game with multiple facets to explore - aside from making videos, taking courses and odd jobs, there's also a social element to the game. In a way I'm reminded of The Sims, but with a much narrower focus.
That being said this is an early access review, and there are early access flaws. The pacing of the game feels a little awkward, in part because you're encouraged to rush through the earliest part of the game (in which you live at your moms home as a kid in high school). By default you basically are going to study enough to do well on 1, maybe 2 tests, and then immediately move out with your best friend and ditch school. I would have liked having to go through at least five months (or better yet, an option on how long you have to live like this). The task juggling also toned down later on and money ceased to be a real concern after a point, so more random events (they are in there, I just don't see them often) would be appreciated. The UI is still a bit clunky in a few areas, but the bottom line is I like what I see despite the issues present.
The devs are responsive on the forums and there are plenty of subforums, including ones for different languages.
It may still be a work in progress, but it's very promising thus far. Keep your eye on it.

It's always sad to see such a cool idea ran into the ground so hard.
Crusader kings 2 does not feel like a game. In fact, it's hard to defend as a game when you spend more time watching your computer screen blankly than participating in any kind of strategy or diplomacy. This is so you can desperately watch a map that looks like a boardgame, questioning why you were ever given a functioning cerebral cortex just to waste it with this♥♥♥♥♥♥ so the game can instruct you that after wasting real time hours it has finally given you the "ok" to get some sort of progress or feeling of worth. The "progressfdsf" in the form of a province soon turns into nothing but a huge damn headache, there is nothing gained but more stress. But don't worry, one way or another CK2 will find a way to rob you of it and do it's best to convince you to uninstall it.
There is no progress. Every step of the way CK tries it's best to prevent you from feeling any sense of victory, accomplishment, satisfaction and definitely no fun. When "political intrigue" or "strategic warfare" fail, the game will do acrobatics with it's own appalling mechanics that would make circus ole  stare in confused disgust, several times it will straight out lie about heirs or some small mechanic to completely rob you of anything you deem worth your time in this mess.
The roleplaying appeal it appears to have is actually paper thin and puddle shallow. I could feel more like im taking part in history by wiping my♥♥♥♥♥with a copy of dynasty warriors. I would actually feel bad about it though, since dynasty warriors has depth when compared this abominable effigy of a strategy game. The events and traits are laughably few in number and the most you get from the NPCs is the cold blank stare on their portraits. They look like they've been playing CK2. No wonder everyone in the middle ages is portrayed as so irrationally moronic.
Nothing sticks, nothing is ever really "yours" so you never feel attached to it. You will waste hours just trying to dig yourself out of pit after pit, hammer through roadblock after roadblock. I suspect this game is a philosophical commentary on the "exercise in futility". You have no kingdom or provinces, you have a vomit colored splotch on the map, that you are given no reason to love or care about while ck pokes the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it with a hot iron, giggling like a mentally deficient sadist who you will slowly realize you have no desire to interact with.
It's like someone out there thought up a brilliant monty python-esque comedy on the ridiculousness of fuedal dynasties - and then some absolute moron decided to make a game out of it. No matter what role you think youre playing in the game, youre really just a fool for paradox in a medieval comedy where you waste $40 to be medievally♥♥♥♥♥♥upon. I really can't press this enough, do not waste your money on this farce of a product. If you want a cool historical experience, or any sort of enjoyment whatsoever, please check out CIV 5 instead.
