Contrast has a brilliant idea - what could happen if we could shift into shadows and live in the umbral world? The developers really had lightning in a bottle here, and the 1920s setting is just perfect. The game also deals with two of my favorite themes in fiction - that being "what is real?" and the image of the double, the reflection, the...other.
You play as Dawn, the "imaginary" best friend of Didi, a young girl who appears to be retreating into fantasy to deal with the break-up of her parents. While running around a beautifully imagined world you shift into shadow to solve various puzzles. I want to live in this video game. There are not many games I can say that about, the only other one being Deus Ex: Human Revolution. The atmosphere is just THAT good. This would be the perfect game if it were not for one molar-crunching flaw. The controls are a nightmare. The sticks are too twitchy, the buttons are unresponsive and the camera is epileptic. You'll be shouting and swearing a LOT during this game. I finished it in four hours and I'm happy I stuck with it to the end, it's just a shame that no updates have been made to fix the bugs.
And if you think that the voice of Didi's surrogate dad is familiar, it's none other than Elias Toufexis who also voices Adam Jensen in Deus Ex.
There is amazing potential here and, for the most part, it's a wonderful game, but the controls cripple it.
There are 22 trophies/achievements (I could only manage 15) and trading cards included, as well as a lovely soundtrack album.
It's a good game. It just is a little confusing about why the girl is out of the shadows but not anyone else, except dawn. And the ending feels open..

Interesting, but the controls can be a bit clunky.  The story is good, the visual style is right up my alley, and the puzzles never get too frustrating.  Now that I've played this I regret not getting We Happy Few before it's price sky rocketed, because I'd like to see where the developers go from here, but I didn't like this enough to pay $60+ for their followup.

The concept of this platformer is intriguing, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired.
Contrast's story is a mess. It revolves around a small girl, Didi, wanting to fix her family matters, and Dawn (the silent character the player controls) helps her in this endeavor. Didi comes across as fickle, being sad one moment and ecstatic the next, and such inconsistencies also exist in the opinion she holds of her father. I'm still not sure whether she truly loves and respects him or if she thinks he's a giant mongoloid who has trouble getting dressed.
There is a lot of world building missing in this game. I don't know why it's three-dimensional world in which two-dimensional shadow people live, nor why there are some people who can shift between the shadows and the actual world. The ending tried to shed some light on it, but it was ultimately a vague non-explanation.
The gameplay is where I thought this game would shine, but I often had to battle against the clunky controls. The camera is often not where I wanted it to be, and would move in wide sweeping patterns if I tried turning it while moving. Some mechanics didn't always execute properly, ending up with me either having to start from the beginning or dying.
Sadly, I can't recommend getting this game, even when it's on sale. It looked good to me at first, but playing it just ended up with me becoming frustrated that the game isn't as polished as it should be.

There's a lot that can be said about Chivalry: Medieval Warfare, but it all boils down to this:
RRRAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAH!
Basically, you run, you shout, you chop people's limbs off in the most satisfying way imaginable, and you get good, and then you chop even more limbs off plus smash some heads in with a giant hammer (that stuff never gets old). Do some objectives, come hither, oooo look: a rainbow!, run some more, duel, duel on TO servers, get scolded for duelling on TO servers, go on a duel server, get rekt, go back to TO and behave! Rinse and repeat. Fun, fun, fun!
It's like being inside The Kingdom of Heaven (the film, not the actual place) with all its visceral beauty and gore. It will get your heart racing and you'll feel every slash, every bash and every stab. Decent headphones are a must - there is no sound more awe-inspiring than that of someone's helmet, skull and brains being mushed into a sticky pulp with one drop of a maul. It's just beautiful!
Stick around and you'll meet some of the nicest people around (at least EU-side, but I do have friends in the States too). Community-driven events and antics happen all the time and you can count on veteran players helpin you out with tactics, optimisation and anything really. Sure, there are a few bell-ends too, but every game has a few, nothing to be concerned about. Talk to me if you need anything and I'm sure 99% of players over 50 lvl will say the same.
In terms of graphics - little bit outdated, but it's UE3 so there's no surprise. Sound design is superb, rivalled only by that of Alien: Isolation and I'm not saying it lightly. Playability? Let my 1100hrs of gameplay speak for themselves (at the time of writing this review).
In closing: don't be a scrub, join in on the fun!
P.S. DEATH TO ARCHERS!

Turn-based dungeon crawler which you can control for about 90%, the other 10% is up to RNGesus. The idea is that you've got your own guild of adventurers (dungeoneers) which you send out on quests to earn fame and glory (translation: money). The adventurers in case are (more or less) mindless minions... sorry... "highly capable employees"... which have to be coaxed... darn it, I meant "encouraged"... into doing things for you.
First, you need to attract them ("expand the guild") which gains you the manpower to send out on quests. You do this by using money which the dungeoneers gain for you on said quests. You can expand the guild with various rooms granting various boons which can (or cannot) be used in the following adventures.
Secondly, you need to pick a quest for your minions, sorry... I meant "valued employees" to go onto. You pick these on a map. There's not really a way to know if you're going to be able to handle it or if the rewards will be worth the effort. You've just got to jump in. If your dungeoneer happens to be killed quite gruesomly... Well, whatever. There's always more dungeoneers. Death is permanent, but as in corporate life, no one is irreplacable. You can always retry an adventure.
Once in the adventure, it turns out the dungeoneers have a will of their own and need to be enticed to complete said adventure. If it's not interesting for them, they'll leave and go do other stuff.
The adventure is turn-based. Each turn you get five cards which can either be new rooms to add, treasures to place around and monsters to fill the adventure with. By use of these (entirely random) cards you yourself generate the dungeon, the monsters the dungeoneers encounter and the rewards they reap. The dungeoneers find their own path based on what's ahead in their field of vision (mostly just the next room or the one beyond that) and it's up to you to guide them in such a way the complete the quest and don't f--- up.
Battles with monsters are fought by use of a cardsystem based on RNG which means you can either damage the monster or defend yourself. Loot afterwards is also a cardsystem based on RNG. All the aforementioned cards come out of a deck which you yourself have some control over by expanding your guild. Remember when I said "you can expand the guild with various rooms granting various boons which can (or cannot) be used in the following adventures"? Yep. That's these cards.
Other than this, not much more to say. Graphics are handdrawn and look rather good. The soundtrack is excellent (I love the narrator). And the humour inside the game left me snickering more than once.
All in all: Worth it.

My name is Nick "@UncleLono" Rehfeldt and like most PC gamers I have a steam backlog. I've resound to play & beat them all and chronicle it in a series of reviews. Today we are looking at LA NOIRE.
I'm suppose to be reviewing these things as I beat them, but I'm also not about to subject myself to forcing completion for the sake of building up a portfolio of reviews that I won't even get paid for or end up meaning anything. Not that there wasn't a lot to enjoy in LA NOIRE.
To reveal my bias, I'm one of those people that has loved the 1950's aesthetic and style ever since Fallout 3 graced my life years ago. I love old-timey noire detective stories, I use to love the cartoon parodies of them I'd see as a kid. So a little while in my early 20s I even rocked a beige trench coat, feeling that it gave off a "good guy aura" akin to a hero pro-wrestler wearing white boots.
Love LA NOIRE should of been easy, and even easier as I had played it when it first came out on consoles way back and recalled loving it. Now a chance to play through it again, but with the additional DLC cases? What was not to love?
I'll tell you what's not to love, and it's that LA NOIRE is a Grand Theft Auto style game with glitz and big production values when it could've been more easily a game done in the TellTale series style. So much of the gameplay didn't need to be here, and I'm just talking like the little things like walking down the steps of the police station, to driving the car, to approaching each suspect... I mean compare it to TellTale's The Wolf Among Us (Which is also a detective game) it gives us the same same story beats, the action, the intrigue, without being bogged down by the trappings that come with being a Grand Theft Auto clone.
And to top it off, those extra DLC cases? Nothing to write home about, and contributes very little to the overall story.
I'll give LA NOIRE a mild recommendation, but only if one has already played The Wolf Among Us and hasn't yet touched this one.

One thing I suspect divides reviewers of this game is whether they remember the original Bionic Commando - if you do, that will set your expectations accordingly and you will go in expecting a platform game with solid weapons where the main fun is in the experience of using/swinging around on the arm, and yes, slightly repetitive gameplay at times. If that is what you are going in for, this game hits the spot perfectly
If that is *not* what you're expecting, though, it could feel like something of a let-down, because while it starts out looking like a fairly story-driven FPS, runs through the standard Super Soldier stuff like Metal Gear Solid/Rambo/Deus Ex/Commando etc. (you are the ultimate warrior of bygone days, called upong to reluctantly return to service and save the day), it really is just a platformer. I think this could cause some to take a dim view of the game, which is understandable.
Anyway, the whole thing is better than I was led to believe, and is a solidly implemented nod to something *like* the original in 3D. Swing, kill, get out of the line of fire, kill, swing, get a better gun, swing, kill - like spiderman with guns, as a platform game.
Swinging on the arm is done brilliantly, guns work well and you get upgrades regularly (one at a time like the original game, some would have liked to see a pack full of weapons to switch between but in fairness that might not make sense given the character). Boss battles are well done, satisfying and interesting without any of the tedium and brokenness that seems to plague many games' boss battles. There is one possible exception on the boss battles thing, but a) it is spoilerish and b) doesn't ruin the game.
Overall, this platformer scores well. Before you play, watch some videos of the original 2D game and see what you are signing up for - and if you decide to go in knowing that Splinter Cell it ain't, this game is good, solid, old-fashioned fun.
Overall, graphics aren't particularly fabulous, it's a (fairly) repetitive platformer, and nostalgia would not have carried it alone, but it scores an 8/10 from me for one reason, something that is missing so often from games: Playability

This game is amazing and an upgrade in pretty much every aspect from its predecessor.
The graphical style has been shifted from slightly cartoonish to a somewhat more realistic this time around. A lot of people have enjoyed the comical look and feel of the previous game, me included, but I do have to say I prefer what they are doing now for one simple reason: the love put into every little detail art-wise is staggering. Every item has a nice icon when picked up and everything is lovingly detailed while in the actual world and not in your inventory. A simple example would be the health potions (or any potions, for that matter). Put them on the ground, zoom in as far as you can and admire the interestingly shaped flask adorned with gems and golden inserts.
This attention to detail translates to armours for your characters (and NPCs) as well. I can hardly remember the last time I was so excited about finding new gear and seeing it on my characters in a game. But the good news does not stop there. Because the sequel now has an option to select your race (human, elf, dwarf, lizard, undead), they all come with their own armour style. This means a leather chest piece will have a completely different and unique look depending on which race you put it on. The humans are what we could most relate to, the elves are clad in natural-looking clothing made of twigs, leaves, feathers and so on. The lizards, being a proud and aloof race, reflect this in the beautiful and exquisite-looking armour they wear.
One thing that immediately jumped out at me when I first played the game was how crisp and colourful everything was. Zooming in as far as I could, I quickly found the culprit - the textures have been much, much improved this time around. No longer is zooming in only a way to try and spot that possibly hidden trap door under a rug. It's now also completely fine to truly enjoy the attention to textures (and thus details) on various surfaces and items.
I have personally enjoyed the music in the first Original Sin. After the unfortunate passing of the composer, Original Sin 2 has a new composer, whose music you might have heard in games like Crysis 2. And I have to say I adore the soundtrack. The instruments picked are fitting, the tracks ranging from calm, dark, creepy, cheery and so on, but all having a pretty epic feel. All I can say is - I have found myself just standing in an area to listen to the music and enjoy the surroundings.
But oh, dear. I'm dragging this out and I haven't even gotten to the gameplay part. Like before (and rightfully so), this game is staying firmly in the turn-based combat shoes with a hefty slice of RPG elements to top it off. The developers have recently changed how the base stats work, which make improving them much more meaningful and give satisfaction when leveling up. Combat is enjoyable, although currently somewhat broken as the improved AI can sometimes like to stun-lock you with various combnations of crowd control spells and abilities. But that's simply something they will be polishing and changing before release. Having said that, combat is fun, the animation (while still work in progress and unfinished) fun to watch, as are the surface effects where you can electrify a pool of water or blood, slow down enemies with oil and then ignite it, etc.
There is currently no voice acting in the game but it is planned, although I believe Larian have said there will not be full voice acting due to the sheer amount of text in the game. As for the latter, the dialogues are enjoyable and the story more serious this time around. However, there are still parts of the game where I got quite a good laugh, so fear not - the comedy relief is still present here and there.
I could go on and on and on. But the simple matter of fact is, if you enjoyed the previous game, you will most likely love this one. If you haven't played the previous game but enjoy games such as Baldur's Gate or Pillars of Eternity, this will be right up your alley.
The amount of polish is astonishing, the music is beautiful and so is the art direction. The only downside is that the game is not yet finished and the wait is killing me!
Be aware that, at the time of writing this (02.21.2017), the game ONLY includes the first act, so you can not play through the game in its entirety at all.

I want to like this game, I really do. I'm just not feelin it.
I remember the original bionic commando in all it's glory back in the NES days.
This certainly tries to recapture that glory and maybe for some people it will be enough.
For me it's just not there.
For starters the controls are horrible. Unresponsive and crude are the best adjectives I can give for it. For one thing they can't even be bothered to use a readable font when instructing you. Press the "i" button... I pressed the i button, I pressed every button on the dam keyboard until I realized what they wanted was the j button. Do you know how much "j" looks like "i" ? well it shouldn't unless you use a terrible font.
But suffer through the tutorial and you can get to a point where the controls are playable. Not fun per say, but sort of usable and I was able to beat all the tutorial "challenges".
On to the game itself. I realize you don't typically play a platformer for a storyline. But wow, this is bad. It's so bad I would prefer they not have put one in at all. One page splash screens to launch each mission would have been preferable. Instead you get treated to page after page of back and forth dialogue that amounts to a meaningless pile of drivel peppered with cliche threats and taunts.
If you can't be bothered to make a story decent then at least keep it short and relevent towards moving you from one mission to another. Don't give me long winded conversations about nothing interesting. Even the almost valid enemy coversations (that you hack into for hints about how to beat bosses) is dripping with cheese in the worst ways.
I digress... gameplay. It feels like it's trying to be bionic commando but the entire game just feels... slow. Bullets fly by like butterflies that you could just reach out and swat if you wanted to. Movement is clunky and the entire game is like swimming in butter.
I pushed on, treating it more like a puzzle game than a shooter. Though the minimalist puzzle mechanics seem to only be there to funnel you into more shootouts.
There's a myriad of enemy troops but they all come accross as lazy and are beaten with essentially the same tactics. Level designs are short and feel meaningles. Boss fights were simplistic exagerations of the basic mechanics that only really become difficult when the controls don't respond in the way you want them to (which is frequent...).  Conceptually they were too easy to beat, but then the controls cheat you out of what you are trying to do and you get to start over. In the end boss fights felt unsatisfying.
Beyond the main gameplay there's two other modes you get shoved into:
1. hacking. at first these are frustrating, you weren't told what the controls are and trial and error will make you fail them (setting off alarms). once you do figure out the controls they are so simple to get through you wonder why they bothered, its just a waste of time. Spin cube, throw ball, spin cube, throw ball. I'm bored...
2. top down shoot outs (between missions). On the world map when your helicopter flys over a convoy, she parks and lets you out to go walking around shooting things... Why? There's no logic to these stops, we could have flown past them or around them or.... Sadly these sections (as much as they don't make sense to the overal plot) are actually slightly more fun gameplay wise than the actual platforming game. The controls function without too much slippage and you actually get to use your bionic arm against enemies (even if its only to knock them back ~ where as in the main game your arm does nothing to them). Not that I'd want to play an entire game of this, they are once again too easy and not all that interesting.
And that's where I am. I beat the tutorials, I played a few missions, I did some hacking and fought some convoys when my pilot decided to land between missions. But... meh. Overall I was bored. I took a break to get a drink and realized I had zero motivation to bother getting back into the game.
I wanted to like this and for those who really need to scratch the nostalgia itch maybe it's on OK game. But it's just not cutting it for me. I'm bored and the controls suck really bad.
How do you play? I don't know but I like it!

Dwarfs!? is a strangely addicting game. If you enjoy arcade games, where the main objective is to beat your high score (or someone else's high score), you'll probably love this game.
The way you score is by getting as much gold as you can, while trying to stay alive--but, you're dwarfs aren't the brightest and will insist on digging into caves filled with water, lava, and monsters, so you'll have to keep a close eye on them, which becomes harder and harder as the game progresses.
The F2P version has the two easier difficulties unlocked and each can be played in 5, 15, 30, and 60 min sessions (but beware, you cannot save the game mid-session).
The only problem I've encountered is in long games, where you have thousands of dwarfs in the field at one time, my computer starts to lag--which makes the game very difficult and frustrating to play.
Overall, this is a fun, simple, casual game that can keep you entertained for hours or opened for a quick 5-minute session.
[NOTE: If you buy the full version, your personal scores and achievements will transfer, but the F2P version has different global leaderboards, and your global score will not transfer.]
[EDIT: For those wondering, I personally own the full version (non-F2P), which is why my play-time on the F2P version is so low.]
Concerning the DLC...
Dwarfs - F2P Skirmish Pack (Recommended): Comes with 3 modes (Sandbox, Rush, and Dark). Rush and Dark modes bring new challenges to the game and can be a lot of fun. In Sandbox, you can experiment. In Rush, dwarfs spawn CONSTANTLY and you can only let 200 die. In Dark, you cannot see where caves or minerals are located.
Dwarfs - F2P Difficulty Pack (Recommended): Unlocks the two harder difficulty levels (Hardcore & Tedi Hardcore) for Arcade mode.
Dwarfs - F2P Endless Mode Pack (Not Recommended): Exactly like Arcade mode, except it's endless and you're allowed to pick the map size as well as the difficulty. Beware lag. Also, no high score is recorded.
Dwarfs - F2P Summer Carnival Pack (Extremely NOT Recommended): Was a prize for a Steam summer sale years ago; a very simple mini-game that is completely different than the base game.
Dwarfs - F2P Base Defend Pack (Not Recommended): A cute little tower defense mode that's rather different from the base game.

Super fun and funny the first 3 hours,..
...then it turns into an annoying repetitive grind. The Artstyle is endearing, the voice over of the rhyming bard is funny, until you heard it all, and when you are just trying to grind out 500gold in 10-30 gold chunks, because you only have the Boss levels available to you (most which are timed), hearing the mockery of the Narrator wasn't funny anymore, but insult to injury.
After I cleared the first area, i hadn't unlocked the new classes, as the first area taught me that equipment unlocks are more important, so eventually I hit a wall, where each new Class costs 500 gold to unlock, and not all the classes are viable for each dungeon. Meaning I had to unlock 3 classes (because i didn't know which ones would work for me), until I finally could progress. And I had to do so, mostly in 20gold chunks.
The game also has no replay ability, because you cannot go back and play Quests again, at least not where I am now. Maybe there is an option at the very end, when you defeated all, but I cannot imagine such. I assume it will be the same randomly selected boss. If you at least could select the boss stage, but you can't even do that. You pick a class, that might or might not be suited for the randomly selected boss, providing little to no ability to level up your tier 1 characters.
Maybe I just got severely unlucky with the RNG, but I swear it seemed like I always got the stage least suited for the character I had selected.
New Classes you unlock get progressively more powerful, and there is a difficulty spike between Area 1 and 2. With my rewards from the Area 1 I focused on unlocking Tier 2 gear, assuming, wrongfully, that I could keep using the Tier 1 classes for Area 2. No dice. Certain monsters simply cannot be beaten by Tier 1 classes without significant investment into gear, which requires beating monsters. Catch 22.
So I was stuck grinding for the new classes and it soured me on the game. The game length is perfect for a quick 5-10 minute game, unfortunately the lack of replay ability holds the game back.
Even without being salty about the grind, I didn't feel the game is worth the price of admission. I do not believe this game should cost most than 5 bucks. Matter of fact, I think 99cents would be the perfect price. The artwork is funny and lovingly, and the Bard is funny... but there is just not enough meat here that I would say justifies a higher price.
Since Steam doesn't let me post a review without saying binary if I would recommend it or not... the sole fact that I had to grind this painfully between Area 1 and 2.. makes this a “not”, otherwise I would have said “yeah, give it a look”, it certainly would be worth picking up at a sale. So if you read this far, and still want to try it, focus on getting new classes. Oh and Trickster Talisman is best talisman.. you cannot beat +1 loot.
Is it just me, or does this game get incredibly boring after a very short time? I mean, ye, it's good, but it does get very repetitive.

Even when you can choose to speed up the slow game (to an uncomfortable fast) and turn off the mockery, one has to question why they were there to begin with. Great game. The first has become a favorite of mine and this one seems to be improving upon in in a lot of ways. However, there are a few things that I think could use some work. As this is an early access game, I truly hope that the Dev's are looking into these reviews. I have no idea how to give them constructive criticism outside of this forum. I guess I will try their website next.
My issues: The new armor system is an awesome addition. It changes battle strategy in amazing ways. However, it is truly unfortunate that no status effects can be given to anyone who still has even a sliver of corresponding armour. This ruins the early battle efficiency of a number of spells and abilities, and unless you spend time wittling each enemies armour down before killing them off (a terrible tactical plan) most AOE skills (namely spells) have very little value. My suggestion to fix this would be to have each point in an armour type give a percentage resistance to corresponding status effects, rather than prevent them alltogether. This would still provide benefits for having the armour, but it would allow a chance for status effects to happen, increasing the usefulness of a lot of skills early in the battles.
Other than that, most of my issues are simple things that are undoubtedly going to get fixed through testing: permanent blindness issues that carry over into new battles, lack of companion options outside of original 4 (meaning no tank option without building into it), a beginning where I felt like I was running around talking to people for hours with no real direction and no winnable battles.
All in all, this seems like a great improvement on an already amazing game. I can't wait for the final product.

Usually I don't really care about the F2P games and I tend to ignore them, because most of the time they're crap and P2W games. But somehow I still decided to give the Warframe a try and to my surprise I even liked it.
The game has its share of problems, but it's a decent game for a F2P game.
Lets start with what I like about the game.
What I like the most is that the game doesn't have any paywalls on items, only the cosmetic items costs currency that you have to buy with real money. You can unlock all the warframes (classes) and weapons just by playing and grinding the game and crafting them.
That's another thing that I like in the game, crafting. Unlike any other MMO, Warframe doesn't have real loot drops, kinda. Instead of loot drops, certain enemies or missions will give you item blueprints and after obtaining the right materials you can craft those items at the foundry (crafting station).
Then how about the things that I don't like.
First of all, and probably my biggest concern, is that there are too much stuff that the new players need to know. The game simply throws all that stuff at your face and doesn't care explaining any of it. New players will either quit playing because of the overwhelming odds or find themselves spending more time on youtube watching "beginners guide" videos than playing the game. I really hate this in games, but then again, this is only F2P game. Even after +60 hours, I still have to spend almost more time out of the game than in it, researching stuff that the game doesn't bother explaining.
Another thing that I'm not really fond to is one part in the crafting system. Even if I like the crafting system, I dislike how long it takes to craft anything. For weapons you usually have to wait for 12 hours and the warframe crafting times are even worse, 3 days. You can speed this up buy spending real money on it, but I think its not really worth it.
As every F2P game has microtransactions, then how bad is it in this game?
As I mentioned before, I'm not a real fan of F2P games because of those microtransactions, I think that in Warframe it's kinda balanced. You don't have to use any real money at all if you don't want to. Real money only skips the grind for you, but its overly prized. Which is why you should only use the real money currency to buy more warframe and weapon slots, which are kinda limited when you first start the game. However, the game does give you free 50 platinum (the real money currency) for new accounts, which can get you either 1 additional warframe slot and 4 weapon slots or 2 additional warframe slots.
So, it's F2P game, but you're still forced to spend platinum if you want to get more warframe/weapon slots, so aren't you forced to spend real money on the game anyway?
The answer is no. The thing is that you can sell items that you don't need to other players, in exchance for platinum, so you don't have to spend any real money on the game if you don't want to. However, it takes time to get decent items that are worth to sell, so it's not something that beginners can do immediately  (I've been playing for a week at this moment, and I still don't have any items that are worth of selling)
There is one particular system in the game that I despise which is the Prime Vault system. Every time the game receives some new Prime gear, at the same time some of the older Prime gear are put into Prime Vault, meaning that it's no longer obtainable in the game. This makes the game kinda unbalanced, because the older players have advantage over the new players because they have that Prime gear that the new players cannot obtain anymore. Prime gear is basically improved version of some warframe/weapon. The reason why the game has such system is because according to DE there's not enough room for all this stuff in the game, so they have to remove the older gear to give the new gear room, which sounds ridiculous to me. However, there is a time when the Prime Vault gets "unsealed" and few of those older Prime gear becomes available for farming, but from what I've heard the Prime Vault is unsealed only twice per year and it stays open only few weeks. But at least the new players have that small change to get the old Prime gaer during that time which they wouldn't get otherwise.
Overall, I think that Warframe is pretty decent game for a F2P game. I might have to warn you though, that if you are like me don't intent to spend any real money on to the game, the endless grinding can get repetitive. Which is why I only play for few hours at a time if it gets too repetitive.
Pros:
+ F2P, but no paywalls - real money only skips the grind
+ Unique loot drop and crafting mechanic
(+ Space ninjas)
Cons:
- No tutorials
- Extremely confusing for new players
- Prime Vault - new players are at disadvantage because of it
- Peer-to-peer connection
- Sometimes the grinding can get repetitive
- Crafting is time consuming
Verdict: 7 / 10 - Fairly good F2P game

For this review I'll split up the different aspects of the game into categories and then provide my final thoughts. At this point I've played Dust Force DX for 6 hours, ands have completed all of the default levels, bronze levels, and all of the silver and gold levels of the first area with double S rank.
Story:
You're not buying this game for the story. There is a minor one conveyed through a single opening cinematic.
Music and Art:
Both are done in a very simplistic style. The art isn't something that will blow you away. It adds to the atmosphere of the game, and doesn't make it difficult to tell where the environment ends and where you are. The music is very peaceful. It will keep you playing, keep you interested in the game, and keep you from hating yourself. There is really something very peaceful and soothing about the soundtrack and did a lot to help the game. Great music.
Controls:
The controls take a little bit to get used to, but once you understand them they are very easy to use. They usually make you feel like it's you're fault for failing, which is what you want. I say usally because there have been a few times when it was their flaw and not mine. I would press one direction and the game wouldn't pick up on it, and it would cost me the level. Other than a few isolated incidents they've worked exactly as I've expected them to.
Mechanics:
Every mechanic that you use in the game is given to you the second the game is booted up. It's is your responsibility to master them and force them to do what you want. This is a plus in my book. I love games with few movement options that I can learn and perfect.
Difficulty:
It's a hard game. It is more difficult than any other ultra hard platformer I have ever played. It sometimes becomes infuriatingly tedious and makes me want to stop playing, but there is a significant sense of gratification when you complete a challenge that tells you to keep going. However, I don't think that this is a game anyone can play and achieve a double S rank on every level. I had a feeling that this game would be good, but I had no idea that it would be THIS GOOD
Contrast's gameplay mechanic is pretty good, over all - even though there are some areas where the controls can be a bit fiddly, or the jumps can take a few tries - but where it really shines is in the art style and characters, the setting, and the story.
Personally, I love the character designs. Dawn's proportions seemed off to me at first, but this is explained later in the game in an extremely interesting plot twist that I won't spoil for you. Didi is adorable, and her character is well written. (and it's refreshing to have a companion npc that you don't have to wait around for - nine times out of ten she got to the objective before I did)
The story takes place in a version of the 1920's that floats somewhere between noir, steampunk, and fantasy. This setting is incredibly fun to run around in and is handled very well, in my opinion. (Well... except for one bit where the movie Mary Poppins is referenced, that line sort of takes you out of the 1920's for a jarring minute. But this also happens in one of my favorite parts of the game - a very Limbo-esque shadow puppet show - so I don't mind it too much)
Speaking of Mary Poppins, however, brings me to the story. Dawn's role in the game gave me a very film-noir Mary Poppins feel for some reason. As Didi's imaginary friend, you accompany her in her attempts to bring her family back together, help her father get out of a bad situation, and learn more about a famous magician performing at her father's circus (again, no spoilers). There are some deep (occasionally dark, but not too bad - the T rating is fair) themes throughout, and I'm willing to admit that I cried twice during some of the emotional scenes.
Also, the soundtrack is absolutely amazing. I honestly don't know what else I can say about it, it just is.

TL;DR : I liked the story and the characters very much, and found it to be an enjoyable read.
8/10 Stars
PROS
There are three very different love interests (all male) - a lovestruck human childhood friend, an arrogant light elf classmate, and an older dark elf detective. Characters are well developed and acted with believable motivations.
After you complete the story once, you unlock the "killer's diary", where you learn more about who the killer was and his motivations. I haven't seen anything like this in other VN games, and I felt it was a unique and valued addition to the killer's character development.
The final scene story perspective is told from the POV of the love interest, not Mia, and it gives interesting and unique insights into the character's thoughts.
The artwork was pretty and well done, and the characters changed facial expressions, eye movement, blushing, etc as they reacted to the story.
I really liked the "killer's diary" aspect of the story. It did a lot to change my impressions of him from being an amoral monster into someone who was just hopeless and desperate and pushed too far so he snapped.
Appropriate background sounds - seagulls at the park, the creaking of a door opening, etc. really help set the mood.
NEUTRAL
Music was nice and appropriate to the scenes, though since there are only 4 different songs it felt a bit repetitive and "looped" after awhile.
There were minor spelling and grammar mistakes, but it's not overly horrible for a translation.
Mages in this world seemed to be split into different specialties - elemental mages, necromancers, etc - but it's never clearly explained just what a universal mage is. Is that a mage who just hasn't chosen a specialty yet? I wish it would have been explained a bit more.
CONS
It was initially hard for me to like Mia - she is a young girl who recently lost her parents, she is having trouble adjusting to living with her uncle and going to a private school, and she is totally out of her element to deal with being stalked by a serial killer. I mostly dislike the way she lies whenever she's upset or nervous, and that's a LOT of the time. You would think with all this "practice" lying that she would be great at it, but nope - she's horrible at lying. She did become more likable as the story went on and she gained some amount of self-confidence, but she isn't a very strong female lead. Mia is a believable character, she just didn't work well for me as I prefer strong female leads to the "rescue me, damsel in distress" female leads.
It's disappointing that Professor Goldstone wasn't available as a love interest. He has such an interesting backstory, and I can see a wonderful alt story where Mia could end up with him.
For the achievement collectors: Two achievements (Aleistar's bad & normal ending) are bugged - this has been reported, and the designer blames steam/renpy for the issue - but since changing the language unlocks the achievements, I'm not convinced that is accurate. One also wonders why the issue was never fixed, if it was only a language issue?
Final Thoughts ...
Despite the weak female lead, spelling/grammar errors and bugged achievements, I really loved this VN. I would buy VN's from 7DOTS again.

Little Lords of Twilight is an interesting yet simple game with clearly defined objectives: destroy the opponent with tactics. There isn't much of a learning curve and the tutorial points out everything you need to know. You quickly start to understand that the defensive line to protect your portal is important. The voices used for the protagonists can be a bit eerie, but then that's the sort of game this is ;). Lady Frost isn't much of a lady, that's for sure!
I particularly enjoyed the camera zooming in shortly for the attacks and the variety of weapons/ spells used. There's some humorous animations for the characters (like Monster Herk cracking his spine) to help lighten the idea you're going into battle with spells and wizardry. On the topic of visuals - the graphics look great and the artwork is spot on.
The different levels will see varying scenery and obstacles placed in your path making you think about strategy more. You get around 40 seconds for your turn enabling you to spawn an accomplice, heal, move, attack, etc. There is a points system for weighing up the different characters and increasing their abilities, and you get a choice of passive or active upgrades on level-ups.
One thing I'd like to point out - the game seems focused on PvP battles - which is fine - however at the time of writing this review, there wasn't many ways to connect to those friends. If I remember correctly, it uses Facebook friends for some of the matchmaking rather than having any sort of integration with Steam and that's certainly something which could be addressed in the future.
The gameplay seems quite smooth and the dialogue isn't over-the-top at all. I won't lie in that there are other games which are built around the same architecture which do things a little better, but then this isn't marketed or advertised as that sort of game.
It runs extremely well on both computers I've tried it on, without any sort of hiccups or crashes. The CPU/ GPU don't get utilised even by 50% when running alongside other mundane tasks (like browsing the internet or having Spotify playing in the background).

"Never give up!" is a very strange game for me, because I like it's setup, I like it's lore, I like all the main characters, but I really dislike the plot. This is a mystery game without any real mystery (sadly, that is a case with quite a few otome visual novels). You will probably figure out, who the killer is, during your first meeting with him and even if you won't, you will surely know before the final confrontation. There are two things that could save this game in my eyes: if it was a good thriller (it isn't and trailer pretty much spoils any "surprise" there could be) or if it was a good romance (which it also isn't, because characters simply do not have enough time to grow and develop their relationships). I think it would be much more interesting game, if the "killer" aspect was cut of completely and it would be just a magic-school life type of visual novel. There just isn't enough time, nor build-up to convey any sort of message, make you feel bad for the killer or for his victims, or even get some satisfaction from getting good endings with the guy, that you've encountered, maybe five times during the whole game.
Even for the low price, it's still a disappointment.

This is a PvP turn-based strategy game i first stumbled upon when it first released on mobile and has cought my attention right away. Visuals and art design of heroes and environments look amazing and obviously alot of care has been put into it. With its steam release it has only gotten better. Originally the game had only two playable heroes, but as time went on more and more were added and it seems they want to continue that trend going forward, and all of these heroes are free which is an added bonus.
The game has a useful tutorials (about 20 or so) that you can do at any time and completing it gives you extra ingame currency for you to spend ingame so it is a nice incentive to do it. That said, you only need to do the first one to open up PvP matchmaking which is great.
Gameplay itself revolves around strategically moving your hero and its minions around the board in order to outsmart your opponent and thus prevent him from taking over your portal or killing your hero. There are number of power-ups placed around the map that give boosts to your hero or provide healing. You only have a limited amount of time to make decisions and so every second counts which adds even more to strategy aspect of the game. One thing i found different from other simmilar games is that here you have a day/night cycle and depending on which it is your abilities change and your hero gets eather weaker or stronger making things alot more interesting and not as monotone as you would see in other games.
Reward sistem is quite interesting as well, you get a currency called Madblings which you get for eather winning or losing, and you can use those to buy cards that unlock new abilities for your hero or skins to change its apperance.
I do have to point out that there are some exlusive skins for your heroes that you need to buy with real money, but prices are quite small, around a dollar, but these are not necessary to play the game and you can play for free without the need to spend a dime as most things can be bought for ingame currency that you get ingame by just playing and so i don't consider this game pay to win at all.
There is a ranked PvP sistem in place as well which you can partake in after you have done seven matches so you can test yourself there against the best and earn some great rewards. Friends and public rankings are also available for you to check out and see how you stand against others.
For the time i played, PvP seemed to give you a balanced opponent to fight which maybe has one level over you or is on a same level so that is quite good for new players just getting into the game.
The game can also be linked with your Facebook account so you can play with same account on your mobile or steam and you can share your moments with your friends, which is a nice touch.
I did not experienced any crashes or glitches in my time playing which means that if those were present at some point, are constantly worked on and fixed if needed which is great for the game and should keep people playing.
I do have to point out one thing that i didn't like much and that is the fact that you cant see any tooltips when you hover over your abilities mid-fight and so if you don't know your spells and traps well you could find yourself a bit lost and lose on that precious time so i do recommend going over your spellbook and learning what your spells do for maximum result.
Overall, the game is quite fun to play when you have that extra bit of free time on your hands and a great experience for both casual gamers and those that are more hardcore as the game is easy to get into.
Highly recommend to at least try, you will not regret it.

I have been playing this game for the last few years and watched it grow.  With almost 1400 hrs in game at the time of this writing I fel I know the game pretty well. You can use cash purchases to short cut some crafting time or get access to some gear that you might otherwise need to run missions to get.  But nothing is exclusive to the cash store, everything is available in game for free.
Over the past year or so they have put in tons of improvements and they are constantly adding new content.  The game is what it is, a team co-op procgen mission grinder, but it does it very well.  The graphics are top notch, the content is fun and engaging, the story is great to follow but you can also ignore it and just dive in to the fun, and the "classes" are unique and entertaining.
There are very few games I would recommend as highly as Warframe.  It is one of the few games that I keep coming back to for years and years.

Aside from the bugs this game has at the moment(I hope they will be fixed in time), the game is excellent, pick up and play sort. A joypad is required if you want to experience this game.
I shant lie, the game has a learning curve but in time the more you play it, the more you will start to see how the maps are laid out for you to master them.
Naturally it is all about timing, one mistake can cost you a round being lost but! if you can recover by your other opponents mistakes then you are still in with a chance.
Matches can last between 3-5mins tops so there is plenty of fun to be had. Also you can play this 4 player offline as well which is pretty cool if you have friends round and 4 joypads to spare.
Currently the multiplayer side is slightly buggy ie game crashes, inconsistant glitches causing hte screen not to follow the players, freezing on loading screen etc But you can look beyond that to enjoy this game once it starts ;)
There is also a single player missions to do but the multiplayer side is it's main selling point in my opinion.
Also with multiplayer comes the Ranked matches, once you feel ready, you can play against others and improve your rank status, though same with multiplayer issues of crashes and lag might occur but not often!
Finally the nicest thing of all is the map making tool, the replayability is provided with a mass of cutom made fan maps for you to play with bots(if the map supports them) or with your friends, some will be completely awful and crappy but you will come across nicer made maps for competitive play.
General Zod's Verdict
*Note: Would strongly recommend having a joypad when playing this game to get the best experience of speedrunners, via keyboard it can become problematic if your keyboard has issues of not allowing multiple keys pressed at the same time, esp when it comes to wall jumping and this game has a fai few areas of wall jumping ;)
Pros
- Excellent 4 player competitive play
- Fast paced Fun (learn the maps and you will master it)
- Nice animations / style
- Easy pick up and play
- Replayability with custom maps
Cons
- Still buggy in some areas causing crashes to the game, including lag bugs...
- UI for lobby/Ranked games could do with some work!
- Lobby/Ranked match player finding will take a while!
Overall if you love competitive games, you want to play something that you can just pick up and get going, speedrunners is highly recommended! if you feel it is not worth the value, get it via a sale ;)

Mass Effect 2 continues the adventures of commander John (or Jane) Shepard who's doing everything what's to stop the reapers from destroying all intelligent life in are galaxy. What can be said about this game is that the gameplay is more action oriented than previously which is not necessary a problem unless you preferred less action and more story driven narration with planetary exploration. As in this instalment you do not land on planets to search for resources but instead the whole planet hologram is shown and you scan it moving a pointer around it. Is this way better? Again it all depends on your preference but perhaps Bioware thought that after few hours people would start to get bored exploring such vast areas with so little to find as they did not have anything more interesting to do with it. Another new thing in the game is something in a style of a quick time event but it's not a matter of pressing the correct button like A or Y but more like interrupting a scene with bad or good decision. I must say that sometimes it brings a bit more tension, so that's a nice addition. As for your decisions, you still have two clear paths to pick just like in Star Wars KOTOR series and the first Mass Effect. I am not saying it's bad however if you are looking for something like in the Witcher series where sometimes you really struggle to choose what's right and later see how they impacted later on the story you will not find it here as this game (in my opinion) was always as an alternative to Star Wars were there is a visible distinction between light and darkness. What really impressed me in this game is that so many of your decisions from ME 1 found their way here which in a way gives you a unique experience from the start and I think it was done better than in the last game of the trilogy.
Let's talk about the visuals. They are very good, character models have been updated to meet the standards and look very nice, textures are sharper and the visual style is kept the same. Audio is also on high level, actors perform very good and match their in game hero. Also can't say anything bad about the music.
To sum up Mass Effect 2 is a solid sequel quoted by many to be the best in the series (it might be). Of course it's not a perfect game yet any negatives are not big in my opinion to spoil the fun. Very good game 9/10.

I beat this game in about 3.5 hours. Got most of the stuff too. I liked the music, it was nice. Had a good concept, ie switching between shadows for 2d and normal world for 3d. The story was pretty good too, especially at the end, and the way it presents the story visually is very unique.
That's about most of the good things I can say about this game. Is it a platformer? Not a very good one, often jumps are very janky and awkward. Is it a puzzle game? Not really. Most of the puzzles weren't very challenging or interesting from a gameplay standpoint. Either the "puzzle" took no thought (like I accidentally solved a large chunk of the puzzles, or you just have to watch a shadow for about 30 seconds for an obvious solution), or the way it was presented was poor but the puzzle was good. Is it a colectathon? Not really, most of the collectibles are in plain sight. The game is very unpolished, I ran into invisible walls time and time again. I was unable to progress at least 3 times due to bugs, and had to restart from a previous save. It's way too short, and yes short games are fine if they take their concept far enough but there were definitely plenty of ideas for puzzles that were totally overlooked. There is a particular item that you need multiple of to progress, but the tiny amount required is laughable, especially when most of them are so easy to get.
I would say it had a good concept, but poor execution. I was hoping for so much more depth in a game with such a neat idea. If you're just looking for a decent story with unique visuals, you'll probably enjoy this. If you're looking for a game with intelligent puzzles, I'd say there are several better options: Portal 1/2, The Swapper, Braid, and Limbo to name a few. If I had the option, I'd probably give this a neutral rating because it's not terrible, but unfortunately I can't.

Never Give Up is a stunning visual novel developed by Salamandra88 and published by 7DOTS. A beautiful young girl named Mia Silverlight suddenly finds herself caught up in a diabolical series of events in her city as someone has started killing half-bloods which are half-human and half-elf hybrids. As a half-blood herself, will Mia be able to avoid getting caught by the killer, find true love and discover the secret her uncle is hiding? The police believe that it's nothing more than a regular maniac obsessed with racial purity but detective Blackwood and Mia's uncle, the magician Silverlight, have their own opinion about this case. They think that the killer is a necromancer going after the souls of half-bloods who wants to use them for some horrible ritual. How the story unfolds for our protagonist is completely up to you?
Suprisingly, the illustrations in this visual novel are non-manga inspired which is a breath of fresh air as most titles in this genre tend to lead towards that particular style of art. The developers really did a wonderful job with the presentation of this novel as it is quite pleasing to the eye. Truth be told, I actually enjoy the wonderful and very colorful C.G. art in this title much more than I do the more prevalent manga-style and would love to see more novels illustrated in such a manner as Never Give Up. The art is just gorgeous and really stands out on it's own. Also, as the dialogue is spoken, the characters often convey emotions through various facial animations, eye movements, blushing, etc. which truly injects some life into the people as the story unfolds. Just a slight difference in a characters eyes alone can ellicit an array of unspoken emotions to the reader. Just as well, the sound quality is really terrific, crisp and quite immersive which is what you want in a good visual novel. For example, when a character enters a room you will hear a door open and close and if a carraige ride is taken one can distinctly hear the galloping of the horses across the cobbled pavement. The sound really is expertly done in this title.
I really enjoyed this visual novel. The protagonist is a very interesting young lady and really makes you feel for her plight, you also get to meet a gallery of wonderful characters and the narrative is quite intriguing on it's own merits as well. Interestingly enough, I was able to achieve a good ending on my very first read which is unusual since I tend to make the absolute worst choices whenever I read a novel with a branching story and usually get the worst possible ending. This story has some replayability as there are 12 possible endings, there are also Steam Trading cards to collect and Steam achievements to unlock as well as a C.G. gallery and a ample amount of settings at your disposal. I would definitely recommend Never Give Up to fans of the visual novel genre as it makes a truly great addition.

I got this game on mobile before buying on Steam, mainly because my phone isn't that great and can't really handle 3D very well. The Steam version is an exact port of the mobile version, right down to the UI. While the mobile version is free to play, the Steam version charges $10, but you do get 50,000 of the in game currency and a free hero (Herk).
The game itself is really simple, but it forces players to think very quickly since each turn only lasts 45 seconds. The tactical aspect is quite significant, since bad positioning will generally cost you the match. Players have to take into account not only the enemy hero and hirelings on the board, but also the enemy's mana reserve. Going head to head with an enemy with full mana will easily see you taking 2 damage the next turn just from spells; in addition to any damage from the hero and hirelings.
That said, there's really not enough explanation on spells and unit abilities in the game. For example, Veroline's Gnome hireling can attack enemy units without line of sight, it has a range of 2 including diagonals suring SunPops, but a range of 2 in a straight line during NightFalls. This kind of information isn't shown anywhere clearly and you won't learn it unless you spend some time using the character.
However, I would still recommend this game because I think there's great potential for it to grow in the future. Support from their help line has been responsive, so I'm optimistic that improvements will be made to the system.

Little Lords of Twilight is a wonderful little gem I recently discovered on Steam that I find myself returning to whenever I have a free moment. LLoT is a PvP based game that magnificently combines turn-based strategy, with a fun card collecting combat ''MagZik'' (magic) system. You can use 4 characters (heroes). Each one has their own unique abilities and 2 minions to battle for them.
In short, the gameplay of LLoL is where this game really shines. The turn-based strategy system mixed with unique character abilities and a card based magic system works very well to make LLoT a simple to grasp yet complex to master game. I could tell from the start the developers (BKOM Studios ) really put a lot of love and effort into this game to make sure the ''genre mashing'' of the battle system works flawlessly together. Speaking of the battle system...wait there is more! In a lovely twist a day/night cycle is added which alters character appearance and abilities. This adds an interesting twist to the player's strategy. Wait, there is more still! Each player has 45 seconds to complete their turn requiring the player to develop their plan swiftly. I love this time constraint. This truly makes for intense battles where one mistake can cost victory.
LLoL's atmosphere is immersed in a day/night cycle that tides the balance between good and evil. Where our heroes do battle in the realm of Zikverländ. The tides of day and night (SunPop and NighFall) fight for control over those trapped here and it is up to you, the player, to see who emerges victorious!
Is this game alive? When I look at the animation-esque art style I often think that. The characters appear to be hand drawn and move just as you'd expect them too. Veroline is especially beautiful to watch. Her ''Raggedy Ann'' doll movements are as authentic as you would expect from an animated doll. A wide use of the colour palette makes the battlefields of Zikverländ look lavish amidst the day/night cycles.

Erie and spooky. Mystical and and quirky. This is where LLoT gets to show off its sense of humor. The musical scores fit each battle stage nicely. The heroes sound effects help give each one their own distinct personality.
You would be hard pressed to tell this is a mobile to steam game. The controls were implemented perfectly to suit a mouse and keyboard. Hit boxes of clickable items are precise so you don't waist valuable seconds of your turn trying to enter commands.
I love a good PvP experience and LLoT nails it perfectly on the mobile platform and as I said before it transitions to steam wonderfully. Players have so many strategies at their disposal none of the 30 + matches I have played have been alike. I have played some matches that were over in 2 minutes and others that were a 20 minute strategic grudge match. With close to 100 MadZik card spells it is assured that no 2 players spell layout will be alike. I highly recommend LLoT to everyone, not just fans of PvP. This is the perfect game to have a quick match with a friend while you ride the city bus or at home gaming.
There is only one thing that I feel really could improve the LLoT experience overall on Steam. That would be implementing a feature that allows you to play with your steam friends. As of now, you can only play your friends via your Facebook friends list.

This game is not the greates of its genre or the year it was released, but it certainly does not deserve such a low rating in reviews. Lets talk about some of the common points made the negative reviews for this game.
- The game has linear. It certainly is and the game is described as one. This is not an Open-World Rpg, it is a Tactical one.
- The story is not good enough. Well the names might be awkward to hear for the first time, but after a couple of times listening to the great narrator you ll get the hang of it. The initial lore of the game can be learned from the game manual, the story is told through a narrator and codex pages acquired after certain events in the game enriching the lore.

This game does not deserve this score. It seems people jump on hate-trains to eagerly.

A fun game, but it spreads its content a bit too thin.
The music's good(though I dare you to find the player who didn't mute the bard after an hour's play, tops. I mean, he's not bad, but... it just gets pretty repetitive, pretty fast, because there's more game than there is variety to his songs), the art is cute and functional and the basic gameplay is really solid, conceptually.
But it comes apart in two places. Firstly, by the time you're a short bit into the game, you've really seen all it has to offer. The relatively low scaling of the abilities means there aren't really any you're only going to discover later in the game. And all of the options are on display pretty much from the word go, so there aren't any additions popping up later on.
Secondly... it's just a bit too easy, really. The only thing that can really trip you up is random chance, like being forced into a fountain that gives your enemies Concealment so you're pretty much playing blind. But short of that, you've pretty much always got a clearly superior option lined up for what to do. Oddly enough, making enemies "weaker," with Predictable, actually makes the game more interesting since it lets you plan multiple rounds ahead, rather than just picking the obvious counter/solution to what the enemy is playing right here and now.
Lastly, the game does have a bit of false advertisement. The way its presented suggests that it's about manipulating your adventurers' varied motivations to get them to go where you want in the dungeon... and that's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The adventurers always go for the nearest monster and/or treasure, pretty much a beeline. And I've seen no variations in their behavior at all, not even when they had "Battle Scars" that were ostensibly meant to alter it.
If there's a genuine difference hidden somewhere, it's obfuscated by the fact that the dungeon crawls are very short and your actual *need* for manipulating their behavior very limited. Due to the fact that *you're* the one placing the dungeon corridors as well as most of the generic dungeon encounters, you can just make them a straight path to where you want them to go.

No... Just no.
In a universe where Baldur's gate, Icewind Dale, and Neverwinter Nights doesn't exist.  Confrontation would still be a clunky uninteresting game, of repetative combat, linear gameplay, and lacking upgrades.
But in a universe where Those three games do exist, as well as many more, there's nothing to recommend with Confrontation.  The story is weak, the enemies are repetative, the characters have no real upgrade system to speak of, there's no inventory outside a minor weapon/armor upgrade system that feels cheap, and the gameplay is monotonous.
There's no "Exploration" in this game, you play through linear levels with a very similar party.  The combat is mostly fast paced which requires either a lot of micromanaging before the battle starts, or a lot of pause and resume.
The problem with this is that all the combats are the same, in the classic Fallouts (or even the modern ones) there's snap decisions that require a pause system because it's a new enemy, or you need to utilize a large inventory.  In this game, a simple autocast system would have made the combat dull.  Well duller than it already is.
There's a FEW interesting ideas in the game regarding death, but overall, I played two of the maps, and neither were that enjoyable.  I mean how many of the same soldier in the same formation do you have to kill to show you "understand" how to kill them.    In between battles, you heal up so it's not even like the game can wear you down with multiple waves of enemies.
If you're considering this, buy Baldur's gate, Icewind Dale, Disgaea, Wastelands 2, or something along those lines.  This game, well maybe if you've played all of those and simply MUST have yet another game, and can ignore a poor story, and uninteresting characters, then maybe buy this one, but honestly, you should have more than enough hours in any one of those other games.

This game has a lot of problems. The driving and shooting mechanics are clunky, the graphics don't really stand the test of time, the quicktime events are laughably simplistic, and the side quests/exploration aspects of the game are shallow and ultimately pointless. The facial animation software was innovative for its time, and granted it does look pretty good considering the games that were released around the same time, despite being nothing special today. But don't get this game if you're expecting typical Rockstar fare, mindless shoot-em-up action-adventure fun, because it isn't that at all.
That all being said, what you will get is an engrossing story with well fleshed-out characters and a one-of-a-kind detective experience that requires careful attention and punishes mistakes if you aren't thorough. Despite all of the technical flaws of the game I found myself constantly compelled forward by the plot. I wish the game had done away with all the "action" subgames and focused more heavily on the investigative mechanics, but as a whole it works I guess. Your decisions also don't really matter much, other than the fact that poor job performance earns you lower "grades" for each level (which don't matter in the end). But at the end of the day I had to ask myself, "Did I have fun playing this game?" and the answer is yes; therefore I feel that my money was well-spent for the experience I got.

Date: 2/17/16
Review Number: 18
Game: Dustforce DX
From (Creator Publisher): Hitbox Team
Played On: Steambox (w/ Controller)
Steam Price as of Review: $9.99
Total Time played: 30 Minutes
Review:
Another day, another review from the wheel of insanity.  This time the randomizer brought up Dustforce DX, a platformer from Hitbox Team which apparently is about four people dealing with janitorial work as an art form.  Now, I am always down for unique and interesting takes on new games and all, but for some reason the idea of having your characters doing what they do because they want to keep the floors obsessive clear of leaves just seems a bit off even to me.  It doesn’t really get too much in the way of gameplay though, and that, surprisingly, is quite interesting, the controls are quite simple once you get into the swing of finding exactly when to dash jump and double jump.  The engine uses a surprisingly robust set of physics rules to control the player's movement, and i could easily see someone trying to spend a lot of time trying to really dig into the specifics of the movement of the characters.  In truth, I think this is the sort of platformer that would appeal to perfectionist platformers, both for the almost OCD nature of its story, to the demanding requirements of the level ranking systems.  For folks who love that sort of thing, this is a definite buy.  For everyone else, it’s still pretty good, and probably worth keeping on a wishlist for the next sale.
Game’s Fate: Uninstalled.  Its pretty, but just isn’t interesting enough for me to enjoy, but I can see where plenty of people would enjoy it.
Buy/No Buy: There's nothing wrong with this game, but it’s just not interesting enough to me to be worth the full price.  Keep in your wishlist and buy it when it’s on sale.

TLDR: Don't buy this, it's free on mobile and mediocre besides.
Beyond the appealing visuals, this game doesn't offer anything that isn't being done better in Duelyst. This is a vanilla RPG-style tactics game where your spells are random via a 10-card deck of singletons. As you level the characters, you unlock new passive and active abilities, and there is some customizabilty in that you sometimes have to pick between two abilities, although your ability choices can be changed between matches. The object of the match is to either kill the other character, or perform the equivalent of a touchdown by passing through their starting point. There are a few buffs around the playing field (HP, MP, Movement Speed), as well as some obstacles that you must walk around. You may also summon one minion per turn, having up to two minions on the battlefield at any given time. This game is pay/grind to win, in that you purchase booster packs of new spells with an in-game currency that you can of course purchase with real money, or earn by playing matches and completing daily quests.
Frustratingly, there is no way to get more information on anything mid-match. You can not check what your spells do once the match starts, you are only given a thumbnail image to guess by. This is often problematic, as my beginning deck had multiple cards with different images of lightning bolts, all doing slightly different things. You would think with the extra $10 I payed to play this game on the computer, they would at least add some features that are commonly found in similar games like Hearthstone, Duelyst, etc. This lack of information extends to the items you pick up on the battlefield, enemy player and minion stats, the specific details of status ailments, etc.
{Edit}: There are ways to access information in-game but they are rather unintuitive.
Another large gripe I have with the game is the lack of character diversity and depth. Among the 3 starting characters, the only differences I could notice was that one was able to move an extra space every turn, one could fly over obstacles, and the third had one extra unit of range. All characters have the same health, all do 1 damage per attack, and all are only able to have 2 minions on the battlefield. The minions are also virtually identical in function. As far as I could tell, each character's card pool was identical. No class specific cards like in Hearthstone or Duelyst. This game also enforces an arbitrary turn order, without warning you about skipping steps. You must move, summon a minion, attack, then cast a spell. If you do anything before you move, you can't move during that turn. If you attack before you summon a minion, you can't summon a minion that turn. Their FAQ said this is to prevent "unfair" hit-and-run tactics. In my opinion, limiting minions on the field, restricting turn order, and other hand-holding tactics inevitably lower the overall amount of strategy in the game.
But the most frustrating thing about this game is that I paid $10 for a game, only to find out it is free to play on mobile, and utilizes microtransactions. I had to check their FAQ for rule clarifications, and that's how I found out I had been bamboozled. I'll probably invest a few more play sessions of this game over the next couple of days, but I fear that it will be hard to forgive the game for essentially tricking me into buying it.

Noone can see an imaginary friend. And your imaginary friend can't see anyone. Except for their shadows. And you can become a shadow too. Sound interesting? Good, because it is.
You are Dawn, the imaginary friend of a young, clever, lively and kind hearted girl named Didi. She can see you and you can see her. And her only. Every other human being is invisible to you. But not their shadows! I guess this is the point of view of an imaginary friend. Instead of going to bed Didi wants to follow her mother to see her sing at the club just to meet her lost father. So our quest is to help Didi in this adventure.
Contrast runs with Unreal Engine 3 but the most important aspect of the game is not in models, polys or effects but the ambience, settings and style of characters and locations. The story is set in a city which looks like it came ot of the 1920s. It doesn't look like a normal city, though, it looks more like a dream, or a child's fantasy point of view as there are empty spaces, floating surfaces, incredible machines, giant roller coasters in tiny buildings. Everything in a dark atmosphere with desaturated colors (with few exceptions).
Of course with such a setting the most fitting music genre is jazz. Too bad the soundtrack is mostly made of a bunch of tracks where the most noticeable are the main menu theme and Didi's mom singing (which are the same).
Here comes the real best. Contrast is a 3rd person platform, so you run and jump like usual, there are puzzles to solve in ordeer to proceed and so on. The most important feature of the game is that the main protagonist, Dawn, can adhere to walls becoming a shadow and walk over other objects shadows and so on. The more you proceed the more interesting becomes as shadows will come ot from the most unthinkable objects and there will be one of the most original and unexpected "minigame" which will exploit this temporary mechanic to a longer and very interesting section.
Well, it's short. Interesting, involving and surprising, but short.
And few sections require a very high level of precision when you place objects that will project shadows you will have to walk on. More precision than you could expect.

I'll start by saying, I love this ♥♥♥♥ing game. I can't stop playing it, however, I do equate it to flogging myself; against unrealistic/broken physics and metagamer movement exploits of these failures.
I don't recommend people buy it until a few key issues are addressed.
Level 1-16 are a whirlwhind of fun for non-meta gamers. After you reach a certain level (takes 1-3 days), you are cast into a 'non-noob' rank pool of players. As a competent gamer, I was completely stunned by the immediate brick wall you face when you 'graduate' post lv 16. There needs to be a game-mode which enforces a HALO-style rank/matchmaking system so that players can be matched together based on an average recent skill.
I've noticed there are two types of players in Chivalry: Those who play and move their character based on their perception of real life physics [and] Those who exploit the game engine's weak grasp on realistic physics. Some gamers prefer to win at all costs; even if its sprinting, jumping crouching and swinging 100 pound claymore from left shoulder to right shoulder as if it were a twig, all at the same time. To make the physics worse, the devs have decided to add a speed factor to swinging a weapon based on how fast the player can move the mouse. What you'll find is players with LOW DPI mice, huge mouse pads, spamming tons of keys, jumping, crouching, looking down and swiping their mice wildly across a huge mouse pad. The client [you, the player] cant even properly render the movement-spam these players are producing, while you're dying to a sword you didn't even see swing. It makes any logical/reaction-based sword strategy extremely difficult to execute. The developers need to implement better physics based on the gear the different classes use. Weight factor should be reduced if a player opts to carry less weapons or equipment. Remove the ridiculous fast-mouse-power-swing idea. Slow player movement down or show me videos where people can wear full body-chain mail, have a tower shield on their back, jump 5 feet in the air while crouching into a cannonball and managing to swing and hit with a claymore before they hit the ground. This isn't Call of Duty guy-.. wait..
If player 'effectiveness' were ranked, there wouldn't be lopsided servers in almost every occasion.

As a fan of card- and boardgames, Guild of Dungeoneering scratches all the right itches. From the quirky artstyle, amazing music, tongue-in-cheek-yet-still-relentless humor, Guild of Dungeoneering on more than one occasion reminded me of a real-life board/card game Munchkin, especially Munchkin Quest. This is, needless to say, a good thing for tabletop veterans.
GoD's actual game mechanics are more remniscent to an old computer game called Majesty, in that you have no "direct" control over your character, you can only "lure" them across the board by placing treasures, or by placing monsters that are less dangerous than the ones they were originally about to run into.
The actual combat is done by using cards in a deck. Every character class has their own base deck, and every character starts a dungeon run at level 1. To gain a level, a character has to defeat a monster with a level that is either their own or higher, and upon leveling up, you are often presented with additional health (varies per class) and items. These items usually come down to additional cards for your character deck, and can provide you with different attacks, blocks, counters, heals, and sometimes more subtle forms of combat.
GoD is a typical case of easy to learn, hard to master. Don't be fooled by the adorable graphics and the light "feel" of the game, there is a lot of content here, and more strategic depth than first meets the eye. This is an addictive game, and just perfect for both players that are prone to doing "just one more run", as well as those players whose time can *only* afford a quick run.
