I am only part way through this game at the moment. Having bought this title on the holiday sale 75% off for £3.74. Compared to its regular list price of £14.99.
Would I recommend this game, the answer would be no. There are better action rpg titles around for the same price. It does feel clunky at times. There are pathing issues. though I do like the visuals, the lore and some of the mechanics. That is why I picked up Aarklash: Legacy to give this series another chance.
If you have bought this title, and are having issues with reading the manual. For some reason, the manual is not accessible via the right hand menu in the library. So you will have to google steam powered + confrontation manual to get it.
There are no loot drops what so ever. You can only upgrade armor and weapons via weapon stands. Which are located sporadically around the various maps. Other upgrades include glyphs, which are obtained via plinths a giant magic rock.
Main Screen - On the campaign menu there is an Additional Content button, but when selecting it. There is nothing listed, and I cannot find anything regarding additional content.
The main menu is located right at the bottom of the screen. Where you can access options, switching profile and quiting the game. It looks out of place on the main screen, compared to the other buttons. Which have a UI element to them.
Gameplay
Naration - The naration feels like the old pen and paper DM, explaining things to you. Other than that it is uninspired.
User Interface - In game with the party interface it does look nice and clean. Though the minimap is rather lackluster, even worse when bringing up the full map. You cannot zoom into the map. Though it does leave white dots showing where you have been on the map. It does seem out of place compared to the rest of the UI.
Character Panels - Pressing I gives you the character panel, which shows you their attributes, skills, armor etc.. One gripe is it does not include all of the stats. Which are on a seperate panel pressing O. So you will not be able to see when increasing attributes what they are improving. The tooltips on attributes do specify what they improve. Also their class should be on the panel as well.
Skills and Armor - I would have liked a way to respec my characters, this feature is in Aarklash: Legacy. So I can make the party I want, with the builds I want.
Healing - Some characters have a heal over time. Others have an aoe heal. There is the option of using bandages to heal. But you can only use them on other characters, not on yourself. Frustration can set in when due to pathing you cannot reach the character you want to bandage.
Codex - Only accessible in the main menu, and not while you are playing the game. Also they have missed adding lore and character biographies to the character entries. Character entries only have a visual model of the character, plus a list of their abilities. In Aarklash: Legacy you are able to examine enemy units and their abilities.
Combat - Rushing blindly into rooms, will definitely get your party killed in this game. Some fights do take some strategy on what to focus on, what to crowd control. Line of sight, and pulling groups away from patrols. So you do not end up in some crazy cluster frak wipe, when a party member gets feared. Combat is mainly pausing, chaining some commands, such as move here, attack this, use this ability for each party member. Unpause then watch the fight unfold, pause and reissue commands when required.
Multiplayer - I have not tried multiplayer, but according to the forums and how this title was recieved. Do not expect any.
I do not know what the original price listing was for this title at launch. This title does feel unfinished, and would need more polish. Personally I would not have released this title as is. It should have undergone some closed or open beta testing. Taken onboard player feedback and improved this title immeasurably.
Anyone who has played this title and has not gone all angry german kid. Deserves medals and a parade, Personally I think it is worthy of a visit by an Enforcer droid and vaporized. Am I going to play the game to the end, yes I am. To see if anything can be redeemed before summary vaporizing.

Another detective game that suffers from a rigid system of obscure choices made by unimaginative designers.
This game suffers from the same symptoms that make a lot of detective games nearly unplayable: a poorly designed interweave of evidence and choices where many choice are correct but only one is "right."  A few spoiler-ish examples follow:
In short, this is Multiple Choice Test: The Game.  Where there are multiple correct answers but you're looking for the one that's "most correct" according to the writer.  There's even one case that is entirely failed or succeeded based on the last, illogically premised, interaction with the final suspect (see spoiler #2).  If you want to play with a guide, you'll probably have a good time.  If you want to actually play the game yourself, prepare for some undue frustration.

It's a very simple game based on oldschool shooters. There isn't anything special to it - you walk, kill enemies on the way, collect items for score, reach the end of the level, rinse and repeat.
While the game is nothing special, it works inside its own premise. It's also a very short game (can be beaten in about one hour) with 14 levels plus one bonus level and 7 weapons to use along the way. Two of the levels are also horseback levels, which was actually an interesting change of pace, even though those levels could have been better designed.
The game does have some quite weird gameplay issues, mainly about hit detection and enemy behavior. You can hit enemies through walls and they can hit you through walls as well, but if you can get enemies behind a wall, they won't actually attack you and you can just aim at the corner of their sprite and kill them. At the same time, if you turn your back to an enemy, they'll then be able to move from whatever corner they're behind, which is actually quite dangerous if you somehow can't see an enemy, specially if it's a melee enemy since those can drain your health very quickly. Lastly, enemies can hit you easily, but you can't hit them as easily - and even collecting items feels weird.
Nonetheless, for the very cheap price the game has, I can safely recommend it as a one-time experience.

Metro Last Light Redux is the sequel to the critically acclaimed Metro 2033 and once again you take on the role of the young ranger Artyom in the post apocalyptic ruins of the Moscow metro.
And right of the bat : Metro Last Light is a worthy successor and in many ways even better than the original.
The first thing you'll notice is that stealth is actually a viable option this time around and it works. No more glitched throwing knives or enemies that can spot you in complete darkness. If you fail to sneak around a group of enemies they will instantly call for backup, making the game harder but in no way unfair or frustrating. Both options work equally well.
However sometimes enemies do not spot you even though they clearly should have. But most of the time it feels very good trying to get to the next mission objective without ever being seen.
Last Light looks absolutely stunning and while graphics are not everything, I never felt like I was playing a nice looking tech demo. Performance wise the game ran really well on my machine and only in one level I could not get over 30 frames per second no matter what graphical setting I chose.
The atmosphere was incredibly tense, with great sound design and music. If you run out of air filters for example, Artyom will start breathing heavily and you think you're going to suffocate yourself.
The same goes for the guns in the game. There is a large variety with some customization options like sights, extended magazines or silencers. All in all the gunplay felt nice, and I especially liked the pneumatic weapons which have to be charged up before being able to fire.
I really liked that in some parts of the game you will encounter foes that are pretty invulnerable to firearms and can only be defeated by using your flashlight. Of course these sections are pretty dark which makes for a great atmosphere.
What I also really enjoyed were the extra missions that let you see certain parts of the story from another perspective. These were really fun, but it's easy to miss them because they are hidden away in the menu.
Most of the time the game is very linear with a strict path, but in some cases there are small side missions to complete which will reward you with loot like ammo, guns or new air filters.
One of my main issues with the game are the bossfights. All of the boss enemies you will encounter are basically bulletsponges that will occasionally charge at you, but not anything else really. So it's just a matter of running around in circles, evading charge attacks and spraying bullets. Not very challenging and just extremely tedious. A few twists to spice things up would have been nice.
Also do you remember charging headlessly into an enemy stronghold in Metro 2033 and instantly getting killed by a trap? Yeah, those were the times. Sure it was annoying, but also a slap in your face to be more cautious.
This time around traps do not do any real damage whatsoever and the only thing they will do is scare you when somthing explodes in your face and maybe alert some enemies nearby.
I really liked the constant danger of Metro 2033 and this is one aspect of Last Light that did not make any sense for me. It just took away from the experience of an always hostile environment.
One other thing I would like to mention is that the games started crashing more and more towards the end. In the last 2 hours of gameplay I had about 4 or 5 crashes to my desktop which was really annoying.
I do not know the cause of this, but I think it should be mentioned nontheless.
Metro Last Light is a great game with an awesome atmosphere, slightly better gunplay and a stealth option that actually works. If you enjoyed Metro 2033 there is no real reason to skip this game.

Catzilla is going to be the new standard of benchmarks, it provides accurate results which can be compared with other systems and it has really nice looking graphics test.
A "benchmark" it's a kind of software that can be use to compare the performance between two or more computers, speaking in software terms. You can do a benchmark on everything that can be measured, computers performance or procesing power can be easily measured.
They turn more and more useful when the number of results and people who uses it increases, if we have 10 or 20 results is not really useful to compare because most of the systems will use different hardware, but when the number is enormous like 3dmark results (we are talking about millions of results). Benchmarks are essential to know if your system is running well and has optimum performance.
Benchmarking with games is not accurate because they don't use "timedemos", when you run Catzilla on diverse systems every part of the benchmark lasts the same time and renders the same frames, the results are based on how many frames your computer renders PER SECOND.
No and no, you can't fight Catzilla or control any caracter, this kind of software was not made to play with it.
.Measure
.Compare
.Test stability when Overclocking
It is ESSENCIAL to know the capabilities of your computer's hardware, there are so many different graphics cards out there, you need to know which performs better, then you can evaluate its price/performance by your own.
Enough talking, lets see what Catzilla can do!
Catzilla consist on five different test:
*Main Test
*Fluid Test
*Physics Test
*Fur Test
*Raymarch Test

Absolutely spectacular remake of one of the most iconic games from my childhood. Bionic Commando was one of the very best games for NES, and remains a very fun game to this day. This remake is a faithful rendition of the old classic with updated graphics.
I was wary when I first got this game, afraid they may have added new controls to make full use of an XBox controller. But that apprehension went out the window as soon as I started playing. The graphics look beautiful, I was stunned to see how good this old game looks with new visuals, and I was amazed to find they kept the old control scheme: D-pad (or left joystick) and just two buttons (A and B). To any of you who might be thinking "wow, just two buttons, OMG WTF???" you're missing the point of this game. It's old-school platforming fun, with a really good plot and great challenges that really make you think.
This is the kind of game I want my kids to play (whenever I have them in a few years). The mechanics are a bit frustrating at times, since there is no "jump" button, no "run" button, or any of the other frills you would find in most third-person shooters. Instead, you have just two buttons: one to shoot your gun, and another to shoot your bionic arm, which functions basically like a grappling hook. You can shoot the grappling hook in exactly 5 directions: straight left, straight right, 45 degrees up-left, 45 degrees up-right, and straight up. Though this might seem like a limitation, it's actually an integral part of what gives this game its challenge and creativity. Back in the day when this was programmed for NES, it was the pinnacle of gaming, and today, it's a wonderful challenge that gets better and better as you play longer and get used to the controls. The reason I want my future kids to play this kind of game is that it really forces you to think outside the box. For example, there are some areas that seem impassable, but with a bit of thought, you can jump off the platform, turn back and catch onto it, then swing past and catch another platform with a little bit of timing. Things like that are what makes Bionic Commando something unique in the world of gaming, teaching kids (or nostalgic adults) how to think outside the box and work with what you have to overcome challenges.
As I mentioned before, the graphics look great. It's not absolutely stunning, definitely not on par with Skyrim or The Witcher 3, but still very good. If you played the NES classic like me, then you will be absolutely blown away, but for people who are new to Bionic Commando, it probably won't stun you. There's nothing wrong with the graphics, it's just obvious that it's a minimalistic platformer. The tutorial reminds me of Frozen Synapse, while the main game looks similar to Valdis Story: An Abyssal City, but less cartoony.
Speaking of the tutorial, you really should play it when you get to it. If you haven't played Bionic Commando before, you'll need the time to get used to the controls, and if you have, you could probably use a refresher course, especially since you'll be using an XBox controller instead of the NES controller. Please, for the love of God, don't try to play this game with your keyboard. For one thing, I don't think you can get a true feel for the game without using a real D-pad and real A & B buttons, and for another, some of the reviews have stated that in later levels the key binding is messed up which is very problematic when you're facing a Boss Battle where one false move could spell your doom. I'm actually seriously considering getting a USB NES controller specifically for this game, but it works great with an XBox controller so there's no need for that unless you're just nostalgic.
Sound quality is excellent, I think it does a great job of staying true to the classic sounds while updating them to the modern era. The music sounds like a revamped version of the original soundtrack, and the sound effects are a perfect blend of just enough chiptunes to make it feel older, while still maintaining a level of modern quality.
Overall, this is a spectacular game that I would recommend to anyone who is a fan of platformers or looking to try one. With various difficulty levels to choose from, it has great replay value, and it's simple to learn but difficult to master. $10 isn't that much for a game these days, and Bionic Commando goes on sale pretty regularly so I'd say it's definitely worth every penny.
Oh, who am I kidding? I can't try to write an unbiased review of Bionic Commando: Rearmed, this is a faithful remake of one of the first video games I ever played. It's awesome because I said so, now buy it and love it.

This game hits a serious sweet spot for me. Paris. 1920's. You are an imaginary friend of a little girl whose parents are a 1920's version of Jessica Rabbit and a father who wants to make good but goes about it in all the wrong ways. Add a great jazz and noir feel and you have Contrast. Now I'm not going to go into the whole story. Suffice it to say, it has a lot of heart, and it had me tearing up at the end. Though the game does take place through the eyes of a child, Didi is not stupid. She knows what is happening to her parents and the dire circumstances they are in. Of course, it is up to her and her imaginary friend Dawn to save the day!
The idea behind the platforming is brilliant, as Dawn is able to slip into the shadows (literally) and go between 2D and 3D spaces to solve puzzles. This is a brilliant idea that I wish could have been explored a little more. I was sad to see so many crate puzzles, but this is a nitpick.
Now as nice as the gameplay is, the setting and the music are the stars. This game is unlike anything I've seen. The music has a classy noir feel. I'm just glad its available as DLC....The level design is amazing. You will visit different areas of a circus, fixing things to make them work, nightclubs, cinemas, and automaton workshops. The city between levels is nicely done but I wish there was more world to explore.
This game is short. I don't know if that is a bad thing, because the game was fun and well done. The story was well told, with a very satisfying ending. Throughout the game are collectables that expound on the story and give very important details. I know I will be replaying to get all the extra bits.
This to me was an original platformer with a great story and puzzles that could be challenging, but shouldn't make you run for a walkthrough. A definite must for those who are drawn to this time period and atmosphere.

is now released! If you prefer a written form, check out the text below!
Let’s talk about the
of Autocraft first, and I will be supremely direct here. It seems to me that the game tries to hinge on the simple graphical fidelity train that Minecraft started. Most models seem deliberately low in their polygon count, leading to this peculiar art style, which could be okay if it would not be as highly inconsistent as it currently is. For example when looking at the astronaut, the model is actually quite detailed, thus creating a harsh contrast. Moreover, the choice of colours and in general the shading of the objects (I don’t even want to say texturing, as there is no real texture to it) seems inspired by smooth pastels, which again contrasts the rest of the aesthetics in terms of providing futuristic, edgy models. The overall appearance suggests that the developer does not know which way the game is supposed to look, lacking a clear artistic vision. The missing anti-aliasing does the rest to inflict screen flickering on your eyes wherever possible. Suffice to say, Autocraft does not give a good impression in terms of graphical fidelity. The same can be said about the overall
. Generic, monotone background tracks trot along while you are playing, never peaking interest or requiring any attention.
But technical facets do not necessarily make a good game bad and horrible gameplay is not rescued just by splendid graphics. Therefore, let’s talk about the core of Autocraft: the
, consisting of building vehicles and afterwards steering them through the physics simulation to reach a certain point on the map. The building aspects of the game are actually decent. The camera can be rotated freely, parts mostly react like you would expect and all parts snap to the backbone of your vehicle making the building rather intuitive. Additionally you can remap the keys required to steer interactive parts, thus allowing fancy mechanisms if you are creative enough about it. Sadly, Autocraft wastes said potential as you are mostly required to limit yourself incredibly to reach the bonus star requirements. Additionally, even when you try fancy things, they usually end up not working as intended and often a simple solution of flying plane, rocket or standard car is the solution to every level I have encountered. What is the point of a wacky building game, if we can’t creatively use the level design to design vehicles of our weird twisted minds?
Immediately when taking your firsts transport out for a ride, you will notice that the physics engine is so obviously terrible that you wonder which, if any, laws of physics have been applied to Autocraft. The worst part is again inconsistency. In a particular level, I was pressing W constantly and restarting in between to display how broken the simulation is. Even though the vehicle is spawned in the same spot over and over, and even though I just press W constantly, thus accelerating constantly, the bounces, breaks and side-ways reactions seem utterly random. If your game consists of essentially one gameplay element, you better make sure it is darn good, and currently the physics of Autocraft are anything but that.
At least I got a mild chuckle out of Autocraft when taking roughly ten minutes to build a giraffe, which I then took for a leisurely stroll through the sandbox mode. Seriously, these are the things I would want to do in a crazy building game like this. Huge machines, completely unreasonably flying vehicles and rocket boosted drag racers. Well, you could build rocket boosted drag racers, but Autocraft fails to display any sense of momentum, thus the whole endeavour is actually quite boring.
, even in its early access state, I have to say I do not see a bright future for Autocraft. The inconsistencies throughout the game are frustrating and frankly there are too many other good competitors in this genre for Autocraft to take off. The ideas are interesting, but in terms of execution it seems as if the developers are crushed below the weight.

This is a simple yet brilliant game. You play a rather unique role of a Dungeon Master by placing tiles, monsters and gold. Yet also play as the "dungeoneer" also, who moves by itself (via motivation, for example gold is more important than an empty room), yet the combat is based on a card system in which you control. You can gain additional cards via loot which can only be obtained from monsters. You will need to fight in order to level up and gain further loot to handle the boss fight in said dungeon.
When you enter a dungeon you will always start without loot and at level 1, which may sound off-putting but considering the games formula, it is incredibly effective.
The early-mid game can be a struggle at first due to a learning curve, lack of money (to upgrade your guild to get better heroes) and not knowing what dungeons contain what. The game unfortuantely gets easier later on when you get top tier heroes, but I still found it enjoyable until it's end.

Metro Last Light Redux is the sequel to the critically acclaimed Metro 2033 and once again you take on the role of the young ranger Artyom in the post apocalyptic ruins of the Moscow metro.
And right of the bat : Metro Last Light is a worthy successor and in many ways even better than the original.
The first thing you'll notice is that stealth is actually a viable option this time around and it works. No more glitched throwing knives or enemies that can spot you in complete darkness. If you fail to sneak around a group of enemies they will instantly call for backup, making the game harder but in no way unfair or frustrating. Both options work equally well.
However sometimes enemies do not spot you even though they clearly should have. But most of the time it feels very good trying to get to the next mission objective without ever being seen.
Last Light looks absolutely stunning and while graphics are not everything, I never felt like I was playing a nice looking tech demo. Performance wise the game ran really well on my machine and only in one level I could not get over 30 frames per second no matter what graphical setting I chose.
The atmosphere was incredibly tense, with great sound design and music. If you run out of air filters for example, Artyom will start breathing heavily and you think you're going to suffocate yourself.
The same goes for the guns in the game. There is a large variety with some customization options like sights, extended magazines or silencers. All in all the gunplay felt nice, and I especially liked the pneumatic weapons which have to be charged up before being able to fire.
I really liked that in some parts of the game you will encounter foes that are pretty invulnerable to firearms and can only be defeated by using your flashlight. Of course these sections are pretty dark which makes for a great atmosphere.
What I also really enjoyed were the extra missions that let you see certain parts of the story from another perspective. These were really fun, but it's easy to miss them because they are hidden away in the menu.
Most of the time the game is very linear with a strict path, but in some cases there are small side missions to complete which will reward you with loot like ammo, guns or new air filters.
One of my main issues with the game are the bossfights. All of the boss enemies you will encounter are basically bulletsponges that will occasionally charge at you, but not anything else really. So it's just a matter of running around in circles, evading charge attacks and spraying bullets. Not very challenging and just extremely tedious. A few twists to spice things up would have been nice.
Also do you remember charging headlessly into an enemy stronghold in Metro 2033 and instantly getting killed by a trap? Yeah, those were the times. Sure it was annoying, but also a slap in your face to be more cautious.
This time around traps do not do any real damage whatsoever and the only thing they will do is scare you when somthing explodes in your face and maybe alert some enemies nearby.
I really liked the constant danger of Metro 2033 and this is one aspect of Last Light that did not make any sense for me. It just took away from the experience of an always hostile environment.
One other thing I would like to mention is that the games started crashing more and more towards the end. In the last 2 hours of gameplay I had about 4 or 5 crashes to my desktop which was really annoying.
I do not know the cause of this, but I think it should be mentioned nontheless.
Metro Last Light is a great game with an awesome atmosphere, slightly better gunplay and a stealth option that actually works. If you enjoyed Metro 2033 there is no real reason to skip this game.

- Endlessly roaming around wasteland planets in the stupid rover has been replaced with scanning planets from orbit and occasionally mining their resources using a little mini-game you won't have to play very much.

- Long boring speeches have been replaced by snappy dialogue. I LOL'd plenty of times.
- Depressing characters have been replaced by characters with actual depth and humour.
- Absolutely terrible in-mission music has been purged and replaced with admittedly unmemorable but generally enjoyable music.
- Completely unwieldy inventory system has been replaced with an upgrade system that will have you hunting down every credit .
- Good story revelations at every step of the way

To that end I'm  changing my review to positive, there is no reason for it to be negative now.

Here are the things wrong with this game.
1) The tutorial is too hard. Instead of spreading the 3 tutorial levels out over time the game requires you to be able to execute even the advanced mechanics right from the beginning. I imagine some casual players may not even be able to complete these 3 tutorial levels. These levels also lack any kind of flow, and so they're also just bad levels in general.
2) The tutorial is too short. The tutorial doesn't explain some very key movement mechanics that are profoundly unintuitive to the point that they are literally the opposite of reality. There's a hidden "charge" system the game never explains that allows you to either dash or jump in mid-air. Not all of the cases where the recharges happen are explained and so the player is left without enough information to even begin to tackle anything past the first 15 courses. The player is forced to look up a guide online or spend a lot of time randomly button mashing in order to progress.
3) The "overworld" is dumb and confusing. Instead of the devs bothering to figure out which order the levels should be in the game has you exploring these 4 zones between the worlds in order to find new levels. Sometimes this requires executing extraordinarily difficult platforming tricks as well as a key obtained from doing really well on previous levels. The layout of this zone is very confusing, and it is very very very very very frustrating having to deal with a dumb mini-game just to get to the next course. The courses are hard enough on their own. I already did well enough on the courses in order to get the key. Just let me pick them from a menu, and don't lock content behind meaningless redundant skill gates you didn't think through properly before you implemented. It's very easy to get stuck.
4) Keys aren't explained. The game doesn't explain adequately how to obtain keys. This leads to being stuck until you look up a guide online that explains how to get more keys.
5) Key colors are difficult to differentiate. I'm a little bit color-blind. The game has like 5 key colors. I can only differentiate between silver and "the rest of them." They bothered to make the key icons look different, but not the locks. So good luck being able to figure out where to take a key you just obtained because a) the lock colors are all very similar and b) you might not even be able to get there due to point #3.
6) Character differences are not explained.  2 of them are quite similar while the other 2 are quite different from all others. It would have been nice to have been told by the game why I should ever choose a different character than the default.
In conclusion, I do like this game, but don't be afraid to look up guides on how the mechanics of the game work. It's really not fun if you don't do that.
I also want to reiterate again that the entire concept of The Nexus feels very much like the dev fell in love with their own "clever" idea, and never bothered to think through the ramifications of what they were doing. I'm sure it took a lot of time to build and design, but it only ever serves to frustrate and impede player progress to new courses. Just save yourself the trouble and look up a YouTube video that shows how to navigate to all the courses along with a map of door lock colors. You will have a much better time of it.

It's a shame. I really enjoyed watching speedruns of Dustforce. I had high hopes that I'd be able to do the same stunts that several of the top players displayed in various playthroughs. Unfortunately, this game has ultimately taught me the difference between watching videos of Dustforce and physically playing Dustforce.
+Pros: Beautiful music (very relaxing!) and art. Fun to watch. Competitive for the speedrunning community. High replay value*
-Cons: Stiff controls, hard to master even after brushing and practicing the tutorial several times, confusing hub world, definitely not worth the $9.99 price tag.
Summary:
While the gameplay looks impressive, the controls are extremely stiff and difficult to master (actions like jumping are delayed once the button is pressed, not immediate). After the tutorial, you'll have to perform the actions you just learned to enter a door that leads to a hub world; this took me a bunch of tries (I just wanted to play the game already!). There's no sense of direction in this hub world; I found myself entering harder levels earlier just because I was wandering around aimlessly. Without a sense of direction (especially on a first playthrough), casual players will find the difficulty going all over the place rather than easier--->harder levels. With an insanely steep learning curve and a non-linear flow of gameplay, I don't feel enticed to explore this game further after 5+ hours of trying to work with the game's mechanics.
*Because Dustforce drives players to complete levels as fast as possible, much of the core gameplay revolves around beating your personal best time. I've had some experience with speedrunning games and personally, I can't find enjoyment from trying to beat my times if I cannot enjoy the controls and core mechanics of the game first. Dustforce isn't something I can recommend to anyone unless they find entertainment in learning every inch of mechanic possible in this game through countless repitition and muscle memory

Who would have guessed: a 2D indie platformer can be challenging and difficult and yet be--gasp!--ENJOYABLE?! Considering there seems to be a trend for games that confuse challenge with stress and difficulty with laboriousness, this game is kind of a miracle.
For starters, it has a learning curve. Yes: an ACTUAL LEARNING CURVE. You have some brief tutorials to help you get the hang of the controls, with are fairly complex and prety tricky to get right, and soon you're in a "nexus" which you can traverse and unlock levels. These levels come in different difficulties, and you hve to beat a certain number of easier levels to get keys and unlock the harder ones.
As usual, the controls define about half of the playability and the fun of the game, and they work quite well here. It strikes a balance between fast, fluid, complex and challenging. Yes, it can get annoying and a little innaccurate at times, but those flaws seem to be more due to the natural limitations of keyboard controls rather than the game designers letting them suck deliberately because "that makes it HARD!!!". The only thing that does annoy me is how the gravity works: within a millisecond, you'll switch from "gently floating down" to "plummetting like a stone". I don't think this adds anything to the game.
The levels are good, and range from flowing and pleasant to devilishly hard. So far, I've played more than half of the levels, and only one was seriously beyond my skills. The others, at their most difficult, are reasonably doable. Also, you're not expected to simply reach the end of the level: the more dust you clean up, the higher your "Completion" rank goes up, and the higher the combo you get at the end, the higher your "Finesse" rank (it took me ages to understand what that meant). The higher your ranks, the sooner you get keys to unlock the harder levels. Also, if you're really perverted, you can try to improve your time and improve your rank in the scoreboard. If you like speedrunning, you'll have a field day.
Finally, I really enjoy the art style. The visuals are pretty, cartoony and slightly dreamy. The music is nice, and whomever wrote it did a pretty good job at imitating Tycho. Also, you get to choose from four different characters: the guy in blue, and... er... four others. (another gripe I have is that you have to choose your character EVERY TIME you start a level. Sheesh, why not choose once, at the beginning of the game, and let me change it later if I want to?)
I'm glad I got this game, and I'm glad for the time I spent on it. I still have quite a lot to play, but I'm already satisfied. Fans of platformers should definitely take notice.

If you first hear the name Autocraft you might just think you’re dealing with some kind of Warcraft clone with cars here. Let me reassure you that it doesn’t come even close. In reality this is a fun game for all of those who have ever played with Lego or K’nex. That’s exactly right; Autocraft wants you to use your imagination again.

First and foremost this is a puzzle game, but building stuff is also a very important part of the game. There aren’t any real objectives except to get to the goal. You start off in ‘building’ mode where you have the opportunity to build a vehicle. At first, this will be a car, but a few levels in you’ll be building an airplane and later on even boats and robots, among other things.
Every couple of levels you’ll learn something new to do so it gradually teaches you all the things you can do. These ‘tutorials’ aren’t too deep. As a matter of fact you’ll be doing everything yourself. The game doesn’t limit you to the developers’ ideas, it allows you to experiment with things yourself and maybe you can even find a different way to do things. I do have to admit that this is pretty hard in the beginning, because you only have a limited amount of building blocks available and you’re probably going to need them all just to understand the game’s mechanics. Still, it’s possible.
And I wouldn’t say it’s impossible but it’s damn hard to get to the end of the level without crashing at least once. Building things is a learning process and a fun experience in itself. It’s very satisfying to see a crafted vehicle do exactly what you want it to do.
I haven’t mentioned the controls yet but they’re really easy to use. Just dragging objects onto other objects will attach them to each other. You can smoothly and quickly drag them to other places, too and by keeping Control pressed you can quickly add the same parts to other pieces and by pressing and holding Alt you’ll be able to quickly delete specific parts. Easy as pie.
As I said there aren’t any real objectives but there are optional objectives you can complete like setting a speed record, collecting a star (‘hidden’ somewhere in the level) or by using a specific amount of blocks. Completing these objectives will earn you more (different) blocks that you can use in Sandbox mode where you can express your imagination and creativity more freely.
Sandbox mode is exactly what it sounds like. You select a level and you start building things with the blocks you have acquired. You’ll also be able to load objects from other users into your levels and then just have fun with them. Fans of Lego and K’nex will have an excellent time here, even if interaction with objects is fairly limited.
The game, at the moment of writing, has 37 levels to complete. The first couple of levels are easy and can be seen as an introduction to the game really, but around level 10 things start to get more difficult. You can play this until the end of time, but if you’re going to finish just the levels then you should be able to complete them between 10-20 hours I think. It depends on several factors so as you can understand it’s a very rough estimate.
As far as the graphics are concerned Autocraft looks really beautiful. This is the first game, I think ever, that reminded me of Mario Galaxy. The graphics have the same style with lots of colors and specific shading. It looks beautiful in motion and the screenshots don’t do it justice. Not entirely, at least. One thing I would like to see though, are more animated objects in the background. It feels a little barebones sometimes, but you’re usually probably too busy building anyway.
The music is kind of subtle but what’s there is calm and soothing, and maybe even a bit futuristic. It’s well done. As for the sounds; crashing, using your engines and blocks connecting with each other all sound realistic enough to keep you immersed.
Autocraft is a fun game that’s all about completing puzzles by building vehicles. If you ever played Turbo Dismount but wanted more freedom and creativity then this is the game for you. I had a great time with it and I’m sure many share that sentiment. I know the game isn’t yet complete, but I’m positive the quality will only improve (it’s already very polished). I’m curious to see what the final product will be like. Recommended !

Crusader Kings II is beyond a doubt one of the most immersive strategy games I have ever played. The sheer vastness of options is overwhelming and means that you will never be at a loss of things to do. Twisting history is one of the most rewarding aspects of the game. Want to form the empire of Brittania? You can do that.
There are hundreds of in game random events and the amount of time and effort you put into your characters makes you feel more immersed. In fact, when your beloved character dies after having ruled for 70 years you do feel somewhat saddened. The game definitely brings out emotion, such as when your only male heir dies, invoking large amounts of rage in you.
The county management, the politics and the combat are all polished beautifully. The AI is also top notch, although there can be some strange marriages by AI rulers (sometimes Kings wish to marry your lowborn courtiers!) The DLC's also offer many hours more playtime and are well worth getting as they expand your gameplay options exponentially.
This is a true masterpiece Grand Strategy title from Paradox and I would recommend it to everyone. 10/10.

Confrontation is a simplistic linear action RPG. You will face few choices throughout the game the biggest being which generic heroes you want to use at any given time.
What ever happend to the deep RPGs? The ones driven by skill, story and exploration?
In Confrontation you take control of a number of Griffin Hero's as they travel through various hostile lands in the search of secret enemy cloning labs. Although the back story and lore in the world of Confrontation seems pretty interesting the game never manages to portray it in a favorable light. Everything is locked into classic fantasy stereotypes and even the slight steampunk elements feels bland and unimpressive.
The gameplay is your standard team based action RPG, you control 4 heroes that level up as you go along and upgrade their various abilities. Unfortunately the strength and usefulness of the heroes and their abilities are quite skewered and many of them is not worth using outside of their required sections. On normal difficulty almost all of the fights can be won by simply clicking attack on the enemies as they pop up although some micro management is required that is mainly due to the horrendous AI that makes your heroes go idle at the end of their action unless they are literally standing next to an enemy.
Graphics and sound are of the lower end of the "We actually spent money on it" range and generally UI and menus seem slightly dated and underdeveloped.
I'd love to have evaluated the multi-player but nobody seems to be playing and looking around on the official forums this seems to have been the case from day one.
All in all this is a game to avoid. It's boring and bland and has little to recommend it. The developers have had no interest in supporting it past release and there is no community to make multi-player a viable gamemode. Truly a wasted purchase.

This will be my first review but unlike some other reviewers, I've played it more than 12 minutes.
The short: If you liked the original Wolfenstein 3D, you will probably enjoy this game. However if Wolfenstein did not float your boat it is unlikely that this will interest you.
Now for the longer version: As several posters have pointed out, the game is made using a free asset pack. However as far as I know the maps and campaign seem to be original (if I'm wrong, feel free to correct me). There are two 7 level campaigns and one unique bonus map for a total of 15 maps. As of this review, there are a few bugs that need to be ironed out mainly involving the mini-map display but the game ran without hiccups and seemed very stable on my machine.
Much like Wolfenstein 3D  the game takes place on one plane with walls that have the same height and a uniformly coloured ceiling. It also shares some of the quirks that Wolfenstein had; corners can be used to your advantage to block enemy movements and pick them off at your leisure.
As a huge fan of the Wolfenstein 3D and Doom it was nice to play an old school sprite-based FPS with non-regenerating health and simple mission objectives. I feel I got my money's worth.

Fun.  Simple.  Challenging.  Free.
Fun:
It's an interesting mix of micro and macro.  I could generalize this game to about 5 elements and from those, 10 problems that can arise from those that you need to have a strategy for.  What exactly those are, you'll have to find out for yourself in game.
Simple:
As I said, not much to keep track of on paper, but the sheer mass of your colony will quickly grow.  I usually try to expand in a single (of 4) direction so that my camera doesn't have to move as much (now we're getting into some of my secrets for holding certain top scores).  Solutions are also simple, but then we get to Challenging...
Challenging:
While solutions to issues are simple, there's an easy way to do things, and an efficient way.  Then keep in mind that the same issue could be coming up in several places suddenly.  The game I just played, I had 3(!) shaman caves bust open within a few seconds of eachother.  Luckily, they were all near to eachother so I only needed to build one fortress to get all 3 under control.
Free:
Yes, it's free.  But listen, I recommend the 'difficulty DLC'.  The higher difficulties are much more interesting, and it's 3 dollars.
And look how many hours I've played this!  Albeit it's over a period of 3 or so years, for a free game that I spent 3 dollars on, nearly 100 hours as of this writing is nothing.
Conclusion:  I feel comfortable in calling this game a classic.  Think Galaga, or that old Donkey Kong game where Mario runs up those ramps to rescue the princess.  It's pretty simple, but the replayability is definitely there.  Go play it!

There's a good game in here IF you have the patience to learn to put up with and work around the HORRIBLE CONTROLS. Interesting story, interesting characters, interesting world, interesting gameplay mechanics, ABSOLUTELY TERRIBLE CONTROLS. I can't stress that enough. I think the good outweighs the bad here, but I seriously hope Compulsion has learned how to program decent controls by now (especially since We Happy Few looks like an interesting game, and I want to try that too).
The puzzles are inventive and a lot of fun to figure out. It's rewarding to have those "Aha moments." However, a puzzle/platformer like this requires very precise controls, and this game doesn't have that. The last thing that should make a game like this more difficult is wonky controls, but that is definitely the case here. It will cause several deaths and/or increase the number of attempts you have to make at each puzzle--even when you already know what to do.
The biggest point of frustration is, sadly, the central mechanic of the game's puzzles: switching between a 3D color plane and a 2D background/shadow plane. You hit a button to switch planes; that works. You hit a different button to dash through thinner shadows in the shadow plane; that works too. Where the whole thing falls apart, however, is when jumping from one level of shadow object to another where there's something that will launch you into the air or force you through a tight space. When that happens, the game will often--seemingly for no reason--push you out of the shadow plane and back into the 3D plane automatically, requiring you to start a puzzle all over again. Puzzles like the drum cymbals in the magician's lab are unbelievably frustrating because of this specific control issue. To get around this, you'll need to master the timing of jumping back into the shadow plane in that split second between being pushed out and falling; but even that's not always possible.
This game is short, so the frustration won't last too long. But I do recommend it. Again, there's a lot to like here if you can see past and work around the clunky controls.

Bioshock 2 is probably the weakest of the trilogy, but that is not to say that it is a bad game by any stretch of the imagination.
It plays in a very similar way to the original, except this time you play as a Big Daddy, however that is where one of the main problem the game lies. You expect playing as a Big Daddy, you should be a giant  kickass killing machine, yet you still seem to have problems fighting off the same splicers you faced in Bioshock 1 as a human, I felt underpowered considering I was playing  as one of the  major toughguys from the first game.
The remastered version looks gorgeous BUT there is a problem with the resolution on the game, so if your monitor is  above 1920x1080, the picture will be cropped and if you drop it down to 1920 to see the full screen, the picture quality for some reason suffers. Also, near the end, the game has a bad case of "oh you did the task, but now you must do THIS task to finish... oh, and THIS task... and you are done, except for THIS task" It does feel a bit like things were added to extend the playing time of the game (10-12 hours overall)
While it might sound like I am complaining about a lot of stuff, it's more of a warning to those who need to know this kind of thing. If you liked Bioshock 1, then this continuation is a no brainer.

Tumbleweed Express is outstanding. It bills itself as a sort of Tower Defense game and while I am usually not a fan of that genre, I loved this game...a lot. The main missions are not terribly long, and there are but 12, but they're replayable as hell and I never once felt like I was "grinding" when I was going back to some old levels for loot. The gameplay is fast, thrilling, and challenging (yet somehow never frusturating).
There isn't much story to speak about, and the characters are lovable yet flat. I did pick up on an underlying theme of "progress vs the old fashioned way", and I thought that was very neat, and something I didn't really expect from this game when I bought it. As you deck out your own Tumbleweed to go on your journey, you use more and more fancy gizmos and gadgets, like Tesla guns, a radar, etc. And that line between old and new really starts to get blurred in the game when you realize you might just have to adapt to the new technology to finish your quest. I could get into deeper ideas like "becoming just as bad as your enemy" but maybe I'm reading into it too much. All I can say is that I truly was not expecting it from this game.
Building up your own train and customizing it in this game is satisfying to the point of nearly addicting. You start with two cars and you get more cars, better guns, armor, and speed boosts. I do wish there were more customization options.
This is a can't-miss game for $5 bucks. I got it for $4 on sale and that feels like a steal. I would absolutely pay more for a DLC, hell, even a sequel with more train customization, bigger branching levels, more fleshed out story and characters, more weapons....the possibilities are limitless. For their first game Digiriballers have made a knock-out, and I will follow them wherever they go next (which should be Tumbleweed 2 :D)
(P.S. Don't skip the credits! The song played during the credits and the sketches are a true delight.)

I've never played a game quite like this. In this game you are in control of the Tumbleweed Express, one of the very few remaining trains after the advent of dirigibles has left trains behind. The fellow responsible for dirigible technology has sabotaged most remaining trains, and so yours is a rare sight indeed.
As for the actual gameplay, your train follows the track and you control the main cannon at the back of the train. You can buy different types of cannon as the story progresses, although two of the four types are utterly useless. One cool aspect is that you can add train cars, which increase your income per mission and also allow you to mount smaller, automated versions of the guns you put on the caboose. Every stage is completed just by reaching the end without being destroyed by bandits, rivals, or dirigibles. There are several upgrades you can buy between missions, and you can replay completed missions for more cash. You can also complete side objectives in those missions.
All in all a fairly simple but also quite fun game. I definitely recommend it unless you don't like aiming and firing cool guns.

Despite the fact that I'm very used to categories of lengthy games (min 35 hours, up to several hundred where there's MP), I found my experience with the Metro series quite immersive. The story cannot fail to intrigue you and will indeed make you jump into Artyom's boots. Yes it's just about 10 hours on normal (9 if you don't take it with leisure, probably 15-20 if you go for harder modes) but they're gonna be really intense.
As it appears Last Light has officially been included in the novel's canon too (on of the endings of the game precisely) I feel safe to say there's no point in playing Metro 2033 without going for LL too; meaning that LL is not just some made-up story totally unconnected to the original book.
I can't even argue with the choice of the so-called 'moral points'. If you want a certain ending (the canon and harder one) you must act like you think Artyom would have. Do things without rushing, listening, being over-philosophical, stealthy, and so on. Also consider that they're not defined 'moral points' anywhere on the official site, media, whatever. Likewise, there's no good or bad ending. I think an explanation to the standard finale would not that
Anyway I had to get over the fact I couldn't get the 'good ending'. And if you're either the 'righteous vengeful' or the 'guns blazing' type you'll have too.
As for the DLC’s, they are overall pretty good. I have no idea how much the packs were priced when they were released, so I cannot say a thing about the playtime/cost ratio – this is the redux version of Metro LL so I’ll just consider them bonus missions tossed in for free and judge them for their quality only.
Most people in the reviews have around 10-11 hours recorded, and mention no DLC’s at all, meaning being detailed about them may prove useful to readers. I have not played the Sniper team and Pavel levels, and the tower either. I may refer to the missions with names that don’t precisely match with the ones in-game. To sum it up:
Kshatriya – The longest of all and probably one of the most enjoyable, though I barely played this one. You impersonate a Polis stalker off to collect ‘artifacts’, so it’s mostly about scavenging stuff. The map is said to be really big and expands as you explore it. Overall I’m sure most will enjoy it.
Reich – You jump into some Fourth Reich war hero’s boots, known as Hans. The mission is pretty short, but I appreciate the effort the developers made to give us some experience with our favourite factions. Try it on ranger or hc ranger if you wish, it’s really a bloodbath of reds.
Anna  – It gives you the chance of re-taking the first mission on the surface, but in Miller’s daughter’s rags. I liked this one a lot, because it gives you the chance to relive moments in the main story but from a different perspective. The mission is short as the Reich’s one more or less, but adds some details to the plot if you wondered why
. And it’s sort of cool to see Artyom fight on his own, if you got involved with the character.
Khan – Another good one. It covers another piece of the main story but with side characters, namely Ulman (you) and the the namesake of the mission. You accidentally meet with the latter after stopping the communists’ train, and eventually stumble across a station Khan has a past with… You’ll see for yourself. It’s relatively long compared to the previous 2, but still plays for some 20-30 minutes.
Developer level – Enjoyable for a while. The museum doesn’t offer much but it’s still nice to take a closer look to all the vicious beasts and humans you encountered in your escapade. The range and arena offer you a bunch of challenges that may be of interest if you like shooter (FPS in my jargon) games, well… for the shooting and killing. I had a lot of hopes for the Arena because battling mutants could be extremely cool, but it was a let down to see only minor enemies are featured. No librarians, bears or big momma’s for you.
Through the fire – Not sure that’s its name, but it’s the one with the spiderbugs in D6. You impersonate an unnamed stalker who has just teamed up with 2 supposedly ‘tough’ guys in a bar. At normal it probably lasts some 20-30 minutes, so it’s not that bad. It’s not much of a challenge, but the ending makes you feel like wanting a sequel.
I think that’s all. I loved the bonus missions altogether, because they helped cope with the fact that the game was over and I had to go on with my life. Story driven videogames are like books if they feature good narratives, story-telling, and they always leave you in a state of confusion and what not. Considering I played Metro 2033 and Last Light as if they were a single game, for a total of almost 24 hours, I could say I lived an entire day as Artyom. Let’s all hope our dear Slavic developers come up with another game, but even if they did I doubt they would set it in Moscow again.

I've devoted over 500 hours to this game over the last 3 years and I don't regret it at all. With such a massive amount of things to accomplish it almost never ends. From pvp to quests to farming with your friends to just goofing around and trying out new builds, the game is super fun. I thought I'd give my honest opinion on the game and why I think it's one of the best mmo's out there today.
Pros:
The story has come so far and is very immersive. Very rich lore. However if you don't pay attention to what's going on around you you'll be very lost. A lot of the story isn't told directly and has to be told through quests and paying attention to the world around you. For example, how the different factions interact with each other and what their goals are, is explained through doing missions and putting together puzzle pieces by listening to what the NPCs say.
This is a farming and hard♥♥♥♥♥grinding game. If you don't like the grind for better upgrades, parts for weapons or certain drops/events then perhaps this isn't the one for you. Although the payoff feels so good when you finally get the item you were farming so hard to get and now you get to craft your item and show it off to your friends. A wide arsenal of weapons and gear you can pick from leads to an unlimited possibility of builds, along with customizable mods to add to your weapons and warframes in order to make them fit your play style, make them stronger and more efficient. Making everyone you meet along the way unique from everyone else. Oh, did I mention that every weapon and Warframe can be acquired for FREE!
That brings me to my next point where this game is absolutely 100% free to play. The only thing you must pay real money for is cosmetics, which you'd only get if you really wanna look cool (Hence the nickname for the game "FashionFrame") or want to support it. Everything in the game can be acquired and there is no p2p aspect to it at all. No monthly subscriptions. No secret p2w shortcut (Although if you do pay a hefty amount of money you can aquire things very quickly. But what's the fun in that?) and no DLC's. Screw that. Everything can be acquired with a bit of farming. The real money ingame currency is called Platinum and can be traded with other players for parts for weapons and such. This gives the game an entire thriving economy. Don't have any platinum? Farm for parts and items people are looking for and are to lazy to get themselves and sell them. That's how I earn my platinum. Platinum can be used to buy almost everything in game from weapons and warframes to cosmetics. Although I save my platinum for specific items that the ingame market does not offer that people are selling in game.
The community is amazing in this game. When I first started out I had no idea what I was doing. I did a public mission and met a guy who was so far into the game. He saw I was new and asked if I had any questions. So I asked away and got familiar with the game very quickly as he showed me around and helped me acquire my first new warframe. Out of my entire time playing I've never seen one toxic or negative person. Everyone just wants to help each other and have fun. Best gaming community out there if you ask me. And joining a clan will help you by not only finding a few more friends along the way but getting your hands on some new gear only acquired by being in a clan, which are very easy to join. You'll grow a very strong pride for your clan and alliance which gives a competitive feel for when your clan goes to conqour dark sectors, which are areas that are controlled by clans. As for the development team they are very interactive with the players. Answering questions and listening to the players ideas and thoughts while responding with real care and interest. They are very indulged with their game and the players love DE as well <3
The graphics are stunning and utterly remarkable. I have a pretty crappy computer setup yet I manage to run the game smoothly on medium setting and it looks awesome. I can only imagine how it looks at high. The color scheme to the art style is perfectly fitting and almost feels realistic at times or something straight out of star wars. Nothing is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or seemed to be created in a lazy fashion. The detail and creativity that went into the development of this game really shows. The gameplay is very smooth as well and very simple. Some of the jump techniques might be a little tricky at first but can be easily mastered with a bit of practice. It has all the aspects of a shooter game and the aspects of a melee game such as parry, heavy hits, light hits and combos to slaughter your enemies with. It always feel good to see your enemies littered with bullet holes or to see them vaporize or get sliced up into little pieces. The UI is kept simple and easy to read along with the other utilities in the game like the arsenal menu and the foundry (Where you can make new items for yourself)
Now here come my cons:
The game is very unique in so many ways and has come a very long way to get where it is today and I honestly think it is one of, if not the best, mmorpg game that's completely f2p. But the only thing that is not unique is the tilemaps. The maps in this game start to get very old after awhile of playing them. Although as you progress through the game you get to go to different tilemaps but they all tend to get old eventually. They're recycled and reused. If you're doing a mission on venus on land and you go to another mission on venus on land they will be exactly the same tilemap. Although they do spawn you in different areas on the map every time and the maps are fairly big so atleast you get to enjoy them a bit more before you start to figure out where everything is. The enemies are kind of the same way too. As they are reused fairly often. They can also be a bit clunky at times. But I think that adds a bit of humor to the game.
After acquiring most of your wants and needs in the game after the countless hours of grinding and researching the game starts to lose its drive. Since there's nothing more you want, why keep playing? This has happened to me on multiple occasions. And updates for the game tend to come out every month or so, which add tons of new gear and a new quest and frame to farm which always brings me to play again and see what's new. The game is constantly being improved and can be played forever if you'd like.
Not sure if I should consider this a con or not but I'm gonna put it in here anyway as some people might think it is. When I first introduced the game to my friends they all thought it was just another shoot em up game with no skill(Even though it is technically a shoot em up game), as they tend to see me mashing my keyboard and coming out on top. I explain to them that at lower levels enemies are super easy to kill. It's just to make it easier and make it more appealing to beginners so they're not discouraged or get frustrated at hard enemies. As you progress the enemies get immensely harder and more challenging, making strategy key. Some might be turned off by the game not being challenging at first is the point I am trying to make.
Warframe is always improving and is always adding new elements to the game. If you're looking for a new game to spend hours in and get lost in its rich gameplay and community then this is the game for you. As long as you don't mind the grind it's an amazing game to immerse yourself in and meet awesome people. I highly recommend this game to anyone or to at least try it out. A big 10/10 for me. Thank you DE for such a fantastic game that I will continue playing for only Lotus knows how long.

Almost to 100 hours now, so I feel it's time for a review. I'm hooked on this game and Plains of Eidolon hasn't even released yet. I'm going to go over how Warframe handles the 3 core pillars to an RPG experience: Mechanics, Progression, and Customization. Then I'll talk about the business model.
Mechanics - Warframe has fun mechanics. The shooting feels good. Once you find some weapons you enjoy using the gunplay is as good as any shooter you'll find. The warframe abilities are fun to use once you get the hang of them. Melee combat is fun once you understand how stances, combos and channeling work. Where this game's mechanics really shine though is in its movement system. Not only is the movement speed fast, but once you master sliding, double jumping, wall climbing, rolling, and all of the movement "combos" you can pull off, the game offers more mobility than any shooter I've played.
Progression - Warframe has one of the most complicated progression systems I've ever seen in a game. You craft weapons and warframes, then level them up. The higher level they get, the more mods you can put in them. The mods give a variety of buffs and offer a wide variety of ways to build your weapons and warframes to suit your playstyle. You can get creative with them and completely change how certain weapons function. For example: I got a sniper rifle named Vectis Prime, to prepare for the Plains. Vectis is a semi-auto rifle with only a 2 shot magazine but fast reload speed. I got a mod that increases the damage of the first shot by 40%. Then I got a mod that reduces mag capacity but increases reload speed. So now it only holds one shot at a time, but with yet another mod that further increases reload speed, it reloads almost instantly. This makes it function more like a bolt-action rifle. On top of that there are flat damage boost mods, and elemental damage mods. You can combine different elements for new damage types, such as heat damage + poison damage = gas damage, which makes a cloud of AOE poison damage on impact. Really, this is all just scratching the surface of the complex yet rewarding progression system.
Customization - The customization options in Warframe are vast. For cosmetics, your Warframes and Weapons not only have skins you can obtain, but also seperate cosmetic armor pieces. You can also customize all the colors of your items. Then you can customize your playstyle through your choice of Warframes, guns and melee weapons. You have much more freedom to play with what suits you, because most of what determines how powerful a piece of gear is depends on the mods that were put in it. So even the weapons and warframes you get early in the game can be viable at end game, if you put good mods into them. You can also customize your spaceship, inside and out. Clans have huge customizable dojos. You can also choose a companion. These vary from small flying robots similar to Ghosts in the Destiny series, to space dogs and alien cats. There's even a mutant dog thing you can grow from a tumor that develops on your neck when you get infected by a virus that spreads through the player base.
Now, the elephant in the room. It's Free to Play, so there's a ton of Microtransactions. The premium currency, Platinum is kinda expensive, but here's something that's not discussed enough when it comes to this game's business model. TRADING. You can trade in-game items to other players for their premium currency. So, say you find a rare blueprint. You can go into trade chat, or one of the trading bazarres, find a whale with a bunch of platinum who wants to buy your blueprint, and boom, you now have the premium currency without spending a dime.
Awesome game, can't wait to see what Plains of Eidolon brings to the table.

Short version: simple but fun.
If you played Death Track: Resurrection, you can think of this as a simplified version--the maps are all flat and not nearly as diverse; yet the graphics are still half-decent.
If you're big into racing games you may or may not like the fact that you can get through 95% of this game without braking. In fact, there's an option (enabled by default) to auto-accelerate just so you don't have to hold down the throttle the whole time. Still, the small but interesting selection of weapons and ability to choose two different weapons separately, combined with the different map types, has allowed it to keep my attention.
The music is also decent.
Unlike the few other racing games I've played, there's also no announcer. Hallelujah.
One little nitpick: the game doesn't save to an AppData or Documents folder and instead writes your profile information directly to the registry. So you can give yourself all the currency you need to buy the weapons, performance upgrades, and armor upgrades. Nice for cheating but not for transferring a profile between computers.
Again, this may not be for everyone--I like its simplicity but others may see that as a flaw.

Its noir / pulp / theater / vaudeville setting will appeal to fans of those genres, as it has surreal environments with dark, moody European esque streets which the player traverses. I would recommend checking out actual gameplay videos, as I don't think the trailers here depict the game's pacing or more laidback atmosphere well.
I like that the story is presented in somewhat obscure ways, in which you watch "flashbacks" from shadows cast upon the alleyways, to find out more about the father, his lover, and their daughter, as they struggle to make payments to unsavory characters. The platforming mechanic of warping into and out of shadow areas is novel at first, but its implementation can seem a bit strange at times too (i.e. figure out which picnic table umbrellas to open, to make a shadow casting a line for you to navigate on the 'shadow plane' that your character can warp into.., or later an at-times tedious elevator puzzle in which you push elevator buttons to change the cast shadows on the wall to be able to warp into the shadows and then progress upward, etc...)
There are some platforming staples including collectibles, a dash ability to smash through previously unseen areas, etc...
The daughter character can get a little annoying in a "child character always scared / whining / crying" type of way at times, but the voice acting in the game is well done overall.
I think this game deserves more recognition than it ever got, as it is pretty relaxing to play and the stylized setting itself is pretty well done with a unique platforming mechanic, if you're a fan of old theater / noir type of environments and can look past the game's somewhat visible-graphical age, I think you may enjoy it.

I'm going to address this as both a remaster and as the base game. Let's starts with the game itself. It's a decent sequel to a legendary game that has a fine story with some interesting characters (Gil Alexander being a standout to rival Cohen and Steinman in some respects). The game loses some of the visual interest of the last game due to very much (intentionally) looking run down, however it doesn't benefit since these are areas that hold no visual notoriety. The character models are ugly as sin, partly due to artistic design (which is fine), partly due to dated tech. This results in looking decent from a distance and animation not being too bad but up close they're pretty rough to look at. The music is haunting and the voice acting is great. Mechanically, I feel it's more fluid and punchier than the original BioShock and the wave based Little Sisters gameplay encourages entertaining tactics. You acquire a pretty generic assortment of guns but they have good feedback at least. The game seems more like a part 2 to BioShock save the characters which isn't awful but means you don't see anything that new. The hacking minigame is much better I should note. Finally, the game runs goes long enough to be satisfying and not become worn down. If you need more BioShock, it'll fill that hole, it just won't really blow you away like the original. As far as remasters go, it's♥♥♥♥♥♥ Still buggy at points and it still looks super dated so if you already own the original and have no real incentive to pick up the remaster, avoid it.

Divinity: Original Sin was one of the greatest co-op multiplayer RPGs on the market. Playing on a higher difficulty offers those same options, but often at an extreme cost; for example, you wanna run around stealing everything from everyone?  Be ready to fight off an entire town (and likely die miserably in a pool of your own frozen, electrified blood).
If you're a fan of classic, co-op, turn based RPGs, get on board.  The Divinity: Original Sin titles offer you that ride you've been looking for.

To be fair, Guild of Dungeoneering is a time-waster and shouldn't be viewed as more than that. Don't expect a depth to the degree of Binding of Isaac, this is a game you play during lunch break... I think.
+ Replayability: This game has so much randomness going on that no single game will be the same as the previous one, and different classes keep the game interesting for a while.
+ Dungeon length: Usually, you'll be out of a dungeon in about 5 to 10 minutes unless you get unlucky and the first enemy kicks your butt in 3 turns. You can even quit the game in the middle of a dungeon and resume where you left off.
+ Loot system: Being able to decide what kind of loot your characters are able to get is a good idea, and it works nicely. I would like to see a similar concept in more games.
+ Humor: If you like traditional RPG's, this game takes a huge loop with the genre and creates a comedy out of it.
- Negative dungeon rewards: Remove them. Period. Nobody wants to finally beat that mimic boss after losing numerous characters due to RNG, only to be 'rewarded' with 1 permanent health loss, or a less controllable character. It's just a bad gimmick that shouldn't exist.
- RPG: Let's just be clear that it isn't one. Not in the slightest.
- Extreme randomness: If you know even in the slightest what you're doing, the only thing you'll lose to is to RNG, and it happens a LOT. You don't draw any blocks against that ettin? You die. You didn't get a dungeon tile that gets you to the boss in time? Death! A random monster drawing 2 unblockable attack cards in a row? Guess what, it's another death you couldn't do anything about.
I'm weighing this last point in very heavily, because it changes the game from a light-hearted fun dungeon crawler into an excersize in frustration very quickly. On your lunch break, you'd like at a cat burglar literally throwing cats and making terrible cat puns. You don't want to close the game because your cat burglar died to a bad fountain you have to place straight before the dungeon boss, but sadly, that happens way to often for this game to stay entertaining.
Dont buy this and save yourself the regret .

TWISTED METAL: FISH EDITION!
(with a dash of agar.io for extra flavour)
Ever dreamt of being a fish?
Ever felt the desire to eat everyone around you, except for your family?
Ever wanted to swallow a gigantic ballbag under the sea?
If you answered yes to any of these questions, Feed and Grow: Fish is the game for you!
Feed and Grow: Fish is one INTERESTING game. I really didn't know what to expect when I picked up this title, other than the whispers I'd heard from some of my buddies regarding the game's recent popularity on YouTube. I've been looking for a game I can build a new series around, so I decided to pick it up and give it a shot. Now, at this moment, I haven't spent a great deal of time with FAGF, so this review is more of a first impressions than anything else so please, don't take it as gospel, as there is still a lot about the game that I don't know.
With that out of the way, FAGF is essentially an educational game that teaches people about the food chain. The objective is basically to eat anything and everything smaller than you (and sometimes bigger) until you level up and grow, at which point you can then start eating bigger and more nutritious sea creatures! The possibilities are endless! By eating other fish, you level up and gain coins, which are then used to temporarily unlock other fish. Depending on the fish you choose, you have different abilities and attributes that either make the game easier or harder. Think Twisted Metal, but with fish.
There are also a three different maps that you can play in, though I have only tried the river and the ocean. The ocean was a very narrow, straight forward map that gave nowhere near as much flexibility as the ocean. The ocean was ENORMOUS, and there were plenty more fish and plants around to help you level up, though the number of hostile high level browerags, tiger sharks and eels is borderline insane. Good luck surviving more than a few minutes! I know I couldn't.
All in all, FAGF is a fun, beautiful looking and mechanically simple game, though the game itself can be quite challenging and I'm starting to understand why it's recently gained the popularity that it has. I believe there is a free version that you can get on Gamejolt, but it doesn't have the multiplayer capabilities that the Steam version has, so if you're into MP and want to support the devs (which are two young brothers), then this is the way to go.
Hope you enjoy Feed and Grow: Fish as much as I have been!
