At it's very core, Battle Riders is a racing game that wants so much to be an early PS1 game. If it were, this game would be really fantastic, but despite my "recommended" below, I do not entirely recommend it without knowing EXACTLY what you're getting into. For the record, ten minutes was all I needed to learn all I had to about the game.
Primarily, you're going to be driving around a track with opponents. Most of the races seem to fit six or more. Their AI isn't the greatest. If the game has rubber banding, it's obvious and if it doesn't, then that's a shame because it feels like it does. Racing carries a decent sense of speed, although *how* much speed you can't really tell. It's an arcade racer, so I'll forgive it for that.
However, it seems you earn more credits for destroying your foes than you do racing. This encourages you to lag behind, to kill as many of your opponents as possible. That's a big problem for me, and in my opinion ruins a lot of the economy of the game. Racing levels should reward more for racing than killing, and vice versa.
The driving physics feel floaty in straightaways and tight in turns. It's exactly the reverse of how you'd expect this to feel.
You'll spend a decent portion of your time firing upon your foes. You have two weapon slots, left and right. Very awkwardly, you fire these independently, with two separate keys for firing. It's different I guess, but I cannot say that it is better.
The guns themselves have very low ammo counts, they don't feel like there is any spread, and you can comfortably drive and shoot without the fear that your driving is going to mess up your shots.
The various weapons have no kick, do not feel like they're firing anything other than an animation, and feedback for when you are shot is minimal and lackluster. In short, the combat is not fun.
Truth be told, that's where the game is strongest and weakest. Sloppy driving is fine, because you can get used to it. Poor feedback on your weapons is fine, because you can get used to that. The "arcade" portion where I can judge the style, realism, customization and so on, is where the game tries to set itself apart.
The style of the game is really really similar to many games I played from 1995-1999 in terms of design. The mad max, minimal asthetics, and a texture quality that is low enough to notice but not low enough to complain about, all feel like I'm taken back to that time. The music is forgettable, but again feels like a good old ps1 game.
The customization might be the one point where I don't feel I have enough information. There certainly are lots of items to upgrade with, but fewer than I'd like to see out the starting gate. Credits don't feel like they're hard to earn, and so there should be lots of options to open up. Also, it feels good to have a game let you unlock stuff via playing the game instead of playing a slot machine loot box.
However, while this is the strongest part of the game, it's also the weakest. Tracks have little to make them visually interesting. I'd have looked at Pod Racer or Mario Kart 64 before designing levels, were I the developer. The cars have a nice design in general, but specifically there really is nothing setting them apart. The devs could have taken a note from Carmageddon's books to ensure everything has character. And while the graphics sit firmly between PS1 and PS2 era games (higher res than both, texture quality somewhere between, and a level of polish more often seen on the PS1 than the PS2), they're nothing to be excited about.
Oh and it was a little weird that I had to control the menus using a mouse, but I can drive with my controller. That's a big design flaw in my opinion.
The game isn't good. It has basic design choices that force the player to play against the game design rather than with it, if they want to be optimal. The lack of early unlocks makes wanting to drive a chore and the racing physics and ai both feel bad.
But that's today. That's after playing dozens of racers that learned these lessons much earlier in their development and this is a game from one man as a passion project.
So I'd argue against myself and say that the game achieves the goals of it's designer. It is an arcade racer of yesteryear, and if I had this game on PS1, closer to launch day? I'd have played the crap out of this game. It's not going to give you new nostalgia, but it's also totally worth the 5 bucks or so that the developer is asking for.
---
TL;DR: The game feels old, plays old and would be more at home 15 or 20 years ago. But it's a single individuals effort and for that and the low price, it's not a bad game.

This was my first CAPCOM game that I had ever played. I know that CAPCOM has thousands of other games, but after my experience, BCR was probably one of the best to start with. I hate platformers, so when I found out this was a platformer I was a little turned off. However, I had just bought the 2-pack with BCR and the sequel, Bionic Commando, for sale, and I hate jumping into a story without any prior knowledge, so I decided to play through the first one for some background info. After I got used to the controls, I found this game extremely fun. I made it through the first couple of levels pretty quickly, and proceeded to continue with the game. In BCR, there are enemy encounters, and I felt cocky, so I decided to initiate one. That's when I got a big surprise; some parts of the game are played in top-down/isometric shooter mode! Now, most people would just be like,"Oh, well... That's pretty neat!" but I have been on a Diablo-esque hook, meaning I have been hooked on the top-down/isometric playstyle of Diablo and other games, so I was really intrigued by this. Sadly, enemy encounters are very short, but they aren't really a main part of the game, so that's to be expected. All in all, I'm hooked on this old relic of a platformer and can't wait until I play the sequel!

I obtained Dustforce as part of a Humble Bundle, and it turned out to be one of the weakest entries of the set. Having enjoyed Super Meat Boy, I thought taking on another challenging speed/flow platformer would be good fun, but Dustforce didn't measure up.
In premise, Dustforce seemed like a lot of fun. Ninja janitors! Fighting-game style uppercuts and kicks, used to navigate hazards and literally clean house! Some lovely sprite work and a fantastic soundtrack enticed me to give it a go.
Unfortunately, Dustforce turns out to be one of those games where only the hardest of the hard core need apply, and no lesser player has any hope of wringing some entertainment from this sharp, unforgiving stone of a title. Unless you master the moves immediately (perhaps by some years' experience playing Street Fighter on the competitive scene?), you will fail constantly, progressing to the end of even the earliest levels only by determination and brute repetition. That in and of itself is not irredeemable--that's part and parcel of SMB's shtick, after all. However, the insult to injury is that speedrunning is mandatory. You cannot barely squeak out a level completion and advance in the game; you *must* achieve a ranking score in speed and thoroughness in order to earn keys to open additional levels. If you don't, well, enjoy replaying the first world a lot, because that's all you'll get to see.
There is something to be said for defying the predominant game design pattern of "if you just play long enough, no matter your skill, you will win." And no doubt a truly elite button-pusher would revel in it here. But if you don't consider yourself such a chest-thumping master, you would do well to give this game a pass.

Guild of Dungeoneering is unique, charming and pleasant. But it's also weird and it tries its best to prevent you from getting attached to it on the long term. Buy it on sale, just to enjoy the first few hours of discovery.
This game is really charming and unique. Its paper and pencil art direction brings you back to the good old days of mapping dungeons on graph paper in D&D, and that's awesome. This is nicely supported by a funny, light and pleasant atmosphere, both at the visual, narrative and musical levels.
Gameplay-wise, Guild of Dungeoneering is definitely an experience you have never had before. It kinda plays like a guild manager, but it mostly plays like a dungeon crawler, and it also plays sorta like a dungeon builder. All of that at the same time. So if you like discovering new game concepts, this game will certainly not disappoint. It's greatest gameplay strength lies in a card-based battle system that's simple, fun, and well supported by juicy feedback.
So just on these strengths, the game deserves to be at least tried.
Ok, let's say it outright: this game is weird and unorthodox. But not in a good way.
First, the core concept of the game is extremely unclear. Who or what am I playing as? What is my goal? What motivates me to go forward? These are questions I have not found answers to, and it made me stop playing after 5 hopeful hours.
Upfront, the game tells you that it's the guild that matters most. It's the title of the game after all, and you're given control of this adventurer-recruiting structure right from the start. However, in reality, nothing supports this. There is no narrative goal related with the guild, and there is no gameplay related to how you choose to expand, nor any intrinsic reward in making the guild bigger or personalized. You quickly realize the guild is simply a fancy upgrade UI. Disappointing.
So what are you then? Well, you also play as a roster of disposable adventurers. Unfortunately here too, the game offers no explicit goal. There are dungeons for you to attack, and there are hidden regions on the map, presumably containing more dungeons. But that's all you'll ever get in terms of long term goals. After a while, you're not quite sure anymore why you should keep slogging through these similar-looking dungeons.
Just to add to the confusion, when you attack a dungeon, you must build parts of that dungeon as you move forward. You are given some random dungeon elements to place, and it's up to you to min/max your way to victory. Why is this feature there? The game never gives you any narrative justification, and it contributes to blurring even further your identity as a player. Furthering this unclear feeling, you don't directly control your character's movement in dungeons. So you play your characters, but not completely, and you create the very dungeons you're attacking, but not completely. All of that without anything telling you what's the end goal and why you should care. The game is really intent on not letting you feel attached to anything.
All of this to say that while the game system is quite fascinating to explore at first, it severely lacks any hook for immersion or motivation. I quickly realized there was nothing to keep me playing. As a whole, Guild of Dungeoneering feels more like a nifty toy to play with for a few hours, than like a formal game to invest into. And that's too bad.

Great story; solve cases while uncovering the past of the protagonist in a plot that thickens more and more as you progress. I'm going to focus on the negative aspects for the review, these are minor remarks compared to the quality of the story, character development and case design.
The game has some flaws, some dialog options (truth, doubt, lie - responses) get a bit of imagination to guess what Phelps is going to accuse the other person of, but on the other hand choosing lie you can back down after your accusation if you feel like it leads in the wrong direction. The problem with that is that, especially if abused, it defies the point in actually trying to read the other person reducing it to "♥♥♥♥ it I’m not sure let's just press lie and see what Cole says, push comes to shove I’ll just make him apologise".
Some of the clues are "circumstantial" their presence is generally not annoying unless overdone
.
There is one case in particular in which one of the actual clues is well hidden, also partially due to being barely significant in real life logic, and precludes a dialogue option, this can lead to you getting stuck on a crime scene for way longer than necessary, but there's really only one instance of this happening.
Navigating around L.A. is not hard but can be a bit annoying for several reasons.
Trying to get directions at the start of each route: there is no route displayed on the minimap and, if you don't feel like opening and closing the map or learning it, pressing "F" you ask your partner for directions: he'll tell you to go right left or straight at the next intersection, this in my opinion is great immersion wise. The problem with this is that during scripted dialogue it's difficult to get him to guide you especially if you're going fast.
On this topic: your partner won't give you directions while you're receiving a call from the station for one of the secondary missions, which can be annoying if you want to ignore them and you're a bit lost.
About traffic: the AI does not behave like humans (unsurprisingly) when driving but only somewhat mimics a real driver, and not only in situations like "being caught in a car chase" but also in basic behaviour at an intersection with traffic lights on it. Here's a little list of things that are wrong with the AI:
- if a car has to turn right it will gladly ignore the red light if it thinks it's not going to collide with anything;
- it will often prioritise cars turning left to cars going straight coming from the opposite direction. The first times (if you're roleplaying following the rules) this can lead you into accelerating off the green light and having a car cut you off, you'll get used to it after a while;
- if a car feels like your pathing intercepts its own, it will break, even though had it kept its speed up you would have passed behind it.
When you're travelling with sirens on the AI drivers (unless they're being chased or a key part of the chase sequence, in which case their pathing is scripted) will do two extra things regardless of your position and speed relative to them:
1. slow down and move to the right most lane unless there is another car directly in the path or unless they're following behaviour 2. While this would generally be appropriate behaviour for real drivers as well, in most situations, the AI applies it brainlessly, sometimes resulting in rather amusing nonsensical situations that very well could be considered obstruction of justice;
2. not go across an intersection. While this is almost always a good things it means that a road block like situation can be created if all lanes are occupied by cars waiting at the stop line. This is because not occupying the intersection takes priority over slowly going to the right-most lane.
As said these are minor flaws that i wanted to point out just to make you aware of what you can find so that you're prepared to face it, I overall would recommend this game, especially during a sale.

Mr. Hunter sat at the end of the bar nursing his Red Bull and Stoli.  It was ladies night at this corner dive, and the university girls that filled the place earlier had long ago left for their primary engagements.  Now the bar contained four occupants, of whom only three were concious.  The moment of reckoning had finally arrived.  It was dark, smokey, and last call.
That's when she walked into the bar.
She blinked once, then twice as her eyes adjusted to the dark and she lowered the hood of her cloak.  Neon light gleamed off of the red of her hair obscenely.  Her gaze landed on Mr. Hunter like a spell.  He found that he could not look away from her as she crossed the room liquidly.  Her cloak was a deep red that matched her hair.  The dress underneath was a heart attack.  Her eyes never left Mr. Hunter as she ordered her drink; "Macallan 27 year, neat." The bartenders sarcasitic reply was cut off when he found a bottle of Macallan 27 where he left the Dewars."  It may have been the magic trick, or it may have just been her striking beauty, but no one noticed that her voice was weaved together from the screams of a thousand tortured souls.
Mr. Hunter caught himself staring and attempted to recover, channeling his best Bond impression:  "My name is Hunter.  Card Hunter."
She grimaced in embarassment for an instant before regaining her composure.  Her voice was intoxicating, alluring.  "Don't try to be something your not, Card Hunter.  I'm not out looking for bells and whistles.  I don't care about top flight graphics.  I sought you out, Card Hunter, because you have what I am looking for.  Solid gameplay.  An original system.  Replayability.  And perhaps more than anything, a sense of whimsy.  People tell me all the time I can't let my hair down and have fun.  Maybe I am too dark.  What do people expect?  My name is Darkest, after all."
The bar had faded away somehow by now, and they were sitting alone somewhere he couldn't comprehend.  The air reeked of sulfur, or was it tobacco?  His head was swimming from more than just alcohol as she touched the tip of his nose with the tip of her finger,  quietly making a beep-like noise.  Her eyes were red in the light of the twin moon.  His thoughts would wander, threads sewing as they tangled together, chaos breeding.  First they were in the bar, then a hotel room, now a barren planet with purple skies, then a deep cave seemingly carved from the very darkness.  His sanity was hanging by a thread she held between the silver blades of a pair of what look like safety scissors.  He started to chuckle at the absurdity of it all.
Her voice was distant yet loud, jarring in its calm tones, musical and chilling.  He couldn't move a muscle, but it didn't matter as long as she kept talking.  "It is long past time for me to mate, my sweet Card Hunter, and to bring an offspring into this world.  I spent far too long searching the darkness for what was hiding in the bright light the whole time."
She smiled shyly, while the glint of unending hunger flickered in her eyes.  "I'm sorry that I will never be Mrs. Hunter.  Almost as sorry that you will never know your spawn.  I promise that you will feel only the pleasurable type of pain."
The first wave of estatic oblivion had already began to wash over Mr. Card Hunter when he managed to croak out two words of a question.
"Darkest Dungeon, my sweet innocent Card Hunter.  And our child will be Guild of Dungeoneering."
TL;DR?   If Darkest Dungeon seduced Card Hunter, Guild of Dungeoneering would be the resulting love child.

Like so many other people who negatively reviewed this game, I wanted so badly to like it. I thought "Wow, a game where you have to read the facial expressions of characters in order to determine whether or not they're lying to you! Cool!" But as another reviewer put it, it's a game of second guessing your second guesses. When someone looks to be telling the truth, you think "That's too easy, they must be lying," and of course you're wrong. And Aaron Staton/Cole Phelps switching from good cop to loud, angry bad cop was so abrupt that it made interrogations impossible to get through without laughing.
This also feels very much like an open-world game, but there's very little to do beyond the main quests and some short side quests. The A.I. on vehicles is not great, either, since you'll be speeding down the street with your siren on and sometimes cars will literally stop in the middle of the street, creating a barricade that will force you onto the sidewalk. Car chases are kind of rubbish, as well, considering the cars of the people you're pursuing are somehow resistant to being spun out, while your own car spins out at the slightest touch from a gangster's car.
The game also gives you frequent flashbacks to WWII at the beginning of each case, but most of them feel like they're not even necessary--it would have been enough if that history had been revealed through dialogue between characters. The game sets things up for Phelps to take down corruption within the LAPD, and yet
And let's talk about the fact that this game has two moments--one involving a tar pit and the other a bulldozer--that the game actually apologizes for. Someone must have realized that these moments were so annoying that they decided to take pity on the player and give them the offer of skipping over them to continue the game. Not to mention that at one point, a crook escapes police custody and runs into a warehouse where he magically conjures up a shotgun. I found out the hard way that this guy was a sorcerer because--using my incredible powers of observation as a detective--I saw him enter the warehouse unarmed. I round a corner and receive a pointblank shotgun blast to my face. Awesome.
I love film noir, so I was hoping this game would allow me to feel like I was "living" in one of those films, but so much about the story and gameplay was unbearably frustrating that I can't imagine I'll end up playing through this again. Thank god I didn't pay full price.

Tumbleweed Express is a rail shooter with tower defense elements. A rail shooter where you protect a train on rails....yup. Anyways, you control a 360 degree rotating turret on top of a caboose in an old west steampunk world where blimps and dirigibles have overtaken railroads as the main method of cargo transportation. You inherit the tumbleweed express from a dead family member and as the new owner it's your job to ride the rails to glory.
The graphics fit the theme of the game prefectly and so does the music. It also sounds like the narrator is using a fake southern accent and that's a bit off-putting. Game progression is stage based with the option to replay each stage as many times as you want. I'm glad you're able to do this because the difficulty curve is sharp and soon enough you'll become overwhelmed by all the crap coming at ya from all around ya.  Upgrades include cool stuff like being able to buy more cars for your train so you can add automated turrets. You can also hire engineers that'll repair your traincars and different types of gunners that will also shoot stuff on their own. There's also turret upgrades and different types of turrets you can purchase such as cannons. I'm not too far in it but it looks like there's a lot to this game. Each stage has multiple side-objectives you can enable to get a bigger reward if you complete them however it also increases the difficulty of the stage. And since you can replay each stage you can experiment with those to see if the risk is worth the reward. There are secrets hidden in each stage too that will uncover more of the story but they aren't necessary.
All in all it's a fun game and a fresh rail shooter that does a good job at being different. In fact probably one of the only rail shooters I'd recommend because I haven't played that many. The developer is really nice, productive and vocal with the commuity so that's a plus in my book.  It's cheap so pick it up if all that sounds good to you.

I had very high hopes for this starting out.
One of Lynnea Glasser's previous works, Creatures Such as We, was what first sparked my interest in CYOA games (though it was later with Choice of Robots that got me seriously into them) so I bought this as soon as it was available. I ended up not doing my first playthrough for quite a while and by then the reviews had started to show up. I was surprised and honestly a bit disappointed to see the overall ratings. They caused me to delay even longer. All that aside, though, my actual thoughts on the game.
Firstly and most importantly: this was EXTREMELY engaging for me. I'm sitting here at 9am, with about 4 and a half hours put into navigating the story and then several more thinking about what I'd just read. That should speak for itself.
A lot of people mention how this is a "message" game and while I can't really dispute that it didn't feel that way to me. There were definitely some, uh, "PC" elements but they never detracted from the story. They were well couched in the themes and elements of the setting that they felt quite natural... most of the time. Though, as always, with this type of content your mileage may vary.
As for the actual writing and editing... top notch. I really don't think there's any argument here, whatever people may think of the content. I may not exactly at my best due to sleep deprivation (and if there are any errors in this: sorry) but I didn't notice any typos or anything of the sort. The writing was concise without being too brief and generally quite evocative. Aaaaaand speaking of concise... the length. My first playthrough definitely took less than an hour and the many half-skipped-over proceeding playthrough, totalling about 5 or 6, only ate up about 3-4 more.
Now, I'm far from done with this but already this isn't a bad amount of time for a CYOA game to keep my attention. My only real complaint is that I find myself unable to get a lot of the things I want to happen to happen. I don't know if this is a lack of freedom, overly harsh choice requirements or my own addled ineptitude but it's getting pretty annoying. I may have to ammend this section in the future, but for now it's... a problem. Not a huge one, but still.
Anyways I feel like I'm in equal parts rambling and entirely missing the point of a review so I'll wrap this up. Interesting, complex setting with generally interesting characters and some pretty seriously dramatic branching paths.
I give it a "pretty great" out of 10.
(Again, apologies for the probably massive number of typos and errors both grammatical and logical.)

Elsword is a game that I have always heard about from friends, but I never really paid attention to it. And with good reason; the title of the game doesn't sound that promising - just something formulaic, but that is beside the point.
The game itself starts out alright. There are 8 characters to choose from, though unfortunately there is no customization at the start of the game, meaning if you pick Elesis (which I did), you're going to be seeing quite a few Elesis characters that all look the same. This goes for the other 7 characters as well; the character you pick is a stock character. In a way this makes sense, as the cut ins have art for the characters themselves, and to be fair there is
customization, though you would have to do it with items you find or buy items from other players or the cash shop.
The graphics are charming and polished; mind you this is no Crysis or TERA, but it does its job nicely. The game is set up as a sidescroller that uses some 3D elements; it can make for interesting gameplay but at times can get a bit confusing as to what platform you should be on and thus have to backtrack to get to the intended platform and not the one in front or behind. Character design is pretty good, at least for the girls. The guys I find to be a bit too immature (though Elsword himself gets a bye since he is only 13), but hey, that's just me. The game world too is alright; the cartoony atmosphere certainly fits and doesn't get tiring or fussy. Sounds are standard for MMOs, and they don't sound bad here. The characters I think speak Korean - the game was voiced both in Korean and in Japanese and they aren't speaking Japanese here - though these are usually soundbytes when the character starts or finishes a dungeon or quest, and for all I know they are probably just speaking jibberish as supposed to actual Korean. However, that is neither here nor there, and thus the sounds are pleasant.
Controls are good; they're intuitive and it is easy to pull off combos, though I do wish the combo screen at the bottom was constant throughout your levels, as once you get your first job it is gone forever since my guess is that the developers assume the players know their characters' movesets. This isn't a problem with a character like Elesis, who is rather straightforward with her combos, but someone like Ara Haan or Eve can get a bit confusing. Fortnuately, there is an action guide provided with the skill menu that shows the combos, but again, the combo screen should not go away. On top of that they do get a bit slippery, causing the character to spaz out a bit before gaining full control.
Otherwise gameplay is generally good. There are very few sidescroller MMORPGs that can run smoothly, and Elsword is one of them. The storyline is a bit campy at first - Elsword is no Deus Ex or even Mabinogi - but it is engaging and for the most part solid. There really isn't so much as far as grinding goes either; dungeons take care of a good chunk of the EXP, and it is painless to level even up to your 2nd job. Dungeons can get a bit too easy, especially with a party. The "Very Hard" dungeons don't provide much of a challenge and the normal ones can be easily soloed. This is both a good thing and a bad thing. Good because one is able to not be bogged down by challenges, bad because it can get too easy and thus a bit more tedious to do. On the whole though, gameplay is good.
One of the major factors of any free MMO is the pay to win factor. Here, Elsword does okay. You don't have to pay for job advancement nor actually exploring the game nor doing anything else (though I might have barely scratched the surface here). There is a gachapon system, and the game does entice you to buy them; the server flashes messages of people getting rare items from the gachapon. Though like any other gacha, it is gambling.
My major gripe about Elsword is this though: you have to pay to unlock the full skill bar and the full hotkey bar. Right off the bat the game gives you skill hotkeys and 3 item hotkeys, with 4 more skill hotkeys and 3 more item hotkeys locked out unless you paid up for them. Elsword also has you pay for more inventory space, which can get a bit problematic if you keep getting junk items while looking for something in particular. However, the hotkey issue is more important; Elsword is the only game I know of that locks out hotkeys. Inventory space and bank space is common in MMOs; Mabinogi did that, Maplestory did/does that, and so on, but this is the first time I had a game lock out some of the controls. It is a stupid way for the game to get money from its players, but by the same token, being restricted to only 4 skill keys is pretty damn, well, restrictive. In short, locking out hotkeys is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
In the end, Elsword is a good game. It is a good old fashioned beat-em-up sidescroller that doesn't have many similarities - only Maplestory comes close. It's a good timewaster, that while I think might be questionable in its money making scheme, is otherwise an enjoyable, fun game.

Like so many other people who negatively reviewed this game, I wanted so badly to like it. I thought "Wow, a game where you have to read the facial expressions of characters in order to determine whether or not they're lying to you! Cool!" But as another reviewer put it, it's a game of second guessing your second guesses. When someone looks to be telling the truth, you think "That's too easy, they must be lying," and of course you're wrong. And Aaron Staton/Cole Phelps switching from good cop to loud, angry bad cop was so abrupt that it made interrogations impossible to get through without laughing.
This also feels very much like an open-world game, but there's very little to do beyond the main quests and some short side quests. The A.I. on vehicles is not great, either, since you'll be speeding down the street with your siren on and sometimes cars will literally stop in the middle of the street, creating a barricade that will force you onto the sidewalk. Car chases are kind of rubbish, as well, considering the cars of the people you're pursuing are somehow resistant to being spun out, while your own car spins out at the slightest touch from a gangster's car.
The game also gives you frequent flashbacks to WWII at the beginning of each case, but most of them feel like they're not even necessary--it would have been enough if that history had been revealed through dialogue between characters. The game sets things up for Phelps to take down corruption within the LAPD, and yet
And let's talk about the fact that this game has two moments--one involving a tar pit and the other a bulldozer--that the game actually apologizes for. Someone must have realized that these moments were so annoying that they decided to take pity on the player and give them the offer of skipping over them to continue the game. Not to mention that at one point, a crook escapes police custody and runs into a warehouse where he magically conjures up a shotgun. I found out the hard way that this guy was a sorcerer because--using my incredible powers of observation as a detective--I saw him enter the warehouse unarmed. I round a corner and receive a pointblank shotgun blast to my face. Awesome.
I love film noir, so I was hoping this game would allow me to feel like I was "living" in one of those films, but so much about the story and gameplay was unbearably frustrating that I can't imagine I'll end up playing through this again. Thank god I didn't pay full price.

Beneath the somewhat amusing exterior this is at heart a deck building game. A bad deck building game.
You start with a deck of 7 cards determined by your hero and, props to the devs, the decks can be markedly different. Which leads into the two main problem I have with this game:
1. The skills and methods of clearing a dungeon (identifying enemy card themes and building appropriately via random mc random loot drops) are never explained or elaborated on and there is no way to know what cards an enemy has outside of experience. This makes things a little grindy as you can't build a deck to beat the boss mimic without knowing what cards the boss mimic uses... and so on.
2. The randomness. You draw three cards from your deck of 14 - you can't redraw, you can't flee combat and if you can't win this battle with these go back to the start and try again. That was a nice 5 to 10 minutes you just wasted. You also have no real control over what equipment (extra cards for your deck) you find as it too is entirely random.
These two combined lead to a game in which you win a lot of trivial fights only to get destroyed by an enemy whose deck you couldn't anticipate or lose to a bad draw, throw away your entire deck and start again in the same dungeon.
It was fun for the first 45 minutes.

Bioshock 2 is a game that didn't need to exist, but I am glad it does. 2K Marin created a follow-up that manages to upstage the original Bioshock in nearly every way. The clunky combat of the first game is overhauled, giving encounters an improved pace and players far more options. Environments are appreciably larger than the cramped corridors of the first Bioshock, with the added bonus of higher fidelity visuals and prop density. Even the narrative has higher emotional stakes due to interactions with various NPCs that possess believably complex motivations.
My only qualm with Bioshock 2 is that little effort is made to fill in backstory. Brand new players or those returning after a hiatus will be utterly lost. Much of the lore from Bioshock is essential to understanding the passage of time leading to Bioshock 2, meaning a thorough playthrough of Bioshock is required.
As with Bioshock Remastered, I caution against playing this updated version. Developer Blind Squirrel Games put nominal effort into reworking Bioshock 2. Other than adding settings for modern displays and tweaking textures, there is nothing substantial here. In fact, just looking at the Steam forums reveals a number of issues exclusive to the remaster. Crashes, game breaking bugs, and lost saves are common. Since Bioshock 2 Remastered comes with a copy of the original Bioshock 2, play that instead.

A fun, tactical and strategic game where you: build an Adventurer's Guild; recruit random classes; explore dungeons; collect gold; expand the guild; gain access to higher tiers of equipment and classes.
What's odd about this game is that you don't have direct control over your hero. He/She has a lust for gold, so similar to the game, "Majesty 1" you entice him/her to walk in specific directions, by throwing a purse of gold coins on the floor.
Every time you enter the dungeon, you start off naked and weak, so the goal is to level up from fighting level 1 monsters, while avoiding the level 3 monsters.
Another odd thing is that there are gaps between the rooms in the dungeon.  The goal is to bridge the gaps, similar to the tile game, "Carcassonne". Each turn, there is a draw phase, where you are given a random assortment of room tiles, creature tiles and rare purses of gold. You can place up to 3 tiles per turn, so there's a puzzle aspect to planning your moves.
The combat is surprisingly deep with concepts such as: unblockable attacks; first strike; bleed effects and magical damage over time. If you are tired, it's easy to get complacent and make a mistake.
The game is full of cheeky, British humour and the emphasis is on fun.

I spent 6-8 hours playing through this game on tablet and bought the steam version just so I can write a review.
As a fan of choose-your-adventure games for a year, I rank The Sea Eternal as my number one favorite due to the emotional complexity the game delivers (my second favorite is Choice of Robots, due to its multidimensional characters).
The Sea Eternal is well written, typo-free except for one minor mistake, and has a very fluent flow. You play as a merfolk living in a mersociety. I love that the game does not bury you with tons of merfolk backgrounds in the beginning, but rather introduce you to the society through several dialogue choices scattered throughout the game. Many dialogue choices inform you of some relevant truth before you make the choice.
Character development is average in The Sea Eternal, but whatever it loses in character dimensionality, it makes up for with its huge plot. You are placed in the controversial world of merfolks in which the very concepts of your life, memories, and identity are a well plotted scheme. Throughout your journey, you will inspire younger versions of yourself to either fall for or avoid the scheme. I myself have had the misfortune of pushing everyone I care about down the cliff. But the fact that you will inspire others to fall despite sensing that something is off is just what makes The Sea Eternal so beautiful.
If you enjoy choose-your-adventure games with mind-blowing plots and don't mind melancholy, you should definitely pick up The Sea Eternal.

I've played it a bit. It's aight.
And for the record, you don't need any DLC to take advantage of any of the mechanics upgrades made over time, only to play early starts and various religions as your ruler and dynasty.
I understand what many people say about the "DLC policy" but the game has been out for over 5 years.  I personally own all of them, and unlike some of the other paradox games and other games at that, if you play multiplayer, you play with all the dlcs that the game host uses as well.  Could the multiplayer use some work? Of course, but the point is that the producers make the DLC available to any of those that want to play with them.
Next point, there is a very active community, if you want to play a multiplayer game with more than just close friends, or try out some DLC with a mentor just leave a comment in the forum and I guarantee someone will be willing to host a game and play at least a century or two with you.
As for the price point regarding DLCs, I would recommend that anyone that wants it wait till a sale, and there are certain DLCs that give much much more content than others, again if you go on the forums helpful players will point you in the right direction.
Regardless of the negging DLC naysayers, the best thing to do is take what they say, or any player reviewer with a grain of salt.  Am I a bit opinionated? Of course, ive clearly played the game for about 80 days worth of real time I enjoy it just that much. (That being said I am a huge buff of medieval history, even studied it)
Finally for new player ill leave my own personal opinions on the DLCs that are great if you want to really get more out of the game:
-The Old Gods (rolls back start date 2 centuries to 867, and allows play as all pagans)
-Charlemagne (rolls back start date another century to 769, huge amount of events added)
-The Republic (which allows players to start as any of the trade republics around europe in any start date available)
-Sons of Abraham (adds Judaism as a playable religion, many new events, and new Catholicism mechanics)
-Rajas of India (allows players to play any ruler on the Indian subcontinent)
-Horse Lords (allows players to play as any nomadic horse-based warrior group such as mongols, cumans etc.
-Sword of Islam (allows all muslims to be played, even more events added)
There are 6 additional DLCs that are largely flavor based, combined they add a huge amount of new mechanics and events, but are really for veteran players that know the base mechanics and have played through several game periods and are looking for something extra.  Some add interesting goals for existing countries, some add things like pandemics and secret societies, but overall my initial statement stands.
TL:DR this is a great game, give it a chance, even at its base content youre still getting at least several hundred hours of play.
Final word of warning: this game plays entirely different than EU, it is NOT a macro game, you do not have just a simple functioning empire that you can then just look at trade and whatnot, you need to manage your family, marriages and on top of that manage holdings etc.  it is extremely in depth just like other paradox games and as of me writing this, is going to continue growing at least till the end of 2017.

Pros

Bright, colourful and detailed levels.
Special abilities.
Easy to use controls.
Cons
Once a fish is unlocked, if you die, you need to spend your points again to play as it.
Slow movement speed for a short time when spawning.
Not enough playable fishies, come on, add crabs, octopus, crayfish, lobsters and all that.
Only one classic type game mode (crab king is a yearly event). A few more could liven it up.
No public multiplayer.
Small levels, and only 3 to choose from.
No main menu music, and very little actual ingame music at all, apart from chomping noises, and water sounds.
Granted, it's early access, but it needs A LOT more improvement in the months to come.

The slogan 'Ninjas play free' is not really accurate in a way that yes, you will play a character with Ninja-like skills but this is far from a stealth game and you shouldn't get this if you want to play a stealth game. A slogan like 'Ninjas become space elite soldiers for free' would be more fitting but you get why this is not the one Digital Extremes chose. This is a co-op shooter with lots of rewarding grind and playing this feels amazing. You jump and fly around, use your Warframe's (a special exoskeleton-like armor) special abilities to feel like a superhero and complete missions all over our solar system. Unlike other games of this type, this game is not getting dumbed down from patch to patch but instead kept interesting. It is definitely nothing for those of you that absolutely need the 100% because that is most likely not going to happen and you should not aim for that. Instead have fun with the progression you do make and the different builds you create to go really fast or make a lot of things dead at the same time.
AS FOR THE GAME'S FREE TO PLAY ASPECT:
Despite what some people (that have played the game for 10 minutes and then dropped it) might tell you, this game is not pay to win.
People say this because most gear, when taking a look into the market, has to be paid with Platinum, the game's paid currency. But fear not, the market is the lazy way to get items for nutbags with too much money (or those that want to support the devs idc).
Instead where you get your gear is the foundry. For this you will have to obtain blueprints (which can be bought from the market with the game's regular currency) and farm resources.
There is also the opportunity to trade your gear with earlier mentioned nutbags in order to obtain Platinum without having to pay for it.
In short: Get this. Play this. Now.

UPDATE: Over the past few days I have been talking to the developer and they have been extremely open to suggestions, discussion, et cetera. They requested I spend some more time with the game then edit this review accordingly.
I obliged to this but since I now have a relationship with the developer, my opinions have the potential to be biased, so I will leave the original review below this.
I will also change the rating to positive based on my interaction with the developer, but it should be noted that my original selection was negative.
The developer noted that though this is a port from IOS/Android they have updated textures, graphics and resolutions for the PC release. Other PC specific updates include 60 FPS, track and handling fixes for vehicles.
In my original review I had a small gripe about the odd control scheme to which the developer has addressed as necessary due to a ghosting issue with modern keyboards. I am unsure as to how that would be fixed. Controls are also customizable.
The developer noted that health pickups also give you credits to spend on upgrades when playing modes where they do not provide health. I would personally like to see the extra step taken to have different icons entirely when health packs come into play.
Gameplay-wise after spending some more time with the game, my opinion is slightly more positive as I tried out a couple more of the weapons and vehicles.
However I do believe the game is still rather shallow in both gameplay/mode variety and the tracks on offer. There are only eight or so tracks included in the game.
Certain modes are also locked until you win enough races on career mode, which results in playing through the same tracks multiple times with little variation.
Survival mode is still a very weak aspect to me as it becomes to easy to just destroy the other cars from the back of the pack. I did have an easier time ahead of the AI in this mode once trying the mines as a weapon.
While my overall experience is still mediocre, this is by no means terrible. As I stated in my original review, it's one of those times that I wish Steam would allow for a middle of the road review instead of the positive/negative system.
In regards to the developer, I am very pleased that my interaction with them has been so positive. In the past I have had indie developers throw fits at me via email or even in my Discord server. I do not condone that behaviour.
Having a developer openly talk about and discuss my review and their own game in such a positive way is something I will support and gladly work on with the developer.
Indie devs reading this, please be like OneManTeam.

This is one of those times I wish I could give a game some form of in between review.
Battle Riders is an alright mobile port. The game runs fine with no frame dips and the general gameplay is perfectly usable with mouse and keyboard.
There are a few places where the game still says "tap to continue" and other small, mobile oriented things that put me off a bit.
The controls are with the arrow keys or WASD. Oddly you shoot with K/L or Z/X which is a weird decision, but it works.
The gameplay is alright and works fine. It's not terribly engaging after a few runs and some modes work much better than others.
The survival mode is almost broken as if you just stay at the back of the pack and blow up all the other cars they can't hit you back and you will win. This mode should have been in an arena instead of the standard tracks. Health pickups also don't work in survival mode but are still there anyways.
Battle races are the main mode, they are fine. You race and blow up cars so they respawn and you get ahead. Very simplistic and can feel sort of cheap as the AI will widdle down your health and you are guaranteed to explode unless you are lucky enough to hit a health pack. It feels like there is no way to avoid getting wrecked sometimes.
If I had played this game on IOS or Android I think it would have been a better time because my expectations are simply lower. There are better combat racing games available on PC and Steam at the moment. That being said the game works fine and isn't the worst mobile port on the planet.

Haven't had so much fun when playing racing game in a long time. The mechanics are simple, but car handling on the road is really well-done.
Battle Riders is a racing game. Plot twist: there are also weapons involved. You race around in your car while trying to destroy other racers. There are multiple game modes and three bonus types (ammo, boost, health) spread across the tracks. While the premise sounds simple, the execution is surprisingly fun.
-	Old-School racing feel and great car handling. The car really feels good to control. And the game is just fun.
-	Decent AI opponents: the AI is not unbeatable, but you’ll definitely need to practice and you will get surprised a few times when it takes you down right before the finish line.
-	The car models are great: those feel like a battle cars on the track. The feeling of car weight is also there, which really makes you feel like you’re driving a heavy, albeit fast, vehicle.
-	The cars are also upgradable, which gives a sense of progression for the game.
-	The music and sounds are alright. It puts you in the racing mood + engine roar/tire screech is really well done which is detrimental for immersion in the racing game.
-	No joystick/keyboard control in menu: you’ll have to put your controller down and navigate with mouse
-	Can Get Repetitive: there are 9 tracks for ~100 campaign levels. Might not seem that bad, but campaign split into 3 parts. First part only features 3 tracks. That means those 3 tracks repeat over 32 missions. Yes, I enjoyed riding on those tracks for the first ~5 times. After that: that’s the first time I seriously wished that the game I like was shorter rather than longer. And to get all tracks / cars in solo racing mode – you’ll need to grind through all these 100 levels.
-	The backgrounds are somewhat bland. There are track surroundings, but behind them it looks like an infinite empty space, especially noticeable in the city tracks.
-	Extra mention goes to the strongest weapon, railgun: the shot does good damage, but it not feel powerful at all. It’s just a small red dot that appears/disappears when you actually expect something like a railgun from quake 2, leaving a good trail of particles for a few seconds.
What surprised me about the Battle Riders is the car handling. It just feels really great to drive and succeed on turning. It reminded me of driving in Need For Speed 2 and Need for Speed 3 – when you get so excited that your body literally follows the cars turn direction (I’m sure you know that feeling if you played racing games when you were a kid). The only serious drawbacks is the lack of multiplayer (would be tons of fun) and a small variety of tracks: there are 9 tracks, multiplied by two (the reverse directions are also possible). It might sound a lot, but first 32 races happen on 3 of them and it really starts to feel somewhat grindy to go through the same road over and over again, even if it includes reversed tracks. Other than that - the description of the game mentions “adrenaline pumping, high octane action and a lot of fun” and I agree to it. Despite the flaws – I can strongly recommend the game. If you love racing games and aren’t afraid of practicing the same track over and over again – that’s the game for you. If you are simply looking for a good game but maybe lack patience – that’s also a solid choice, but wait for 50% discount.

Free-to-Play done right. The game is engaging and fun, and you can expect to play without playing anything. Cosmetics and inventory slots cost platinum, which is the in-game currency that you pay real money for, but even platinum you can earn through trading in-game items with other players.
The game itself is a gorgeous co-op third person shooter, and the controls are really good (once you change the default key bindings). Combat is a combination of big guns, parkour and meelee weapons, which earns Warframe the title Robot ninjas in space.
The developer is still adding new content. While possible to enjoy everything for free, this is the kind of game development I like to support.

A good game with some jarringly stressful levels at the end, namely the upper swinging section in 11 where you have to be very precise and a slight mispress of the claw arm button, which your press only has to be off by a milisecond, means having to re-navigate the bottom section to get back up for another most likely unsuccessful try. Then you have the final albatros level. It just ♥♥♥♥ing sucks. The first part, your claw arm doesn't work half the time on some of the platforms in one section, an obvious game glitch, and the rest is just a pure stress test. If your doctor ever wants you to take a stress test, tell him no thanks, you have already played Bionic Commando Rearmed. The last albatros level is the worst level I have ever seen in a video game. It was so incredibly stressful and so bull-shi--y that I just got tired of it and gave up and uninstalled the game because I just stopped caring, never to be ♥♥♥♥ed with again. You get through three door tests that are stupid enough in their own right, then the next section has changing platforms and collapsing hook grapple points. I was laughing at how stupidly stressful it was and just quit and am done with this game. Such a shame, all that work for such a truly God awful last level.
Everything is good, but it will take some getting used to for most people because it is a platformer without a jump button. The idea is that your bionic arm is so heavy that you can't jump but you can sure as hell use it to swing around the levels awkwardly and that is the whole thing that made Bionic Commando unique in the first place, since the original. Everything works fine and it is a challenging game so some things are going to be immensely stressful in the levels but it is do-able with practice. The challenge levels in particular are probably the hardest, most stressful things I have ever done in my life, Unfortunately a lot of the picky awful programming that forces you to have perfect timing in the challenge levels trickles over into the story missions. On the 10th challenge I had no idea how to swing up to do it until I checked a youtube video. Even after watching how it was done I still had no idea how to do it until I read some detailed comments under the video and even then I still pretty much did it by luck. I gave up after the second set of them. The third set of challenges just got too stressful. I have never in my life seen anything require you to be so incredibly precise. If you don't swing right even for a milisecond you fail. If you dont hit the button within the right milisecond you fail. There is quite literally zero margin of error in the challenges, but thankfully they are not required so I am just enjoying the story levels. The graphics are awesome, the music is superb and is the best part of the game, the weapons and enemies solid, the animations realistic, and the gameplay is smooth. The only real way the game could be improved is if the dumb overly picky swing section in 11 was fixed and the last level wasn't so nightmarishly bad.
The combat is ♥♥♥♥ing stressful as well because there is no recovery time so one hit and you are sometimes bouncing around like a pinball into other hits and you can either be killed in no time or be easily bounced off a platform and fall a long, long way down and have to reclimb the level which absolutely sucks. If only your guy wasn't such a stiff heavy snail with incredibly picky claw arm swing controls then it would be less frustrating.
6/10, nothing but pure stress at the end. Get the 2009 Bionic Commando instead. The swinging in it is not done very well (gee what a surprise!) but it is not too bad and the game is still enjoyable but very short. The claw arm idea instead of a jump button is a very neat idea but it really should stay in these games and not be adopted by any others. Catch it (the 2009 3D version) only on sale though for $5 or less because it is a very short game.

LA Noire differs from other typical open world games. Instead of being the criminal going around causing chaos, you're quite the opposite.  You assume the role of detective, which is nice for a change, and solve various cases around 1940's Los Angeles. There aremany things I enjoy such as the detailed city (right down to the "Hollywoodland" sign), the soundtrack is great, the interaction between you and the people you confront are realistic, cutscenes aren't boring, almost like watching a TV series, and the ability to gather evidence and use it against those you suspect of the crime. The cases were also fun to be a part of, and the characters were also interesting. Facial animation was a key factor into making the game, and it makes the character interaction way more realistic.
Obviously, no game is perfect. There are a few things that I found flawed in this game.  One being that despite the game being open world, there isn't much to do other than follow your key objectives in the current case you're working on, or drive around and wait for dispatch to radio you in on a street crime. You can also drive by key landmarks, but other than that there isn't much.  Street crimes can sometimes be repetitive, mostly gunfights that you can end fairly quickly. Interrogations really make you think, and analyzing people's facial reactions are crucial to determine if someone is lying or telling the truth, but sometimes they can be tricky, making the game frustrating, but  despite how good/bad your skills as a detective are, you still end up finishing the case, but are ranked at the end on how well you did.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who loves crime/mysteries.  There aren't too many open world games where you assume the role of a detective and solve the crimes and the 1940's noire style is a great touch that will surely impress you.

Contrast has been sitting in my Library for a while.  It always looked interesting, but never made the cut on new games to install.  Eventually, it made it on my Hard Drive.  And I'm glad I found the time to play it.  The game offers a unique light and shadow gameplay gimmick.  Your job is to help Didi find her parents and help them through the night to find success and hopefully more.  The story, which is played out entirely in shadows on the wall isn't anything to write home about, but because you are forced to witness it and interact with it at times it means that you will know what the story is and it works well for the game.
The platforming is good, the animation is smooth.  I will say that the camera was a bit of an issue at times and that the 3D transition into 2D shadows can often times become a bit tricky, but never impossible.  The puzzles were great, never too difficult to leave out to dry, but difficult enough to at least make you think.
The game is rather short and all achievements are easily accessible.  However, the ambience that the game sets with its jazzy tunes and its french influence makes for quite a fun ride.  Definitely a game that I would recommend for those looking for a good platformer to play.

In this game, you fight for no side as you need both darkness and light to get from Point A to Point B. I have never been this frustrated and fascinated with a game before. The controls take some time to get used to, so some necessary actions may take a while to do. I absolutely hated the moving shadow parts that you had to climb in order to get somewhere or in order to obtain an object. That, and the parts where you have to jump or speed past a shadowless area while in shadow form. It took me forever to get past them, but I pushed through anyway because I wanted to know how the story would end. Didi is a little girl with the misfortune of belonging to a broken family. Her father is nowhere to be found and her mother is a singer at a nightclub. Dawn is her imaginary friend-slash-babysitter who literally has the ability to walk in the shadows. Together, they try to solve the puzzle that is Didi's true identity and save the day.
Speaking of puzzles, those are exactly what this game consists of. You'll have to think your way in, out, and around everything. It pays to be curious as there are collectibles to gather as well. These play a big part in explaining what the story is about. You also need to collect luminaries to power up certain objects. A good tip would be to think out of the box. Some solutions may surprise you and make you go, "Why didn't I think of that before?". I loved the graphics of this game. It's a bit dark, but charming in its own quirky way. It would have been better if they used more musical pieces though. This game is pretty quiet and, therefore, anti-climatic, but you'll be too busy listening to the gears in your head moving anyway, so it's a passable requirement.
All in all, the game is a good mix between challenging, fun, and eye-opening. 7/10

Bottom line: This was a fairly charming and fun game that blends a shooter and tower defense. While the gameplay is not terribly deep, I can easily say I got my $5 worth.
Positives: I love the premise just because it is so silly -- you're a train that's retaking the west and stomping out airships, crazy rocket cars, and other weird things.  The graphics are sufficient but the aesthetic of the game is better; it definitely feels like its own world.There are contracts and time challenges to undertake which provide a level of difficulty and replayability -- it can get pretty hectic with all the contracts going and you speeding along with your boost. The actual gameplay is solid though judging ranges on some of the weapons isn't easy. Getting the various upgrades allows some options as to how you outfit your train and creates some strategic choices, though that's more of an early to mid game concern.
Some minor drawbacks: I thought the narrator's voice acting felt a little forced and muted; I almost think it would have been better just as text. I felt the  weapons were a bit unbalanced. It almost always felt like either the regular cannon or tesla cannon was the best option because of distance and predictability of shots (except in a few cases, like the Drillcar Jim boss). I feel like it should have been a little more situationally balanced so that using the flamethrower or TNT is a clear choice in more instances. For that reason and because once you have enough money you can buy everything, I felt the strategy involved in outfitting your cars was a bit too simple.
Ideas for future enhancements: It would be nice if after a level you could get some stats on your cars, like how many each killed, whether it was marshalls or weapons, your hit percentage, damage done, number and types of enemies killed, etc. Just something to add a little extra motivation to keep replaying (and perhaps turn into a calculable score for a leaderboard). A workshop to create levels would be pretty sweet, too.
Overall, though, for $5 it was a good deal of fun. The developer(s) seem very helpful, involved, and excited about their game, so I'm glad to support them.

To start off, let's do a quick summary of what Elsword is:
Elsword is a Anime Styled, Side Scrolling, Free to Play, Class-based RPG Fighter in which you are given the choice of 9 different characters to fight with, level up and "evolve" so to say. Each character has different skill trees which can be chosen to fit your personal gameplay style.
Like to play as a Free Knight and acquire pyromancer abilities? Choose Elesis! Like being a Tank for your team? Choose Chung! How about being an Archer to attack from long range? Choose Rena!
This selection of characters is great for all kinds of players and helps broaden the audience for this game. It has typical elements which you can expect from an RPG: Armour, Special weapons, potions, grinding etc. These elements fit well into the world of Elsword, helping you defeat bosses in dungeons to earn XP and gain better armour and weapons!
Speaking of bosses, there may be repetition with such bosses as Banthus but besides that, they are both challenging and rewarding. The game itself seems to get very addicting when you are trying to level up your character and get them to their next form or "evolution" as I've said before. The stamina bar is used to prevent addiction. This bar is gradually used up as you complete dungeons and once you are out of stamina you cannot do any more dungeons for the day. Stamina is refilled every day though as well as having unlimited stamina at weekends so all you fanatics can play to your hearts content.
In closing, I believe Elsword is a fun, vibrant and addicting game and I recommend it to all of you anime or RPG lovers.

Since I've logged so many hours in this, my mindset while playing has changed immensely. I tend to stick to more casual difficulties, which is not how this game starts out. You begin with gear that is minimally powerful but once you start gaining Mastery Ranks (the equivalent of your overall character's level) you unlock a plethora of tools at your disposal and what once seemed impossible becomes trivial.
This is one of the few Free-To-Play games I have spent money on and it has felt well-spent. The community can be helpful at times but it has its few toxic elements. Prepare for some fast-paced space ninja action. More details below.
I don't feel like this review does much justice for how much I've experienced in this game. If you're going to try it out, hook up with a clan that has veteran players. You can play a lot of the game alone if you like but you will have a much easier time with other people, especially if those other people know what they're doing.
Here are some resources that will make a beginner's Warframe experience much better:
UPDATE: Plains of Eidolon. Hell of an expansion. It had a pretty rough start of generally bugginess and progression imbalance. The new expension area is pretty much self-inclusive, as in most of the content contained within can only be acquired through progressing in the Plains. The stockpiles of resources many veterans like myself have acquired do little to advance you further than a dedicated new player could reach. Originally, the grind to progress in the Plains was pretty rough, but just about every update since then has drastically eased it (Bounties now reward for each stage completed; standing gains were multiplied; blueprints purchased were made reusable; Plains resource costs were reduced). Plains of Eidolon has raised my score from an 85 to a 90, and I look forward to future free roam expansions that they have teased.

If you liked Darkest Dungeons even a little bit, you'll probably love this little gem.
Your guildies (The npcs that occupy the guild you are building) trudge through the dungeons you make (a turn based component - a little like old-school pipe dream with only 5 tiles to pick from a turn) and you as the "dungeon builder" can only indirectly influence their direction. When the guildie meets a mob the deck building game starts. Each class of guildie has a specific set of cards they start with in their combat deck. The Apprentice mostly magic attack, the bruiser mostly physical attack, etc... As they progress through the dungeon killing mobs, more cards will drop and it will be up to you to choose which ones should go in the deck (choosing 1 card out of 3+ typicaly) based on what you think will get your guildie to the goal condition. Many of the goal conditions seem to be combat related, so this little deck-game is pretty important. If you like deck-builder card-games, this game component might appeal to you.
In any case, I'm having a blast and I've only played for a few hours. If you like Darkest Dungeons at all, you will definitely like this game, and this game is way more forgiving than DD. The difficulty curve in this game seems a lot less steeper. (In my opinion).

Ah, the hard-boiled detective world of the 1940s. The subject of many a detective novel by Dashiel Hammett, Raymond Chandler, Elmore Leonard and others, this genre has a name that instantly evokes dark and gritty. That name is noir. And it’s played pretty much perfectly in this game. While the game’s not totally perfect and there are a few annoying snags, the technology behind it is pretty impressive and you can definitely get a few hours out of playing through and exploring post-WW2 Los Angeles.
As former Marine Lieutenant Cole Phelps, a rookie cop in the LAPD, you work your way up from the bottom to the top, then strangely down a step, but how you get there is not for me to say. You start out on the traffic desk, solving crimes on the beat before rising to Vice, investigating a military-surplus morphine distribution ring. From there it’s on to Homicide, where you investigate crimes seemingly very related to the Black Dahlia murder, committed just prior to the game’s start. Finally, a scandal that rocks Phelps, and the department to its knees sees you busted down to Arson, where a mad bomber is disrupting peaceful living in suburban Los Angeles.
Gameplay is quite a bit different from the standard Grand Theft Auto clone. You can free-roam between desks, but while you’re in a case you’re pretty much rushed on to the next objective. Auto accidents are counted against you, so you’d do best to “fast-travel” to your destination by letting your partner drive.
Once you’re at a crime scene, speak with the coroner and conduct an investigation. Examine the body (all of which rendered in pretty horrific detail; this is where that Nudity descriptor comes in!), finding any and all relevant items and questioning witnesses. This pattern is followed throughout the places and people of interest you encounter, but there’s a twist thanks to the awesome facial scanning technology built into the game:
Each person you meet has basically had his or her actor’s facial performance recorded and mapped onto the model, such that you really have to read his or her expression to determine whether they’re lying. You can choose to doubt them or catch them in a lie with evidence you’ve acquired; but if you choose the wrong response, you’ll be penalized and your suspect will clam up. By the way, if you’ve paid attention to various TV series in the last decade, you’ll recognize some faces: Aaron Staton from Mad Men, Greg Grunberg from Heroes, and others.
There’s not a whole lot to do in the otherwise massive environment of Los Angeles and Hollywood; you can respond to up to 40 street crimes spread out across the ‘desks’; you can find 50 golden film canisters throughout the game world; locate 20 real-world landmarks; and that’s basically it. There’s no real replay value to speak of, and the gunplay is repetitive; the fistfights are interesting, but they don’t last too long.
For what a great first impression this game makes, there’s not a whole lot of reason to come back time after time. I give this three out of five stars. I really wanted to give more, but the games need to give too, and this one wasn’t doing it for me.

Some people play Portal (and its sequel) only for its quirky, witty humor, but Portal is one of my favorite games of all time for another reason: its puzzles. Why do I mention Portal? Because if you enjoy the puzzles in Portal and Portal 2, I think you'll enjoy the puzzles in Contrast.
Like Portal, Contrast is a puzzle platformer. The challenge isn't just in getting from Point A to Point B - it's also about HOW. And, like Portal, Contrast adds an exciting twist. The shadow-shifting element is perfectly designed: it's very simple to understand how it works, but figuring out how to use it is challenging and fun. The puzzles aren't tear-your-hair-out difficult, and neither is the platforming skill required, but it's still hard enough to be rewarding when you finally get it right. The game's later puzzles have you manipulating the position of light sources and even shifting objects - like boxes - into the shadow world with you, so the puzzles never get stale.
The story is short, but interesting. The voice acting is absolutely superb, especially in scenes where tensions are running high. The world is beautifully crafted, and it really does have a fun 1920s vaudeville
In summary: I desperately wish there were more of this game. In fact, I think the brevity is my only complaint about Contrast. I hope there's a sequel, or at least another puzzle-platformer from this developer. If you like puzzles, and especially if you liked Portal, you should play this game.

This game is a product from a joint effort namely
(A professional Russian company with over 400 employees) and
(who can't seem to get a web page together). There are six in this particular series at the moment done by alternating enterprises.
This is a 'Time Management' game meaning it’s a game that tests you in your ability to successfully plan when exercising conscious control over the amount of time spent on specific activities to reach certain goals. This is all laid out on the framework of a story where you become stranded on a fictitious island parroted with some symbols and beliefs to that of Easter Island which is all made apparent thanks to Moai (great big head monoliths). The natives thinking that you are a gift from above promise to help you on your way again as long as you help them first and return the island back to its former glory. Unfortunately this means you are getting the raw end of the deal as you endeavour to gather, construct and defend the island against hordes of annoying cartoon ghosts, an active volcano, frost bite sickness and several notorious tribes and bandits.
The first ten levels are nicely presented as a learning curve which have a generous amount of time allocated to them that it would probably be possible to blindfold yourself and randomly click away at the screen and you would still pass all 10 levels with 3 stars. However after this the difficulty really ramps up and even with successful planning your heart pulse will raise and you will be forced to wipe sweat from your brow if you intend to continue to try and master a 3 star rating for all 64 levels.
The progression of the story is all nicely illustrated in story book animation while a well done narration helps in maintaining the mood and the need to progress. Several artwork backdrops and game concepts contain an odd nod and wink here and there to Easter Island folklore, however I must admit some liberties have been taken there as well (ghosts/moai).
In a game like this a sense of completion and achievement is made when one nuts out a perfect strategy against pressing time management. The game successfully tests the gamer in whole range of ways and never did the 64 levels feel like I was doing the same thing over and over. Neither did it ever feel like one strategy fits all. As each level adapted, my game play and techniques had to adapt too.
My biggest surprise is this, for the first in the series alawar and toyman did a number of things correct in their time management game which other companies have definitely failed to implement or master. Some of which are...
* When each level begins you have the ability of running your cursor over each object on the map and see the different requirements needed, this allows the player to really think about a method of execution before beginning. As soon as you click the first item on the map though, the game is on.
* While time and resource requirements are very challenging at times they were never impossible. This helped maintain the games reputation for being a casual enjoyable game. Many companies fail to take into account the transition of app design and PC. Distances needed to travel on a large pc screen with mouse and pad can be quite significant in comparison to touchscreen which many companies fail to take into account.
* The versatility of strategy tested here was quite praiseworthy. There were a few levels which required you thanks to limited land resources to even 'destroy' current resources when you had enough and construct different resources so that you can reach all stated goals. Many time management games I have played have NEVER tested this concept and often a one tactic fits all.
There are many things to enjoy with this (2013) gem which kept me entertained for well over a week. Definitely worthy of a gander if it ever goes on sale.

Contrast is an enjoyable puzzle platformer that has some unique mechanics, a great storyline but suffers from a few small gameplay issues.
The shadow / light mechanics are unique and they work (most of the time) very well, making for some intriguing puzzles. The storyline is ambiguous but definitely interesting.
The music and graphics are also fantastic, and better than I thought there'd be. I'd also recommend the soundtrack if you enjoy soundtracks.
The game does have a minor annoyances when it comes to gameplay. Occassionally I found the controls a little clunky which made some more technical puzzle jumps hard. There were also a couple of glitches when trying to jump and shift into a wall.
Overall those were only minor grievances and I easily lived with them. For its price, it's still great value for money.
I recommend it if you want a nice but relatively quick puzzle platformer with some unique mechanics, a great storyline and fantastic music; just don't expect a 100% perfect gameplay experience.

So, I have played all of the Metro games starting from 2033 to Last Light, and then I played both redux versions in that same order. I have also played only Last Light on Linux (more specifically, xUbuntu 15.10 using most up to date proprietary tested nvidia driver).
I want to make a note that there is a huge performance difference on the same hardware with the linux and windows versions. Not surprisingly the linux version is not graphically optimized, even with vsync on I am getting huge tearing. Also 16x filtering is still very jagged and highest settings on linux do not come close to highest settings on windows. I should also mention that with the same graphic settings I was getting a consistant getting 30-35 fps in windows and in linux I would get anywhere from 17-24fps.
For those of you with GTX cards dont let this scare you, I am testing this only with a single nVidia gt 750m, if you have a better card than that then the linux version might be very well playable for you.
I think that 4a needs to do a lot of tweaking to the linux release of the game before its as smooth as the windows version.
