I finally finished my first proper playthrough and what better time to write a review of this game?
If you're looking for an intense strategy game, perhaps even one that's a bit simple, just stop looking at this game. This is by far the most complex strategy game I've played. I spent roughly 60 hours on one playthrough and many of those hours were just sitting and waiting for a certain event to happen or to pass a certain point in time.
The tutorial then, although it shows you the various game elements and how to interact with them it does not put them into context. I started my first playthrough directly after going through the tutorial and I failed miserably and just didn't appreciate the game.
I left it alone for a month or so and then looked at one of the tutorial guides on Youtube. I highly recommend that you do this as well, you get a basic understanding of the game and how all the various parts of it interact and affect each other.
With that said, don't think you'll know everything after watching some tutorials. The learning curve is steep but it is also highly rewarding. There is nothing sweeter than figuring out a way on your own to claim an entire kingdom without even going to war.
The complexity of the game is also extremely frustrating at times. At one point my heir changed his culture without me knowing it, and when I died and he inherited my domain I ended up fighting civil wars for roughly 100 years because a foreigner was the ruler.
That's just one example, I could list many more, but in the end I find it a lot more rewarding and fun than I find it frustrating to play this game.
This review was written while only playing the vanilla version of the game. If you buy the various DLC's they'll incorporate a lot of new functions, intricacies and a whole lot more stuff to learn.
If you have the time to dedicate to learning this game, and if you like complex strategy games, just buy this. You won't regret it. You have literally thousands of hours of playtime without the game becoming boring.

Bioshock 2 is the sequel to the cult classic Bioshock, an incredibly atmospheric horror-shooty affair. In many ways, Bioshock 2 improves on the original, in many ways it doesn't.
THE GOOD:
Combat was always very satisfying in Bioshock. This game is no exception. New weapons improve upon the original game and the ability to have both a plasmid and weapon selected at the same time is a definite improvement; as a result combat is much more fast-paced and exciting.
ADAM is much more scarce in this game, though by the end I still had around 300 spare. This is a drastic improvement to how common it was in the original game, which left you with near-no challenge.
THE MIDDLE:
Hacking is MUCH easier in this game than it was in the original, provided you have good reaction time. I personally don't like this, as hacking was already fairly straightforward, but you may feel different. Hitting a blue segment while hacking will give you a bonus with whatever you're hacking, so that's also nice.
THE BAD:
For somebody in a metal diving suit you seem to be made of wet cardboard. Enemies do massive amounts of damage. There are plot reasons for this however plot should add on to gameplay, not sacrifice it. In addition to taking much more damage, the number of health kits and EVE you can carry has been reduced from 9 to 5. You can purchase more slots for them at a Gatherers Garden, however this seems like a needless way to make the game more irritating.
I use the word irritating because it isn't more difficult. Difficulty remains at the same level, but I found myself dying much more in Bioshock 2 than in the original game. I often defaulted to revival-scumming in order to take out tougher enemies as there's no penalty for using Vita Chambers, save only being revived with half health.
(Do note that you can turn off the ability to use vita chambers, though I usually play with them on because I'm a filthy casul)
In addition, and what I believe the most damning thing is: THIS GAME IS SHORT. SERIOUSLY.
It took me less than 8 hours to finish this game. That includes most of the optional stuff. The original game took bare minimum twice as long to complete. From a sheer price-to-time POV, this game isn't worth more than $10.
I still enjoyed this game, but pick it up on a sale. It isn't worth full price.

This is, in short, Baby's First Sims. It is exactly like The Sims, except for that it's vastly less complex, and you're focused on only one potential career. It takes only 20 minutes or so to completely master the complexities of it, and from there on out you're on autopilot until the credits roll.
But there's also (for the moment) no replayability. Until the other career modes are in, nothing will ever need to change. You might restart and make a visually different character... but there's no change to the challenges or the gameplay for this.  You wouldn't pick a different skill tree to level up, because they don't meaningfully change anything, and regardless they all level up so easily that you're racking up skill points constantly even if you're half-assing it. And even half-assing it is more than enough effort.
I recognize that this is a casual game, not meant to be a deep simulation, but even within that framework this is a disappointment. This plays more like a Freemium iPhone game, a sort of half hearted mobile edition of... well, the Sims again.
And all of that's a shame because the concept is interesting. Attending gaming conventions, product launches, managing one's BRANDDD... all of that could be very cool, but here it is very not. Each of those events lets you mingle with other players, or participate in some sort of side moment where you sometimes do nothing.
I guarantee, however, that this isn't presently worth your time. I also doubt that once the other career modes are in, the formula won't have changed enough to earn an updated review.

Oh boy, I've been waiting long for this one to be released on Steam. It's been on steamdb for more than a year!
Anyways, Ground Control II is an RTS game made by Massive Ent. (who made World in Conflict afterwards) and initially released in 2004. The key feature of the game is that you don't build bases here, you earn points by killing enemy troops and capturing control points and call in reinforcements to the landing zones you captured.
The game doesn't have a lot of units and only two playable factions, but every unit has an alternative mode that can drastically change its capabilities (a standard NSA trooper can turn into a heavy rocket trooper that is very effective against vehicles, but can't move); two identical Viron (the second faction) units can meld together to form a unique third unit (that has an alternative mode as well). So the game offers a lot of freedom as to how you use your soldiers.
The highlight of the game for me has always been the campaign. I would go as far as to say that it is at least on par with campaign of Startcraft II. It has cool cinematics, very neat sci-fi aesthetic and surpisingly good story. I am a casual RTS player, so this game is one of my favourites because of it. Not to mention that the game still looks gorgeous. I remember how astonished I was as a kid by sky reflection in the water. The music is very good and extremely fitting as well.
One thing needs to be mentioned however, ONLINE MULTIPLAYER IS DEAD. You can still play locally though.
As for this version of the game, it works fine on a modern system, but has no improvements over original release (not even Steam features like cards and achievements, which is a shame).
That being said, for 5$ it's a steal. Buy it, have a blast with campaign (it's pretty long) and it would be well worth it already.
Although the game is straight up grind, I gotta say that it gets pretty addictive...

Many of the things other people have mentioned are valid criticisms of the game, but I feel a lot of the negative feedback is a bit harsh for a game still in Early Access and only 2 months old.
It is an incredibly clever and well-thought-out game, but it does have some things that hamper its potential. That said, I spent a solid 20 hours just on one campaign, which is no small time investment. Consider how much more replayability value this game will have as they come out with more and more content. Given the amount they intend to deliver in the weeks and months to come, I don't think $15 is such a steep price to pay, especially at this point in the game's lifespan. (For me, I go by the "what is my time worth" rule. If I get paid $10 an hour to work, and I paid $15 for the game, I essentially had to work an hour and a half to play the game for 20 hours, and when I consider that, it feels like a fair tradeoff.)
Here is a point where you have the opportunity to help shape and refine the game alongside the creators through careful examination and multiple perspectives. Trial and error is what allows a creator to determine what works and what doesn't. In this instance, you're not just paying $15 to participate in the existing experience. You're paying that fee (which is nominal compared to many other titles lately) to help the developer figure out and provide you with the game you want.
Personally, I'm happy with the game as it is. Knowing it's still in early access, I can accept that there are some bugs here and there. The developers are admirably vigilant in their updates and constantly keep in touch with the community to let them know where the project stands. I would recommend buying it sooner rather than later, in case its price happens to increase with the additional content (unless they've indicated that the price is fixed).

Ever wanted that game where you're a knight in shining armor and you can cleave your foes in two!? No!? Well too bad, because this game has it!
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a multiplayer game which does exactly what I stated previously and nothing more. What's better than seeing your worst enemy's head chopped off and into a pit? Nothing, because it's a sight to behold.
There is a story behind this game which is explained if you play the tutorial, which is a great help, as there are a decent sum of buttons you need to learn before you storm the castle. There are four classes each with their own unique abilites; Archer, Man-at-Arms, Vanguard, and Knight. That goes from least armored to most armored, some doing more damage than others. Two teams, a Red vs. Blue style, the Agatha Knights and the Mason Order.
If you're not too huge for multiplayer like myself, fret not, you can fight bots. This isn't like any other game though, there's no difficulty setting. I'd place the bots at around an average player's style, they don't really counter your attacks much, but that makes it all the better if you're there to smash some skulls and nothing more. Though the AI is rather dumbfounded when they see themselves in a TDM, you're better off placing them in a free-for-all in a small map so you can get the most action possible.
The one downfall to this game though is it's price. Twenty-five dollars doesn't sound too bad with all the good things to it, but if you wanna get some cool looking weapons without having to rank up, you're gonna have to spend some extra cash to make your character look like the person you want. You'd be better off getting it on sale for 5$-10$ and buying the DLC for it as it will probably be on sale too.
Overall, though, this game get's an 8.4/10 in my book. It's fun to shout at your comrades or your computer as you gloriously stomp on your enemy's dead bodies and chop off their balls because you're one of those people.

Since I've logged so many hours in this, my mindset while playing has changed immensely. I tend to stick to more casual difficulties, which is not how this game starts out. You begin with gear that is minimally powerful but once you start gaining Mastery Ranks (the equivalent of your overall character's level) you unlock a plethora of tools at your disposal and what once seemed impossible becomes trivial.
This is one of the few Free-To-Play games I have spent money on and it has felt well-spent. The community can be helpful at times but it has its few toxic elements. Prepare for some fast-paced space ninja action. More details below.
I don't feel like this review does much justice for how much I've experienced in this game. If you're going to try it out, hook up with a clan that has veteran players. You can play a lot of the game alone if you like but you will have a much easier time with other people, especially if those other people know what they're doing.
Here are some resources that will make a beginner's Warframe experience much better:
UPDATE: Plains of Eidolon. Hell of an expansion. It had a pretty rough start of generally bugginess and progression imbalance. The new expension area is pretty much self-inclusive, as in most of the content contained within can only be acquired through progressing in the Plains. The stockpiles of resources many veterans like myself have acquired do little to advance you further than a dedicated new player could reach. Originally, the grind to progress in the Plains was pretty rough, but just about every update since then has drastically eased it (Bounties now reward for each stage completed; standing gains were multiplied; blueprints purchased were made reusable; Plains resource costs were reduced). is a gorgeous looking, underrated puzzle game which I think deserves more light. In this review I will try convincing you to give this game a shot.
The game gives you a feeling like 1920 noir films which  are so awesome. The main character is named Dawn, which is drawn with awesome art style. She looks like an acrobat with  make-up which I really loved. The story follows a young child named Didi, who lives with her mother and really misses her father
. Her parents have some problems and the whole story revolves around this family. Didi needs Dawn to help her find her father. The game implies that Dawn is a figment of Didi’s imagination and only she can interact with Dawn. Be sure to collect all collectables because they add more details to the main story and for Dawn’s character
.
I was browsing the collector’s edition art book and found a passage which perfectly described the world in a way which I never could, so I decided to share the quote with you. I usually neglect the art books in most games, but for this game I decided to take a look.

If you have already seen any gameplay videos or screenshots you will see that this game has a pretty neat mechanic which really stands out. There are many areas where you can turn into and play as a shadow in the wall to solve puzzles. This key mechanic is required to reach some places.
Now this is great, but the game is quite broken in its implementation. You have a button for entering and exiting this shadow mode the game has its own mind and will randomly decide to exit the shadow mode. This is extremely frustrating, because you need to redo the whole puzzle section again. Graphics are pretty decent for a game which is quite old. In the beginning of most games there is an “Adjust the gamma settings”  option and I usually just keep the default settings, but oh god I could barely see anything with the default setting. Due to not being able to see much in the game my playtime was extended.
The first time you open the game you will be welcomed by a sweet song, which  is beautifully relaxing and right on spot, and set up a good mood for playing this game. Another game with such an opening is L.A. Noire, which is very dear to my heart.
The story  about Contrast’s own original score is quite interesting in my opinion. They used local Montreal voice actors and jazz musicians. The lovely voice from the main theme song is of Laura Ellis. Initially the studio asked if they can use one of her own songs for Contrast’s first trailer, and due to the trailer’s huge success they asked her to perform for the rest of the game.


Puzzles are very easy and the whole point in solving them is to play with light and shadows. Most of the puzzles are timed ones but the timer didn’t raise the difficulty at all.
The collectables are very easy to locate. Since they shine and glow, they are not very tricky to spot. Most of them are letters, pictures, newspapers and posters. The total amount of collectables is 26. There are things called luminaries which are located throughout the game
and do not count towards any achievements. They are rarely required to progress, and some are quite tricky to collect since the game is very broken at times.
Contrast offers very easy achievements, which can all be done in a single playthrough. While most of them are story related, 2 will offer some difficulty since they must be done without falling
. Again luminaries
count towards any achievements. The total amount of achievements is 22.
Well I felt it was very light hearted for me which is great. I didn’t want to get involved with a game which requires a lot of time and effort to complete and in this aspect Contrast was perfect. I really love games that question the theory of multi universe and alternative dimensions and I really like that Contrast is hinting a little towards that area. It made me rage a couple of times, because the game is very broken but at the end of the day I was pleased with it. The game can be finished in one sitting. On scale from 0 to 10 I will give Contrast 7/10.

You dive into your first dungeon and they let you know just how expendable your first character you receive by naming the class "The Chump".   The battle system is very straight forward and the cards do a good job letting you know what it is and what it does.  Essentially this game is a deckbuilder game in which you always begin each dungeon at level 1 with the same basic deck in which you must upgrade via winning weapons and items from battle in which you can carry 4 different pieces of. Each class has a different basic deck and so if you get somewhat bored or find that a class is better suited to fight in the dungeon than you can change to that class and see new possibilities open up for you.
This game is GREAT...... until.... you get your character killed. Normally this is something you can kind of avoid but there are times in which you can't since there is some luck involved.  No problem though you get a free character of that class and off you go.  Oh? Your character killed again?? Well no problem there's more where that came from.  You quickly realize that losing a person is like losing a piece of hair.  There's no progression of characters at all.  The only thing you need to do is build up your guild until it gets really powerful and then win the game.
This game is basically a no stress game that may appeal to the audience looking to wind down and just have some plain fun.  However if you're like me who is a hardcore gamer that needs to feel challenged to have fun than this game is not for you and will eventually become boring.
I am going to give this a thumbs up and recommend purchasing this game but hardcore players beware.

Mass Effect, the ultimate RPG in Space.  For those who played Mass Effect 1, Mass Effect 2 was an improvement in almost every aspect.  It continues the amazing story of Commander Sheapard off to save the galaxy, recruiting the most interesting personalities along the way and exploring their stories as well as the lore and background of the universe.
Whether you are a fan of RPGs, adventure games, or shooters, there's a bit of everything in the Mass Effect series.  Bioware continuese their amazing tradition of storytelling, while making the combat more interesting and fluid than the first game in the series.  The only small drawbacks were the at times longish travel times and perhaps initially the inventory system which seemed over simplified (though playing through the first game again, I am reminded that simple is not a bad thing).
Mass Effect 2 is a can't miss game for most, and it stands up well today in 2013 (although it isn't the prettiest game, the gameplay and story make it a sure hit).  If you have not already played it, you should certainly pick it up, if for nothing else, for one of the most dramatic opening sequences of any game in recent history (in particular if you played Mass Effect 1), and one of the most exciting and dramatic, as well as meaningful endings as well.

I haven't played much of it because I had a really crappy computer so I couldn't run it smoothly, but now I have a new computer that I can run this game perfectly on and I'll tell you the first 10 minutes of the game I kept thinking "This game is freaking amazing, I love it so much." This one is a decent improvement over the original one, but try the original one first. You have to if you want the true experience of the storyline.
The combat is vastly improved. Not perfect, but very good. It suffers from the common console port mistake of putting way too many actions on the same key. You cannot rebind this, these actions are tied together, even though they shouldn't be. Like crouching and running. I've found myself crouch behind a cover instead of running away because the cover just happened to be too close to me.
The graphics are good, but the texture quality is severely lacking. It is obvious that they use the same textures for the PC version as they do on the consoles. Very blurry, and ruin the close-up shots. I recommend modding for higher textures. The graphics can be improved to the point that the game looks almost like a 2014 title, if you use mods.
The voice acting is improved from the first game. The first game really only had good voice acting from a few characters, this one brings most of them up to decent quality. The male protagonist was actually pretty lousy in the first game, compared to the female one. In this game his voice acting is much better.
I highly recommend it. Unfortunately the third game isn't available on Steam, but if you have no problem with Origin, I recommend that game too, just include DLCs so the ending will make at least a bit more sense.

It's a glitch, buggy, slog of a survival game that'll leave you frustrated and angry instead of feeling like you just accomplished something amazing. Ark has a great premise, but the game itself is fully of technical problems that negatively impact player experience and it takes forever to get to any of the worthwhile content.
What are some of those problems?
-My computer exceeded the recommenced hardware specs by double yet the game barely functions on the medium graphics settings. Unless you're running Ark on a super computer, you won't be able to experience Arc's full visual capabilities without serious lag.
-You know how in most video games you'll will be stuck walking if you've exceeded your max carry weight? Yeah Ark doesn't do that. IT'll start slowing you down before reaching your max carry weight and will immobilize you if you're carrying to much. That might be more realistic, but it makes for annoying experience once you need to starting grinding (and it's an island full of tamable dinosaurs. Nothing about it is realistic!)
-Speaking of grinding; it takes *forever* to get anywhere in this game. My first 6 hours of game play were grinding for materials to build a base, to gain xp, to unlock the items needed to tame dinosaurs, so I'd know what new materials to grind for. Rinse. Repeat. All while dodging aggressive dinos and trying to locate your own body to get back the materials you just spent 2 hours collecting but lost in a raptor attack you couldn't defend yourself from. If you want to build anything like you see in the trailers, be prepared to spend most of your time grinding instead of exploring the area and taming dinos.

They finally got it working!
With the December updates they finally worked out the kinks with DX11 related crashes. I read somewhere that audio reverb causes crashes so with that feature disabled I ran through the entire game as well as Minerva's Den without a single crash or problem.
The mouse lag is present but people aren't realizing that this isn't so much a game development problem as it is Microsoft Windows. I can't get into the detailed explanation but some games have a strange lag or hitchyness to it despite a solid 60 FPS with v-sync enabled. Many people wonder why and attribute it to poor game code. This actually has something to do with Windows handling the fullscreen display rather than letting the game handle the fullscreen display. I know that doesn't make much sense but trust me...turn OFF v-sync in game and then go into your GPU's control panel and enable FAST v-sync there as well as triple buffering. The game will run as smooth as glass.
I know this title caught a lot of flak when it released but people need to realize that what they did was done for a reason. They updated the game to DirectX11, worked out the audio issues and the strange physics issues and got it marketed to a whole new generation of consoles. This means that kids that never got to play it or never even heard of it can now play the same classics we enjoyed!
They then went as far as to give this remaster out for frickin FREE to all owners of the original games...and people had the audacity to complain about it when it didn't work properly! Sure enough they came back and patched it multiple times and got it working (at least for some of us) when they didn't have to do any of that for us.
For a review of the game itself, see my other review on the original title which is actually more unstable for me than the remaster.
Really fun to play with friends on a boring afternoon or just whenever!

I want so badly to like this game, because there is so much that is good and inspired about it, but the execution was botched in the sorts of ways only Rockstar can manage.  Superfluous but mandatory connection to an unreliable server.  Terrible graphical glitches as a result of a pointedly incompetent console port.  Unskippable cutscenes that lead seamlessly into action sequences, at which point you need to react right away.
There are some major problems with the basic mechanics of the game, too.  For one thing, it looks and feels like an open-world game, but there is literally nothing to do in that open world except drive between predetermined mission points.  So the beautifully-executed 1940s Los Angeles setting is largely an exercise in tedium.  Crime-scene investigations are handled interestingly, but your avatar both moves and handles objects so slowly that you will
be tempted to skip possible clues in favor of getting to literally any other type of gameplay.  Interviews are exercises in frustration: there's really no way to know what a particular dialogue option means, so you'll be trying to follow up on an investigative thread and suddenly your avatar is angrily shouting at a suspect over nothing.  And the crown jewel in the game's design— reading the facial expressions of suspects as you talk to them— is
, with the facial expressions all so cartoony that it's a matter of second-guessing the game designers: which of these incredibly fake-looking expressions are
to look fake?
But here's the thing: it's a beautiful game, when the graphics are working.  And the concept is brilliant, and the story is interesting, and the setting is great.  It's just: none of it works very well.

Oh boy, I've been waiting long for this one to be released on Steam. It's been on steamdb for more than a year!
Anyways, Ground Control II is an RTS game made by Massive Ent. (who made World in Conflict afterwards) and initially released in 2004. The key feature of the game is that you don't build bases here, you earn points by killing enemy troops and capturing control points and call in reinforcements to the landing zones you captured.
The game doesn't have a lot of units and only two playable factions, but every unit has an alternative mode that can drastically change its capabilities (a standard NSA trooper can turn into a heavy rocket trooper that is very effective against vehicles, but can't move); two identical Viron (the second faction) units can meld together to form a unique third unit (that has an alternative mode as well). So the game offers a lot of freedom as to how you use your soldiers.
The highlight of the game for me has always been the campaign. I would go as far as to say that it is at least on par with campaign of Startcraft II. It has cool cinematics, very neat sci-fi aesthetic and surpisingly good story. I am a casual RTS player, so this game is one of my favourites because of it. Not to mention that the game still looks gorgeous. I remember how astonished I was as a kid by sky reflection in the water. The music is very good and extremely fitting as well.
One thing needs to be mentioned however, ONLINE MULTIPLAYER IS DEAD. You can still play locally though.
As for this version of the game, it works fine on a modern system, but has no improvements over original release (not even Steam features like cards and achievements, which is a shame).
That being said, for 5$ it's a steal. Buy it, have a blast with campaign (it's pretty long) and it would be well worth it already.

Guild of Dungeoneering is a turn-based dungeon crawler where instead of controlling your hero, you lay out the dungeon for him to explore. As you build his surroundings using the dungeon cards, he must simultaneously make hasty decisions in order to accomplish his quest.
Will your hero rob the dungeons dry of their gold and loot? Or go on a blood thirsty rampage and kill everything in sight? The choice is, well, not entirely up to you.
THE GOOD
I NEED A HERO
-Your selection of heroes is about as classic as it gets. From the cat burglar to the methodical apprentice. As you level up and progress, you unlock tiers of the basic hero classes each with their own fighting style ready for you to exploit. The way you play your quest heavily relies on your play style so study each class carefully.
DORK SOULS
-Don't be fooled by it's cute and fun aesthetic, this game is as brutal and challenging as it is adorable. Each dungeon requires strategic planning and swift execution to accomplish each feat. From defeating bosses to looting large chests. You don't know what lies ahead in every corner. Fountains that drain you of your abilities, Zombies shambling to eat your brains, dead ends and timed attacks, every corner is littered with death and you only have yourself to blame. How could you put your hero through all this?
FIGHT STICK NOT REQUIRED
-Should you choose to fight your opponents, that alone is no easy task. Each enemy has their own set of abilities that enable(or disable) their potential power. They have strengths and weaknesses that you can exploit with a set of attack cards. You gain level and items that earn you new cards to add to your variety of arsenal. How you plan to use them is all up to you. This is turn-based card fighting at its finest. Oh, the game also fronts perma-death so don't get too attached to your heroes because you will die. A lot.
STRANGER THAN FICTION
-The narrating bard will sing your every move. Kill your hero and he will taunt you and make you feel guilty. Succeed and he'll cynically praise your efforts but keep an open-mind of your impending doom. It definitely keeps me entertained and I find myself arguing with a software made to ridicule me. Sometimes his foreshadowing is creepy and bodes well with the atmosphere of unknowing. Needless to say, the soundtrack and commentary plays a big part in the game.
_______________________________________________________________
THE BAD
PLEASE SIR, MAY I HAVE SOME MORE?
-I love this game and so far, I'm not tired of it. I'm scared of the day that I might though. Don't get me wrong, the game is not lacking or anything but I'd like a bit more variety and surprises because so far, it's literally the same missions over and over again. Now I'm not saying there is something wrong with that, there's nothing wrong with it, it's fun as hell! But there's gotta be something more to this right? We'll see.
______________________________________________________________
THE VERDICT
-Guild of Dungeoneering is a unique experience. Emphasis on experience because it's more than a game. Any game that manages to keep me intrigued for 10 hours straight with minimal colors and modes has already achieved legendary status and I have ADD. It's fun, addicting and well worth the asking price. For any of you looking to challenge yourselves in the most non-threatening of ways(I didn't know it was possible to achieve this! Take that Dark Souls!) get this game and start crawling!

I really am enjoying this early access preview. I highly recommend this game to people who liked Baldur's Gate, Dragon Age Origins or the first Diablo - it has very similar gameplay to both of them.
It isn't very fast paced - in the sense it isn't, I don't know, whatever modern kids are playing requiring twitch reflexes. But it is engrossing, has  a story and requires a lot of tactical thought - you *feel* smart when you win a battle, and that makes this game enjoyable.
It has magic, item gathering, crafting and enjoyable fights. I really recommend this game, even now, even if they add no more to it - I've played a lot of hours (20+!) which is well worth the price.
Problems - this is an early access, so i thought i'd leave this feedback for the developers from my point of view.
1. Walk speed can be a little slow - I don't mean in combat, but the island you find yourself on is large, and there aren't many teleport locations - this is particularly so for the last fight scene at the docks, where I had to guide my characters over beaches and up mountains. Its all very pretty, but also a bit of a waste of time. I know wandering around increases involvement, but could they maybe wander a little faster?
2. Crossbows are annoying. After firing one in combat there is a little animation and a sound effect - all very nice - but that just take up dead time. This is turn-based, so there is *literally* nothing to do when waiting for this animation. Please get rid of it.
3. Is there some way to stop a character moving in combat? sometimes you accidentally click the screen and you can't stop the character from moving until they get to wherever they're going - necessitating a reload often. Please let me jsut stop a character!
4. My team found a level 8 or so staff early on in the game (~ at level 3? It did 100-120 damage!). This was fun - what was going to be my lead warrior dual handed quickly became a mage. But it also meant i was overpowered, and able to waltz right out of the keep and up to the final boss, killiing everything, easily. As a thought, this meant the battles i faced weren't too hard - teleport enemies in front of main character, kill, repeat. I'd like the battles to have been harder, i really didn't have to bother about elemental or height or anything fancy.
5. The last battle - i could sneak past the shriekers and teleport enemies into their field of vision. Maybe this is intentional, but it makes the last battle way too easy - it ended up being just my team and one mage against the giant worm-thing. On another point, when I did this teleport-into-shrieker move, two enemies saw my thief and chased after him. He ended up sneaking back past the shriekers - but the enemies just ran right into the shriekers' line of sight. Seems pretty stupid of them to wander into their own trap and die.
6. Braccus' armour is broken and needs to be fixed. The armour gives varying curses - perma fire, slow, disease - i think from the chest, leggings and gloves? And the helmet makes you always warm (and 10% res on cold). This should probably be noted. Altho the character *says* they're cursed when first put on, this is easy to miss, as you're probably still looking at the full inventory screen and cannot see your character's thoughts.
Interestingly, giving the character wearing the helmet a resistance to warm also removes the 10% cold curse, which I suppose makes sense but is a bit annoying.
Worse, the ring further seemed to cause a permanent reduction in memory - my character would have 10 memory slots available, but only 8 of them were ever usable. Sometimes this would rise to 9, sometimes drop to 7. Something is buggy with the way the memory attribute is applied from the ring.
Similarly, my character always had to wear the ring because the +2 constitution it gave wouldn't "disappear" from her health pool - so while her con would drop 2 points, her health would still be ~400/450 (healing wouldn't raise it). This was a pain as one of her feats gave her an accuracy boost at full health, so that annoying ring had to always be one. Other +con rings don't seem to do this, only Braccus'.
7. I never understood what lucky charm did - one of my characters had it at 5, but it never seemed to do anything? Maybe that character was meant to be the one that opened crates? If so, seems a little annoying to have as a skill, and if so the tooltip *should* say what the conditions are for it to be useful (i mean, if one character has lucky charm, does it apply if a different character opens a crate?).
8. Teleport is v. powerful, and lets you control fights too easily, especially if everyone has it. Too poweful, really.
9, Same with the freeze spell, makes hydrosophist and aerothurge must-have's, as you can control an entire battle simply with these two schools.
10. fire and posion are meaningless right now, much better to freeze/stun/teleport/heal. the speed boost from fire isn't that handy, and the armour recharge isn't that useful when you can disable foes so simply
11. I never found the undead fighter who apparently appears after helping the pigs, although i did help the pigs.
12. The three necromancers in Braccus' library area would just get up and sit back down and play cards each time i beat the stuffing out of them. They were angry at me (-45 reputation) but it seemed weird they just sat down each time.
13. The rogue skill that lets me hit for 5x damage when sneaking is broken. I would often be in sneak, in backstab position, and would use this skill - but the moment the skill takes effect, i'd be seen, and then my rogue would... just miss the hit? Maybe I was doing it wrong, but sneak-hitting never seemed to work, although i had 6 or 7 points in sneak.
Also, one time i did this 5x move and a *different* npc saw me - and began a conversation. The hit connected, and the target was reduced to 0 health but was still standing and ran to do battle with one of my team, while the rogue had a dialogue with a guard about paying a fine. Seems a bit broken. (The other times i used the 5x ability were in combat, and i'd still break cover and the move would just not connect. Made it a worthless move to have).
14. The special power ups are generally useless - demon and leech and all are either too costly (why not demon+ice king? makes each one individually useless) or too niche (comeback kid?) or redundant. On the other hand, glass cannon is a must have for an archer who hangs back, and the one that gives +20% accuracy, when coupled with high magic/physical armour is just too much.
15. I didn't have a one-use problem when repairing items (either bug or A/B testing maybe?), and i think that is for the best. Repair is already irritating - if you're trying to make it so that items are handled carefully and can be destroyed, consider instead having longer battles - the one where void weevels or whatever kept appearing is a great example. That way you're holding out on hopin your equipment lasts!
16. I never bother with lore - it is simpler to pay to id items - maybe let lore increase crit chance or something more useful than "id items and see enemy resistance" would be nice. improve bartering? increase magic crit chance? something!
17. when you eat someone and get a skill, it should be inherant. otherwise, elves just have to have high memory stats. maybe limit the number of slots for these eat-given-skills?
18. i liked the source points, altho i didn't use the spells much it was nice to have another limit and i imagine there are some fun things you could do to make fights challenging.
That's all - it looks like a bunch of negatives, but the game is really really good. Get it!

After playing Ruse and liking it very much, I wanted to try other Eugen games.
My eyes fell on Wargame: EE and Airland Battle, buying both of them for just 15 bucks during the black friday sale.
My expectations were quite high after Ruse. Disappointed by
RTS games  in a modern setting of the 2000-2010 period, i was glad to see the good reviews of the early Wargame games.
And it is a good game,
The main problem I have is that the game heavily favors high-speed, multitasking tactics. As a gamer which favors slow, chess-like gameplay, this is just too much for me. I cannot keep up.
Is this the fault of the game? I've been thinking for a couple of years since I bought the games for that.
And the answer is: Yes, it is. All legendary RTS games have one thing in common and that is that they support numerous strategies and tactics.
Wargame is more about "who is the quickest" and is going for giving the player an adrenaline shot during playing. Which isnt bad per se,
The good things?
The game engine is fantastic, the units are well-balanced and I like the refreshing road Eugen has taken. It is not just a C&C-formula rehash like so many other RTS games. They also still support this game, even though it is years old and there are newer Wargames out there. The multiplayer community is tiny, but consists mostly of good people that help you anyway they can.
I regret buying these games though, even for 15 bucks I can't enjoy myself playing. And that's what it should be all about. Therefore, I can't recommend this game.
If you want fast gameplay and an adrenaline rush doing it, you should absolutely buy it though.

Pleasing to the eye, ear and mind, dustforce is a great platformer that will keep you sweeping for hours on end.
-Gorgeous art style, full of charm and character with consistently themed levels with sprites to match. One of the things I love most about this game is the soundtrack, its mellow tones are relaxing and blend seamlessly with the gameplay, softening the frustration at my inept cleaning.
-Gameplay is consistently challenging, but as you repeat levels you gradually learn the layout and the best/fastest way to clear each and every obstacle. There is nothing more rewarding than when you get that perfect run (well, not perfect, but as good as I'm going to do). The momentum based character movement did take some getting used to, but after much practice it allows you to flit through a level like a breath of wind.
-The main area in which Dustforce is lacking would be the tutorial, it provides a good basic understanding of the movement mechanics and will make a player reasonably competent. However, to play dustforce to its full, flowing potential it is a necessity to go on youtube and watch tutorials and examine the manouvres and tricks used by the best of the best.

This game is absolutely brilliant. If you never played Bionic Commando on the NES, you don't need to do so to enjoy this game as it is better in pretty much every way possible. There are however plenty of eastereggs and funny references that fans of the original game will appreciate.
The difficulty level has been stepped up with multiple difficulty settings avalible, and the AI is very impressive for a 2D platformer. All the boss battles have also been completely changed for the better, and if you choose to play in coop their behavior adjust so that team work is required to destroy them. In the original game weapons had very little importance, but this time around every weapon is uniqe and has its own useful applications, which is nice given that the enemy variety has been improved as well. If you were unaware, the gimmick in this game is that you cannot jump and have to rely on using a grapple hook arm to get around. The arm functions pretty much the same way it did in the original game, but with some added features such as the ability to pick up and throw barrels as well as some enemies.
The ONE issue I have with this game is that if you play on a keyboard you won't be able to control your RC rockets separately from your walking, which makes the final encounter notoriously more difficult.

This game is extremely polished for being free-to-play. It truly reminds me of World of Warcraft. Many MMO's try to be like WoW, of course, but Allods actually succeeds quite well, with most of the negative aspects of WoW (aggressive and rude player base, endless raid-gear-raid loop) yet to be seen. I can also vouch that gPotato, the playing service this game comes with, is a much better alternative to beanfun!, which is what games like Divina use. No annoying shortcuts or popups or anything, and the site is far easier to navigate.

Allods comes with a quick built-in tutorial at the beginning to let you get the hang of things, but it's a fairly standard MMO when it comes to controls. Combat is fluid and isn't simply point-to-click. Quest descriptions are long, so if you want to get absorbed in the world, there's the option to. I usually just scroll to the bottom and see what I have to do, though, with the occasional full reading of my quest log. So far the quests seem pretty standard; nothing you haven't seen here in terms of talking to people, killing creatures, collecting items, and going to places.

Onto aesthetics: this game is pretty beautiful. The colors are wonderful without being overpowering and the environment is very immersive. Like I said, for being F2P, I'm impressed at the stunning visuals, and quite enjoy the lighthearted fantasy setting of the League, though the Empire's areas are cooler. The animations are very well-done, as are the various faces and bodies of NPCs. For some reason, my elf is a fairy, but hey, I've never played a fairy character before, so it could be fun (also the NPC names are Russian-sounding and there are Russian signs in towns, likely because the makers are Russian). The map system is very similar to WoW's (the maps look almost identical in style) and even includes a feature called Automove (similar to that of Divina) so you can make a straight-shot for your next quest location without having to waste time paying attention to where your character is walking; enemy aggro is even reduced when you use Automove. Customization isn't too involved, but there are enough options to keep my character from looking like everyone else's. Even the log-out screen is nice. I really like some of the effects; for example, when I shoot an arrow, the arrow gets lodged into whatever I shot, including enemies. The voice acting is a bit robotic and the combat a tiny bit awkward by default what with both the basic attacks and special attacks crammed together on the hotbar (you can change this, of course), but it's not too shabby. I especially like how you can "plan an attack" e.g. hold an attack for the next enemy you target if the first targeted enemy was killed while you were casting.

One of the most irritating things about most MMO's is the endless running around to turn in quests. There don't seem to be many straightaway paths to anywhere you need to go, mindlessly increasing the amount of time it takes you to do anything without being any fun. Luckily, Allods implements a teleportation feature that gets you from place to place relatively quickly, though the quest placement is still odd. The quests are also very hard to do in order since they don't seem to follow a logical progression; some quests will require you to stay in the same area, and then one of them will make you go to the other side of town. Are you supposed to continue questing where you end up, or go back to the start area? Both? Seems like a waste of time to go so far to begin with, then. The music also fades in and out at seemingly random times (and also gets old quickly), so I prefer listening to my own music while playing. It's not cool that you have to get what's called a megaphone in order to talk to other people in the world chat, though, and the mandatory group/instance quests for the Empire are an annoyance since you can't progress if you can't find anyone to do the instance with you. The League has no such thing required, though.

Decided to try this out, conversations between NPCs were first to get my attention. They speak different languages with some english words inserted in the dialouge but there are english texts to accompany them, although the grammar's relatively poor. Gameplay's linear (go from A to B), you move pretty slow despite running and pretty much a point and shoot on one kind of an enemy early in the game. Graphics-wise it isn't top notch (depsite the max settings), although it's not going to bother you if you don't really care about those types of details.
Upgrading your gear isn't really well explained at the beginning of the game, just some form of text description on some of the recipes to craft upgrades but you are really only given a vague idea of how to go about it. You'll figure it out yourself - considering the fact that the enemies are very tough to deal with even at the beginning of the game, upgrading your gear is essential. It seems without upgrades at all it'll be one kill - one death, then you respawn at the furthest stage (e.g. You started stage A and got killed in stage D, you respawn back to A with respawned enemies which you have to kill again). With minimal upgrades you'll manage to get 2-1 KD, but otherwise don't bet on sweeping stages easily.
Lastly and also one of the most disappointing features of this game - No Saves! Or rather, it autosaves only on essential cutscenes with NPC, otherwise quitting afterwards will delete any progress you have made in the game - that means upgrades, inventory items, money, progress, etc. This no longer makes the game any more enticing to replay after one session.
Overall won't really recommend this game right now, as you can tell from the review already. There much better ones out there to get. If they can remedy most of the cons, I say for $3 it's ok to purchase but wait for an update.

"Cleaning up dust wasn't as much fun as I thought it'd be." 5/10
I never thought I'd see the day where I wanted to play a game that revolved around cleaning up dust particles, but nevertheless, here we are. They say never judge a book by it's cover. Well, never judge a video game by it's screenshots. For this game appeared to have it all, but managed to fall short. Let me start out by saying that I loved the art style though, along with the soundtrack. In fact, the soundtrack is probably the best part about 'Dustforce' and is exactly what you want in a platformer. As for the controls, they are nowhere near as bad as some of the people on here make them out to be, and personally I found them to be quite good. The only thing that stinks is how they make you assign the controller buttons yourself, as opposed to just having them preset for you. I wouldn't even dream of using a keyboard to play this game.
As you may already know, this game was made with speedrunning in mind. Speedrunning is something I enjoy watching, but not performing, and had I known that beforehand, I would have skipped this game entirely. I mean, who makes a game specifically tailored for speedruns? Getting to the end of a level as quickly as possible? Where's the fun in that? No, I like to take my time, look around, really take in my surroundings. And besides, isn't the whole fun in speedrunning, coming up with the fastest method on your own? It just doesn't make much sense if you ask me. Aside from that, there's pretty much nothing else to do in this game but run from door to door playing level after level for the best time. No bosses, no enemies, just jumping from one platform to another, climbing wall after wall, sweeping up that dirty dust.
There just doesn't feel like much of a reason to continue playing 'Dustforce' after an hour or two, unless you care about posting the highest scores for all to see. Which is basically where 99% of the incentive to continue playing comes from; the highest possible score. On the other hand, I can definitely see how people enjoy playing this game. Like I said, the soundtrack is great, the art style although simplistic, works quite well, and the controls are pretty good.

Where objectivism was the ideology of BioShock 1 it's collectivism in this one, and while I usually pretty much loathe politics or sociology or whatever this game made those topics interesting for me. I'd say that the first 3/4 of the game are very similar to BS1 (annoyingly so, even) but the last part is exceptional and unique with wonderful endings. (There a three different flavours of endings (Good, Neutral and Evil) with about seven or eight different cutscenes.) The characters are astoundingly well done. Where in BS1 it felt like somewhat decent people turned into monsters thoughout the game it's the opposite here; even the bad guys turn out to be humans with their own understandable motivations. The decisions you have to make also are way more difficult and meaningful than in the first part of the series.
There's one rather short sequence where you play as a Little Sister and it is breathtaking.
Gameplay-wise I'd say that BS2 is a step up from BS1. It's a bit tedious at times, the weapons aren't that remarkably, the plasmids are, well, pretty much the same you already know. The one thing that annoyed me a lot was that both the hacking multitool and the camera are in the weapon wheel; quite often I accidentally selected these non-weapons during combat.
Someone who likes shooters will probably appreciate the mechanics more than I did. I focused on the story and thus the gameplay wasn't that interesting to me.
Minerva's Den is a worthy DLC. It took me about four hours to complete and the plot and characters are as great as in BS1 and the main part of BS2. As always there's a great plot twist in the last part and the ending was touching. I liked the art style even more than in the basegame, and that's saying something.
Truth be told, I can recommend this game to anyone who likes a good story. As I have not played the original version of BS2 I can't say if it crashes more or if the changes are appropriate. I'd say that BS2 is a game you absolutely have to play if you liked BS1; I can't make a choice between the original or the remastered version though.

Warframe is the best game.                    Boom! That's my review, if, that's all you care to read.

Warframe is a really great game, but it's prabably not the best game. But would you like to know why it's so great? Read on! Warframe is great because of many reasons. Warframe is that game where you will find yourself flying threw the air, and shooting enemies as you "fly". Except you are not flying, you are jumping, and then gliding, and jumping again midair to countinue your "flight" (as you gun down enemies), but when you land you slide and attack some poor foe with your sword and he dies. Warframe is also the type of game where you can run around, collect energy and kill everything that comes in your path with your powerful arcane abilities.

But that's just a typical warframe mission. I think what makes Warframe truly great is not the thrill of fighting hundreds and winning, but the storyline. Warframe has a highly detailed storyline and a large amount of lore. In Warframe, you learn the story by doing quests. These quests can sometimes feel repetitive to finally finish it, but I've found that those ones were optional. The main quests are really in depth in the storyline, and will make you wonder why you didn't do that quest sonner. Also if you are a new player reading this review, know that these quests (especially later on) will have HUGE reveals, which will change your view of the game.
But while I personally may think the quests are the best part, they aren't everything. Some people will say Warframe is like Destiny or Destiny 2 these days, but I haven't heard many good things about Destiny's and most games Customization. Warframe has (currently) 33 warframes- each with different abilities and stats, and over 300 weapons. All warframes, weapons, and really almost everything you can own, is customizable down to each individual color.
Now that's a lot of stuff, and most new players to this game will see that they need to buy warframe/weapon slots and assume it's ptw. Warframe has one major currency called platinum, and true you can buy it, but platinum is actually very cheap. many people get thousands of it without spending a dime, because of the trade chat. Basically, you do a mission, collect a item (which is worth plat) and sell it to someone else.
Also warframe has some really good devs. As of right now, warframe is a very different game than what it was when it was released 4 years ago, but in less than a week the new update PoE will add a open world map. This open world map will officially raise Warframe up to the level of Destiny 2 and many other brand new games. In fact, most people are referring to this update as Warframe 2. DE (the devs) will not stop there however, they mentioned that thet may add one of these maps to each planet.
There is so much more I could say, but I feel this review is getting a little long, and congratulations to whoever read it this far.

Warframe is a game about grinding. It's that simple. Every aspect of this game is grinding. Doing missions, farming for materials, even trading and building, is grinding. To get to a planet that you need you must complete a whole bunch of missions and then do a bunch of meaningless tasks just so that you can be taken to a next planet, rinse and repeat, until you get to the planet you wanted in the first place. Every single item requires resources, and lots of them. The more you progress the more bullsh*t amount of resources are required to make better gear. Normally, this is okay as you also gain signifigantly more resources in most games, but nope. Not warframe. There is only a tiny gain in resources as you progress from planet to planet. And even once you have the resources, the whole f*cking building mechanic is a time-waster. Want that great weapon so that you can play away on sunday? Nope. Wait 12 hours. Want that awesome Prime frame to work on and dominate during your weekends, the only time you have to play games because your week is crammed with work and you need to make a living? Nope. Wait three days, come back next weekend, when i can f*ck with you some more. The way to get better weapons and frames, is also, guess what? Grinding. You need to buy new weapon blueprints, wait 12 hours for them to finish, and then take about an hour to level it up to rank 30. Repeat this about 10 times and you can level up your mastery rank. Meaning you can then get more advanced gear. Once you get up to the higher mastery ranks it just becomes a huge joke. If you ever find a master rank 25 player you will see that he/she has literally every single weapon, frame, sentinel, and companion upgraded to level 30. Thats hundreds of f*cking weapons. I veiwed a master rank 24's profile and he had, no joke. 81 days in warframe. Thats 1/4 of a whole f*cking year down the toilet. Think any casual, or pro gamer would ever want to do this. warframe lures you in at the start by making everything cool and easy with the grinding, but i have been playing for a long f*cking time, and i'm only mastery rank 6. That's right, 6. And i'm not even a casual player. I play many times during the week, going way over the 'casual' mark in terms of playtime. Honestly, there isn't a single aspect of warframe that isn't grinding. F*ck even the trading, is grinding, waiting, and wasting your f*cking time. You'll spend hours getting things worth selling and get almost nothing out of it. And that brings me to my next bullsh*t topic, platinum. Everything that does not require grinding you have to pay for. Yep. You pay to not grind. And it's not cheap either. It costs 75 platinum for a f*cking colour pack to make yourself look half-decent. You could spend a FULL day on the trading market to get it, or, pay around 10$ to get it. What. The.  F*ck. Bullsh*t.
Summary: Warframe is a f*cking mess of grinding. Do not play. Do not ever play.
Ever.
Edit: I was quite angry during the writing of this review, and now aknowledge that i was only listing the negative aspects. While warframe has a sh*t ton of grinding, the developers did not steep that low, there are workarounds and things to help you surpass this. And to be honest Trading is not that long of a time. Switching reconmendation to positive because warframe may have alot of grinding, but it is an amazing game.

As of right now, for the English players out here, this game is in broken English, and understanding it is far and few. I've tried for the longest time to get though the tutorial sector, "Sector 0", and their explanation of what to do is completely misunderstood and trial and error isn't seeming to work. Wait until there is an English guide posted with controls and gameplay basics before picking up the game, or, at least playing it. Because that way, you'd at least know what to do in the game.
EDIT: After 2 hours, I was able to finally make sense of it. It is possible to understand after a while if you're an English player, but it takes time and quite a bit of trial and error.
As for the gameplay, it's pretty repetitive. The game consists of: Shooting things, unlocking locks, shooting some more things, unlocking more locks, shooting more, crap ton of more locks to unlock. That's about it. :/
There is a lot of running from "point A" to "point B" to go back to "point A" to see if you can though yet, just to go to a "point C". A Bunch or large green orbs that teleport you to random locations on the map, but you feel obligated to go into them anyways because there is just so much damn walking.
The walking pace in the game is like a snails movement, and the sprint is more of a below average walking pace.
All of the max upgrades can be acquired within the first level, taking out all of the challenge of even fighting anything. Running into an enemy feels more like a nuisance at this rate, kind of like a gnat flying around you.
The "level", "sectors", "tasks", whatever you'd like to call them, are incredibly large for what the game is, making the game a walking/unlocking locks simulator, and going from "point A" to "point B" is always 100% boredom.
The game rips and tears non-stop while playing, and it's jumpy at all times.
During most cut scenes, you can still somewhat control your character, to it's a bit awkward. During the movement cut scenes, you can even press shift to move slightly faster, or as the game calls it, "sprint". If you have your weapon drawn before a cut scene starts, your entire HUD will overlay the cut scene. If you accidentally click more than 1 time to start an interactive cut scene, you will have a permanent text overlay on the bottom of your screen. For example, don't click "E" twice on the first lock in Sector 0, you will be forever annoyed with the rest of the game til you restart the game.
There are tons more bugs from here, and a good number of annoyances.
For the $4 the game costs, if you're going to achievement hunt and grab some steam trading cards along the way, go for it. The achievements are pretty simple, and pretty straight forward. But, for a few of them, the "task" achievements, you must complete the entire game, and that's several several hours of gameplay, walking, and unlocking.
If you're looking at the game for the gameplay, and a possible game for entertainment, your money is probably better spent elsewhere.

Dustforce is slick, fluid, relaxing. Well, providing you're any good at it.
I'm not very good at Dustforce, but I still enjoy it a lot. I'm pretty clumsy with both a keyboard or a controller, I'm fairly certain the input doesn't matter, a skilled player can dance through the levels whilst a clumsier player like myself will find multiple ways to blame the controller whilst really it's the player at fault.
Completing a level isn't good enough, you have to go over and over, to get that S / S rating, shaving off seconds, perfecting a route, figuring the perfect peaceful and flowing pattern that will earn you a perfect and you can move on. Practice makes perfect.
The animations are beautiful and smooth, matching the gameplay style and giving everything a wonderful flow. The soundtrack is amazing, helping your mind hit that half-focused, half-zen-like concentration zone.
I'll never complete Dustforce, I'll never get S / S on many of the levels, I'm not even good enough to even GET to many of the levels in the hub world (they're hidden away out of reach, requiring a certain precision and timing of skills to climb to them)... But I still enjoyed the game, and I'd recommend it to others... It's a fun way to spend a couple of hours. Providing you're not going in for 100% completion, anyway. Only madness or a godlike zen-state await those who would dare.

Allods Online was one of my favorite free to play MMO's out there, and while I cannot read Russian well I remember enough of the game to get by. Allods Online is one of those games that starts out great and slowly and, seemingly inevitably falls pay to win. As much as the peak time for playing Allods has passed, lower pop, more pay to win days ahead you can still find fun in Allods. The style is something I don't feel anyone has really replicated well, one of the more unique free to play MMO's from around 2010.
In Allods you start by picking your race, the two factions each have three races. The races of the Empire are Orcs, Xadaganians (Empire Humans), and the Arisen (aka Russian Necrons). The races of the League are the Elves, the Kanians (League Humans), and the Gibberlings. These Gibberlings need a bit of an explanation. You see the Gibberlings are one of the most unique races I have seen playable in an mmo because you play three of them, at once all animated together! Gibberlings are pretty much tiny 2 foot tall badger people, they fight and live in groups of three, so for every action they work together to accomplish they each have there own role to play. As an example if you chose a sword and shield class chances are your Gibberlings will have be carrying a sword, one with a shield and one running around doing anything else!. Don't worry though, Gibberlings are not "micro" heavy, its only the animations that are fun and exotic, otherwise they play like any other character.
The classes of Allods Online are broken down into archetypes, each archetype reflecting a slightly different class per race. the archetypes are Warrior, Paladin, Scout, Healer, Warden, Mage, Summoner, Psionicist. Not every race can play every archetype.
A bit of background lore now, in Allods an a time long past there was a terrible cataclysm that sundered the worlds into islands and nations that float through the "Astral". The Astral functions like a primitives idea of space, filled with energy that you can traverse with Astral ships, sailing from one world or island to the next. This is one of the more attractive features of Allods Online, and while I wont go into it heavily here, it has much bearing on end game. You will learn more about Astral and the history of the world if you play Allods.
Overall I have to say I really do enjoy Allods even if it is pay to win now in 2016. I hope at some time in the future we get the english version of the game available on Steam!

Here we have it: Allods Online (Theres a TL;DR at the end in case you are lazy)
Back in 2009/2010, among the huge pile of crappy MMOs, this wonderful game emerged. With a big budget, nice graphics and an interesting storyline it promised to be a great and riveting adventure. And so it was, but only during the 1.0 version of the game (as I like to call it "vanilla" allods) because at first there was no cash shop. It got introduced later into the beta, but it didn't upset the balance that much, yet.
Then comes the first big expansion which forced quite a lot of cash shop stuff into the game making it borderling unplayable for non paying players. Even if you decided to be supportive, and buy the cash shop currency from time to time, you usually found yourself wondering if its worth it. Cash shop aside, at least the content was fun during this phase! But that was quick to change.
Soon further expansions arrived, making the game more and more into a unfun tedious grind which required even more money invested than before to play properly, or nerves of steel if you were a free player (farming is not fun I tell you).
In my opinion the game is now a shell of its former self and not worth getting into. Yes it is true, many people spent thousands - some even 10 thousands of euros/dollars/whatever currency on this game.
If you are a new player looking for a fun temporary MMO then I can recommend this game to you. Download it and play it (but don't bother paying). Levels 1-40 will probably be the most fun, and then you'll feel the fun gradually drop off as you climb towards the max level, and then you quit. That's the only thing this MMO got to offer.
I guess the original devs leaving early on did make an impact after all...
TL;DR - Pay2win concept taken to the extreme, probably one of - if not the worst example of pay2win (or should i say pay2lottery and pray4win?) ruining a good game which had a lot of potential

Heyo folks, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for Darkness Within: In Pursuit of Loath Nolder by Zoetrope Interactive and Iceberg Interactive.
Darkness Within is a game that’s heavily inspired by the works of the famed author H.P. Lovecraft and is one of the most true to his work games that I’ve played. The story follows detective Howard E. Loreid as he investigates the mysterious murder of a man named Clark Field. Throughout Howard’s investigation he encounters strange beings, hearing noises, having vivid nightmares and many unusual occurrences begin happening to him.
The game takes place in the fictional town of Wellsmouth and you will visit many locations around the town. Locations include Howard’s home, his office, Clark Field’s home, Loath Nolder’s office and a cabin. The game also has nightmare sequences that take place in unique and mysterious areas as well. It’s also worth mentioning that the game doesn’t reference any of H.P. Lovecraft’s works except for a single easter egg in the game. It focuses more on its own unique storyline that was heavily inspired by the famed author.
The game uses an old school style of movement where you must click the mouse in the direction you’re facing when an arrow appears. When you move you go ahead one space making movement a bit tedious but its not wholly annoying. You can move the camera in a full 360 degree angle to view your surroundings completely. Exploration is done in a linear fashion with only a few rooms and a couple hallways in each area. It’s difficult to get lost while exploring because of this.
If you happen to miss a puzzle on the previous day you can complete it the next day. There’s a lot of puzzles to solve in the game and while some can be easy, others are quite difficult to figure out and not easily noticeable. The game requires a lot of patience to complete. After a while it feels like you’ve played the game for hours on end because of it’s slow pace, but it’s still a very good experience throughout.
If you happen to play on normal difficult you’ll be able to use the hint system to help solve puzzles. There will be times when you’ll need to underline useful keywords or phrases in letters or documents that you find in your journey. There will also be hidden keywords to look for in each document for you find. The think system is a bit different from the hint system. It allows you to combine keywords or items to figure out different parts of the storyline or to make items for puzzles. The think system is used quite a few times during the course of the game and will help you uncover various missing pieces to the storyline.
Overall, Darkness Within: In Pursuit of Loath Nolder is very true to the works of H.P. Lovecraft but it likely won’t be a game for everybody. It requires a lot of patience to get all the way through and it feels like it takes longer to beat than it actually does due to the sheer amount of puzzles and its movement style. I managed to beat the game in over 8 hours and that was with a guide to help with the tougher puzzles. It’s quite long and equally time-consuming but it was an enjoyable experience throughout.

Solid horror point & click detective game, with a heavy focus on the detective work.
Sadly it's not flawless. A major part of the second and third part of the game involves studying notes and underlining vital parts to obtain clues. Unfortunately this process has various problems that can be exceptionally frustrating:
- Sometimes underlining a section in a document will make the player character respond to it and leave it underlined but NOT give a clue. Then later, after discovering something else, you are supposed to NOW read the document and underline that part, despite it ALREADY being underlined, to unlock the clue. It can happen quite often that the player is already one step ahead of the game in figuring out how relevant a certain passage may be, but the game is refusing to give a clue until the previous step is undertaken.
- On one occassion a player has to underline a word (let's say 'flowers' to avoid spoilers) in the second paragraph of a letter. However, the same word is already in the first paragraph and it refers to the very same flowers. Underlining the first instance does nothing, while underlining the second instance of the word DOES reward you with a clue.
It's minor things like that that can make you get hopelessly stuck in this maze of lengthy documents and locations as you try to figure out what you missed, despite not actually missing it. You know you're on the right track but the game is simply preventing you from progressing because you have to underline something a second time for no reason, or you're not underlining the right instance of the word in the same document. This forces you to either painstakingly go over every single document you have access too again and again, or look up a walkthrough.
It's these flaws that prevent the game from being excellent. Instead, it's simply 'good'.
If you like Lovecraftian horror and detective games, and you don't mind that involving a serious amount of paperwork, then
will be right up your alley!
Edit: Finished it! Ending was disappointing. A minor reveal at the end I had already guessed at about an hour into the game, so that had zero impact on me. And lots of unanswered questions still...
Enjoyable game, but certainly no masterpiece.

Ugh. Once again, great expectations on my part are met with disappointment. Looking back at the reviews, a lot of people seem to have low standards ("best lovecraftian game I've ever played" and so forth).
What's good in this game:
- graphics are old but the art direction and overall atmosphere is good if you like mysterious mansions
- sound effects and music are good and contribute to the disquieting vibe, but they overdo a bit the "spooky" sounds.
- good writing in the various documents and letters you find, the universe they depict is alluringly occult even though it screams "I wanna be Lovecraft" in your face without any subtlety
Now for the (unfortunately overwhelming) bad:
- very annoying movement interface, you have to spin around like an idiot to find clues and the arrows that can lead to the next area, and it makes me dizzy. I never get dizzy in any kind of FPS game, so that's saying something. This made me miss the static screens of other point and click games, or the free 3d movement of other adventure games.
- the objects to click are not obvious from examining the screen, you have to scan everything with your cursor. Pixel hunting is back, only now it's more annoying: a cupboard might or might not be interactive, same for interesting looking objects and documents which sometimes are individually clickable and sometimes are just part of a larger static scene, without any indication. The game would really have needed a key to show interactive hotspots (like Black Mirror 2/3 or Book of Unwritten Tales.)
- investigation system that seems very interesting at first (clue-combining, text-underlining and so on), but you rapidly realize that the game doesn't anticipate many logical combinations the player might make. You end up guessing at how the game wants you to put things together to progress, even though you already understang where the story is going.
- nonsensical story. It has a lot of promising elements and many story threads open up, only for the game to end on a cliffhanger without answering any questions it raised. It's not really Lovecraftian, either, as (minor spoiler)
- there are basically no characters to interact with in the game, a striking contrast with most adventure games. The few in-person dialogues you have are with rigid puppets with questionable voice acting.
Sadly if you thought that the sequel Darkness Within 2 was gonna complete the story in a satisfying manner, it doesn't (actually adds even more plot holes), moves to glitchy and awkward 3d movement, and loses a lot of the mystery and atmosphere.
If you want a good psychological horror point and click adventure series with a satisfying story, I recommend Black Mirror 1-2-3 instead (especially II and III which are examples of how to design an adventure game).

Contrast is a puzzle platformer that will tug on your heartstrings. It's stylized (in a very Parisian way), has some great voice work, and will leave you thinking about it long after the credits have rolled.
The gameplay is experimental, yet simple. The use of light and shadow to shift from 3D to 2D and back works wonderfully, and forcing your brain to think in multiple dimensions leads to the best kinds of puzzles. There are just enough secrets and collectibles to keep things interesting and promote exploration without being annoying in this small but well-realized world. You'll notice jokes and easter eggs in the background while progressing, and it's rare that you'll ever feel lost.
My biggest gripe is that the controls are just clunky enough that a few spots requiring precision movement can be very, very frustrating. I rage quit twice as a result.
The short and sweet story is totally worth the time, invisible walls and all. All the collectibles and optional dialogue only serve to enrich the experience. You'll think you know where things are going and then a big reveal will twist everything around. Luckily, every new story point makes sense, and they don't come out of nowhere - it's simply the process of learning more about the characters. And the ending is just complex enough to be satisfying while opening your mind to multiple possibilities.
Contrast takes high-concept ideas for both gameplay and story and manages to fit them all into a neat little package. It makes for a cohesive, fun, and memorable game.
