This could have been a great game, fantastic even. It even has the potential to be my absolute dream game, but the actual combat simulation is way to oversimplified and lacks many common RTS control and information features. I've been waiting for a game like this since the 90ies title M1 Tank Platoon. I like the graphics and sound, voices are great, though unit feedback is way to cocky.
It is a mystery to me why the design was kept so ridiculously arcady. The main reason I'm giving it a thumbs down, is because I can't really enjoy playing it without constantly thinking how much better it could have been with just a few more features.
These are my main issues:
- purchasing unit menu is cumbersome, way to many clicks, and why can it not be toggled to remain open all the time
- no way to pause. pausing and giving orders would make the game so much better.
- no adjustbale game speed
- no proper tutorial
- terrible unit placement, no rotation/facing, no formations
- no real air support
- skirmish mode lacks features, no real way to play a more customized battle setup (assign resources to each side, block certain units, display starting positions, etc etc)
- no unit stance (aggressive, neutral, ambush, stealth etc etc)
- no display of line of sight and firing zones,
- no display of fog of war
- no real cover model and usage (walls, buildings)
- no splitting of infantry units
- infantry units can't dig in/fortify
- no loadout selection
- way too few units
@Devs: I love your work, but a few steps towards titles like "Combat Mission" (tactical combat wise), "Supreme Commander" (information wise) and even "Company of Heroes" (cover system, retreat function, special abilities) wouldn't hurt.

Wargame: European Escalation
Eugen Systems
Focus Home Interactive
Real Time Strategy
The first part in the Wargame series of tactical RTS’ had to leave a good impression. Fortunately for it, the dev team behind the game I’m reviewing today, are industry veterans which specialize in the Real Time Strategy genre and particularly the subgenre I’m most found of, when strategic titles come into discussion. The type of strategy that eschews traditional base building and management, for pure unit combat. This subgenre relies however on a lot more patience, studying of the terrain and even your foes, to know precisely what weapons or tactics to use upon. It’s a lot more static than the fast-paced RTS’ so popular today. Starcraft, C&C, Dawn of War, Cossacks, Age of Empires and many other franchises, are as dynamic as they come, with players scrambling to meet their opponents in the open as soon as possible and the infrastructure needed to sustain your army, has to be built fast and efficiently while being maintained at all times with a  various degree of attention.
By  contrast, franchises like: Sudden Strike, Blitzkrieg, Men of War, World in Conflict and Wargame, all focus on the skill of your unit placement, use and knowledge of the battlefield. There is no emphasis placed on a base since you rely on a steady or less, supply of reinforcements. Many times, you even get to choose those new units to enter the fray. It is far more realistic than building a barracks and watching troops march from it. And when you can no longer count on a near infinite number of units recruited through resource gathering, you begin to appreciate them far more and do your best as to limit the casualties sustained by your army.
Wargame: European Escalation is by no means, an easy game. For some new players to this type of RTS, it may come as a nasty surprise, but even your most advanced tanks can fall prey to a well placed squad of rocket launcher-carrying infantry, hidden in a forest. Scouting ahead and before you send your mechanized units, is paramount. Even the falsely portrayed in the media, “death from above” type of assault helicopters, seem fragile and vulnerable if you don’t plan ahead accordingly. There is no “Rock Paper Scissors” ruleset in Wargame. This potential vulnerability of your units can also tip the odds in your favor since the enemy is also subject to the same tactics he might use against you. Alas, the Artificial Intelligence in this game, is quite capable and will not hesitate to flank you instead of just rushing towards the center of the battle. During some missions, it demonstrates full defensive skills and taking over sectors from the enemy shall not prove an easy task.
I will not spoil details regarding the single player campaigns, even if I was pleased by the use of an alternative Cold War era in which the conflicts heat up faster than an ICBM heading for a capital city. That’s an abbreviation for “Intercontinental ballistic missile” by the way. The true “city busters” of our contemporary times.
Unto the gameplay aspects I didn’t enjoy as much (and which ultimately stopped me from giving this title a perfect 10 rating). Besides being a difficult strategic game, you also have to babysit your units a lot more than in the aforementioned dynamic RTS types. Also, you can’t afford to lose too many units since they have a finite number for the entire campaign and unlocking new ones requires a lot of grinding (multiplayer matches are a must, in this case). You won’t be able to unlock all the units for both the NATO and the Warsaw Pact factions, just by completing the single player campaigns, no matter how many secondary objectives you might accomplish. I understand that far better than the already tough AI, would be a real mind, a human player to spar within an MP mode. I just don’t appreciate being forced down this road, in order to unlock a full roster of troops I might actually need during the SP missions.
All things considered, European Escalation is the start of a great strategic series, in the vein of old school classics that can’t be found on the Steam Store (I’m looking at you, Sudden Strike!). And if you are searching for a derivative Cold War scenario about to get warmer than Hell itself, you’re in for a treat. Wargame doesn’t fail to provide a most challenging and fun experience. Once you’re used to the turtle pacing and battlefield unpredictability, you will really feel like an armchair general!
+ Gorgeous graphics.

Metro: Last Light Redux is another game I got first on Xbox. As A metro fan I have played through both games and enhanced versions multiple times and I can definitely call myself a Metro Fan.  I family shared Metro: Last Light Redux for the purpose of this review, I like Last Light Redux enough to definitely give it a positive review.
Last Light Redux does not change much about Last Light overall. it mostly consists of enhanced graphics and fixes. I can at least say that I feel the graphics definitely look better, and maxed out they are pretty amazing. Something I want to note however is that I have experienced a good deal of new bugs in the Redux version, a few of them serious like corrupted auto saves and some random performance issues in certain areas of the game. Even with these I would still recommend the game, as they seem rare enough to not be a deal breaker.
Another important addition to Last Light Redux is that it includes all previously released DLC and new modes to play through the game, for someone looking for the complete Last Light experience I would obviously recommend Redux over getting the original release of Last Light and all the DLC.
Really though, in the end I would say that if you are a Metro fan, and you have not played Redux yet get it and play through it, If you like it chances are you will play through Last Light Redux multiple times. I was able to play through Last Light Redux about three and a half times before I started to get bored.
I recommend Metro: Last Light Redux to fans of shooters, post apocalyptic games, and fans of the Metro series. With its multiple varied story choices and multiple endings, Metro: Last Light Redux is sure to make a decent addition to anyone's game library.

Why oh why aren't there more Chinese historical dating sim games like this? Please make more!
I originally wanted to wait for the English release but I'm too impatient and it gives me an excuse to practice my Chinese... lol and I have to say I really enjoyed it!
- The voice acting:
Voice acting is so on point... especially Zhikong. I'm in love with his voice. Like seriously I don't even care he's a weirdo and a little♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'd listen to him talk mantras all day. haha I wish the main character was also voice acted because I'm lazy and I want someone to read it for me. lol
- The music:
The title song has been stuck in my head for the past few days!!! Ahhh~ It may be because I'm partial to traditional Chinese music but the use of traditional instruments in the bgm is just perfect for the setting.
- The setting:
Speaking of the setting... I LOVE THE SETTING! Like I said I wish there were more games set in ancient China released in the West. I hope more developers think about releasing Chinese games in the West. The game goes a bit into some buddhism-inspired philosophy in some routes (hello they're all monks) which I find interesting. The religion depicted here is fictional (draws from inspiration from buddhist principles) but is not actual representation of real Buddhism. It's generally focused on the relationships and less on the religious doctines. I think most people should still be able to enjoy it even if you aren't religious or buddhist.
///
To provide some context for those who may not be familiar: In order to become a monk, one must give up worldly desires including love/romance/carnal pleasures. To have attachment to earthly things/person is to be tethered to the mortal realm and thus preventing one from attaining nirvana. (Similar to real Buddhism) The temple and monks serve mostly as a backdrop for the story and this conflict of detachment vs. romance is one point of interest explored in the game.
///
- The story:
I think the game delivered a good balance of humor, romance, and angst. Some routes definitely extroted more tears than others. I didn't feel the writing was contrived or cingey (which is a problem I have with most otoges). Typical of historical Chinese stories, this did a pretty good job at evoking a sense of nostalgia and beautiful melancholy... if you ever watched C dramas you know what I mean.
- The love interests:
Few brief descriptions on the male leads:
Zhikong: serene, aloof, obsessive, possessive, a living contradiction, dat voice dayyyum
Huihai: a precious sweet cinnamon roll, basically perfect, so smart and yet so dumb
Ziqing: childhood friend, tsundere, infuriating and endearing, is a lil♥♥♥♥♥♥ actually pretty thoughtful
- Main character:
I liked that the MC is capable and intelligent and isn't a total pushover (unlike some other otoge where the MC is a weak potato and/or immature brat...). She can be silly, sassy, smart, self-depricating... you know, more like a real person and less like a paper doll. Why is it so hard for other writers to give the girls a ♥♥♥♥ing personality?
- Value:
I felt the game wasn't very long compared to some other titles and only has 3 routes but considering the price, it's definitely worth the buy! I liked it so much I wish the game was longer and/or had more routes. I think you get more than your money's worth even at full price.
I'm looking forward to the English release. I may play through it again on the English version to get a comparison.

The style of Contrast is right up my ally - it's beautiful, mysterious, slightly eerie and reminiscent of Ye Olden Times romanticism. That combined with the amazingly original premise of playing as an imaginary friend accompaning a little girl living in a world of shadow people made the game a really unique experience. There's something infinitely thrilling in running along the walls as a shadow, climbing on the shadows of others.
Unfortunately, that's where it stopped for me, but it could well be that I want this game to be something that it's just not. It's essentially a puzzle game, but I personally found that most of the "puzzles" were incredibly easy to solve and the story itself, as much as there was one, was pretty linear, complete with average-to-poor voice acting, thus leaving me wanting more. The full price of Contrast isn't much, but I still have to say that there isn't much content even for that price point - I completed the game in a bit over 3 hours, and that already included several re-dos of some of the sections. I imagine that if one is not as tippy-tumbles as I was, the game is easily completable in 2,5 hours.
Don't get me wrong - I still recommend it (especially when it's on sale) to people who like puzzle games for it has a truly unique style, but I personally just feel like the idea of this game has such potential that it's almost kind of wasted here and I would have loved to see it developed to a full-length game with a bit more depth.
All 'n' all a solid 7/10  for what it is, 5/10 for what I wish it would be.

Es gibt reichlich authentische Waffen, Maps & viele Spielmodi und auch einige Mods. Zudem ist jede Menge DLC in Form von Skins für Rüstungen und Waffen schon für kleines Geld erhältlich. Alles was das Herz begehrt! Natürlich ist Chivalry nicht perfekt. Es gibt schon einige Bugs, aber die halten sich wirklich in Grenzen und schmälern den Spielspaß meiner Meinung nach nicht. Chivalry ist ein absolutes Muss für jeden Mittelalter-Fan.

If you have patience and like the premise of this game (which in a nutshell is survival with dinosaurs), then I do highly recommend it. The game can be played singleplayer, locally, or online.
-
Game has frequent patches, especially after large content updates. These updates are usually at least 100MB and can even get to be over a Gig. Average is probably around 400MB. If you have metered internet, this can cause the game to become unplayable until you are able to download the update.
-
There are still glitches and bugs in the game. From frustrating building issues to dino clipping, these are annoying and require you to adapt your play style sometimes. Other more impactful bugs are still around too, yet I have only had one of those happen (tamed dino falling through map) once in all my play time.
-
Game can take quite a while to load your world. This seems to be worse when starting a new game, though logging into your save still takes a fair while to load in. Logging into an online server, however, is faster as the world is already 'started'. This load time only applies to when you are starting up a world.
-
Game runs well with low-med graphics on my older non-gaming laptop PC; doesn't necessarily mean it will run on other systems, but maybe this info will help someone out there.

ARK is a fantastic game, with issues.
Yes it's poorly optimized.
Yes it has too many items.
But let's be honest: the real reason ARK has gotten so many negative reviews is because of Wildcard's development style.
ARK had very positive review stats until Scorched Earth was released.
Once it did so, a LOT of 'ethics police' pounced on Wildcard for daring to release a paid DLC for a game that wasn't fully released yet.
So?
These same people took to the review section and, in tones of righteous indignation, downvoted _the game_ because _the developers_ decided to release a paid DLC before the game's full release.
The result is that potential buyers get a false impression.
They see all those negative reviews and conclude the game is lousy.
Instead, many of those reviews have NOTHING to do with the game. They are simply objections to the development process Wildcard chose.
And so, these people maddened by the dev path chosen by Wildcard, punish THE GAME, when it wasn't even the game they were objecting to. It was Wildcard's policies.
Some ethics, huh?
"I'll say your pizza is lousy, even though it's fine and it's really the COMPANY I don't like."
The exact same thing happened when Wildcard announced it was releasing the game as a full version. People complained, and downvoted _THE GAME_ because of what _THE STUDIO_ was doing.
And now, I'll write a review that discusses THE GAME, and not the studio's development decisions.
ARK: Survival Evolved.
To be honest, I enjoyed the game more in its earlier stages of development. I think there are too many items now, and that optimization lags behind where it should be. The game feels cluttered and overpopulated.
Additionally, there are certain animals that just make the game less fun to play, notably the Terror Birds and the Troodons. Insofar as they are the only dangerous animals around after you tame a fairly fast pet, they render something of a service. They keep you cautious as you venture into the jungle, because they are both fast and effective, especially the Troodons, with their fast acting venom. However, the fact that they are small and annoying tends to make them more of a dangerous nuisance than an opponent you respect. You RESPECT the dire bears and T-Rexes, because they're big and mighty.  But the Terror Birds and Troodons are more like tiny flies with a REALLY bad bite. You don't want to get bit because they hurt, but you have contempt for them at the same time, because they're so small.
They're like potholes in the road: they keep you alert, but you wish you didn't have to deal with them. They ultimately drag down the experience.
What the game really needs is a credible LARGE opponent that roams the island and makes things dangerous for you. But large dinos are so slow, and generally too big, to either follow you or even reach you.
And so that's another failing of the game: once you get a fairly tough, fairly fast mount, you're out of danger. The same problem exists at sea: once you get a Dolphin (Ichthyosaurus), you can literally outrun everything. Even the biggest sea predator, with the most fearsome bite damage, becomes as harmless as a bath ducky.
The list goes on.
Building is irritating because generally it's more work than it's worth. Yes, you can make neat structures, and feel like you've made a digital home. But when you finally look up from your labors and set down your Journeyman level pickaxe, wipe the sweat from your brow, and literally jump into a pool of water in order to drink from it, what have you done? You have a big house. Swell. But it doesn't really protect you from anything. No dinosaurs were going to bother you at that locale anyhow. Everything you've built in it you could have built on a wall-less piece of foundation, and they would have been just as safe. No dinosaurs were going to smash your smelting forge anyhow, so why build the walls? For that matter, why build a second story, complete with a roof?
And that's the real problem of ARK in a nutshell: there's no reason to do anything once you've gotten beyond the basic level. In the beginning, you have to hunt and make clothes so you can eat and stay warm at night. But once you've got cloth clothing, three spears, food, a stone pickaxe and hatchet, what point is there to the game anymore? If it's your first playthrough, you'll probably be so giddy by all the possibilities and unlockable items that you'll just keep going, like I and a lot of other people did. But once the initial enthusiasm runs out, there is no motive anymore. The devs, rather lamely I think, only provided two motives for development once you get beyond the initial stage: finding crates with high level goodies in dangerous places, and unlocking horrible monsters to fight.
With regards to the first goal, what's the point of leveling up your character so you can get high level items? What are you going to use them on? Are you going to use that Mastercraft level hatchet to harvest wood faster so you can build that house you don't actually need? Or are you going to use that Journeyman pike to kill raptors in order to level up, in order to...what, exactly? Oh! to fight monsters! But...all you get for fighting, say, the Brood Mother (giant spider) is a few trinkets, some high tech engrams, and a powerful but very scarce element called Element. That's it: no explanation why you're on the ARK. No story development.
Of course there are pluses to the game too, but it's always easier to list the downsides.
Here are the pluses that stand out to me:
Great projective mechanics. The only game I've played that got projectile throwing this right was Peter Jackson's King Kong. The spear, the bow and arrow, it all feels so right. The mechanics are perfect.
The sheer feeling of freedom. You really CAN go anywhere. Whether there's any reason to do so is another question. But the fact is, and this is ARK's chief feature, is that you're not tied to anywhere at all. You can live on a wooden raft, put all your necessary buildings on it, and live a high tech existance with all you need on the raft (I've done this).
The graphics are phenomenal. The sun beaming through the jungle canopy and glistening across lakes is fantastic. The water effects are great, and the landmasses on the official maps are very well done (except for a few odd places on Ragnarok).
Underwater exploring is exciting and nerve racking. Poking your head around aquatic corners, on edge for an eel to jump out and electrocute you is one of the most exciting things I've felt in a video game.
Being jumped by raptors is almost equally exciting. They're fast, aggressive, very damaging and have a genuinely menacing look. All at once your mind jumps to Jurrasic Park, and you start thinking about how they're supposed to be the most dangerous animal you could bump into. You wonder if you can kill him before he kills you. And if there's two of them, you could panic. It's fast paced and adrenaline filled.
And here's one of the best features of this game: it's authentic sense of atmosphere. Standing next to a campfire at night, listening to the crickets, can really be relaxing and make you feel that you're there. I've never played a game with as much atmosphere as ARK.
To summarize:
Pros:
Fantastic graphics;
Realistic feeling dinos;
Phenomenal atmosphere;
The sheer sense (and reality) of freedom;
Excellent throwing mechanics.
Cons:
No goal to the game;
Too many items, cluttered;
Overpopulated by too many dino types;
No purpose to the elaborate, and well designed, building system.
ARK the ecosystem is great, while ARK the game isn't. The various elements in the game are great, but the implementation tends to fail. The game needed an editor to trim the fat, and smoothly link all the elements together. As it is, it's a mixture of success and failure, but the sheer virtuosity with which they've crafted the experience puts it into the positive. It gets a thumbs up from me.

I almost always have a couple of point-and-click adventures of some description installed and in varying states of completion. I find them to be fairly casual games to play for the most part, that I can play while the Mrs. is watching some rubbish on TV, and that I can simply pause or escape out of when the serious business of being a thirty-something year old child is invariably interrupted. But there are always exceptions, and ten minutes of gameplay is usually enough to tell when you’re playing one, and these are the ones that are worth savouring; These are the ones that you want to have the house to yourself to play, and even then you’ll wear headphones just in case some rude individual knocks on the door with the misguided assumption that you care about what they have to say. No, good Sir, today is the day that I am playing, The Darkness Within: In Pursuit of Loath Nolder. I care not for your free light bulbs, kindly leave without knocking.
I don’t claim to be any type of expert on Lovecraft, but I have read quite a bit of his work, and anyone who is familiar with even only the most commonly referenced stories would know that his protagonists consistently speak of how they must hide the knowledge they have uncovered at all costs, even unto death. It should come as no surprise then, that when a game comes along that can truly own the tag of “Lovecraftian”, that it’s going to be f*$%ing hard to piece together what secret cults, madmen, and good old-fashioned wizards and necromancers, are trying so hard to keep secret. The Darkness Within is an excellent game for quite a few reasons, the most straightforward of these however, is that it’s honest.
As Detective Howard E. Loreid, the player uses a unique and somewhat complex inventory/problem solving interface, to sift through the information and puzzles that are uncovered throughout the course of an investigation into a man’s death. This interface is used to make the mental connections between certain clues and items found throughout the game, and you’re made to work for it a lot of the time, just like a real detective. There are no shortcuts. You will paw over documents multiple times to unlock the secrets they contain, and there will be no picking up of random items in the hope that they will come in handy later. Oh no, if you want to pick up that pot in the kitchen and carry it around, you had better have already figured out why. And how good is that!? It makes sense. It also forces you to pay attention and remember where things are, and where you might need to revisit to get what you need later.
The locations are well crafted with plenty of suggestively dark corners and creative use of lighting, and do an excellent job of setting the mood for the unfolding story. These locations are also very faithfully “Lovecraftian”. Gambrel roofs, brooding forests, tunnels, and richly-appointed studies all make an appearance, and the supplementary material that is found within these environments is also very faithful to a true Lovecraft horror. I can’t get enough of all the diagrams and sketches, and all the little extras that go into making a game that has depth. I love it. There’s plenty in The Darkness Within: In Pursuit of Loath Nolder to satisfy fans of stories like, “The Case of Charles Dexter Ward”, and, “The Statement of Randolph Carter”.
Zeotrope Interactive have proved that they understand the importance of sound, and lack thereof, to create suspense in a game. Creaking floorboards, whistling draughts, and oppressive bouts of silence are all used to great effect, and the hauntingly-crafted musical tracks provide excellent ambience to their respective environments.
The character models do have that classic PS1 kind of look about them, but honestly, for me they add a subtle level of creepiness to the game that I actually find very endearing. I like my horror games to be weird and kind of f#%*ed up in that way, so this period-style character animation fits perfectly for my taste.
If you like Lovecraft, and I’m not talking about bull$#it tentacles and cartoon plush toys; I’m talking about well researched, and caringly executed homages to classic literature, then you will like this game. Just be mindful of the fact that this is not a game for those with lazy brains who just want to grind out yet another point-and-click. This game is about a detective working to solve a mystery, and sometimes you’re going to have to take a second look at things to fully understand what is going on. Likewise, it’s not a game for people looking for easy jump scares or Penumbra-esque games of hide and seek; This is a game for people who understand what was considered “horror” at the turn of the last century. At the time of this review you can pick this game up for $1.99 US during the 2016 Summer Sale, and that’s an absolute bargain for the quality of game you will get in return.

Darkness Within: In Pursuit of Loath Nolder, though containing superb writing, is difficult to recommend due to its unintuitive UI/inventory system and an overbearing difficulty.
UI/Inventory:
The game uses an interesting concept where you must combine clues you have found into a "Brain/Think" panel. As another reviewer pointed out, I had to look up in a guide how to simply open an envelope. I had the envelope opener and I had the envelope, yet I couldn't figure out how to open it. Shouldn't this raise an alarm that the inventory system is a bit wacky?
There is another clue system where you must find specific information in texts and underline clues. When the pages of texts become 5+ pages of information, this becomes tedious and frustrating. While I enjoy reading and encourage it, reading for the sake of finding 1-3 words per page in a multiple page document simply becomes silly. This actually has the opposite effect of the joy of reading. You are no longer reading for the joy of reading. You are being forced to read for clues and it's no longer fun - it's disappointing.
Story and Writing:
The writing is superb. There is tons of backstory and the world/environment is beautifully brought to life through language. The characters are developed well and the world feels alive. This is definitely the strongest appeal to the game.
Graphics and Sound:
I liked the graphics for this game. The visuals create a dark and mysterious vibe that brings the story to life. The sound compliments the visuals quite well with heavy sound effects such as clocks ticking, floorboards creeking, doors slamming, casettes playing...
Overall:
The story and writing is superior quality. It's honestly some of the best writing I've seen in a game. It was impressive. Unfortunately the inventory system and the way you combine clues is simply not intuitive. If I had to look up a guide simply to understand the basic mechanics of the game then that means one two things:
A) The game developers did not take enough time explaining the inventory system well or
B) The inventory system is overly complex and not intuitive
I think if the inventory/clue/underlining system was improved and made more clear, it would tone down much of the difficulty of the game. You want to have a balance of difficulties in a game like this, but also you want your players to experience the story (it's written so well!) By making the difficulty so high you are actually deterring your players from finishing the game because of the frustrating experience.

A point and click Amnesia, this game is one of the few, like Amnesia itself, that delivers real Lovecraftian atmosphere and the psychological horror of a man struggling to keep his sanity while going mad.
Unlike most so called Lovecraft inspired games, and other media, that just confront the player with some tentacles and turn into an almost hentai-like parody of Lovecraft, completely missing the point.
Anyway, that sums up the good parts of the game, the downside is the aged point and click format. The UI is convoluted, it showers you with text, and worst of all you may know or see items, but can't interact until you've solved a puzzle so that the game has decided that the protagonist will pick it up WTF!
Instead of rewarding the logical mind these invisible barriers punish the logical mind, very bad game design.
Conclusion; only buy the game if you are really into Lovecraft (like me), or really into point and click adventures, so you can deal with the flaws. Even then, get it only at a really good sale.

This was a fun adventure game with both a humorous and dark storyline. It should take you around 8 - 10 hours on your first playthrough. In this game you will assume the role of Edna with her trusty sidekick Harvey as you attempt to escape the asylum in which you are housed so that you can find out the secrets of the past. As with most adventure games you will have a full inventory which you can use to interact with in multiple ways. Almost every item can be offered or used in some way to get some hilarious dialogue / reactions.
This game was created as part of a university thesis and also the first game that Daedalic Games published. Unfortunately there are a few different bugs in the game but there are work arounds that can be found in the steam forums but most of these issues can be resolved simply by changing the language of the game to German momentarily. The reason for this is due to translation issues in the code.
Please don't let this put you off, the moments that may require the language to change to German do not seem to contain much speech or text relating to the story.
If you a fan of point and click adventure games then I recommend give this one a try, personally I enjoyed the story as well as the puzzles and I also look forward to the next installment in the series as well as other Daedalic Games I play in the future.

June 2016 Edit: Well, the devs listened to the feedback and gave players the options to turn off battle scars (still in in the trophy mode). Thank you devs. Just go into the options and turn it off. You'll be very, very happy you did. Thus, I'm changing my rating back to 7.0 and giving it a big thumbs up.
I've played this game a lot since its release through its various updates and Pirate's Cove DLC. I want to recommend this game, but there is one glaring update that they did that ruined the game--Battle Scars. First off, I want to say I completely understand why the devs wanted to put this into the game. See how it worked before is that you'd take one class, or maybe one of each of the two types of classes, physical and magic, and one or two of the trinkets and run the entire area (which was basically a level). You'd take all the gold you got and dump it into the upgraded items for each tier, and that would be that. What the new Battle Scars system does is completely prevent you from doing that by burdening your character until you have no chance to win. You continually gain those scars after almost every successful run. I've had 6 on one character, and almost every single one is a negative. Oh, and the worst ones match up exactly with the trinkets meaning the devs are explicitly telling you that you have to buy all 4, but you still have to buy all 4 (3 on the final level) gear upgrades to have any chance to win. If that wasn't bad enough, they also added in a one quest time out on the class that just died so you have to buy at least 2 classes per level (you do get one good class when you start the Pirate's Cove area for free; the other two in there are horrible) or waste time waiting for your chump to die. The worst scar by far is the one that drops your hand size by 1. Your starting hand size is 3 btw, and pretty much every single monster has at least one card that drops a card from your hand which almost always hits when you can't block it leaving you top-decking the entire time, with the usual results.
Did I mention there's a Steam achievement for completing the game without anyone dying? Yeah, it is now impossible so if you're a completionist, don't buy this game. Oh, and no, you can't just dismiss a worthless character. There's no retirement system so you could have that character class become useful again other than death. And again, you get a battle scar 99% of the time when you complete a mission. Combine that with the normal card-based RNG, and the game will have you throwing up your hands in disgust/anger pretty often. I just can't recommend the game unless you're desperate for fun (it does work well on a low-tier PC as my ancient PC can attest) even when it is on sale.
Pros:
1. The original soundtrack was amazing. Why they changed that with Pirate's Cove, I don't know.
2. The graphics are minimalist but look great.
3. All of the classes are unique, and they play like you'd expect them to. Same for the enemies.
4. The times where you get sychronistic gear for your hero and obliterate enemies with ease are a blast.
5. Pirate's Cove is a must-buy. It adds a lot of gear and a whole new area, which gives you plenty of time to play with the tier 3 classes and gear which wasn't the case with the base game.
Cons:
1. Battle Scars. Battle Scars. Battle Scars. If they took them out, my rating would jump 3 points immediately. Totally horrible addition to the game.
2. There are some glaring imbalances with enemies. Some are way too powerful to the point you never want to fight them (looking at you Bandito along with a few level 1's which are just inexcusable) while others are just a cakewalk (namely the level 3 burning enemies).
3. There are a couple of character classes that just stink. Granted, there are only 3 of them, but man are they glarely bad. The two that aren't the Drunken Sailor from Pirate's Cove and the Barbarian. You can tell the Barbarian was bad in the original because the Drunken Sailor is basically an upgraded version.
4. The individual missions can vary wildly in length. Some are over in 10 minutes while others are just a ridiculously long slogs no matter how good or bad your room card RNG is. I'm talking 45 minutes to an hour. The game just stops being fun after about 25 minutes in a mission because you're fighting the same three level 3 enemies over and over getting nothing but gold out of it as your equipment is already perfect.
5. The Pirate's Cove DLC did break the game slightly with one piece of equipment, the Spyglass. It turns every physical attack into a Ranged attack. As a level 1 uncommon gear, that severely dampens you ever wanting to play a magic user. Granted, that lessens over time as you add way more gear which lessens the frequency of it popping up, and you get the Ranger class in tier 2.
6. The Room Card RNG and pathfinding will frustate you to no end. You will have runs where you won't get any of the room cards you need (you get 5 cards every turn which consist of room, enemy, and gold cards). Usually, this is fine, but there are several timed missions where you will lose just because of that RNG and not because of anything you did wrong. The devs have never actually addressed the lack of any impetus on getting to the empty quest rooms. This means that your character will go anywhere but there unless you specifically remember to take gold instead of great gear towards the end of those TIMED missions. Also, your character will automatically go to a fountain room, even negative fountains (unless gold or an enemy tempts him), so when you get the battle scar that makes your first room card a fountain room, the game gets a lot tougher for no good reason.
Rating: 4 out of 10 (7 out of 10 if they remove Battle Scars AND They DID!!!)

It has a VERY steep learning curve, but for strategy fans, I can't recommend it enough, its a very unique game. Basically, the goal is to last as long as you can, its over when ether you lose your last piece of land, or if your ruler dies without a heir. Its very complex, but so worth it once you get the hang of it. I mean really, how many games come along where you can say you had the Pope assassinated? Unlike a lot of strategy games, its not so much about build this and conqure everyone, its more about surviving and the political intrigue of the times. People will try to fabricate claims on your land, your second wife may try to have a son you had with your first wife assassinated so that her child will become the rightfull heir. You can start in Ireland and work your way up from count, to king, then conqure Scotland and England to form the Empire of Britannia. You can stratigically marry off your daughters to prestigous people of other countrys, then their sons will have claim to those lands. Theres different rules too, which you can change so that daughters can inherit, or that women can even inheret on the same grounds men do. There is a LOT to the game. The DLCs add even more, such as being able to play as pagens and sacrificeing your prisioners, if thats more your thing.

The squel to Mass Effect (1)!
In the sequel to Mass Effect (1) you will continue to play as Shepard from the first game (The same character if you imported him or her) on a new quest.
This time around though you will notice something almost immediately; Combat has changed!
Now the game has changed around more to a cover based shooter compared to what the first game was (I mean, there WERE some cover based shooting in the first, but now its radically different) and also you are now using limited ammunition.
Some people welcomed this change, some didn't. I personally am still on the fence about the changes to combat.
But its quicker, more actionny than ever. Also you can only use one power at once since other powers will be put on cooldown once you activate a power (In the first game you could maybe use 8 powers at once but had maybe a minuter cooldown).
The question is though, is it fun? Oh hell yes, the combat is fun. It also makes it more interesting trying other classes and trying out different choices in the first game in order to see what will change in the second game.
Storytime eh? Yeah yeah.
This time Shepard will be summoned by the corporation "Cerberus" and is tasked to find out why an alien race called the "Collectors" are kidnapping humans, so its up to you to find a new crew on you voyage amongst the stars and find out the grim truth about the kidnapping of humans...
One thing is sure; this game is more grim than the first and third game. No dance on flowers here.
While the story to me is not good as the first but the interactions with the crew and characters keeps this game going. They also cut out the unnecessarily exploration bits (Love it or hate it) and major loot collecting has been removed entirely (Although you can do some cool research/upgrades in your lab).
**And yes,i need to put this into here; Mass Effect 3 mini-review!**
Mass Effect 3 is the last game in the Mass Effect Trilogy. While the combat was the best out of the three (According to me), the story took a major backlash thanks to the ending.
But, while the ending in the third game is absolotely horrible i can tell you one thing; The journey is a good one.
The sad truth though is that if you want to play Mass Effect 3 you have to buy it elsewhere than on Steam...

When I first found out about the crew of Dustforce and their follies in amateur game development, I became very anxious to play this game and to support them. However, playing the actual game has shown me that good intentions do not necessarily translate into a full experience.
I think that Dustforce's biggest problem is how it defines 'skill' and 'difficulty'. Dustforce has very little in the way of rewarding a player, only giving out keys which are used to unlock a handful of harder levels. When most of the game's content is unlocked from the start, the player's only remaining motivation is the scoreboard. When one takes a cursory glance at said scoreboard, one notices very long strings of players who complete the level in virtually the same amount of time, give or take a fraction of a second. Not only that, but the requirement of sweeping all dust in a level for a perfect score causes every level, regardless of size, to develop a 'one true path' that sacrifices exploration and player experience for the sake of a higher score. This makes the game extremely tedious to play, boiling itself down to memorization of a level and restarting the level at the slightest mishap.
I'm aware that the game is designed with the speedrunning community in mind, but one reason as to why speedrunning is so highly valued in those circles is the fact that speedrunners interpret a game in a different manner than the developers, and play it at a much faster speed than intended, entertaining others who are only familiar with a more down-to-earth means of beating the game. Meanwhile, Dustforce's design mentality is rigidly geared towards beating the levels as fast as possible, causing the practice of speedrunning to be rendered pedestrian, and therefore moot.
Aside from the core gameplay, which is admittedly quite interesting despite its flawed implementation, there is honestly not much else to say about Dustforce. I did like how the game's various sprites were traditionally animated, but the artstyle itself is so minimalistic that the subtlties and quirks that normally come with such techniques are lost. The music on its own is good, but not exciting or emotional, causing it to simply blend into the background, when music should enhance the player's experience by being memorable or unique.
When looking at Hitbox Team's upcoming Spire, I'm glad to see that the team is taking more consideration to the skill of the individual and motivating the individual to get better in order to progress further. Hopefully, it'll make for a more rewarding and engaging experience than Dustforce, which, in my opinion, feels like more of a chore than actual dusting.

Whilst most games wearing the tag "lovecraftian" are content with waving a few tentacles about (obviously so lovecraftian, did you know he also wrote a great deal of hentai?), this game gets the subtlety and nuance of his writing.
An dark little point and click romp through the fetid thoughts of a lovecraft fan. At points throughout this game the atmosphere was almost tangible, oozing from my monitor, gripping me within its eldritch grasp. The puzzles and thoughts kept my mind racing, jumping from conclusion to conclusion, waiting to uncover the next secret or clue.
I am all praise for this delectible slice of true lovecraftian gaming, but one does feel it necessary to point out some of the flaws.
If you don't like lovecraft, this probably is not the game for you. This game is Lovecraft to the bone, even crediting him as the creators biggest inspiration.
The graphics. Now if unpolished graphics are enough to put you off this game, then you sir are a fool and i already know that you would not enjoy this game. But yes, the graphics and 3d models aren't the best, but that does not detract from the experience in the slightest. Hell, i'd even say that the unnaturalness of the charcter models adds to the creepiness.
Knowing where to go next. Occasionally you can be left stumped. You've found a clue, YOU know where you want to go due to thinking ahead, but in the game you haven't found the exact clue that the game wants you to find. Having to double check everything is tedious.
One small problem I had, which i intend to remedy, is the shear number of loose ends for instance
.But I'm sure going over parts again would clear these up.
Overall I highly recommend this. Nothing new to Lovecraft fans, just the same cliches, but they're the same cliches we know and love. Difficult though it may be, the story is intrigueing and I couldn't get enough. A must play for fans of this style of game.

I've read most of Lovecraft's works and I love lovecraftian horror. This game has lots of it, I daresay it's at least as lovecraftian as Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the earth. Especially in the beginning you can barely make a step without finding a Lovecraft or even a Poe reference - a madman who escapes from an asylum, a town called Wellsmoth, a protagonist called Howard, a poet called Pickman, a book with incredibly lovecraftian short stories and poems which was probably written by the developers (amazing work!), darkness, fear of the unknown, a secret cult, a raven, a "volume of forgotten lore" and a detective story. Seriously, it can't become more lovecraftian than that.
But then there's the gameplay. Most of the riddles are ridiculous. You sometimes have to find hints by reading (very long) documents and underlining the right info. Sometimes you don't even know what you are searching. Sometimes you have to come back to a document you read 2 hours before, because you can suddenly underline information you couldn't underline earlier because you haven't triggered it by finding information in another, completely unrelated document (at another place) you didn't even know you had to find. You can't even take these documents with you - that's backtracking at its worst. Sometimes you don't even find these documents because you can't click them even though you are standing right in front of them - because you aren't standing at the right position.
I also had a bug where an item vanished from my inventory, so I had to edit my savegame to be able to progress any further.
I really don't see how one could be able to finish this game without a walkthrough. There is an activatable hint feature, but it usually only gives you hints when you don't need them or they are just plain useless. "There must be something in this house that helps you find the solution" - thank you, but in which of the 10 rooms did I miss something? Reading long, boring texts over and over again without even knowing why isn't fun at all, even though it's quite the charm of being a detective.
Talking about being a detective, the story disappointed me a lot.
You have investigate in the case of a man who was found dead shortly after descending into a well under his house. According to the info you have he found something and wanted to get rid of the house immediately - so obviously the game starts by finding the well and climbing down. Oh, and there really is something, and shortly after the "real" story starts because you don't know whether you are mad, whether you are dreaming, whether you are a sleepwalker, whether you are whatever. You get suspended, but you keep investigating in the case.
You keep meeting people and finding information that make you think "Damn, I really want to know what this is about!"
Well, none of these question get answered. You don't find the resolution of the case, you don't find out who these people are, you don't find out what the thing in the well was, you don't find out what happens while you are unconscious (which happens several times), you don't find out what your nightmares are about, you don't even find out what's the matter with Loath Nolder.
I know it's part of the charm of Lovecraft's works that several things stay unresolved, but this game doesn't resolve anything at all. And this is why I don't recommend this game at all, because after the struggle with these horribly designed riddles I'd at least expect a good ending.
If you love Lovecraft as much as I do, give it a shot, but don't forget looking for a good walkthrough before you do. Otherwise you probably won't be able to enjoy the partly exciting story which is almost TOO lovecraftian.

Guild of Dungeneering is a very stylized dungeon-crawling card game in the vein of something like Order of the Stick or Munckin Quest, but is missing some really key elements to make it great.
Game loop:
- Choose a hero / Special Ability card
- Choose a quest
- Through card-exchange guided combat, you fight enemies and level up.
- Collect money from quests,
- Buy new classes, abilities, special cards.
Pros:
- It looks great
- Since your heroes start at level 1 each quest, you are just as able to beat any quest as any other.
- It is fun collecting loot in each quest to get more powerful and complete objectives.
- Funny sense of humor.
- No Permanent "lose" condition. You can fail a mission but are not really penalized for it.
Cons:
- You dont really have a lot of control over what is going on. Specifically:
--- You dont control what path your hero takes. They just take the quickest route.
--- There is no deck building, other than equipment cards you get on each mission (which are reset after missions)
- The game lacks a lot of depth. For example:
--- You place rooms down in the dungeon to decide your path. However, rooms themelves have no other function. Unlike games like Munchkin, there is no reason to place one room versus another other than getting to a specific place. It would have been far better to have 1) A "Special" room deck that got mixed in with other normal rooms with rooms that had perks or penalty trade-offs and 2) Have rooms/halls that maybe hurt you on the first turn on the next fight or gave you extra hitpoints, etc. Just any reason to make them special.
--- The actual guild screen is customizable based on classes you unlock but serves no actual purpose in the game.
- No persistance with characters at all. They level up in missions but then reset after the mission is over. The persistence is all in the guild, which isnt nearly as exciting as most of it is just unlocked classes.  I would much rather have character persistance and increasingly hard dungeons.
-  While you can control what class you have (Class cards) and extra cards (Equipment cards), it would be nice to have SOME sort of deck building to feel like you are controlling the result a bit more. It just feels too random.  It also get harder as the game goes along (Enemies have like 3+ hits on you almost imnmediatley) and all you can do is choose a class.
- Success feels like hitting a wall enough times (failing) until you finally win.
Overall, a fun game that could have been a lot better. Not bad or great, but i can see someone really not liking it.

BUT, here are my tiny criticisms: a) I don't like the setting at the beginning. I think the setting at the beginning of the first game is much better. b) I don't like those stupid source collars. Rhyms with "horse collar." c) I don't understand the emphasis on height advantage in the fights. There is nothing about being higher than your enemy that would make your weapons 20% more effective! The squel to Mass Effect (1)!
In the sequel to Mass Effect (1) you will continue to play as Shepard from the first game (The same character if you imported him or her) on a new quest.
This time around though you will notice something almost immediately; Combat has changed!
Now the game has changed around more to a cover based shooter compared to what the first game was (I mean, there WERE some cover based shooting in the first, but now its radically different) and also you are now using limited ammunition.
Some people welcomed this change, some didn't. I personally am still on the fence about the changes to combat.
But its quicker, more actionny than ever. Also you can only use one power at once since other powers will be put on cooldown once you activate a power (In the first game you could maybe use 8 powers at once but had maybe a minuter cooldown).
The question is though, is it fun? Oh hell yes, the combat is fun. It also makes it more interesting trying other classes and trying out different choices in the first game in order to see what will change in the second game.
Storytime eh? Yeah yeah.
This time Shepard will be summoned by the corporation "Cerberus" and is tasked to find out why an alien race called the "Collectors" are kidnapping humans, so its up to you to find a new crew on you voyage amongst the stars and find out the grim truth about the kidnapping of humans...
One thing is sure; this game is more grim than the first and third game. No dance on flowers here.
While the story to me is not good as the first but the interactions with the crew and characters keeps this game going. They also cut out the unnecessarily exploration bits (Love it or hate it) and major loot collecting has been removed entirely (Although you can do some cool research/upgrades in your lab).
**And yes,i need to put this into here; Mass Effect 3 mini-review!**
Mass Effect 3 is the last game in the Mass Effect Trilogy. While the combat was the best out of the three (According to me), the story took a major backlash thanks to the ending.
But, while the ending in the third game is absolotely horrible i can tell you one thing; The journey is a good one.
The sad truth though is that if you want to play Mass Effect 3 you have to buy it elsewhere than on Steam...

It's a
adventure from German developer Daedalic Entertainment.
It has references of games such as Monkey Island, the dialogues and visual style has a strong influence of Day of Tentacle. The dark humor reminds us of the first Sam & Max.
Story
The story starts off a bit slowly, with Edna trying to figure out how to escape from her cell. Her memory has been wiped by electroshock treatments. Edna counts on her stuffed rabbit, Harvey, that takes over a form of an imaginary friend.
Gameplay
The interaction with the  characters is linear, although there are many hypotheses of conversation, the result will always be the same and there's one way to resolve the puzzles. The mechanic used by the game is the "tempomorph". So it takes Edna and Harvey back in time to explore traumatic scenes from her past. The memories acquired from this experience provide new abilities to Edna. Control is point & click, along with usual options to interact with your environment in many ways, talking, picking objects up... etc.

Graphic
Graphically, the game features a striking cartoon art with a slightly abstract using a retro interface reminiscent of Lucas Arts-style comedic that fits perfectly into the theme of insanity and dark humor of the asylum. Great voice acting especially for Edna and Harvey; an unexpectedly touching storyline; massive amounts of interactivity. The sound is great at some points, especially when it uses piano and a mix of jazz. Tedious dialogues and repetitive travel sequences.
Conclusion
Edna & Harvey: The Breakout, it's assumed to be a tribute to Lucas Arts. It has an old-school flavor with many of the same annoyances as older games, but many positive surprises as well. so if you seek to revive the memories of the 90s then it's a perfect game to remember the worst and the best that the past has given us.
Once you get past the learning curve, this is one of the greatest strategy games I've played.

"♥♥♥♥♥ wut", or An Easy To Understand Version of The Review (TM)
Kitty Power's Matchmaker is a game with a pretty unique idea: work in a dating agency and help people find their true love. Sadly the game quickly goes downhill after the first hour or so, when you realise that practicaly every date is the same thing but with minor differences, and how A LOT of it relies on RNG. A lot of the crucial data about your client's potential dates is hidden meaning that you often have to just pick someone randomly and hope that it works. When the two characters talk you will often encounter a situation when your client won't like something about their date and you can tell them to lie. In this situation the success is determined by... a fortune wheel. Playing F2P mobile games made me hate these things with passion, and there they are even more vile, since failing this minigame gives you a strike - 3 strikes and the date is a fail. If the partner of your date hates something about them, they just say it straight which can either bring your client down or GIVE YOU A STRIKE WITHOUT ANY CHANCE TO PREVENT IT (well, about that later...)
During the date there are simple minigames, for example the date says "I want something spicy", and you pick one of the three dishes for them. Pretty straightforward. But there are many other minigames that can happen during the date, and it's annoying how many of them rely on RNG. Like a memory game. Or picking if the next card will be a lower one or a higher one. All of them are associated with some situation, like your character telling a story or... trying not to fart (10 minute long laugh track). Like I said, 80 percent of them are RNG, and the only ones that are different are just based on remembering♥♥♥♥♥♥or a simple math problem. Booooooooooooring.
So yeah, you do the date, it goes either good or bad (of course the first option is the best) and then you get dat sweeeet moneeeeeeey my guy.
As you progress in the game you unlock♥♥♥♥♥♥like new restaurants (which get harder over time, but it's the only real difference between them) or options to prepare your client for the date with new clothes or hairstyle. This is a very important feature since it lets you prevent some of the annoying RNG related to the preferences different partners have, but many of these are locked for a long time and you're forced to endure the random chance until you can do it about it.
And they cost money, often a lot of it. So you need to drop a ton of money on a character hoping that you will get paid enough to cover all the expenses. So failing dates is even more annoying since you pretty much lose money.
In all, a RNG grindfest, don't buy.
Dear Kitty Powers' Matchmaker
I remember the first day we met. I heard dozens of people talking about how funny and original you are. When we saw each other for the first time, it was love at first sight. The time we spent together was wonderful. I loved your naughty sense of humour, creative ideas, cartoonish appearance and open minded nature.
But as our meetings became longer and more frequent, things started to change. You gave me this weird challenges that were pretty much luck based, and when I failed sometimes you would punish me, and sometimes you would forgive everything. It was like I had to spin a wheel of fortune everytime I messed up! And I'm not even talking about the times when you forced me to struggle with hard tasks that were often full of random unfair obstacles!
Sure, sometimes you had something different in store, but how was that supposed to be refreshing when it was all either memory games or random luck?
I tried to make our meetings exciting, but you wouldn't cooperate. We kept doing the same things over and over, and when you suggested something different, it was as boring as everything else. Sure, you promised a lot, but you wanted me to spend hours doing the same thing with you first!
So, I think you know what I'm going to do.
You're nothing but a pretty box that promises tons of fun, but I kept getting out the same boring things and couldn't get to the "super cool thing" you had on the bottom.
I can't help but feel that the time we spent together was wasted.
I'm sorry, but that's it.

It has a VERY steep learning curve, but for strategy fans, I can't recommend it enough, its a very unique game. Basically, the goal is to last as long as you can, its over when ether you lose your last piece of land, or if your ruler dies without a heir. Its very complex, but so worth it once you get the hang of it. I mean really, how many games come along where you can say you had the Pope assassinated? Unlike a lot of strategy games, its not so much about build this and conqure everyone, its more about surviving and the political intrigue of the times. People will try to fabricate claims on your land, your second wife may try to have a son you had with your first wife assassinated so that her child will become the rightfull heir. You can start in Ireland and work your way up from count, to king, then conqure Scotland and England to form the Empire of Britannia. You can stratigically marry off your daughters to prestigous people of other countrys, then their sons will have claim to those lands. Theres different rules too, which you can change so that daughters can inherit, or that women can even inheret on the same grounds men do. There is a LOT to the game. The DLCs add even more, such as being able to play as pagens and sacrificeing your prisioners, if thats more your thing.
Fun, awesome, and hilarious, this game is highly addicting and very recommended!

I got this game in a bundle, and was really excited to try it because of all the technical gameplay mechanics - like the complex executions you have to use in order to make your run look as seamless as possible. I had watched a few speedruns on YouTube and was pleasantly surprised with the quality of experience provided by Dustforce DX.
If you like cleaning, artsy and smooth platforming gameplay, a stellar electronic soundtrack, chaining combos, score attacks, and challenging mechanics, then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are great - the detail in the different levels is very high and well-done. The music and sound effects are awesome, and I will provide a link to the OST here because it is that good; I think the only other game OST I ever linked in my review was NEOTOKYO's.
.
The controls are a bit tricky to learn, but the tutorials are very helpful and will ensure you get a firm grasp on the game's mechanics before you start your janitorial runs. You can try using a controller, but the keyboard bindings work just as well. The learning curve is minimal to moderate - one of the most difficult elements of the game is combining the different actions in order to achieve a smooth run. Combos are also essential for reaching many areas in each level and progressing deeper into the game. For example, you may have to wall run upward, double/wall jump several times, and hit a dustball/enemy at the top in order to reach a higher level (and if you do everything except hitting the object at the top, you will not be able to make the climb). Practising and repeating levels will really hone your skills.
Overall, the gameplay is very quick and technical - chaining the proper actions is critical. Once you can achieve a seamless run, the visual aesthetics are so satisfying and rewarding. The main hub will allow you to access the options and all the levels, however, you must unlock new levels by completing preceding ones. There are a good number of levels available for you to test your skills, and the game offers a lot of time value if you are really into speedruns and 100% completion. During your playthrough, you must complete each level in a set amount of time, while maintaining a smooth (finesse) run. If you can finish the stage within the time limit and maintain a good combo bar, then you will achieve a double S rank (best possible score).
For the achievement junkies, there is only one to collect, and this requires you to complete every level by performing the most perfect possible run. I really, really love this type of achievement system in a game, and not the stupid, meaningless artificial-game-lengthener types found in games like Lucius (which I will be reviewing soon) - where you need 20 and 40 game hours when the game takes ~10 hours to complete. No, in Dustforce DX there's just one, challenging achievement that involves you spending quite a bit of time refining your skills and experience so you can obtain those perfect runs.
The game can get a bit repetitive once you've invested a large amount of time, however, the variety in level layout and different enemy types adds lots of playability. There are also different characters with slightly different attributes, allowing for a unique playstyle depending on who you select (ex: one character has quicker drops and longer jump range).
If you like challenging platformers with an emphasis on finesse and score attacks, then you must give this game a try.
Definitely recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

It pains me not to give this game a recommendation. I have spent a lot of hours in the game, and I even come back to it occasionally.  I definitely feel I've gotten my money's worth.  Yet at the same time, Ark: Survival Evolved never rose to the point of being a truly fun and engaging game.  Instead, it became a casual time-waster with ultimately no point.
The game itself is gorgeous, and the worlds you can explore are beautifully crafted.  After encountering a game-breaking bug (more on that later) which ruined my initial Island game, and a bit of time in the Scorched Earth setting, I moved to The Center... and wow, that world is breathtaking.  Sure there are a few persistant graphical issues (purple rain, I'm looking at you), but nothing that seriously marred enjoying the scenery.
I really love crafting and building settlements and player homes.  That is one of the things I found most enjoyable in Fallout 4, and Ark: Survival Evolved gives a new and interesting playset to work with.  Most of my time in-game has been spent crafting, and I have some pretty homes and bases that I am rather pleased with to show for it.  Even if there really isn't anyone to show them to.
Which brings me to the core problem:
If you play Ark: Survival Evolved, you are either going to play singleplayer, with a small group of friends on a dedicated server, or in the open multiplayer.  The last is, frankly, to be avoided at all costs.  The Ark MMO community is unimaginably toxic.  (And the game designers have actively promoted and encouraged toxicity.)  You can go to other reviews to get a full story.  That isn't the point of this review.
The survival elements of this game are very strong.  It takes a fair bit of effort to get to the point where you can sustain yourself.  But once you do, there is no plot.  There is no goal other than to build up to the next level of tech just to run around with different toys.  Mercifully, you can adjust settings to minimize the amount of grind, but even with those adjusted settings, the game is still at heart and MMO, and most of your time will be spent doing tedious chores rather than actually exploring or building.
(And when you are alone, there is no one to really build for other than yourself.  At least in Fallout 4, I have NPC settlers to share my creations with.  In Ark: Survival Evolved, I finished building a grand room with a center table surrounded by chairs... and then stopped to look at all these chairs in a world where my character was the only human alive, and I thought, "This is clearly a cry for help.")
Playing with a small group of friends on a dedicated server will allow you to avoid the toxicity of the MMO community and provide you with companionship that will drastically improve the fun of the game.  But eventually either you or they will succumb to the numbing realization that there isn't a point to anything.  Without a plot, without missions, without goals or an end point, the game simply becomes stale.  And the lack of those things can be felt very early, giving the game a lack of depth and substance that is really required for an enjoyable RPG.
Exploration on the beautiful maps like The Center can be quite visually enjoyable.  However, while there is a lot to see, there isn't a lot to find.   Cool, new, unique places are abundant and I very much enjoy seeking them out.  But once you are there, they don't offer anything.  Just a few resources to mine which, by that point, you have multiple other ways to acquire.  In a way, these places are like empty gift boxes with magnificant wrapping -- the sort you see in Christmas displays at the mall -- more enjoyable for the promise you can pretend they hold than their actual substance.
The best part of Ark: Survival Evolved is the mods.  The modding community has built a lot of incredible content, and adding in mods breathes fresh (if sadly temporary) life into the game, as well as gives you a whole lot of new toys to play with.  I would have abandoned the game completely long ago, but with mods that gave me great new options for base building, or which allowed me to tame and ride a dragon, I kept finding reasons to come back to it and play a little bit more.  And those mods often lifted Ark within enough proximity of being actually fun to sustain my interest for a while longer.
PS: As the game is designed to be an MMO, there are some critical issues with playing it singleplayer or on a dedicated server which the developers refuse to address.  One such issue is that if you shut down the game or teleport away from an area before the resources respawn, they will never respawn again.  This is a game-breaking bug, and the best way to avoid it is to set the respawn rate as high as possible and be cautious in always making sure the last thing you harvested or mined has respawned before leaving an area or shutting down the game.

Pros:
+ VERY Lovecraftian. Maybe almost too much. If you want to play a game where you are the main character in an HP Lovecraft story, this is it.
+ Very immersive. The mood is consistently creepy, and solving the mysteries in front of you almost feels realistic. The game sidesteps some of the traditional Point and Click cliches in favor of making things more realistic. (For example, you don't randomly pick up every object you see because you are going to need it for some convoluted reason later on.) For sure, this game gave me the feeling like I was really in the story.
+ Very good story.
Cons:
- Although the game's problem-solving is normally pretty realistic, this makes the game very hard. Remember how I said the game won't let you pick up some innane object that you'll need later? This means you have to remember where it is and come back for it if you need it. You'll spend a lot of time searching the same areas over and over looking for clues or small things you missed. This game would be very hard to beat without consulting a walkthrough at least once or twice.
- I love the game's emphasis on having to read things in order to put clues together, but the mechanics of making you underline important clues in the documents doesn't work very well. It's very hard to see what the game will consider a relevant "clue."
- Overall, the game can be quite frustrating, and it is very easy to get stuck.
- The story is unresolved, making this game more episodic than standalone.

This game might be fine, if you're into very slow paced games with an unfortunate control setup.
It's 360 degree view but movement in the game is a very limited point-click setup.  This results in very very slow pacing (a step every ten seconds if you intend to run somewhere) and difficulty interacting with your environment.
In addition, the Underline feature means that even though you read something and understand where it's taking you next, you have to underline it using a wonky tool and investigate it again...it's very tiresome.  Another example, you hear footsteps or creaks - it's not easy to move quickly in that direction to investigate.
The way you interact with clues and the tutorial for those features is really unhelpful sometimes.
I didn't progress more than 1.7 hours.  The story is intriguing, and I'm a huge Lovecraft/weird fiction fan so this was promising.  Unfortunately the controls and clue UI got in the way to the point of being too prohibitively frustrating.  One thing on the story is there is a good amount of reading material which I am in no way opposed to, however it is often needlessly flowery and melodramatic.
Overall I found it to be a very frustrating, laborious process and that's not something I look for in a game.  I'm hoping part 2 doesn't suffer from the same problems but I have no idea.

Contrast is a game developed by Compulsion Games, the same people behind We Happy Few. Contrast was Compulsion Games' first game before the development of We Happy Few and the game was published by Focus Home Interactive. Contrast takes place in a Caberat setting where a young girl Didi and her friend Dawn (who you play) set out on an adventure to save Didi's father from losing out more debt on a circus he wants to build
It seems as if Dawn is an imaginary character and only Didi can see her, Dawn also has the ability to blend in with the shadows, this is the main gameplay concept. You, as the player, have the ability to blend in with the shadows and interact with objects and go up to higher levels
Through this you solve puzzles and progress through the story. Although this game is in 3D, a heavy amount of the game is puzzle platforming. The platforming in Contrast is the weakest bit, some of the platforming bits in the game were frustrating and outright annoying
Another issues with Contrast is Dawn's jumping ability, its too weak and so feeble that you have to place Dawn in the exact point that the game wants you to do it, if not, you will die countless times
The story is good although the game is extremely short (finished the main story in two hours and in one whole sitting) and I was expecting the game to be longer, however, with the annoying puzzle platforming bits and the horendous jumping ability, I was happy that the game ended quickly
The voice acting is really good. The game camera and animation is the poorest aspect of the game (including the puzzle platforming segments and Dawn's jumping ability) and you could tell that this was Compulsion Games' first game as the animations and camera work greatly improved in their second game, We Happy Few
However, Contrast is a nice little short puzzle platformer game which although it has a few annoying segments here and there, it is a nice game to play in one whole sitting

Contrast is a very nice little platformer with a really interesting game mechanic; in well lit areas you can turn yourself into a 2d shadow and platform with the shadows on the walls to solve puzzles. This mechanic allows Contrast to give players both a 3d and 2d world to solve puzzles. Great voice acting and good, period appropriate music draw you into a well written story about a little girl and her (imaginary?) friend, as they navigate through the lives of her and her parents. And wonderful animations and artwork help craft this world into a very interesting environment for the player to solve the puzzles that are put into the characters paths.
That's not to say the game is perfect. It isn't. There are some camera issues here and there, not enough to ruin the game but it can pull you out of the story every now and then. Also, if you only play on a keyboard then you may well hate the control scheme. The controls were picture perfect on my Steam Controller but oddly delayed on my keyboard and sometimes locking out certain commands until I reloaded. Stick with a controller. And once it was all complete I really found no reason to go back.
Anyway, for a 3-4 hour game experience Contrast is well worth checking out, but you might want to wait for a sale.

Dustforce is a beautiful platformer with a very high skill cap. The premise of the game is to sweep each level while never letting your combo drop; which occurs when you have not swept up any dust after a set period of time. A flawless continuous sweep gives you a 'perfect' rating, which can unlock keys which you can use to enter more difficult levels. This is not necessary to enjoy the game, though, as many levels are available without unlocks and community made levels are plentiful and just as enjoyable. You can complete levels without perfecting them, though this gives you a worse rating and no key. Earning a perfect rating on difficult levels is really a challenge as the mechanics in Dustforce take hours, maybe even days of playtime to perfect.
The game contains a leaderboard where you can watch replays of the best times to get a feel for how to perfect a level and different paths to take. Only a small handful of players have perfected every level, and I am not one of them. The challenge does not take away from the game, though, it is still a fantastic game with gorgeous visuals and a calming and beautiful soundtrack that I have listened to for nearly 3 years now. I highly suggest picking up Dustforce if you are a fan of difficult platformers and want a real challenge fit for a perfectionist.

“Edna & Harvey: The Breakout” is one of my favorite games. I found this wonderful and funny game by accident, and after only 1 hour that I played, I really liked the storyline of this game. Everything in this quest was beautiful – storyline, dialogues, characters, music and humor. And even despite some bugs, a few of which made me laugh. So, i want to tell a little about this game – In this game the player must help the young strange woman named Edna escape from a psychiatric hospital. She will also be helped by her plush rabbit named Harvey. One day Edna wakes up in the hospital room. She doesn’t remember who she is and how she ended up in a room with soft walls. Harvey, who suddenly began to speak, becomes the best friend of Edna and they together make an attempt to escape from the hospital…
This game about mentally ill people, friendship, and bad memories. This game is fun and sad at the same time. And, playing, I almost didn’t notice this border between my smile and a feeling of compassion for the main character. Maybe this is my personal oddity, but the fact that this game will not leave you indifferent – irrefutable.
