The goal is to navigate your white (primary) cube around the platforms and collect/deliver "relics" along the way. The platforms appear and disappear depending on the position of your cube and the rotation of the puzzle. You can be sitting in the same spot but rotate the puzzle and more/less platform is revealed. You also have to contend with multiple vertical 'floors' with beacons to bump you to upper levels, so there's a lot to think about even before you start picking up the 4 coloured helper-cubes which each have special powers.
Keyboard controls only, and there are several keys to get to grips with: move; rotate; toggle cubes on/off; switch cubes. You can also press E to show a larger area of the puzzle, which doesn't really help to solve the section you're working on, but it is a nice aesthetic that shows the overall beauty of the puzzle.
First of all, I have to say I love the beautiful, swirling plasma clouds waiting below to swallow you up when you fall. These do seem to weigh heavy on my GPU though, it certainly gets my PC fans blowing hard. The rest of the puzzle has a very clear, efficient layout, with different gradients of grey to indicate the vertical heights of the floors.
A couple of improvements I would like to see: a) have a zoom feature (mouse wheel) because sometimes the puzzle doesn't make full use of the screen area, and b) it would be nice if it was possible to drag the puzzle around to look at it from different angles and then have it snap back to position when you let go.
Music is the usual ambient sounds you often find with these types of games. Pleasant but unremarkable.
I used to think I was good at puzzlers but games like this have shown me that I'm a miserable, brainless worm.
There is no easy, getting-to-know-you stage. The difficulty ramps up immediately. Even death has a high penalty, often sending you way back to the start of a section instead of respawning where you died. You'd better remember how you reached your current position otherwise you'll be right back to square one, literally.
Most of these types of puzzlers rely on the level design to provide the difficulty, with a relatively small number of mechanics/options. Here, not only is the level tricky but you also have several different aspects to consider: the position of the cube; horizontal rotation of the puzzle; which helper-cube to use; which vertical level to travel. All of these things combine to make it eye-wateringly complex. If you're going to use a trial-and-error strategy then you'd better have a lot of patience and a good memory, as your brain will be overloaded with options, drowning in possibilities.
The game is linear - you progress through space via your platforms, and if you get stuck there's no option to try a different level for some variety. I normally complain about difficulty bottlenecks but in this particular case it feels appropriate. When you are stuck on a particular section, there are so many different options available that it doesn't become stale, you want to keep trying.
The price is lower than I would expect. The overall production quality is excellent and there is so much complexity crammed into the puzzle that I would be happy to pay twice the price for this. Strictly speaking there is no replay value, but in practice you are going to forget most of the solutions by the time you get to the end, so after a week or two you'll probably be able to replay it as a fresh game.
Achievements, trading cards and Cloud - Windows and Linux supported, to this is a useful feature for dual-booters like myself.
At first glance this looks like another boring push-the-cube puzzler, of which I've played many, but there are so many different aspects to think about that it's one of the most complex, dynamic puzzlers I've played.
I found myself swearing out loud on numerous occasions as I fell into the abyss again and again, having forgotten the same crucial move for the umpteenth time. Then I would take a break and return later to find a solution immediately.
I highly recommend this if you're looking for a hard puzzler with a rich set of mechanics. I'll say the word 'complex' just one more time, in case you missed it.

If you're familiar with the game Scratches (which I also greatly enjoyed), DW1 is extremely similar in gameplay and visual style but with two extra layers:  document research (seeking key words and phrases in text) and 'Howard's Mind' (where clues, observations, and items can be combined to further the narrative and/or help solve puzzles).  The inclusion of the latter should perfectly fit the context of a game about sanity; unfortunately the implementation is a bit disappointing -- the mechanic becomes cumbersome and frustrating, particularly by the end of the game when you have collected dozens of clues to sort through (I would have preferred a system where only unresolved clues stay active and the others are simply archived for narrative reference).
My two biggest complaints would be the endgame (narrative threads fray and split over the course of the entire game but never come back together to provide a satisfying conclusion... this is almost entirely left for the sequel to deal with) and the occasional lack of direction provided to the player (there were a number of times where I had no idea what I was supposed to be doing or why).  Some of the written text was also awkward enough (translation issue?) to break the immersion of the experience.
Flaws aside, however, Darkness Within might be one of the most faithful interpretations of the universe of H.P. Lovecraft presented by a videogame.  That alone is enough for me to recommend it.

The graphics hasn't really changed, it's the same "old" dark, gritty, Rapture. The sounds are the same. The music is still as good. The gameplay is first person shooter with light RPG elements and also some horror at that. The ending felt lackluster, there were no real boss battles, making certain choices made no difference. But I still wanted to find Eleanore and save her, no matter the cost. I can never tell when a game will click with me. Contrast is one of those that I didn't think I'd like, but I did.
The setting of the game is well-realized: art nouveau/art deco with a jazzy early 20th century theme. It was a fantastic change of pace from the usual common game themes, and it was well done here.
As well, the mechanic of shifting into and out of shadow to complete platforming tasks was a neat twist on the usual platforming mechanics. I'm not a big fan of platformers (and this game didn't change my mind) but the novelty of this at least made it feel unique and somewhat fresh.
The story was a nice noir concept, and it doesn't get in its own way with crazy twists - it exists and is fairly comprehensible, while suiting the game and its mechanics.
As for downsides, I found the gamepad controls to be a little "loose" and slippery - movement felt overly-sensistive to me, and I sometimes had trouble controlling my jumps. There were a few puzzles that are not intuitive, but that's OK I suppose - the game isn't meant to be a complete cakewalk.
I'd definitely recommend this if you're in the mood for something unique and noir and platform-y: 4 out of 5.

Crusader Kings II is one of the finest grand strategy games currently on the market. Unlike other titles of the genre, such as the Total War series, Crusader Kings II takes the focus of the player away from battles and warfare - although both play a large role in the game - and shifts the focus to politics, alliances, marriages and above all the continuation of the House. Many times I have found myself praying for my character to have a son, and there's nothing quite so infuriating as the long-awaited boy dying suddenly of the plague or suddenly being thrown headlong into the responsibilites of ruling at the age of three. Although this is all part of the appeal. That sort of thing happened frequently in the Middle Ages, and Paradox have done a wonderful job of capturing the feel of the time. In short, Crusader Kings II is quite possibly the finest strategy game ever made, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who is as interested in the political side of things, which titles like Total War are so lacking in, as they are in battles and warfare. I would also recommend the Game of Thrones mod for this game, which completes the experience perfectly.

Taking what it's predecessor did and improved in almost every way, Mass Effect 2 still holds up as one of the best RPG games of all time. With an unforgettable cast of characters, action packed gameplay, a unique and weel constructed universe and a final mission that is impossible to top. Few games can juggle action heavy gameplay with a rich and engging storytine so deftly.
Would very much recommend, even to those that are normally put off by RPGs. The true depth and complexity of this game is not in stat tables, gear min-maxing or efficient rotations but in the character interactions and choice centric storytelling.
On the negative side, the streamlined RPG mechanics can perhaps be a little too simplified for experianced players looking for variety at the higher difficulty sections. The cover system, while much improved over ME1 still feels a little stiff and clunky at times in the more intense firefights and close range melee fighting is just not viable (both problems addressed in ME3.)
AFAIK the DLC missions are not available through Steam, but if you can find them both 'Overlord' and 'Lair of the Shadow Broker' are by far the best entries, easily standing along side the main game's most memorable missions. Honorable mention for 'Stolen Memories' for changing up the gameplay with a neat little heist caper.
UPDATE: All the old DLC has been made available for free, direct from the publisher!

Summary: The award-winning debut adventure game from the creators of Deponia and The Whispered World now on Steam. The award-winning debut adventure game from the creators of Deponia and The Whispered World now on Steam. Accompany young Edna and her talking stuffed bunny Harvey on a whacky attempt to escape from her padded cell. Experience a bizarre journey all across the insane asylum and far beyond its brick walls.
At the beginning, young Edna wakes up in the padded cell of an insane asylum with no memory of her past. She doesn’t have the slightest idea how she wound up there, but one thing is for sure, she wants out! After all, she feels perfectly sane – and her talking stuffed bunny Harvey agrees completely. Together, they attempt an escape and, in doing so, meet their extremely bizarre fellow patients – from the man in the bee costume to the pseudo-Siamese twins Hoti and Moti. But Dr. Marcel, head of the asylum, will stop at nothing to keep Edna from escaping. What does he have planned for her? And why was her memory erased? Gradually, Edna regains her memory of the time before her detention in her cell…
People who played old-school point & click adventure games, will feel a bit nostalgic when they see four buttons at the bottom of the screen, labeled 'look at', 'pick up', 'talk to' and 'use'. To perform an action, you will need to combine one of those commands with items from your inventory and/or with objects in the game world. For example: to unlock a door you click 'use', next you click on a key in your inventory and then you click on the door.
Striking cartoon art; great voice acting (especially for Edna and Harvey); an unexpectedly touching storyline; massive amounts of interactivity
Edna & Harvey: The Breakout is very much a mixed bag. Its distinctive art style is marred by a problematic interface. Its massive wealth of interactivity is hindered by a handful of vastly unfair puzzles. Its imaginative setting is dragged down by long, often tedious dialogues.
Still, it’s a game I’m glad I played, and that’s mainly because the underlying story about a girl who’s lost her way is so touching. You might think from the premise that Edna & Harvey is a comedy. I’d counter that it’s a tragedy, because no matter what Edna does, either in the past or the present, she can’t escape the circumstances that have made her a prisoner. This isn’t the story I expected Edna & Harvey to tell, and I do love when a game surprises me.

is a point & click adventure game. Its gameplay is classic for the genre: collect items and use them on other items you collected or on objects in the game world. There are no real puzzles or minigames in
.
People who played old-school point & click adventure games, will feel a bit nostalgic when they see four buttons at the bottom of the screen, labeled 'look at', 'pick up', 'talk to' and 'use'. To perform an action, you will need to combine one of those commands with items from your inventory and/or with objects in the game world. For example: to unlock a door you click 'use', next you click on a key in your inventory and then you click on the door.
The four commands add a lot more possible actions to the game. This is both a good thing as it adds more variety and even a bit more depth, and a bad thing as it artificially increases the game's difficulty somewhat by increasing the number of actions to try every time you're feeling stumped.
What's certainly positive, even impressive, is that almost all of the possibilities have a unique 'result'. I mean, in most adventure games you would often get a generic response or one of a few generic responses that boil down to 'I can't do that', 'That won't work' or 'I have no use for that', but in
almost everything I tried got an individual response in which Edna or the NPC at least mentioned the items I tried to use and often made an appropriate  comment about the action I was trying to perform.
On the other hand, it's clear the developers bit off a bit more than they could chew as the syntaxes made by means of the four commands aren't always semantically correct. For example, a coin drops into a coin chute. To pick up the coin, you need to use the command 'pick up' + 'coin chute'. That should be 'pick up' + 'coin', of course.
Also, when you right-click an object, the game performs the 'standard action' for that object. Right-click an NPC and the command 'talk to' will automatically be selected. Right-click an object that you can use or pick up and the command 'use' or 'pick up' will automatically be selected... but not always. Sometimes Edna will simply 'look at' an item she can use or pick up, so the right-click function is helpful but not foolproof. You will still need to experiment with the commands and left-clicks to advance in the game.
You can press SPACE to highlight all the objects on the screen that you can interact with.
is the first game by Daedalic Entertainment I played in which the use of this 'assist function' isn't punished by missing out on an achievement. It's also the first game by D.E. I played where I didn't really feel the need for an 'assist function' because of the clear, basic graphics that make it hard to overlook an item or interactable object.
Edna finds herself locked in a padded cell in an insane asylum and wants to escape. She talks to her stuffed rabbit, Harvey, which seems to help trigger her memory of the events that lead to her incarceration.
While finding a way to escape from the asylum, a background story will unfold but don't expect an elaborate plot. The adventure lies in exploring the asylum and manipulating people and objects to aid you in your escape.
The game's characters are colourful and lively. To create personalities for a handful of mental patients is a risky undertaking. It's easy to make them plain crazy and have them speaking complete gibberish, rendering them little more than over-the-top caricatures, whereas it's hard to give them character and background, and (pardon the pun) to give them reason behind their madness. I think the developers succeeded with flying colours, especially considering the whole game went through a translation process from German to English, during which some nuances inevitably get lost.
The humour is wacky and amusing but not laugh-out-loud hilarious.
The graphics are cartoonish and very basic - crude even. But they fit the atmosphere of the game perfectly.
Noteworthy is the plethora of optional actions that become possible during the game and that actually change the appearance of game world. For example, when Edna finds a pen she can scribble or doodle on dozens of objects in the game world and you will actually see the object changed from then on.
The music is okay. It's certainly not beautiful and it gets a bit repetitive after a while, but it's not too intrusive either. The sound effects, too, are just okay and often I found them absent altogether.
The voice acting is very good. Especially the actress who voiced Edna delivers a fine performance. Only Harvey's voice is a bit forced, which makes it sound a tad annoying but it fits the character and you don't get to hear Harvey that often, so it's not an issue, really.

Most of the problems put before you in
are challenging and certainly require a bit of thinking, but in the end you'll find the appropriate logical solution.
However, for a few of the problems the solution was so far-fetched I had to look it up in a walkthrough. I'll name one example where I was stuck, consulted a walkthrough and concluded I would never have thought of that.
has 7 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 4 while running the game.
Only a few of the Steam Achievements are story-bound and unmissable. Most achievements are completely optional and missable. They usually involve performing all sorts of optional actions like using the pen on other objects like I mentioned earlier. It's refreshing to see some creative achievements here, unlike some other Daedalic games where 'achievements' are given for performing the exact same action 10 times or for using a step-by-step walkthrough. That being said, the achievements are not easy to trigger spontaneously, so unless you want to try everything on everything or make it pretty much impossible on yourself to get most of the achievements, I would at least read the description of the achievements to get some clues about what to look out for. Completionists will want to use an achievements guide.

This game has an interesting plot, challenging puzzles, and a creepy environment. The plot stays true to Lovecraftian fiction if you consider the main character's struggle and even more so if you consider the second half of the plot. The puzzles and clues to solve them are unique and interesting and are sure to intrigue players. The environment is also creepy but I regret to say that there is no sense of an immediate danger so that creepiness dissipates quickly.
However, it suffers from some dated graphics, confusing user interface, some typos (there are some typos in the in-game letters), and some unsolveable puzzles. The character's designs are notably dated however you rarely run into NPCs in this game so it is not that intrusive on your experience. But the user interface will annoy you primarily due to the way you inspect and combine items. Additionally, some puzzles may be too difficult for the casual gamer.
When I played this game I frequently consulted walkthroughs because it was my first point-and-click mystery game and I did not have the patience to backtrack and search. So keep in mind this game requires patience and attention to detail otherwise you might be frustrated if that is not your cup of tea.
You might notice that the end feels rushed and I think this may have to do with the publishing company Lighthouse Interactive going out of business before the game could be published. Also, the development team for this game wasn't too big since Zoetrope Interactive consists of three people. So keep that in mind if you feel like criticizing the game. But regardless it's an enjoyable game that is relatively cheap and you have nothing to lose by buying it if you like point-and-click games.

If you're a fan of classic Point-and-Click mysteries in the vein of games like "Scatches", this one is definitely for you. A variety of beautiful, elegant environments and a rich, haunting soundtrack. Great atmosphere! You play as a police detective searching for the titular Loath Nolder amidst a slowly developing, Lovecraftian-inspired plot. A complex and compelling story builds around you in the form of newpaper articles, books, notes and your interaction with various strange and interesting characters. The puzzles are not terribly difficult, but do require you pay attention to the information you gather on the way.
A few gripes: There is an item and information combination mechanic present that isn't explained very well in-game, so some Google-fu is required. This is also the first in a trilogy and while you can find the first two on Steam, it seems the third game was discontinued in 2014 (having played only this one so far, I'm not sure where that might leave off the conclusion of the story). As a standalone though, this one is worth it.

Here I was, a bit bored and a bit biased about the marriage of a point & click adventure with the theme of horror, but
was a spectacular experience! I've spared 14 hours or so, discovered every achievement, read and re-read every single document, practically poked my nose in every single pixel in the game; but I am still paranoid about missing a piece of the great picture, as any Lovecraftian theme should make you so...
In this gem of a Lovecraftian setting, you play as Howard E. Loreid; a detective that investigates the strange murder of Clark Field, a wealthy man involved in the dark art of occult. The prime suspect of the crime is a man named Loath Nolder, a famous private investigator and an admitant of the local insane asylum. Our game starts with a nightmare, and a phone call coming from our partner, Arthur, in the middle of the night. We're informed that Loath Nolder has escaped...
The game takes brilliant twists and turns, and forces you to investigate odd objects coming from forgotten times, secluded buildings that no one visits and isolated areas of the local geography with dark histories. The atmosphere is carefully arranged to procure a balance between the uneasiness that we feel from a partially observed shadow that lingers in the night, and the raw sense of dread that we suffer whence we face the plain unexplainable. Environment is a huge success to create that lingering, uncanny feeling that haunts us when we are reading a random narration excerpt taken from H.P. Lovecraft's
. It actually uses direct characters and anecdotes from Lovecraft stories like
,
and
.
Gameplay carries two major features that makes the investigation process noteworthy. As you observe events and the environment, you take mental notes in your journal as ideas, observations and suspicions, alongside conversations. You are to pick and add the relevant ideas together to make a thought process to grasp the insight of happenings. This progress of deduction presents the player a unique gameplay. Nothing is presented to you on a silver platter: you actually have to think like an investigator to decide which evidence might go with another to indicate a fact. Another feature is about the documents you stumble in the game. In these kind of games, the gameplay usually presents you your next objective just after you read the document, automatically. Here, you underline the part of the document that you think to be relevant or important and think about it! I mentioned hard work, didn't I?
If you do sincerely enjoy the horror genre - not your common jump scare, or plain human cruelty: an actual sense of gothic that will keep pushing your buttons to keep you awake at night, you MUST try this game. It is brilliant as an adventure, astonishing as a horror game. Plus, it is Lovecraftian!

Taking what it's predecessor did and improved in almost every way, Mass Effect 2 still holds up as one of the best RPG games of all time. With an unforgettable cast of characters, action packed gameplay, a unique and weel constructed universe and a final mission that is impossible to top. Few games can juggle action heavy gameplay with a rich and engging storytine so deftly.
Would very much recommend, even to those that are normally put off by RPGs. The true depth and complexity of this game is not in stat tables, gear min-maxing or efficient rotations but in the character interactions and choice centric storytelling.
On the negative side, the streamlined RPG mechanics can perhaps be a little too simplified for experianced players looking for variety at the higher difficulty sections. The cover system, while much improved over ME1 still feels a little stiff and clunky at times in the more intense firefights and close range melee fighting is just not viable (both problems addressed in ME3.)
AFAIK the DLC missions are not available through Steam, but if you can find them both 'Overlord' and 'Lair of the Shadow Broker' are by far the best entries, easily standing along side the main game's most memorable missions. Honorable mention for 'Stolen Memories' for changing up the gameplay with a neat little heist caper.
UPDATE: All the old DLC has been made available for free, direct from the publisher!

Guild Of Dungeoneering is a fun little Rogue-lite game in which you take on the role of Guild Master of the Guild of Dungeoneering, the underdogs of the adventuring world.
The mechanics are simple enough, you choose which class of adventurer you will take in to the dungeon and which buff you want to have active. Once inside the dungeon you use a selection of cards to build the dungeon in order to complete a quest.
Each class of adventurer uses a different deck of cards and equipping different items will either add buffs to the character or new cards to your deck. Defeating enemies gives you a selection of items to choose from to improve your character or you can sell an item to increase the amount of gold you have to improve your guild hall.
Improving your guild hall unlocks new items, buffs and classes to be used in the dungeons.
This is one of those games that is easy to learn but difficult to master 7/10.

I just finished Bioshock 2 Remastered after playing Bioshock Remastered. Strangely enough, while the first one gave me multiple crashes (which I fixed by leaving all settings as default and saving in a new manual slot every 10 minutes of gameplay), the second game has been a smooth experience all the way through from beginning to end. With the multiple crashes I had to slog through when playing the first, I went into this game thinking I would have to do the same. So, needless to say, I am very happy with my experience; the game is wonderful, the graphics are great, and the story - while not as good as the first - was eventful and interesting. However, the combat is much better in the second game (upgraded plasmids, new skills and tonics, more interesting weapon selection and upgrades, playing as a Big Daddy, dual-wielding, etc.). To conclude, I will say this: always save in a NEW manual slot during gameplay. The first Bioshock Remastered would occasionally freeze while saving over previous data, as well as quicksaving, and would crash to desktop. If you are playing the first game, remember to do this because it will result in loss of saves and having to replay through large parts of the game. I was also able to max out the graphics settings with this game, including anisotropic filtering and antialiasing, which I could not do in the first game, as it would cause it to crash periodically. Again, no problems with part 2, just a smooth and fun experience.

The Mass Effect Series is an another Action RPG winner from the golden developer Bioware. Since 1996 They have released some of the most popular and most powerful story telling experiences, with a track record of producing not a single poor PC game. With the large majority of their games scoring a Metacritic 90 or over this is one of the most acclaimed game developers in history. Playing Mass Effect it is easy to see why, the Space Opera genre of the series greatly aids the ability of Bioware to show off not only their story telling prowess but the beauty of the unreal 3.0 engine. This too comes with it's own pedigree, known widely for it's compromising system specs and the easy nature of programming which has spawned the make something Unreal contest encouraging hundreds of modders and indie dev's. Nevertheless it is a beautiful engine which is improved upon in ME2 with the new iteration, Unreal 3.5. This all makes cruising around the galaxy both an awe inspiring a scenic experience

After completing this game I can safely say I liked it. The premise of building the dungeons your heroes scour was an instant draw for me; simple controls too, only a mouse is required. It has a good variety of randomly aquired equipment, monster and terrain cards all drawn in a childish manner that you will rapidly warm up to.
While the game is good overall it does have some issues that plague it, the first and most obvious being unable to access the options from the main menu screen. When you start the game you're given a brief tutorial that teaches you the basics but does little to teach you about advanced battle tactics. Sometimes during a quest the game crashes causing you to lose all your progress on that level, which can be be very disappointing when you're doing well. Another thing that was disappointing was discovering that you could not go back to previous levels, I was hoping to go back to the old levels to measure my progress against quests and bosses already beaten.
The DLC added many more quests that enabled you to fight new monsters, collect new equipment and recruit new dungeoneers. Unfortunately the pirate quests are easier than most of the main game quests. The new enemies are very interesting to fight though and there were a few times I had to get tactical with my way of thinking. The new dungeoneers while interesting in their own right, seemed a little too gimmick like and had no substance to them; against the trials of the third act they were especially outclassed.
Only one song was added from the the DLC, but like the rest of the track it is high quality and creates much atmosphere. The narration from the bard was well voiced and at times seemed exceptionally annoying, which seems like it was its every intent; however the miniscule options menu does little to help players enjoy either the voice acting or the music in any particular way as there is only a master volume slider and music volume slider.
Once the game is completed you get a giant heap of money that allows you to purchase the rest of the facilities, though this is more a formality as you can't redo quests to test the new dungeoneers which highlights the glaring issue of little replayability. Since the gameplay is relatively simple, playing as different heroes sometimes feels similar with only the synergy between character traits and a characters base card set to freshen things up. All in all, I enjoyed this game and would recommend it as a good, if slightly annoying time waster.

Toonstruck is a point-and-click adventure game that has caught my eye for quite a long time now. I was quite glad that I bought it at a discount! Anyways, after playing this classic masterpiece which combines live-action and 2D animation, like Who Framed Roger Rabbit? and Looney Tunes: Back in Action. Here are my pros and cons:
PROS:
- An all-star cast?! Oh, joy! And I happen to find some familiar voice actors that rung a bell in my head!
-- Christopher Lloyd (who voiced as Judge Doom from Who Framed Roger Rabbit?)
-- Tim Curry (who, surprisingly, voiced Lord Dragaumus from The Mighty Ducks cartoon series)
-- Dan Castellaneta (who famously voiced Homer Simpson from The Simpsons cartoon series!)
-- Dom DeLuise (who voiced Tiger from An American Tail and An American Tail: Fieval Goes West)
-- Corey Burton (who, surprisingly, voiced the english dub of Doublehelix from Asterix and the Vikings!)
-- Jeff Bennett (who voiced as Johnny Bravo from the cartoon of the exact same name!)
-- Jim Cummings (who voiced as Mr. Bumpy from an old-as-heck cartoon, Bump in the Night)
-- Rob Paulsen (who voiced as Squishington from an old-as-heck cartoon, Bump in the Night)
-- and Tress MacNeille (who still voices as Daisy Duck from all that is Disney!)
- Lovely cast of cartoon characters, such as a bird-brain of a royal scientist and a malevolent villain.
- Puzzles and mini-games were very challenging, yet decently fair and possible to beat.
- Neat soundtrack that suits its cartoon-y atmosphere.
- Amazing cartoon references to find, such as WACME (which is a clear reference to Looney Tunes' Acme Corp.)
CONS:
- Some or most of the game were cut-out during its development. For instance, some of the bits on the high-quality trailer here were not found during gameplay, such as this Vincent Van Gogh-esque cartoon character.
- Mouse sensitivity is too 'wacky', if you get my meaning, making you try to move your mouse softly rather than moving it quite fast.
- F1 button doesn't seem to work, as every time I push it, it won't give me the options screen like it said it would do.
- No sequel? Aww... Better get some more people and fans of this game to make it a reality then.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
My final verdict of Toonstruck is that I really enjoyed playing through this game for almost 6 hours time, plus it would at least give me lessons on how would I even try to make a game like this. The cutscenes were both classic and wonderful, from the live-action world to the cartoon world. For that, I would give it a 8.75/10.
If you like point-and-click adventure games such as Monkey Island and Discworld. Hurry up, buy this game, and put it in your collection already! You won't regret it!

Although a little dated and having a few problems here and there, there is plenty of charm left over to win you over.
First, as a warning to those that might make the same mistake I did, despite Steam saying that “Edna & Harvey: The Breakout” was released after “Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes”, this is infact wrong and resulted in me playing the two in the wrong order. This game comes first. They follow each other very loosely in terms of story so there wasn’t much given away, but I think I may have enjoyed ending on the sequel a bit more seeing as this one has a few problems for me.
I’ll start by explaining a few of these problems, as to not end this review on a low note.
First of all the resolution is not very flexible. This is the first thing that really stuck out to me and made it obvious to me that this game is indeed quite a bit older than it’s sequel. You can either go full screen which is stretched quite far, or leave it windowed which is pretty small.
I didn’t really get on with this game as well as some others. Point and clicks, as people who play them often will know, can vary in terms of how logical the item combinations/puzzles will be. It can range from “put the key into the lock” to “this piece of cheese has holes in it, therefore you can use this as a punch card to get past security” kind of logic. This game however, I found myself on guides quite a few times because I just couldn’t grasp what the game was trying to tell me. This was a little frustrating, but maybe I just didn’t mesh with this one very well.
There were three occasions where I had to save my game, close and reboot in German to be able to proceed with what I was doing, as the English version is bugged.
When opening this game you are asked if you would like the language in English or German, and me being a uno-lingual scrub, had to try and find my way around several parts not knowing what was going on (I actually had to ask my multi-lingual boyfriend several times “what’s that word mean?” *Pokes the screen*, which was followed by a reluctant sigh, “Potatoes, Stef. Potatoes”).
For anyone interested/curious, the parts/reasons I had to switch to German were:
- The cafeteria “menu” puzzle
- To unlock the “Lady of Keys” mission achievement
- For the end scene, slides and credits to even play (You need to watch through the credits and start a new game for an achievement. There are parts to read but it was in German so I had to get on the ol’ YouTube for that)
And the last point to my moaning, the achievements are a bit of a nightmare in this game. Daedalic Entertainment do tend to be a little cheeky with their achievements, and I usually strangely enjoy that. They usually lead you to quirky bits of dialogue and parts of the game you would of otherwise missed, or give you strange little challenges to do that really test your patience. These achievements on the other hand, are just kind of tedious. There is some of the stuff mentioned above, but there is quite a few “use this one item on EVERYTHING” kind of achievements.
The second game is better in terms of achievements, but neither of them are particularly difficult to 100%. This one is just a bit more tedious. I would strongly advise that you keep different saves as you go along, as that makes it easier to go back for any achievements that you missed. Although a word of warning, you are only allowed about 9 save slots in this one so spread them out as evenly as you can.
Now with all that moaning out the way, let’s focus on some good stuff.
The Daedalic Entertainment charm is definitely still here. The humour and style that they have going on is generally just great and that’s one of the reasons why I follow them as a developer. Although this game in particular isn’t as polished as some of the others, I personally put that down to it’s age (pretty sure this was their first game) and the developers limited resources at that time. They know how to create high quality, enjoyable games with great story and character.
This little franchise is interesting because it’s quite dark. They cover it in a vibrant, cartoon-like world but I did enjoy that this was made to be a slightly twisted comedic game. It makes for a pair of unique point and click games. The graphics are nice and simple and I find how the characters are drawn particularly strange, but it’s all part of the charm.
The puzzles are quite fun, although I got stuck a fair few times, I respect that they try new things instead of defaulting to the usual kind of puzzles you generally see in these games.
The story is interesting and taps into certain subjects slightly, like psychology and what it is to be “mentally ill”. Which are subjects that I like to see in games, as there is generally a lot more room for twists in those areas. Although not ground-breaking, the story in this game is enjoyable.
All in all, despite some hiccups I enjoyed this game. I would definitely recommend you play this one first like you are supposed to then move onto “Harvey's New Eyes”. It’s a fun game, you just may need to be patient with it at times.
TL;DR : Despite what Steam says, “Edna & Harvey: The Breakout” is the first game and “Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes” is the second. It has an unchangeable small resolution, slightly nightmarish achievements and several hiccups in the English version where you need to switch to German to be able to proceed/unlock certain achievements. But despite all that bad stuff, it has an interesting story, a dark humour which is masked by it’s cartoon-ish graphics, interesting puzzles and that Daedalic Entertainment charm to it.

This is quite the unique platformer. Instead of simply jumping from any ordinary platform to the next, it takes some sort of pseudo-Sonic approach of fast paced, all-surfaces high-octane super-platforming.
Let me be frank: this game is hard. Sure, it does a good job of easing you into it, but this isn't just some casual romp. Be prepared to put all your effort into getting constant SS ranks if you want to explore all the game's content.
The visuals are pleasing and colorful, just a nice view for the eyes. The music is likewise calm and soothing techno, which is just as well to ease you from the rage that will transpire.
The game controls butter smooth, and has a lot of depth from a rather simple means of traversing the maps. I did have one complaint about the controls, namely the lack of complete controller support. Most basic buttons are there, except the menu button. I can't even count how many times I've had to restart, and I have to do it all from going to the keyboard to press escape. Is an extra respec option too much to ask for?
EDIT: Though there is no option to respec the escape menu in the controls, I found that the "instant restart" key in another menu is able to be bound to a controller button, which is quite swell.
Another complaint I have, though not with the game, is the lack of community attention. When exploring the nexus, it is entirely up to me to find the one bronze door that I still have a key for, and it still eludes me because no one has a nexus map uploaded.
All said, it's crazily addictive to the right people, namely: twitch-reflex, practice-based skill games that never stop the action.
